stories.title: London man sentenced in fatal beating
stories.summary: A London courtroom heard on Thursday how the lifeless body of Matthew Harp, 39, was found in a pool of blood at a wooded area behind Mildred Barons Park in east London on Sept. 20, 2024.
stories.author: Nick Paparella
stories.content:
A London courtroom heard on Thursday how the lifeless body of Matthew Harp, 39, was found in a pool of blood at a wooded area behind Mildred Barons Park in east London on Sept. 20, 2024.

In an agreed statement of facts the court was told that Harp showed up to the homeless encampment with two other males armed with a loaded shotgun and a pistol. They had intended to rob the occupants of fentanyl.

After they arrived there was an altercation and fighting going on with the accused Broady Salmon, 31, trying to defend himself and his girlfriend.

At one point Salmon thought his girlfriend had been hurt and he saw Harp on the ground.

“The accused struck the victim on his head multiple times with a metal pole and Mr. Harp died as a result,” said Crown attorney John Lee, reading from the statement.

The next day Salmon would call London police and give himself up claiming that Harp’s friends were threatening him.

In her victim impact statement, Harp’s mother, Darlene, told the court, “There are no words powerful enough to express the pain of losing a son...a grief that will live with me for the rest of my life.”

Before Justice Alissa Mitchell, Salmon who was originally charged with second degree murder plead guilty to the lesser charge of manslaughter along with one count of possession of fentanyl.

Despite the violence involved in the death of Harp, Justice Mitchell agreed with both the Crown and the defence that this was a case of provocation.

That’s why in a submission both sides agree to a sentence of four years with the judge agreeing, “Mr. Salmon’s conduct in the death of Mr. Harp was provoked... the accused had believed that the victim had assaulted his girlfriend.”

With credit for time served, Salmon who had a troubled upbringing has about 21 months left behind bars.

stories.title: Gap to restore pre-pandemic housing affordability by 2036 in Calgary narrowing: Cmhc
stories.summary: According to the report, Calgary must build between 23,000 and 24,000 total new housing starts annually over the next 10 years to close the gap.
stories.author: Adam MacVicar
stories.content:
Calgary is one of the few major Canadian cities where the supply gap to restore pre-pandemic housing affordability levels has narrowed, according to the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC), due to years of record construction.

According to the federal housing agency’s latest supply gap estimate report , Calgary needs between 4,000 and 5,000 additional units annually by 2036 to restore affordability.

“What we’ve seen is years of record housing starts have resulted in a significant narrowing in that gap as builders have stepped up scaling supply,” said CMHC’s lead economist for the Prairies, Taylor Pardy. “It’s actually been cut in half relative to our previous estimate.”

Those figures translate to between 23,000 and 24,000 total new housing starts annually over the next 10 years.

Current trends indicate Calgary is on pace to build around 19,000 total new homes this year, CMHC said.

According to Pardy, the city recorded 27,000 housing starts last year alone as part of three consecutive years of record home construction.

“We’re on track, essentially, this year to maintain well above the 10-year average starts,” Pardy told Global News. “Overall, the market is still looking fairly robust.”

Housing advocates, however, are worried Calgary won’t be able to keep pace with the construction required.

Total housing starts have declined more than 20 per cent, according to CMHC, as projects that began within the last three years reach completion.

CMHC said the slowing construction reflects rising vacancy rates, growing inventories, higher construction costs and “broader economic uncertainty.”

“As a result, we expect supply growth to moderate once the current development pipeline is delivered,” CMHC said in its report.

Alex McColl, a board member with More Neighbours Calgary, told Global News the narrowing supply gap is “a good thing,” but questioned whether the recent repeal of citywide rezoning will have an impact on housing starts moving forward.

“So this council is riding the momentum created by the previous housing strategy, which is good,” he said. “But repeal without replacement reverses the conditions that increase housing supply.”

The policy, which took effect in August 2024 after being approved by the previous city council, changed the city’s base residential zoning to allow for more housing types on a single property, such as duplexes, rowhomes and townhouses, without requiring a public hearing.

The current city council voted to repeal citywide rezoning earlier this year , and the policy change took effect in August.

The move will see 306,774 residential properties across the city redesignated back to their original low-density residential districts.

“Good starts two years ago are now showing good completions today, but we’re also seeing the starts go down,” McColl said. “That worries us that in two years time, we’re going to continue to trend in the wrong direction.”

Calgary Mayor Jeromy Farkas defended the move during a question and answer session with a local Rotary Club chapter on Wednesday.

“I don’t think, with the infrastructure that’s in the ground that it was adequate to be able to take a one-size-fits-all approach,” Farkas said. “But that said, we have to continue to build and we have to continue to build the housing that Calgarians can afford.”

According to a city spokesperson, building permit activity has also shown growth in new communities such as Ricardo Ranch and Alpine Park, and in established communities like Haysboro and Tuxedo Park.

“Altogether, Calgary continues to see strong housing construction which is helping to approach a balance between supply and demand,” the city said in a statement.

However, for lifelong Calgarians like Judy Klassen, the record housing construction can be a concern.

“I don’t like it,” she told Global News. “Look at all the condos they’re putting up . Even in the older areas, they’re building eightplexes on one lot.”

Meanwhile, Calgary city council is getting set to vote on a refined housing strategy with a narrowed scope from 98 recommendations to roughly 10, that shifts its focus to non-market housing.

stories.title: Rat reporting made easier for London neighbourhoods struggling with infestations
stories.summary: This month London city hall expanded its online system for residents to report a number of bylaw related issues, including for the first time, the ability to specifically report rat and vermin infestations.
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
This month London city hall expanded its online system for residents to report a number of bylaw related issues, including for the first time, the ability to specifically report rat and vermin infestations.

It’s part of a comprehensive strategy endorsed by council earlier this summer to address a worsening rat problem in neighbourhoods across the city.

“By adding an option to report rats on the drop-down menu in the Service London (website) portal, we intend to monitor the data closely in response to recent council direction to address rodent concerns,” a statement from the city reads.

Glen Cairn resident Emily McCutcheon describes a rat infestation that has plagued her cul de sac since the pandemic.

“A couple years ago, I was getting five to eight rats a day in the traps,” she says about traps set up around the exterior of her home. “I got rid of the composter about a year ago and haven’t had as many, but I still getting a few a week.”

McCutcheon believes a large field of long grass and weeds behind her home has become a habitat for rats.

“I know some neighbours have contacted the city about getting it mowed, because if this was my lawn, I would be fined for having my lawn this long,” she says.

The city’s new strategy to crackdown on rat infestations primarily focuses on the actions, or inaction of humans.

Both the Yard and Lot Maintenance Bylaw and the Property Standards Bylaw were recently updated.

The goal is to reduce access to resources that rodents need to thrive including food, water, and shelter.

“In situations where debris accumulation in violation of a bylaw exist, staff have reduced the amount of time provided for compliance to ensure that infestations do not have the time to become established,” the city statement reads.

“The issue needs to be addressed as a whole, because one homeowner getting rid of the rats is not going to address this whole problem,” explains McCutcheon.

Meanwhile, residents of a townhouse complex on Shelborne Street say illegally dumped garbage around their communal dumpsters continue to attract vermin.

CTV News originally reported on the situation in early June.

Returning on Thursday, food waste from torn garbage bags was strewn around the dumpsters, and broken furniture was piled behind.

Resident Adil Gahfar says he and his neighbours are at their wits end with the problem and need the city and their landlord to find a solution.

“It’s causing a big issue because it’s all kinds of food and leftovers,” explained Gahfar. “Most of the stuff that comes in, it’s from people (who) drive by, stop their cars, dump all the stuff everywhere.”

Before the end of this year, city staff will present a report to committee proposing a residential rat remediation rebate program.

stories.title: Ottawa launches consultations for a water security strategy
stories.summary: Federal government seeking public input as climate change, rising demand and tensions with the U.S. raise stakes around freshwater resources
stories.author: Andrea Woo
stories.content:
The federal government is asking Canadians to help shape the country’s first water security strategy as competing demands, climate change and tensions with the U.S. raise the stakes for the country’s freshwater resources.

The Canada Water Agency this week launched public engagement for the strategy, which aims to improve freshwater management, protect ecosystems and secure water supplies.

Wade Grant, parliamentary secretary to Environment and Climate Change Minister Julie Dabrusin, who is responsible for the Canada Water Agency, announced the launch of public engagement at a news conference in Richmond, B.C., on Thursday. Similar announcements also took place in Winnipeg and Toronto.

Mr. Grant called water security “one of the defining challenges of our time.”

“With increasingly frequent severe droughts, forest fires or floods impacting every corner of this country, we can see that water availability and water quality are changing,” said Mr. Grant, who is the MP for Vancouver Quadra. “This is the direct result of climate change. We know more must be done.”

The Canada Water Agency was launched in 2024 with a mandate to improve freshwater management and protection across the country. The national water security strategy was first announced in March.

Mr. Grant said the Canada Water Agency is engaging provinces and territories; First Nations, Inuit, and Métis partners; and other stakeholders across a range of sectors. The public is invited to weigh in until Oct. 26, with a summary of findings to be released later this year.

There were few details on how a national water security strategy will improve upon current systems. Asked whether his government would prioritize freshwater resources for human and agricultural use over water-intensive artificial intelligence data centres, Mr. Grant said the agency recognizes the importance of finding more water-protective ways to power AI.

On securing safe drinking water in First Nations communities, Mr. Grant said his government is working with Indigenous communities to ensure that solutions come from the ground up. As of Aug. 13, there were 40 long-term drinking water advisories in 38 First Nations communities across Canada.

Mr. Grant said the development of the strategy is independent from threats directed from the United States, which has increasingly challenged Canada’s water sovereignty. President Donald Trump has threatened to redirect Canadian water to the U.S., criticized the Columbia River Treaty as unfair to Americans and signed an executive order to rename Lake Ontario to Lake America .

Mr. Grant made his remarks at a venue located on the banks of the Fraser River, which is the fourth largest river in Canada by volume and home to the Port of Vancouver, the country’s largest port. Activity across the Fraser River basin generates about 10 per cent of Canada’s gross domestic product.

At the event, he announced $480,000 in funding for three partner-led projects under the Fraser River Freshwater Ecosystem Initiative, a program managed by the Canada Water Agency to support projects that protect and restore the river basin’s freshwater ecosystem.

Among the recipients, the Raincoast Conservation Foundation is receiving $169,000 over two years to work with Indigenous and local communities to bolster water quality monitoring and pollution reduction efforts across nearly half of the lower Fraser River basin.

Peter Ross, a senior scientist at the foundation who was in attendance at Thursday’s event, said the funding will go toward expanding a water pollution monitoring program.

First launched in late 2021 after B.C. experienced catastrophic flooding, Raincoast’s Healthy Waters program will now transition from scientist-led monitoring toward Indigenous and community-led stewardship through training, workshops, online resources and a public symposium, he said.

“I envisage a program that helps to transition us over to a more sustainable water quality monitoring initiative for future generations,” he said.

Working with partners in more than a dozen B.C. watersheds to examine almost 600 pollutants in source water, river water, road runoff, tap water and ocean water, the group has already identified “a number of concerns” in Fraser River watersheds, Dr. Ross said. That includes the presence of hydrocarbons; PFAS, also known as “forever chemicals”; and 6PPD-quinone, a toxic chemical byproduct from rubber tires that is killing local salmon.

The Canada Water Agency launches public engagement as it is being asked to do more with less. As part of Prime Minister Mark Carney’s 2025 budget , which sought to slash the federal bureaucracy and reorient the national economy to respond to U.S. tariff pressures, the agency is facing a $3.8-million funding reduction by 2029-2030, on top of another $1.2-million in “ongoing” savings.

The agency’s 2026-2027 departmental plan said the cuts are expected to result in the loss of 13 full-time equivalent positions by 2028-2029.

stories.title: ‘The neighbourhood has mobilized’: Residents vow to fight Sarnia Road apartment proposal
stories.summary: Residents of a neighbourhood near Western University are vowing to continue fighting a proposal for an eight-storey student development on Sarnia Road.
stories.author: Bryan Bicknell
stories.content:
Residents of a neighbourhood near Western University are vowing to continue fighting a proposal for an eight-storey student development on Sarnia Road.

It follows London city council’s Planning and Environment Committee’s decision to endorse the project.

“There’s no need to go up to eight storeys here,” said area resident Bill Tsioros.

“Too dense of a development for the area,” added Bill’s son, Matt Tsioros.

Each has a home in the Orchard Park neighbourhood north of Sarnia Road near Western. They’re among area residents fighting an eight-storey student apartment building proposal on a 1.12 hectare piece of property at 299-307 Sarnia Road, currently the site of two family homes.

City council had already approved a six-storey apartment for the site.

But on Wednesday, the council committee supported the revised taller building proposal.

“They’ve decided that, ‘well we’re going to apply for eight.’ And that’s what finally set off the alarm bells in the neighbourhood. And the neighbourhood has mobilized,” exclaimed Bill.

“With the congestion already on Sarnia Road, we’re just concerned that a building of this size and density is just going to create massive amounts of through-traffic and spillover,” added Matt.

The proposal, by developer Kimko Inc. along with a numbered company, would have 204 units with 188 underground parking spots.

Ward councillor, Sam Trosow, says the previous six storey proposal was a compromise, but added the new plan doesn’t address real needs.

“Developer has made it very clear that they’re going to be gearing this toward towards a very, very high-end, luxury, upper-income student. And just talking to the students, talking to the representatives of the student government, that’s not what the students need. The students need affordable housing,” Trosow said.

Planning and Environment committee chair, Councillor Steve Lehman supported the staff recommendation to endorse the proposal. He says it’s hard to say ‘no’ when all the boxes have been checked.

“We talk about urban sprawl, and we all want to avoid paving over farmland. There’s only one solution to that, in order to drive housing. And that’s through infill projects like that and get higher density. I think this is an appropriate spot for this type of development,” said Lehman.

The final decision goes to council Sept. 22.

content_blocks.text: Residents of a neighbourhood near Western University are vowing to continue fighting a proposal for an eight-storey student development on Sarnia Road.
It follows London city council’s Planning and Environment Committee’s decision to endorse the project.
“There’s no need to go up to eight storeys here,” said area resident Bill Tsioros.
“Too dense of a development for the area,” added Bill’s son, Matt Tsioros.

Each has a home in the Orchard Park neighbourhood north of Sarnia Road near Western. They’re among area residents fighting an eight-storey student apartment building proposal on a 1.12 hectare piece of property at 299-307 Sarnia Road, currently the site of two family homes.
City council had already approved a six-storey apartment for the site.
But on Wednesday, the council committee supported the revised taller building proposal.
“They’ve decided that, ‘well we’re going to apply for eight.’ And that’s what finally set off the alarm bells in the neighbourhood. And the neighbourhood has mobilized,” exclaimed Bill.
“With the congestion already on Sarnia Road, we’re just concerned that a building of this size and density is just going to create massive amounts of through-traffic and spillover,” added Matt.
The proposal, by developer Kimko Inc. along with a numbered company, would have 204 units with 188 underground parking spots.
Ward councillor, Sam Trosow, says the previous six storey proposal was a compromise, but added the new plan doesn’t address real needs.

“Developer has made it very clear that they’re going to be gearing this toward towards a very, very high-end, luxury, upper-income student. And just talking to the students, talking to the representatives of the student government, that’s not what the students need. The students need affordable housing,” Trosow said.

stories.title: On a sombre anniversary, Gander welcomes the ‘plane people’ back to the Rock
stories.summary: With Canadian-American tensions at a fever pitch, the kindness and generosity of townsfolk still overwhelms 25 years after 9/11
stories.author: Lindsay Jones
stories.content:
In Gander, the 25th anniversary of 9/11 is a time of emotional reunions and conflicted feelings about the Canada-U.S. relationship

Retired air traffic controller Patrick Woodford stood behind a metal gate and eagerly scanned the arrivals hall of the Gander International Airport.

He noticed how much busier it was this week than usual. Dozens of people were milling around the airport’s one baggage carousel and waiting near its two car rental counters.

Finally, he spotted the passenger he was waiting for and raised an arm. Beverley Bass, a petite woman with a short platinum haircut, strode headlong into his arms. “How’s everything?” he said, squeezing his friend in a tight embrace. “How’s everything?”

The two had first forged a connection 25 years ago, here at the same airport, under horrifying circumstances.

Mr. Woodford was the one who helped guide Ms. Bass, the pilot of an American Airlines flight that had been en route from Paris to Dallas, to land on a Gander runway on Sept. 11, 2001.

That day, hijackers affiliated with the al-Qaeda terrorism network crashed planes into the twin towers of the World Trade Center in New York and into the Pentagon in Virginia. A fourth plane went down in a field in Pennsylvania.

Nearly 3,000 people were killed, including 24 Canadians. It was the deadliest terrorist attack in history.

After officials closed U.S. airspace, this tiny airport was the landing spot for 38 passenger planes carrying more than 6,600 travellers and crew – part of an operation that diverted up to 250 flights to airports across Canada.

And the town, with its population of less than 10,000 people at the time, became their temporary home.

Thousands have made that airport busy again this week, and returned to that home for a gathering on Friday to remember the extraordinary generosity and kindness shown by their found families in Gander, as well as nearby communities throughout central Newfoundland.

Residents co-ordinated airport logistics, invited stranded passengers into their homes, prepared mass meals and transformed schools, churches and community halls into shelters.

They took their hospitality to what some still consider an extreme. In what Ms. Bass recalled as a bewildering act of kind-heartedness from Mr. Woodford, he handed her the keys to his truck when they struck up a conversation at the airport while he was on a break.

“Here’s this guy who I don’t even know. He said, ‘You can have the keys to my truck.’ I’m looking at him like he’s crazy,” she said, still in disbelief all these years later.

When she asked if he was afraid she might steal his truck, he told her: “Well, you’re on an island. Where are you going to go?”

To Mr. Woodford, it was just a small act of humanity – of faith in a complete stranger – at a time when the world seemed like it was ending. It was moments like these that, for many people in town, paved the way to lifelong friendships. Like many others, Mr. Woodford and Ms. Bass stayed in touch, visiting back and forth in Gander and Denton, Tex., over the years, celebrating milestones and bonding with each others’ family members.

The emotions of those trying days and the bonds that resulted are depicted in the Tony award-winning musical Come From Away , which debuted in 2015 and has been produced in countries around the world. This year, it returned to Gander for its fourth season.

Gander’s kindness, which became a symbol of co-operation between Canada and the U.S., has also been immortalized in a new Heritage Minute . It is circulating at a time of intense political and economic strife between the two countries.

On Friday, the friendship and connection between Americans and Canadians is nonetheless being venerated at a commemoration service that will honour the victims of the attacks as well as the first responders.

Hundreds of “plane people” are expected to attend an afternoon ceremony at the local arena, as well as dignitaries including Governor-General Louise Arbour; Jean Chrétien, who was prime minister during the attacks; and U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra.

Last week, the Town of Gander defended its decision to host Mr. Hoekstra , who has amplified the rhetoric of U.S. President Donald Trump in the escalating trade war instigated by his administration. Mayor Percy Farwell, who was deputy mayor 25 years ago, encouraged Newfoundlanders to rise above the disrespect and stay true to their welcoming hearts.

“We’re remembering the great tragedy and the great loss, and we’re trying to reflect on those who lost their lives and support those that lost loved ones and that were permanently impacted by those events,” he said during an interview last week.

“We reflect on how we, as a twist of fate, became involved in a specific way – in being able to provide support to impacted people – and how much we value that. Those sorts of things transcend any emotions we might have around the latest Truth Social post or the latest version of trade talks.”

It was a message heard repeatedly about town this week as locals reunited with their “plane people” friends and attended storytelling events, tours of the airport, performances of Come From Away and screech-in ceremonies to welcome visitors at the local Royal Canadian Legion.

Monica Burke, who now lives in the state of Georgia, was on her way home to Seattle on 9/11 when her flight was diverted to Gander. Returning to that legion hall on Wednesday evening caused a flood of memories to come back.

She recalled the spot on the floor across the room where she dozed on a borrowed mattress, waiting to make a call on the one telephone that people were taking turns using. And she remembered Beulah Copper, a legion volunteer, walking in and offering to drive Ms. Burke and others to a pay phone at a nearby hotel.

Ms. Cooper invited Ms. Burke to stay in the spare bedroom in her home, and cooked her hot breakfasts during her stay. Since then, the two have stayed in touch over multiple visits. Ms. Burke thinks of her older friend as a grandmother.

“I just wanted to come back and thank them,” said Ms. Burke. “And then one time wasn’t enough. So I just keep coming back – especially now, being 25 years, a lot of people who were here aren’t here any more, and it’s sad. It’s what happens, but I want to see the people that I can while I can.”

On Wednesday night, Ms. Cooper was again at the legion hall, busy screeching in a bunch of Americans. The welcoming ritual makes “come from aways” into honorary Newfoundlanders. At a long table, visitors from Ohio and New York and Illinois shuddered as they slung back shots of dark Newfoundland Screech rum and Ms. Cooper presented a frozen cod for them to kiss right on the lips (through a plastic bag).

Karen Stringer, wearing an anti-Trump pin and about to get screeched in, said she felt compelled to come to Gander for the 9/11 anniversary commemoration because of Come From Away, which is playing right now in her home city of Peoria, Ill.

“I need to support Canada,” she said. “It wasn’t until years later that we realized what Canada did and I think it’s important that we pay respects to this country and say thank you.”

Strangers from all over the world received comfort from the area’s townspeople during the frightening hours and days after 9/11 – hearing their stories, eating their home cooking, using their spare bedding.

Diane Davis, a Grade 3 French immersion teacher who helped convert Gander Academy into a makeshift shelter for 770 stranded passengers from four flights, inspired a composite character in Come From Away – down to her green Northern Reflections pants and a flowery patterned shirt “that didn’t hide nearly as many sins as I used to think it did,” she joked in a recent interview.

She said that at the time, she was just doing what any Newfoundlander would do. But it has provided her with opportunities to travel the world and keep telling her story – and that’s important, especially now, she said.

“It’s really difficult for a lot of people in the political climate that we’re in right now, where Canada is being so misrepresented and a lot of other things are being misrepresented by the American government. I think it’s really important to keep telling these stories,” she said. “Not to say that we’re any better, but just that we’ve always been there to help.”

Municipal police officer Oswald Fudge and his daughter Lisa, who was in high school at the time, shared their story, too.

They decided to host a special birthday party for the children who were stranded because of the terrorist attack. While only six kids were celebrating birthdays in the days that followed Sept. 11, they organized a party for 60 kids. Some of them were terminally ill and had been diverted to Gander on their way to Disney World.

Within hours, father and daughter had dozens of toys donated by the local Canadian Tire, and filled a 12-foot table with sheet cakes provided by the Co-op grocery store and stacked boxes from Mary Brown’s Chicken.

They also assembled an array of fuzzy mascots – an RCMP bear in red serge, two Cooper the Bear representatives from Co-op, a chicken from Mary Brown’s and the town spokesgoose Commander Gander, worn by Ms. Fudge. There were also clowns and teen girls dressed up as Tinkerbell’s fairies flitting about the room.

“It wasn’t quite Disney World, but we still had bears and chickens and fairies,” Ms. Fudge recalled.

Carousing and playing seemed like a reprieve from the children’s stressful circumstances, she said.

“Done the cockles of your heart good to watch what was going on. It was just an amazing thing,” Mr. Fudge said.

He said that someone recently asked him: If 9/11 happened today, would he still do what he did?

“I said, in a heartbeat. … In Newfoundland and Labrador, it’s not even a question.”

Residents have taken that spirit – and the mayor’s advice – to heart. All over Gander, there are signs of solidarity and lasting friendship between Canada and the U.S. American and Canadian flags placed side by side in the entranceway of the town hall. A pin of the twin towers on a crocheted square at the local arts centre.

The solidarity runs even deeper than what happened 25 years ago. Take the history of the airport, and of the town itself.

After its first plane landing in 1938, the airport in Gander became the main staging point during the Second World War for American and British allies to ferry thousands of bombers and fighter planes across the Atlantic Ocean to Europe. Up to 12,000 soldiers lived in barracks beside and between the runways, a settlement that was abandoned when the town was incorporated in 1958.

“So these people are still our friends,” said Mr. Woodford, the retired air traffic controller who now serves as a town councillor.

He recalled how, in addition to helping land some of the diverted flights in Gander on 9/11, he organized a shelter for the Knights of Columbus. He and his wife Glenda also took in six stranded strangers at their home. His voice cracked with emotion as he described how the daughter of one woman they hosted recently called to share that she had died.

“We didn’t know who, where these people were from, what their backgrounds were. We didn’t do any checks. We were just asked to welcome them, and we did,” he said.

He was one of the local volunteers and political leaders invited to a thank-you breakfast hosted by Ambassador Hoekstra in gratitude for what they did in the aftermath of 9/11.

“I think it might be challenging at times, but the one thing I promise you I will not do is talk politics. This is not a political event,” he said in the lead-up to the event. “This is an event to demonstrate and remember the good deeds. We’re going to commemorate what happened on Sept. 11 and we’re going to celebrate what happened on Sept. 12, 13, 14, 15.”

Every September, Jeanette Gutierrez returns to Gander.

Sitting in the bar at the Gander airport this week, the survivor of the attacks in New York said the warmth and goodwill the town represents have made it a safe haven.

She recounted first visiting Gander with a group of museum volunteers a decade ago. This place and its people, including a local woman she met while being screeched in, have become a refuge.

“It’s just safer for me here, safer in my soul. When I’m in New York it’s awful, but here, it’s not,” she said, on the verge of tears.

“I’m allowed to feel good here.”

With a report from Johnny C.Y. Lam

Mayor Percy Farwell, who was deputy mayor 25 years ago, encouraged Newfoundlanders to rise above the disrespect and stay true to their welcoming hearts.

content_blocks.text: “We’re remembering the great tragedy and the great loss, and we’re trying to reflect on those who lost their lives and support those that lost loved ones and that were permanently impacted by those events,” he said during an interview last week.

“We reflect on how we, as a twist of fate, became involved in a specific way – in being able to provide support to impacted people – and how much we value that. Those sorts of things transcend any emotions we might have around the latest Truth Social post or the latest version of trade talks.”

content_blocks.caption: Mayor Percy Farwell stops by the Compassion Monument, made from a steel beam from the World Trade Center. It was a gift from New York’s Bethpage Fire Department.

content_blocks.text: It was a message heard repeatedly about town this week as locals reunited with their “plane people” friends and attended storytelling events, tours of the airport, performances of Come From Away and screech-in ceremonies to welcome visitors at the local Royal Canadian Legion.

content_blocks.text: Monica Burke, who now lives in the state of Georgia, was on her way home to Seattle on 9/11 when her flight was diverted to Gander. Returning to that legion hall on Wednesday evening caused a flood of memories to come back.

She recalled the spot on the floor across the room where she dozed on a borrowed mattress, waiting to make a call on the one telephone that people were taking turns using. And she remembered Beulah Copper, a legion volunteer, walking in and offering to drive Ms. Burke and others to a pay phone at a nearby hotel.

Ms. Cooper invited Ms. Burke to stay in the spare bedroom in her home, and cooked her hot breakfasts during her stay. Since then, the two have stayed in touch over multiple visits. Ms. Burke thinks of her older friend as a grandmother.

“I just wanted to come back and thank them,” said Ms. Burke. “And then one time wasn’t enough. So I just keep coming back – especially now, being 25 years, a lot of people who were here aren’t here any more, and it’s sad. It’s what happens, but I want to see the people that I can while I can.”

content_blocks.caption: Monica Burke has come back to Gander several times to show gratitude for the hospitality she found here 25 years ago.

content_blocks.text: On Wednesday night, Ms. Cooper was again at the legion hall, busy screeching in a bunch of Americans. The welcoming ritual makes “come from aways” into honorary Newfoundlanders. At a long table, visitors from Ohio and New York and Illinois shuddered as they slung back shots of dark Newfoundland Screech rum and Ms. Cooper presented a frozen cod for them to kiss right on the lips (through a plastic bag).

Karen Stringer, wearing an anti-Trump pin and about to get screeched in, said she felt compelled to come to Gander for the 9/11 anniversary commemoration because of Come From Away, which is playing right now in her home city of Peoria, Ill.

content_blocks.text: “I need to support Canada,” she said. “It wasn’t until years later that we realized what Canada did and I think it’s important that we pay respects to this country and say thank you.”

content_blocks.caption: Karen Stringer from Illinois gets ‘screeched in’ by Beulah Cooper, one of the volunteers who helped travellers in 2001. Kissing the cod is part of a ritual to make someone an honorary Newfoundlander.

content_blocks.text: Strangers from all over the world received comfort from the area’s townspeople during the frightening hours and days after 9/11 – hearing their stories, eating their home cooking, using their spare bedding.

Diane Davis, a Grade 3 French immersion teacher who helped convert Gander Academy into a makeshift shelter for 770 stranded passengers from four flights, inspired a composite character in Come From Away – down to her green Northern Reflections pants and a flowery patterned shirt “that didn’t hide nearly as many sins as I used to think it did,” she joked in a recent interview.

content_blocks.text: She said that at the time, she was just doing what any Newfoundlander would do. But it has provided her with opportunities to travel the world and keep telling her story – and that’s important, especially now, she said.

“It’s really difficult for a lot of people in the political climate that we’re in right now, where Canada is being so misrepresented and a lot of other things are being misrepresented by the American government. I think it’s really important to keep telling these stories,” she said. “Not to say that we’re any better, but just that we’ve always been there to help.”

content_blocks.caption: Retired teacher Diane Davis, who partly inspired one of the characters in the musical, has plenty of Come From Away clothing and fridge magnets at home.

content_blocks.text: Municipal police officer Oswald Fudge and his daughter Lisa, who was in high school at the time, shared their story, too.

They decided to host a special birthday party for the children who were stranded because of the terrorist attack. While only six kids were celebrating birthdays in the days that followed Sept. 11, they organized a party for 60 kids. Some of them were terminally ill and had been diverted to Gander on their way to Disney World.

Within hours, father and daughter had dozens of toys donated by the local Canadian Tire, and filled a 12-foot table with sheet cakes provided by the Co-op grocery store and stacked boxes from Mary Brown’s Chicken.

They also assembled an array of fuzzy mascots – an RCMP bear in red serge, two Cooper the Bear representatives from Co-op, a chicken from Mary Brown’s and the town spokesgoose Commander Gander, worn by Ms. Fudge. There were also clowns and teen girls dressed up as Tinkerbell’s fairies flitting about the room.
“It wasn’t quite Disney World, but we still had bears and chickens and fairies,” Ms. Fudge recalled.
Carousing and playing seemed like a reprieve from the children’s stressful circumstances, she said.
“Done the cockles of your heart good to watch what was going on. It was just an amazing thing,” Mr. Fudge said.
He said that someone recently asked him: If 9/11 happened today, would he still do what he did?
“I said, in a heartbeat. … In Newfoundland and Labrador, it’s not even a question.”

content_blocks.caption: Oswald Fudge was a police officer, and his daughter Lisa Fudge a high-school student, when the planes came to Gander on Sept. 11, 2001.

content_blocks.text: Residents have taken that spirit – and the mayor’s advice – to heart. All over Gander, there are signs of solidarity and lasting friendship between Canada and the U.S. American and Canadian flags placed side by side in the entranceway of the town hall. A pin of the twin towers on a crocheted square at the local arts centre.
The solidarity runs even deeper than what happened 25 years ago. Take the history of the airport, and of the town itself.

After its first plane landing in 1938, the airport in Gander became the main staging point during the Second World War for American and British allies to ferry thousands of bombers and fighter planes across the Atlantic Ocean to Europe. Up to 12,000 soldiers lived in barracks beside and between the runways, a settlement that was abandoned when the town was incorporated in 1958.
“So these people are still our friends,” said Mr. Woodford, the retired air traffic controller who now serves as a town councillor.

content_blocks.caption: Mr. Woodford and his wife, Glenda, opened their home 25 years ago to six stranded people.

content_blocks.text: He recalled how, in addition to helping land some of the diverted flights in Gander on 9/11, he organized a shelter for the Knights of Columbus. He and his wife Glenda also took in six stranded strangers at their home. His voice cracked with emotion as he described how the daughter of one woman they hosted recently called to share that she had died.
“We didn’t know who, where these people were from, what their backgrounds were. We didn’t do any checks. We were just asked to welcome them, and we did,” he said.
He was one of the local volunteers and political leaders invited to a thank-you breakfast hosted by Ambassador Hoekstra in gratitude for what they did in the aftermath of 9/11.

“I think it might be challenging at times, but the one thing I promise you I will not do is talk politics. This is not a political event,” he said in the lead-up to the event. “This is an event to demonstrate and remember the good deeds. We’re going to commemorate what happened on Sept. 11 and we’re going to celebrate what happened on Sept. 12, 13, 14, 15.”

content_blocks.caption: Jeanette Gutierrez, a survivor of 9/11, values the sense of safety she finds in Gander.

content_blocks.text: Every September, Jeanette Gutierrez returns to Gander.
Sitting in the bar at the Gander airport this week, the survivor of the attacks in New York said the warmth and goodwill the town represents have made it a safe haven.
She recounted first visiting Gander with a group of museum volunteers a decade ago. This place and its people, including a local woman she met while being screeched in, have become a refuge.
“It’s just safer for me here, safer in my soul. When I’m in New York it’s awful, but here, it’s not,” she said, on the verge of tears.
“I’m allowed to feel good here.”
With a report from Johnny C.Y. Lam

stories.title: Army reorganization formally takes effect with ceremony in Edmonton
stories.summary: New Manoeuvre Division will oversee all of the Army’s combat resources
stories.author: Gavin John
stories.content:
The long-planned overhaul of the Canadian Army took effect Thursday as a ceremony in Edmonton formally brought its combat role under the purview of a single division for the first time since the Second World War.

The event officially retired the 3rd Canadian Division and reintroduced it as the 1st Canadian Division, also known as Manoeuvre Division, which will oversee all of the Army’s combat resources.

Previously, those resources were split between four divisions located across the country.

The commander of the new division, Major-General Wade Rutland, who previously commanded the 3rd Canadian Division, said the change will put the Army in a league with its allies, though the full transformation will take years.

“What’s actually in the 1st Canadian Division, and you compare it with a lot of our allies, it’s a viable force,” he said in an interview earlier this week. “We think in a couple years we’re going to be much more capable.”

The creation of Manoeuvre Division is part of an overhaul that will also see the Montreal-based 2nd Canadian Division, now also known as the Defence of Canada Division, focus on national emergencies and domestic defence . And Support Division, based in Kingston, will provide infrastructure and other resources to the rest of the Army.

The restructuring is a long-term effort by the Canadian Armed Forces to expand its ranks and prepare for the possibility of major conflict.

Maj.-Gen. Rutland said the Manoeuvre Division is the “expeditionary warfighting division” that will be prepared to fight in the event of a major conflict − overseas or at home.

“We’ll have the highest level of readiness,” he said. “Sometimes defending at home means defending forward. Sometimes it means defending here.”

Dozens of Army personnel dressed in dark green and navy-blue uniforms watched at the Edmonton event as the commander of the Army spoke about past battle honours before offering a blunt assessment of the state of the institution today.

“The Army that we have is not the Army we need,” Lieutenant-General Michael Wright said.

The flag of the 3rd Canadian Division was lowered and replaced with a bright red patch − the new symbol of the Manoeuvre Division − to signal the transition.

Manoeuvre Division will oversee the Army’s three mechanized brigade groups in Edmonton, Petawawa, Ont., and Valcartier, Que. The restructured division also includes four formations: the 3rd Light Infantry Regiment, the 1st Canadian Artillery Brigade, the 1st Canadian Sustainment Brigade and the 10th Signal Regiment.

The federal government has made building up the military a priority, especially as it seeks to reduce Canada’s reliance on the United States for trade and defence in the face of U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade war. Ottawa is also ramping up its defence spending to meet NATO investment targets.

“The division headquarters has to learn to fight as a division headquarters,” Maj.-Gen. Rutland said Thursday, adding that Army personnel will begin conducting combat simulations against a major adversary.

“We need to change now to a division headquarters that has tents, gets its rucksack on, has communications and fights,” he said.

In the meantime, he said, the Army’s work continues uninterrupted. For example, it is preparing to deploy troops to Latvia, as well as to Ukraine for training.

Lt.-Gen. Wright cautioned that the work of transforming the Army won’t be quick.

“Just because it’s the 10th of September doesn’t mean the 1st Canadian Division is completely full of people, necessary people, necessary capability, and able to be that warfighting division,” he said.

“The path toward that starts today.”

He said the new formations are at varying levels of maturity, and the Army’s chief concern is the ability to provide command and control and combat service support.

Much of the equipment the Army says it needs, including ground-based air-defence systems, armoured reconnaissance vehicles and mobile artillery, has yet to be deployed.

Lt.-Gen. Wright said the HIMARS rocket artillery system the government has purchased will fall under 1st Canadian Division command and that by September, 2027, two of Maj.-Gen. Rutland’s units will each have a sub-unit based on uncrewed systems.

David Perry, the president of the Canadian Global Affairs Institute, says the modernization of the military will take years and some of the decisions to ensure that happens − such as supplying equipment − rest with the federal government.

“Realistically, we can’t expect the Army to have much more operational capability than it does today for another three to five years,” Mr. Perry said.

Maj.-Gen. Rutland said a shortage of equipment is not his concern.

“You’ve got to be ready to fight tonight with what you have,” he said. “If we had to bring [older equipment] to World War III, we’d bring it, we’d dig in and we would shoot it.

“I’ve got what I’ve got.”

stories.title: 25 years later, who was the 9/11 victim with a Global News reporter’s name?
stories.summary: A Global News reporter uncovers the life and family of Michael J. Armstrong, the man killed on Sept. 11, 2001, who shares his name — right down to the middle initial.
stories.author: Michael J. Armstrong
stories.content:
It’s an awkward thing to say.

But every Sept. 11 , when the names of the 2,977 people killed in the terrorist attacks are read aloud at the World Trade Center site … I hear my name.

Michael J. Armstrong.

It’s a name I share, right down to the middle initial.

For more than two decades, I wondered about the other Michael Armstrong. Who was he? What was his life like? Who had he left behind?

Years ago, I came across something written by one of his sisters about the family’s efforts to keep Michael’s memory alive. They had created a foundation in his name. So, as I began putting together stories to mark 25 years since the attacks, I decided I wanted to help his family tell his story.

Even reaching out felt uncomfortable.

I knew the email would arrive in his sister’s inbox with one name attached to it: Michael Armstrong. I wondered what it would be like for her to see that name suddenly appear on her screen. And whether I had any right to ask her to open that door.

The ensuing back and forth turned into a visit to her home in Tappan, N.Y., last month.

The walls of Laura’s home are filled with family photos. Michael appears in many of them: Christmas mornings, Thanksgivings, St. Patrick’s Day celebrations, and one where he jumped on their father’s lap. He was goofing around after he as his sister Marian had bought Laura her first digital camera.

“He just had such a hearty laugh,” Laura said. “He laughed a lot.”

“He was just a warm kind of guy and he was great with kids,” Marian recalled.

Dozens of photos have been added to the walls in the 25 years since 9/11. Important events where Michael’s absence is impossible for the family to ignore.

“There are a lot of instances where we think that,” Laura said. “Where he should have been.”

Michael Armstrong was 34 years old and worked in electronic trading on Wall Street with the brokerage company Cantor Fitzgerald.

On the morning of Sept. 11, 2001, Michael was at work on the 104th floor of the North Tower of the World Trade Center, above the floors struck by American Airlines Flight 11.

After the building was hit, Michael tried to reach members of his family by telephone.

His sister Marion remembers that his final cellphone call was to their mother. The family’s copy of his phone statement showed the call lasted two minutes.

But his mother couldn’t make out his words.

All she heard was static.

The family has always hoped that while Michael couldn’t be heard, he could hear his mother’s voice.

For hours that morning, his sisters clung to possibilities.

Maybe he had been late for work. Maybe what they were hearing about the Twin Towers wasn’t as bad as it sounded. They didn’t turn on the television.

“I really thought he was going to be OK,” Laura recalled. “As crazy as it is.”

The next few weeks in Michael’s life were supposed to be special. He and his fiancée, Catherine Nolan, were set to be married on Oct. 6, 2001.

Instead, Michael’s wake was held on Sept. 23, 2001.

He almost wasn’t in the office on 9/11. He’d been at a funeral the day before and missed work. And later in the week, he was scheduled to be off again for his bachelor party.

“We often said, like, oh, you know, so many things,” Catherine recalled. “If he had only left a few days earlier, if he had a dentist appointment the next day.”

“So many days that week he would not have been there,” Marian said.

Those are the what-ifs that can follow a family for decades.

Catherine eventually married and had children. Her youngest son’s middle name is Michael. She also never really left the Armstrong family.

“I always joke that I’ve got the in-laws without the husband,” she said.

Michael’s brother is godfather to one of her children. His sisters remain part of her life. Twenty-five years later, Catherine is still Aunt Catherine to the next generation of Armstrongs.

There is a gravity to grieving — a force that focuses on the pain. The Armstrongs chose instead to help others in Michael’s name.

Within days of the attacks, they established a scholarship fund at Loyola School, where Michael had been a student and remained an active alumnus. In the months that followed, the family established the Michael J. Armstrong Memorial Foundation.

For nearly 25 years, they have held fundraising events and supported causes connected to Michael’s life, including scholarships at Loyola and athletics at Fordham University, where Michael was an enthusiastic basketball fan.

His sister describes it as a place to channel all the emotions that followed his death. It’s also ensured his story didn’t stop on Sept. 11, 2001.

The family’s effort to remember Michael now extends to people who never had the chance to meet him.

His niece, Keeley, says Michael is a normal household name in the family. He died when she was young, but it has never felt that way.

“It’s amazing how much you can know someone through stories,” Keeley said.

Those stories have given another generation a picture of an uncle they never knew: his enormous laugh, his sense of humour, his bear hugs and his habit of teasing his siblings.

But there is still sadness. The next generation of Armstrongs is now approaching the age that Michael was when he was killed.

“We’re now in that stage of life of people getting married,” Keeley said, with tears welling up. “I can’t imagine that you’re supposed to be going to a bachelor party on Thursday, and then this happens.”

But the Armstrongs also remember something else about those days: how people responded to their pain.

Catherine found herself part of a group no one would ever choose to join — women who, like her, lost their fiancées on 9/11.

They found each other in the aftermath. Twenty-five years later, they still get together every Sept. 11 for lunch.

The support came from all directions. There were countless acts of kindness the family remembers from those first days: people reaching out, showing up and trying to help.

It’s something they’ve carried forward through the foundation, the scholarships and the years spent helping others in Michael’s name.

“I can’t look back at that day without thinking about the kindness, the care everyone took with me,” Marian says. “People are so beautiful.”
paragraphs: It’s an awkward thing to say.
But every Sept. 11 , when the names of the 2,977 people killed in the terrorist attacks are read aloud at the World Trade Center site … I hear my name.
Michael J. Armstrong.
It’s a name I share, right down to the middle initial.
For more than two decades, I wondered about the other Michael Armstrong. Who was he? What was his life like? Who had he left behind?

Years ago, I came across something written by one of his sisters about the family’s efforts to keep Michael’s memory alive. They had created a foundation in his name. So, as I began putting together stories to mark 25 years since the attacks, I decided I wanted to help his family tell his story.
Even reaching out felt uncomfortable.

I knew the email would arrive in his sister’s inbox with one name attached to it: Michael Armstrong. I wondered what it would be like for her to see that name suddenly appear on her screen. And whether I had any right to ask her to open that door.
The ensuing back and forth turned into a visit to her home in Tappan, N.Y., last month.

The walls of Laura’s home are filled with family photos. Michael appears in many of them: Christmas mornings, Thanksgivings, St. Patrick’s Day celebrations, and one where he jumped on their father’s lap. He was goofing around after he as his sister Marian had bought Laura her first digital camera.
“He just had such a hearty laugh,” Laura said. “He laughed a lot.”
“He was just a warm kind of guy and he was great with kids,” Marian recalled.
Dozens of photos have been added to the walls in the 25 years since 9/11. Important events where Michael’s absence is impossible for the family to ignore.
“There are a lot of instances where we think that,” Laura said. “Where he should have been.”
Michael Armstrong was 34 years old and worked in electronic trading on Wall Street with the brokerage company Cantor Fitzgerald.
On the morning of Sept. 11, 2001, Michael was at work on the 104th floor of the North Tower of the World Trade Center, above the floors struck by American Airlines Flight 11.
After the building was hit, Michael tried to reach members of his family by telephone.
His sister Marion remembers that his final cellphone call was to their mother. The family’s copy of his phone statement showed the call lasted two minutes.
But his mother couldn’t make out his words.
All she heard was static.
The family has always hoped that while Michael couldn’t be heard, he could hear his mother’s voice.
For hours that morning, his sisters clung to possibilities.
Maybe he had been late for work. Maybe what they were hearing about the Twin Towers wasn’t as bad as it sounded. They didn’t turn on the television.
“I really thought he was going to be OK,” Laura recalled. “As crazy as it is.”
The next few weeks in Michael’s life were supposed to be special. He and his fiancée, Catherine Nolan, were set to be married on Oct. 6, 2001.
Instead, Michael’s wake was held on Sept. 23, 2001.
He almost wasn’t in the office on 9/11. He’d been at a funeral the day before and missed work. And later in the week, he was scheduled to be off again for his bachelor party.
“We often said, like, oh, you know, so many things,” Catherine recalled. “If he had only left a few days earlier, if he had a dentist appointment the next day.”
“So many days that week he would not have been there,” Marian said.
Those are the what-ifs that can follow a family for decades.
Catherine eventually married and had children. Her youngest son’s middle name is Michael. She also never really left the Armstrong family.
“I always joke that I’ve got the in-laws without the husband,” she said.
Michael’s brother is godfather to one of her children. His sisters remain part of her life. Twenty-five years later, Catherine is still Aunt Catherine to the next generation of Armstrongs.
There is a gravity to grieving — a force that focuses on the pain. The Armstrongs chose instead to help others in Michael’s name.

Within days of the attacks, they established a scholarship fund at Loyola School, where Michael had been a student and remained an active alumnus. In the months that followed, the family established the Michael J. Armstrong Memorial Foundation.

For nearly 25 years, they have held fundraising events and supported causes connected to Michael’s life, including scholarships at Loyola and athletics at Fordham University, where Michael was an enthusiastic basketball fan.
His sister describes it as a place to channel all the emotions that followed his death. It’s also ensured his story didn’t stop on Sept. 11, 2001.
The family’s effort to remember Michael now extends to people who never had the chance to meet him.
His niece, Keeley, says Michael is a normal household name in the family. He died when she was young, but it has never felt that way.
“It’s amazing how much you can know someone through stories,” Keeley said.
Those stories have given another generation a picture of an uncle they never knew: his enormous laugh, his sense of humour, his bear hugs and his habit of teasing his siblings.
But there is still sadness. The next generation of Armstrongs is now approaching the age that Michael was when he was killed.

“We’re now in that stage of life of people getting married,” Keeley said, with tears welling up. “I can’t imagine that you’re supposed to be going to a bachelor party on Thursday, and then this happens.”
But the Armstrongs also remember something else about those days: how people responded to their pain.

It’s something they’ve carried forward through the foundation, the scholarships and the years spent helping others in Michael’s name.
“I can’t look back at that day without thinking about the kindness, the care everyone took with me,” Marian says. “People are so beautiful.”

stories.title: Alberta government launches $4M ad campaign ahead of fall separation referendum
stories.summary: Edmonton - Alberta's government says it has launched a $4-million advertising campaign urging citizens vote to stay in Canada in next month's referendum.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
EDMONTON - Alberta’s government says it has launched a $4-million advertising campaign urging citizens vote to stay in Canada in next month’s referendum.

The campaign will advertise online, on TV and radio, and on billboards.

The premier’s office says it’s important Albertans understand what’s at stake when they vote on 10 referendum questions on Oct. 19.

Nine of the questions focus on immigration and constitutional issues.

The main public focus is on the last question, which asks whether Alberta should remain in Canada or hold a second, binding referendum on separation.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Who’s downloading photos of your kid at dance competitions?

Premier Danielle Smith has said she supports keeping the country together and that it’s time to put the issue to rest once and for all in Alberta.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 10, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: How torrential rain is pushing this year’s harvest far behind average
stories.summary: Torrential rains late in the season are adding stress at a time that is already taxing for farmers. The recent moisture has prevented producers from getting into fields and further delayed harvest in many parts of Saskatchewan.
stories.author: Allison Bamford
stories.content:
Davidson, Sask. - Torrential rains late in the season are adding stress at a time that is already taxing for farmers.

The recent moisture has prevented producers from getting into fields and further delayed harvest in many parts of Saskatchewan.

The most recent government-issued crop report shows only 27 per cent of Saskatchewan crops have been harvested, which puts producers far behind the five-year average of 58 per cent.

Rob Stone, who farms an hour south of Saskatoon, is usually ahead of the provincial average.

But right now, he only has 18 per cent of his crops in the bin.

“Bluntly, it has been a bit brutal,” Stone said.

Stone’s area received about 150 millimetres of rain over the course of a week.

He was forced to wait for fields to dry up before he could get equipment running again.

“Everything is in good shape and we need to go, but the weather needs to co-operate,” he said.

Further south, near Montmartre, Sask., the Kotylaks are still waiting for their crops to dry after torrential rains flattened some of their fields.

“In 37 years, this is the worst canola I have ever seen,” farmer Peter Kotylak told CTV News while standing in one of his waterlogged crops.

“The rain came at the wrong time this year.”

Farmers in certain areas have struggled with the weather all year long.

A late snow dump and spring flooding pushed seeding back. Now rain is prolonging harvest.

“The year got off to a slow start and it has just gotten further and further behind,” said Bill Prybylski, president of the Agricultural Producers Association of Saskatchewan.

“It’s been very stressful.”

The recent rain is not only burning time but also hurting yields and potential profits, Prybylski said.

“Some crops are definitely going to be hurt more than others,” he said.

“There will definitely be some downgrading in the quality of the grain.”

Stone expects his wheat and lentils to decrease in grade and yields due to the rain delays.

The potential losses come at a time when farmers are facing record high input costs.

Tariffs and trade uncertainty drove up the costs of fuel, fertilizer, machinery and repairs.

“This is the most expensive crop we have ever grown,” Stone said.

“If the yields are not there, people will be on the wrong side of profit.”

stories.title: Family mourns death of loved one killed fighting in Ukraine
stories.summary: "He paid the ultimate price for Canada and Ukraine,” said an emotional James Bourgeois, Jessy Bourgeois’ father, in an interview with Global News.
stories.author: Klaudia Van Emmerik
stories.content:
The family of a B.C man killed in Ukraine is mourning his death.

“He paid the ultimate price for Canada and Ukraine,” said an emotional James Bourgeois, Jessy Bourgeois’ father.

The 46-year-old man was killed on Aug. 18 in the Donetsk region near the Russian border.

“They got hit by a drone attack, and Jesse was killed instantly,” said Bourgeois. “Another comrade was critically injured and died several days later.”

Bourgeois lived in Nanaimo, where he was introduced to the Ukrainian church.

His family says he quickly fell in love with the people and culture and eventually felt compelled to help defend the country.

“That’s where his heart laid,” said stepmom Dawn Bourgeois. “We didn’t understand it. We didn’t support it.”

Despite having no military experience, Jessy volunteered in November to fight alongside the Ukrainian Army.

He was working as a drone mechanic when he was killed.

“It’s one day at a time, and we try to find happiness every day. That’s all we can do,” Dawn said.

The Okanagan Falls couple says Jessy believed deeply in Ukraine and its efforts to fight for the country,

“He believed in what Ukraine was fighting for — for their freedom — and there was no talking him out of it,” James said.

Bourgeois leaves behind two children.

His family says they will grow up knowing their father was a hero.

“He was brave. He was brave for what he did,” James added.

The family’s grief comes as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy visits Canada, seeking continued support for Ukraine’s fight against Russia.

James says Canada’s support remains important to him, particularly after his son’s death.

“My son lost his life for them,” he said. “I think as Canadians we got to keep backing them.”

Global Affairs Canada says it is aware of the death of a Canadian in Ukraine. The department says it does not keep a registry of Canadians who voluntarily travel to Ukraine to serve, or those who are injured or killed in the conflict.

However, the organization says it is aware of 35 Canadians who have died in Ukraine of all causes since the war began.

Jessy’s body is expected to be repatriated in the coming weeks with the help of the Ukrainian government.

For his family, the grief remains raw, but they find some comfort in knowing Bourgeois believed he was following his heart.

“I’m proud of what he did,” James said. “This was his calling. You look at his pictures, I sure don’t see any fear.”

Instead, he says, he sees determination to help a country in need.

stories.title: Infrastructure investment needed to ‘supercharge’ Canadian mining, BMO analyst says
stories.summary: BMO analyst Matthew Murphy expects mining sector to play central role in discussions at Canada Investment Summit
stories.author: Niall McGee
stories.content:
More investments are needed in vital infrastructure such as roads and power lines to “supercharge” Canadian mining, said BMO analyst Matthew Murphy, a few days ahead of a historic Canadian investment event.

Next week, the inaugural Canada Investment Summit will be held in Toronto to attract hundreds of billions of dollars in international investment into Canada to help cushion the blow of the continuing trade war with the United States. The event is being led by Prime Minister Mark Carney and co-hosted by big Canadian pension funds.

In a note to clients earlier this week, Mr. Murphy, mining analyst with BMO Capital Markets, said he expects the sector to play a central role in discussions at the summit, and he addressed the key question of where capital is needed the most.

In a web panel discussion on Thursday, Mr. Murphy said significantly more investment in mining infrastructure could be enormously beneficial for the industry and reward multiple companies.

“There’s a big multiplier effect on infrastructure spending,” he said. “And that’s what you need for a productive economy.”

Mr. Murphy outlined several parts of the country where infrastructure spending is needed, including Northern B.C., home to major copper and gold discoveries; the Yukon; northern Ontario’s Ring of Fire region; and Quebec’s James Bay region, which has promising lithium projects.

He pointed to past infrastructure investments that spurred new development, including British Columbia installing the 344-kilometre-long Northwest Transmission Line along Highway 37. The additional electricity supply facilitated the Red Chris block cave mine development, the Brucejack gold mine, and exploration projects in B.C.’s Golden Triangle.

Several infrastructure projects that would benefit the mining sector have already been referred to the government’s Major Projects Office , which was created last year by Mr. Carney to both reduce red tape and potentially facilitate funding.

Those projects include the North Coast Transmission Line in northwestern British Columbia, the Taltson Hydro Expansion in the Great Slave Lake region of the Northwest Territories, and the Arctic Economic and Security Corridor in the NWT, a 400-kilometre all-season road through the Slave Geological Province to the Nunavut border.

In his report, Mr. Murphy said that infrastructure investment is one of the ways “to truly supercharge growth” of the Canadian mining sector.

He said that while Canadian mining companies can draw on an educated work force, and have strong engineering capabilities, it’s a major challenge to raise the hundreds of millions in capital needed for such projects.

“Mining investors want 15- to 25-per-cent returns on new projects and that’s hard if you have to carry a big infrastructure load as well,” he said.

Large infrastructure funds, such as those run by Brookfield Asset Management Ltd. BAM-T , or BlackRock’s BLK-N Global Infrastructure Partners, could potentially fill in the gap, Mr. Murphy said. These funds tend to have lower costs of capital than mining companies, and their investors can be satisfied with returns of 7 per cent to 10 per cent, he added.

Some mining companies have already successfully off-loaded the risk of building some mining infrastructure to third parties. Mr. Murphy pointed to BHP Group Ltd.’s BHPLF deal last year with Global Infrastructure Partners that saw GIP pay US$2-billion to acquire a 49-per-cent stake in a power network for BHP’s Western Australia Iron Ore operations.

Canadian pension funds, which have far more money invested abroad than domestically, are also potentially in a position to invest in mining infrastructure projects, Mr. Murphy said.

“We believe more Canadian capital pools can be allocated domestically, while still generating competitive returns,” he said.

Taking place on Sept. 14 and 15, the Canada Investment Summit will feature panel discussions and presentations from Mr. Carney’s cabinet ministers, some of the biggest global investors, and CEOs of several large Canadian resource companies.

One of the earliest sessions will feature a critical minerals discussion with the CEOs of Canadian miners Teck Resources Ltd., Cameco Corp. and Agnico Eagle Mines Ltd., who will discuss how to transform the domestic sector into a world-beater.

stories.title: No shuttle service for Regina Foo Fighters concert ‘due to timing,’ mayor says
stories.summary: Shuttle service will not be available for people attending the Foo Fighters concert next Tuesday, due to timing issues, the city's mayor said.
stories.author: Tavi Dhillon
stories.content:
One of Mosaic Stadium’s biggest shows will not have its typical, game-day shuttle service, the City of Regina said.

While regular transit will run as normal in Saskatchewan’s capital, shuttle service will not be available for Tuesday’s concert because of the timing, Regina Mayor Chad Bachynski said.

“Just due to the timing of the concert, it wouldn’t be possible for us to have that dedicated chartered service,” Bachynski continued.

He said 4 p.m., when the venue’s doors open, is too close to the end of the workday for the city to offer shuttles, adding that Regina decided against it to ensure regular transit riders’ trips home aren’t interrupted.

“It wouldn’t be possible for us to actually take buses offline for the concert,” the mayor said.

Dave Grohl and company will headline the first concert at the stadium in seven years, and the band’s show is almost sold out, Kyle Russell, vice president of operations and experience with REAL District, told Global News. A few last-minute tickets are still available.

The REAL District is not providing transportation services and is advising concertgoers to plan ahead.

“This is really going to be an exercise in planning for coming to and from the concert,” Russell said.

He pointed people to the REAL District website , where information on getting to and from the venue is available.

“Parking’s on sale for the Foo Fighters concert,” Russell said.

Passes can be purchased online.

“We do encourage fans to prepay for parking in advance because we do anticipate a sellout, but the campus is a big parking lot,” Russell said.

“It’s just going to be a really fun night, and we’re looking forward to people coming out here for a full night of great music.”

The Foo Fighters will be joined by Queens of the Stone Age and Mannequin Pussy. The first opening act is expected to hit the stage at Mosaic Stadium at 5:30 p.m. Tuesday.
