stories.title: Canadians born after 9/11 far less likely to fear another terror attack, poll finds
stories.summary: One in six Canadian respondents under the age of 25 believe acts of terrorism can sometimes be justified, the survey found.
stories.author: Adrian Humphreys
stories.content:
Twenty-five years after the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks a public opinion poll reveals a striking generational divide in what Canadians know about the world’s deadliest terror attacks, how deeply they feel its impact, how much they fear terrorism — and even on the question of whether terrorism can be justified.

The poll’s findings suggest personal memories of the shock and horror of the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks change how people think about terrorism.

The nationwide poll of Canadian adults, conducted this week by Leger Marketing for the Association for Canadian Studies and provided to Postmedia, found those under the age of 25 are by far the least likely to say they have good knowledge of the events of 9/11.

Among all respondents, 71 per cent said they have good knowledge of what happened on 9/11, while 17 per cent said they did not and 11 per cent said they didn’t know if they did or did not.

In the youngest cohort of adults, those between 18 and 24, only 47 per cent said they have good knowledge of 9/11, with 35 per cent saying they didn’t and 18 per cent saying they didn’t know. By contrast, those in the oldest cohort, aged 65 and up, 81 per cent said they have good knowledge and only 11 per cent said they didn’t. Across the age brackets, professed knowledge escalated with age.

Age changed how people answered all questions about terrorism.

“It’s a generational divide that’s really driving a lot of the responses on this subject,” said Jack Jedwab, president of the Montreal-based Association for Canadian Studies. “Which makes sense, since those in the youngest cohort weren’t born yet at that time (of 9/11).

“So right out of the proverbial gate that’s going to be an important predictor of how they understand the post-9/11 climate, or the extent to which they think there is a post-9/11 climate, which, in terms of our understanding of the phenomenon of terrorism in this century, that’s the event that has shaped much of the response both in North America and globally.”

For many around the world old enough, 9/11, as the attacks are collectively known, stands as one of those rare events they remember precisely where they were or what they were doing when they first heard the news.

As that day unfolded, people learned that 19 terrorists with al-Qaida, a jihadist group, hijacked four U.S. passenger airliners and used them as deadly weapons. Two planes were crashed into iconic skyscrapers in New York, flattening them, one was flown into the Pentagon, the U.S. military’s headquarters, and a fourth crashed in a field before reaching its target, possibly the White House or the United States Capitol building, when passengers tried to take back control of the plane.

The coordinated attacks killed 2,977 victims. Several times more than that have died since, attributed to exposure to enormous clouds of toxic dust and ash in New York after World Trade Center’s two towers collapsed.

The attacks significantly changed many aspects of life, particularly in the United States but also around the world, including global politics, aviation, public safety, policing and surveillance.

The poll, however, found age also changed how strongly respondents still feel the impact of 9/11 after 25 years.

Asked whether they still feel the impact of the events of 9/11, 45 per cent of all respondents said yes, and 40 per cent said no, with 14 per cent saying they don’t know.

Isolating the youngest group revealed only 27 per cent still felt an impact from the 9/11 attacks, while 47 per cent said no and 26 per cent said they don’t know. That’s much lower even than the next age group up — those between 25 and 34 years old — where 41 per cent said yes and 43 per cent said no, with 16 per cent not knowing. Respondents between 45 and 54 years old felt the strongest lingering impact, at 54 per cent, with 36 per cent saying no. In the two older age groups about half said yes and 38 per cent said no.

“If you have very good knowledge (of 9/11), it has impact. If you don’t, it doesn’t have much impact to you,” Jedwab said. “So, knowledge is really an important predictor of the extent to which you think this is having impact on us today.”

Younger Canadians are far less likely to feel that terrorism is a threat today, the poll suggests. Asked in the poll whether they felt Canada was safer from terrorism now than in 2001, 43 per cent of the youngest respondents said yes, by far the highest. Those feeling the least safe from terrorism were those between 45 and 54 years old; only 18 per cent said yes.

The poll also found one in six Canadian adult respondents under the age of 25 believe acts of terrorism can sometimes be justified, with another one in five saying they don’t know.

Respondents as a whole rejected the idea that terrorism is sometimes justified — 81 per cent saying no, eight per cent saying yes, and 11 per cent saying they don’t know.

“This is a concern,” said Jedwab. “I think there’s a lot of influence on social media that’s working to try to see these horrific acts through some other lens that seeks to identify some root causes.

“This type of view risks creating a severe injustice for victims of tragedies like on 9/11.”

The online survey questioned 1,538 adults in Canada from Sept. 4 to 6. As a non-probability sample in a panel survey, traditional margins of error do not apply. For comparison, a probability sample of the same size would typically have a margin of error of plus or minus 2.5 per cent.

Asked whether they still feel the impact of the events of 9/11, 45 per cent of all respondents said yes, and 40 per cent said no, with 14 per cent saying they don’t know.

Isolating the youngest group revealed only 27 per cent still felt an impact from the 9/11 attacks, while 47 per cent said no and 26 per cent said they don’t know. That’s much lower even than the next age group up — those between 25 and 34 years old — where 41 per cent said yes and 43 per cent said no, with 16 per cent not knowing. Respondents between 45 and 54 years old felt the strongest lingering impact, at 54 per cent, with 36 per cent saying no. In the two older age groups about half said yes and 38 per cent said no.

“If you have very good knowledge (of 9/11), it has impact. If you don’t, it doesn’t have much impact to you,” Jedwab said. “So, knowledge is really an important predictor of the extent to which you think this is having impact on us today.”

Younger Canadians are far less likely to feel that terrorism is a threat today, the poll suggests. Asked in the poll whether they felt Canada was safer from terrorism now than in 2001, 43 per cent of the youngest respondents said yes, by far the highest. Those feeling the least safe from terrorism were those between 45 and 54 years old; only 18 per cent said yes.

Respondents as a whole rejected the idea that terrorism is sometimes justified — 81 per cent saying no, eight per cent saying yes, and 11 per cent saying they don’t know.
“This is a concern,” said Jedwab. “I think there’s a lot of influence on social media that’s working to try to see these horrific acts through some other lens that seeks to identify some root causes.

stories.title: Caisse, B.C. billionaire Ryan Beedie partner to buy and develop industrial property across Canada
stories.summary: Joint venture will target existing, larger-scale structures or land in large cities in Quebec, Ontario, Alberta and B.C.
stories.author: Sean Silcoff
stories.content:
One of Western Canada’s top property developers, Ryan Beedie, is teaming up with the Caisse de dépôt et placement du Québec to buy and develop industrial real estate nationally.

His company, Burnaby, B.C.-based Beedie Holdings Ltd., has sold a half-share in six warehouses and distribution centres to the pension management giant for $500-million. The portfolio includes four Vancouver-area properties, one in Calgary and another under construction in Toronto. Together, they total 2.7 million square feet of leasable space and include facilities used by Sobeys, Aritzia and Amazon. Beedie will manage the properties.

The partners have also agreed to buy or build up to $2-billion of additional industrial properties in large cities in Quebec, Ontario, Alberta and British Columbia. The Caisse has committed $500-million for that expansion. Beedie will source deals and contribute 25 per cent or 50 per cent of the equity capital on a case-by-case basis; the Caisse will contribute the balance of the equity. The remaining will be debt-financed. The joint venture will target existing, larger-scale structures or land where a building can be constructed within three years.

“The Caisse has been clear in saying, as have we, that we want this relationship to continue to grow,” Todd Yuen, president, industrial at Beedie, said in an interview.

It’s the second joint venture this year in the sector for the Caisse, which had $552-billion of assets under management as of June 30. In April, it partnered with San Francisco-based giant Prologis Inc., which owns, develops and manages logistics and distribution warehouses for Amazon, the Home Depot, FedEx and others. With €1-billion ($1.6-billion) in seed assets, that venture, which is 70 per cent owned by the Caisse, will initially combine income-generating properties and development sites contributed by both partners across Europe and Britain.

Rana Ghorayeb, executive vice-president and head of real estate with the Caisse, said in a statement: “By combining our capital and investment expertise with Beedie’s proven operating capabilities and deep market knowledge, we have created a scalable investment vehicle to build a portfolio of quality industrial assets in some of Canada’s most strategic markets. This partnership strengthens our ability to capture compelling opportunities alongside one of Canada’s leading operators.”

The Caisse has remodelled its real estate holdings this decade, boosting its exposure to logistics and residential properties while pulling back on shopping malls and office buildings. It made $4.4-billion of property-related acquisitions in 2025, including data centres and student residences.

Demand for warehouses and other industrial real estate has picked up after two years of relatively lower investment in the sector. There were $6.6-billion of industrial deals in Canada in the first half of 2026, according to commercial real estate services company CBRE. That is slightly higher than the same period last year and does not include the proposed $3.4-billion acquisition of H&R Real Estate Investment Trust. CBRE industrial expert Matthew Brown said industrial investment this year could surpass 2023’s record of $20.7-billion. He said large investors are returning to the space, including pension funds, foreign capital providers and high-net-worth individuals.

The Caisse deal marks the latest step by Mr. Beedie, one of B.C.’s wealthiest entrepreneurs and most prominent philanthropists, to expand the scope and scale of his business beyond the regional development company founded 70 years ago by his late father, Keith. Mr. Beedie has led the company since 2001.

Beedie oversees 24.4 million square feet of industrial space, including buildings it co-owns or manages for others. It’s the largest industrial developer in B.C. and one of Royal Bank of Canada’s two largest corporate lending clients.

In the 2000s, Beedie expanded beyond that traditional base into residential condominium development (it had 944 units under construction at the end of 2025) and financing mining and technology companies. It is the largest shareholder in Artemis Gold Inc., with a stake valued at more than $2.7-billion, and this year it bought a half-stake in one of Canada’s most consistently successful tech financiers, Vistara Capital Partners Ltd. The Caisse deal marks the first time Beedie will manage outside capital.

“This is a pivotal moment for us,” Mr. Beedie said in an interview. “It allows us to scale and become a truly national company.”

Beedie set out last year to seek a deep-pocketed institutional partner to help finance its expansion and enable it to better compete with Prologis and Irvine, Calif.-based Panattoni Development Co. Inc. “To be partners with the Caisse and their millions of pensioners, it feels pretty good to think the work we’re doing may contribute at least a bit to the benefit of Canadians that rely on them,” Mr. Beedie said.

The deal could eventually create a path for Mr. Beedie to exit more of his real estate holdings, given that none of his three adult children work in the business. While “this is not something for the near-term, it’s potentially another benefit if down the road we are looking for more liquidity events, as you have a ready built-in partner to work on that,” he said.

With reports from Rachelle Younglai and Nicolas Van Praet

stories.title: Coun. Susan Stevenson kicks off London mayoral campaign, details platform
stories.summary: "I want every Londoner to be able to look at this city and feel the same pride, the same sense of belonging, and the same hope for its future," she told supporters.
stories.author: Jack Moulton
stories.content:
"I want every Londoner to be able to look at this city and feel the same pride, the same sense of belonging, and the same hope for its future," she told supporters.

Last updated 10 minutes ago[](http://lfpress.com/news/local-news/coun-susan-stevenson-kicks-off-London-mayoral-campaign-details-platform#comments-area)

London mayoral candidate Susan Stevenson speaks during the launch of her campaign at an event in downtown London on Wednesday, Sept. 9, 2026. Geoff Robins/The London Free Press

London city councillor Susan Stevenson officially launched her mayoral campaign Wednesday evening, pledging a more transparent city hall, and safer neighbourhoods just steps away from some of the most prevalent areas for homelessness downtown.

Speaking to a crowd of roughly 130 in her campaign office on the second floor of 284 Dundas St. – next door to the old city hall building at Dundas and Wellington streets – Stevenson, who was first elected to city council four years ago, addressed her reasons for running and revealed the first pieces of her campaign platform.

“I want every Londoner to be able to look at this city and feel the same pride, the same sense of belonging, and the same hope for its future,” she told supporters. “But loving your city also means being willing to fight for it. It means speaking up when people feel unsafe, asking hard questions when the costs keep rising, and having the courage to change course when people are being let down.”

For buyers, sellers, renters and dreamers — London's complex, fascinating real estate market is brought into focus and into context with this newsletter.

It appeared no city council colleagues were in attendance at the event, in contrast to the six council members who attended incumbent Mayor Josh Morgan’s campaign launch Monday.

Stevenson was introduced by former longtime city council member Cheryl Miller, and former Tourism London head John Winston. Stevenson’s campaign chair, Denise Lalonde, also spoke. Also in attendance were former city councillor Michael van Holst and Kurt Holman, the sitting Conservative MP for London-Fanshawe.

London mayoral candidate Susan Stevenson takes a photo with supporters during her campaign launch event in London on Wednesday, Sept. 9, 2026. (Geoff Robins/The London Free Press)

Stevenson outlined her six priorities, teasing out specific promises while reserving some for further exploration in the coming weeks. The priorities include restoring “safety and pride” in neighbourhoods, supporting small businesses, bringing “accountability back to city hall,” improving transportation and mobility, strengthening partnerships, and “leadership that shows up.”

Some of her platform promises include issues she’s raised at city council before, but were defeated by council. As of now, her promises include but are not limited to:

Weekly garbage pickup during the summer

Imposing “good neighbour” agreements on housing providers

Limiting distribution of harm reduction drug paraphernalia

Implementing a downtown parking strategy

Public financial reviews of homelessness and bus rapid transit spending

Hiring an auditor general, and establishing an anonymous “fraud and waste hotline”

Exploring “transit police,” and expanding transit service to industrial areas

Public reporting of council attendance and voting

The 59-year-old Stevenson, presently representing Ward 4 on city council, was first elected in 2022 with 28 per cent of the vote. Prior to being elected, she worked as an accountant.

While on council, her outspoken beliefs on homelessness and open drug use has landed her in the sights of city hall’s integrity commissioner numerous times. While most complaints were dismissed or found no wrongdoing, she was punished by her colleagues twice including a formal reprimand and a 30-day pay suspension.

Speaking to reporters after her remarks Wednesday night, Stevenson said she stands out from her incumbent colleagues specifically for championing recovery over harm reduction on open drug use, and asserts councillors are not provided the information they need to be decision makers on major issues.

“W e did not vote on this in 2022,but in 2026,there’s a very clear path.We can either continue on the path that we’re doing,which is enabling and trying to keep people safe while they’re deeply addicted,or we can create pathways for recovery where people can actually escape the addiction,” she said.

London mayoral candidate Susan Stevenson speaks during the launch of her campaign in London on Wednesday, Sept. 9, 2026. (Geoff Robins/The London Free Press)

On property tax increases, she remained tight-lipped, promising an announcement next week.

Speaking on the council votes needed to pass her priorities, as Morgan saw nearly half of council attend his campaign launch, Stevenson said she doesn’t expect council collaboration to be a problem if she is elected.

“I’m being very clear on what it is I’m running (on),and when I get elected,the mandate from the public is very clear – and council will support it.I have no doubt,” she said. “It’s leadership that takes the stand and sells it to their council,and I have no concerns at all that we needed to do that.”

The first-term councillor jumped into the mayor’s race a little over a week after nominations opened in May, hoping to unseat her council colleague Morgan, who is running for re-election after first being elected mayor in 2022.

Morgan, 48, launched his re-election campaign Monday afternoon, with a four-pillar platform focused on “community, connection, commerce, and security,” and promising “three per cent range” tax hikes over four years, and city hall special constables in public spaces.

Fellow mayoral challenger Kirsten Krose, 42, released her campaign platform in August, narrowing in on public safety, better city services, better traffic management, restrained taxpayer spending, and housing. She also had a campaign launch party this week, Tuesday at Joe Kool’s.

In addition to Morgan, Krose and Stevenson, the other nine registered mayoral candidates are John Feher, Lawrence-Zachary Howe, Barry Douglas Jacklin, Tariq Khan, Dan Lenart, Bronagh Joyce Morgan, Christine Rosehart, Jeff Yam and Mustafa Zeboon. Voters go to the polls on Oct. 26.

London mayoral candidate Susan Stevenson speaks during the launch of her campaign in London on Wednesday, Sept. 9, 2026. (Geoff Robins/The London Free Press)
On property tax increases, she remained tight-lipped, promising an announcement next week.

“I’m being very clear on what it is I’m running (on),and when I get elected,the mandate from the public is very clear – and council will support it.I have no doubt,” she said. “It’s leadership that takes the stand and sells it to their council,and I have no concerns at all that we needed to do that.”

The first-term councillor jumped into the mayor’s race a little over a week after nominations opened in May, hoping to unseat her council colleague Morgan, who is running for re-election after first being elected mayor in 2022.

Morgan, 48, launched his re-election campaign Monday afternoon, with a four-pillar platform focused on “community, connection, commerce, and security,” and promising “three per cent range” tax hikes over four years, and city hall special constables in public spaces.

Fellow mayoral challenger Kirsten Krose, 42, released her campaign platform in August, narrowing in on public safety, better city services, better traffic management, restrained taxpayer spending, and housing. She also had a campaign launch party this week, Tuesday at Joe Kool’s.

In addition to Morgan, Krose and Stevenson, the other nine registered mayoral candidates are John Feher, Lawrence-Zachary Howe, Barry Douglas Jacklin, Tariq Khan, Dan Lenart, Bronagh Joyce Morgan, Christine Rosehart, Jeff Yam and Mustafa Zeboon. Voters go to the polls on Oct. 26.

Limiting distribution of harm reduction drug paraphernalia
Public financial reviews of homelessness and bus rapid transit spending

Public reporting of council attendance and voting

stories.title: N.S. mother continues son’s fight for enhanced government support for people living in tents
stories.summary: Jackie Lowe’s son died in 2023, years before he won a legal case that found that people living in tents were eligible for the enhanced provincial government support
stories.author: Lyndsay Armstrong
stories.content:
A Nova Scotia woman says she is not giving up a fight launched by her son for enhanced government support for unhoused people.

Jackie Lowe’s son, Bradley Lowe, died in 2023, years before he won a legal case on Aug. 5 that found that people living in tents were eligible for the enhanced provincial government support.

The Nova Scotia government responded to the Nova Scotia Court of Appeal ruling by changing the definition of housing to exclude people who live in tents, as was the case for Bradley Lowe.

But his mother said the government response was cruel and she is urging the province to reverse its decision and respect the ruling in her son’s case.

“He was fighting for change, because he saw others around him experiencing the same things he was,” Jackie Lowe said Wednesday.

The August ruling overturned a Nova Scotia Supreme Court decision last year that found Bradley Lowe did not meet the eligibility requirements for enhanced income assistance because he lived in a tent.

Jackie Lowe said her son would have celebrated the August decision, adding that he was someone who was always fighting for the underdog. The family pursued the case after he died with human rights lawyer Vince Calderhead.

Lowe spoke to reporters at a press conference held by the Opposition NDP on Wednesday.

The party introduced three bills related to housing, including one that they called “Bradley’s law.” NDP Leader Claudia Chender said Bradley’s law would overturn the province’s regulation change to allow those living in tents to access the enhanced assistance.

The government introduced the regulatory change to the definition of housing through an order-in-council filed about three weeks after the August court decision. The amended regulations remove the term “accommodation” and substitute it with “lives in a home.”

It also repeals the prior definition for “home” and defines it as a self-contained unit someone rents or owns, a room in a lodging house or a single-occupancy room in a building.

Calderhead, the human rights lawyer, said the province later made further changes to income assistance rules to make people with disabilities living in tents ineligible for a disability supplement.

An order-in-council, signed Sept. 3, changed the eligibility for this supplement to require that the person with a disability receiving the support “must live in a home or board.”

Calderhead said he asked the Nova Scotia Human Rights Commission to investigate this “discriminatory” action.

“This move sends a clear message that people with disabilities living in these very vulnerable circumstances are not as worthy, indeed, are not equal in consideration; in other words: they are not really people – at least not equal in terms of dignity and respect,” Calderhead said in an e-mail Tuesday.

Susan Corkum-Greek, minister of opportunities and social development, said the department was making changes to regulations to provide more clarity in its language so the program can be administered consistently.

Lowe asked members of Premier Tim Houston’s Progressive Conservative government to put themselves in the shoes of someone who is homeless and living in a tent and consider how they would survive on her son’s income assistance rate – which was $380 a month.

The new base income assistance rate has since risen to $410 per month.

Corkum-Greek said she heard about Lowe’s remarks on Wednesday and has reached out in hopes of speaking with her.

“I won’t know until I meet her, but I think we would have a lot of shared space. Because I do want to get the supports that people need, I want to get them access to those supports,” the minister said in an interview Wednesday.

She added that raising the rates of income assistance is a “constant” conversation in her department.

stories.title: ‘Their papa loves them’: 25 years later, Montreal woman remembers husband’s final call on 9/11
stories.summary: Twenty-five years after 9/11, Kimmy Chedel is still carrying the memory of her husband, Frank Doyle, who was killed in the World Trade Center.
stories.author: Lola Kalder
stories.content:
By Lola Kalder

Posted September 10, 2026 6:38 am.

Twenty-five years after 9/11, Kimmy Chedel is still carrying the memory of her husband, Frank Doyle, who was killed in the World Trade Center. Their children were just two and one at the time.

Now, she’s reflecting on the last words they shared and the legacy he has left behind.

Chedel says she first met Doyle in New York. “It was love at first sight. His name tag was stuck to my shoe, and I was just obsessed,” she recounted.

“I couldn’t believe I had met this man. He was funny, kind, caring. He was gorgeous.”

The two would later go on to get married and welcome two children, Zoe and Garrett, while living in Englewood, New Jersey. But on Tuesday Sept. 11, 2001, Chedel says their lives suddenly changed forever.

“I know exactly where I was 25 years ago and how perfect our life was,” she said.

“It wasn’t long after I left the house that I heard on 1010 News that a commercial aircraft had hit the World Trade Center. So I very quickly turned my car around, went back to the house. I’ll never forget. I couldn’t get my key into the front door of the house. My hand was just shaking, shaking.

“I went immediately to the phone, and I called Frank right away, 212-323-484-50. And someone answered the phone, and they’re like, ‘Frankie,’ and I said ‘it’s Kimmy.’ So all of a sudden I had this massive sense of relief because, you know, they’re OK.

“He said, if you think we got rocked in ’93, this was 10 times worse. He said, Kimmy, I was thrown to the floor.”

In 1993, Chedel and Doyle both lived through the World Trade Center bombing, an experience Chedel believes shaped how her husband responded on 9/11. After their phone call, she briefly thought he was safe. But at 9:03 a.m., United Airlines Flight 175 flew into the South Tower, where Doyle worked.

“He called me after the second plane had hit his tower. And on that call he was speaking very deliberately, and he said, I need you to listen carefully. I’ve gone up to the rooftop; the rooftop doors are locked. He said, ‘We’re trapped on the 87th floor. It’s getting difficult to breathe.’ I could hear people coughing. I could hear a girl crying. You could hear glass shattering. And he said, ‘I know you know this, but you need to promise to tell Zoe and Garrett every day for the rest of their lives how much their papa loves them.'”

Doyle then told her he needed her to hang up and call 911 to tell them there were people trapped on the 87th floor.

“I didn’t realize how brave he was on that call, but he was saying goodbye,” said Chedel.

Doyle’s final call came at 9:22 a.m., less than 40 minutes before the South Tower collapsed.

“At 9:59, I’m watching the TV live, and I’m watching his tower collapse. So he had very little time. Their building was hit at 9:03, and they died at 9:59. “

Frank Doyle was 39. His remains were identified through dental records several weeks later. But for Chedel, the process of recovering pieces of her husband continued for years.

“I got seven calls over the next three-and-a-half years. And during those calls they would say, ‘We have his right tibia. We have his left femur. We have his left foot. We have his right foot.’ That was tough,” said Chedel, holding back tears.

At the time, Chedel was raising two young children while trying to navigate a loss that changed every part of their lives.

“I was struggling, I was 37 years old with two babies, but I made sure that they never saw me cry. You know, we slept together in a big king-size bed, and I would cry after they went to sleep at night,” she explained.

Chedel says she kept living for her children. “It was just really important for me to know that they would look back on their childhood and realize that we just kept living, because that’s what Frank would want us to do,” she said.

In the years that followed, Chedel made sure her husband’s memory remained a part of his children’s lives, while turning his love of sports into a lasting legacy.

In 2017, she created Team Frank Africa in Montreal. The organization has helped support 19 schools so far across South Africa in his honour, with Chedel saying many more are on the horizon.

“He was the greatest dad and I just hope that he can see his kids and that he’s really proud of what we’ve created in terms of his legacy,” said Chedel.

stories.title: A convicted killer is here while he challenges the verdict in Mexico. Will Canada extradite him?
stories.summary: Ryan Friesen is a free man in Canada while he appeals his conviction in Mexico for the femicide of his 23-year-old girlfriend Kiara Agnew at an all-inclusive resort in 2023. If a Mexican court upholds that conviction, Mexico could ask Canada to extradite Friesen to serve his sentence.
stories.author: Avery Haines
stories.content:
This is the final part of a three-part W5 investigation series. Read Part 1 and Part 2 .

Watch the W5 investigation “If I’m Ever Found Dead” on our CTV News YouTube channel .

Warning: Graphic content.

Ryan Friesen is a free man in Canada while he appeals his conviction in Mexico for the femicide of his 23-year-old girlfriend Kiara Agnew at an all-inclusive resort in 2023.

If a Mexican court upholds that conviction, Mexico could ask Canada to extradite Friesen to serve his sentence.

Mexico cannot simply order Canada to arrest him. It would have to make a formal extradition request, setting in motion a lengthy legal process in this country.

What happens if Mexico requests extradition?

An extradition request from one country to another is confidential, so there wouldn’t necessarily be an immediate public announcement if Mexico makes one.

“Members of the public won’t know when the Mexican state, or if the Mexican state, makes a request to Canada, ” says Toronto extradition lawyer James Bray.

If the request is made, then Canadian authorities would seek an arrest warrant and take Friesen into custody.

Friesen could apply for bail

Being arrested for extradition does not automatically mean Friesen would remain in jail in Canada while the case plays out.

He could apply for bail.

But Bray says bail is often more difficult to obtain in extradition cases than in ordinary criminal cases, particularly when the underlying offence is serious.

“The courts tend to take bail in the extradition context even more seriously,” he said. “Conditions tend to be a lot more onerous.”

A Canadian judge would consider whether the person is likely to appear in court, whether they pose a danger to the public and whether releasing them would undermine public confidence in the administration of justice.

If bail is granted, conditions May include GPS monitoring and house arrest.

Canada would not retry Mexican case

The extradition proceeding in Canada is not a retrial of the evidence in Kiara’s death.

Instead, a Canadian judge would determine whether the legal requirements for extradition have been met. The case would then move to Canada’s federal minister of justice, who makes a final decision.

Extradition orders can be appealed all the way to the Supreme Court of Canada, but those challenges are often unsuccessful.

“In general, extradition is quite challenging to resist,” Bray said. “The presumption of innocence does not apply.”

Why isn’t Canada already enforcing the Mexican conviction?

The fact that Ryan Friesen has been convicted in Mexico does not mean Canada treats him as someone convicted of a Canadian crime.

Canada does not simply enforce another country’s criminal verdict.

“What happens in the Mexican legal system is very much separate from what happens in Canada,” Bray said.

There is no timeline for when the Mexican court will release its decision on Ryan Friesen’s appeal. The court has had the case for more than four months. But a ruling could still be months, or even years, away.

If the conviction is upheld and the extradition process is finalized in Canada, Friesen would be transferred to Mexico for a sentencing hearing.

The crime of femicide carries a prison term of 50 to 80 years in Mexico.

Ryan Friesen has not responded to repeated requests for comment. His only public statement was in January 2026 when, through his lawyer, he maintained his innocence.

You can read parts 1 , 2 and 3 of W5’s previous investigative series on Kiara Agnew’s murder online. You can also watch W5’s “If I’m Ever Found Dead” on CTV News’ YouTube channel .

W5 is the multiplatform investigative unit of CTV News, continuing its decades-long commitment to covering tough, relevant stories.

stories.title: Is the trade war driving American NHL stars out of Canada?
stories.summary: A handful of American NHL stars are leaving Canadian teams, raising questions about taxes, trade tensions and the appeal of playing in the U.S.
stories.author: Kenn Oliver
stories.content:
Hockey has entered into the Canada-U.S. trade war again. Not over tariffs on hockey sticks or President Donald Trump’s AI-generated meme of himself knocking down Prime Minister Mark Carney on the ice, but as part of the conversation surrounding the departure of American-born players from Canadian teams.

There hasn’t been a flood of players leaving, and plenty of players from the U.S. joined Canadian clubs in the off-season, but when elite players are involved — including three who played for this year’s Olympic gold-medal-winning Team USA — the moves are subject to extra scrutiny.

Asked to weigh in on the apparent American exodus in a pre-season interview aired by Sportsnet this week, the Edmonton Oilers ’ Connor McDavid said he hopes it’s not because they don’t want to be in Canada.

“Canada and the U.S. has had a great relationship for years and years and years, and I hope that continues for a long time,” he said.

Without specifying any players who have left or want to, the Oilers captain reasoned it could be that players simply “don’t see the opportunity to win on that specific team.” He highlighted his organization signing Ryan Shea, from Massachusetts, and St. Louis native Trent Frederic this season.

“Americans still want to play in Canada,” he said. “At least, that’s the sense that I get. They want to play for teams where they see a future.”

Late last month, Michigan-born Winnipeg Jets goaltender Connor Hellebuyck made public his desire to waive a no-movement clause and be traded from the organization after only two years of a seven-year, US$59.5 million contract signed in 2023.

The three-time Vezina Trophy winner who is the league’s best goalie didn’t specifically say he wants out of Canada for a U.S. destination, nor did he provide a list of teams where he’d be willing to move, but NHL insiders believe he’s bound to land with a U.S. club.

After the Jets failed to make the playoffs last season, he made it clear he wants to compete for a Stanley Cup.

“That’s my goal, and that’s all I have left, and that’s what I want on my resumé,” Hellebuyck said in April, according to TSN. “I don’t play this game for the money. I don’t play it for the fame. I do it for my own personal fun and, you know, part of that is winning a Cup. So for me, I’m just looking at how I can get that. How can I get there?”

Should the Jets receive an acceptable offer for Hellebuyck from one of the league’s 25 U.S. teams, he’ll join Brady Tkachuk as the second player from the Team USA squad to be traded from a Canadian club to an American in recent months.

The Ottawa Senators sent their Arizona-born captain to the Florida Panthers on June 21, one of four teams the four-time All-Star submitted as destinations when he made it clear to management that he would not extend his contract before it expired in 2028, according to Sportsnet. The trade came less than two months after he said he was “fully committed” to the Senators and questions about his contract were becoming a “distraction,” Reuters reported.

The Panthers’ pedigree of back-to-back Stanley Cups and a chance to play with older brother Matthew — who’d requested a trade from the Calgary Flames in 2022 — were big draws for Tkachuk, according to NHL.com

Counting Florida-born defenceman Quinn Hughes, the number of departing players from the U.S. squad that defeated Canada in the February gold medal Olympic final rises to three.

The Vancouver Canucks traded the two-time All-Star to the Minnesota Wild on Dec. 12, 2025, after he indicated months earlier that he wouldn’t renew his contract, due to expire in 2027, TSN reported.

Michael Naraine, associate professor of sport management at Brock University, said NHL players May be drawn to certain U.S. clubs — the Panthers, Tampa Bay Lightning, Vegas Golden Knights, or Dallas Stars, for example — for a “multitude” of reasons unrelated to the trade war.

“Would we be talking about this if not for the trade war? Probably not, but I think the trade war has certainly elevated the star players wanting out and not just wanting out, but wanting out to specific destinations,” he told National Post.

Part of it is the “glamour” of their preferred destination.

He said NHLers, like their NBA brethren, operate in an “isomorphic” or “monkey see, monkey do” way, in that when they see a friend or former teammate find success with a club, they’ll want to join them.

At the same time, for NHL players, moving to an American market affords them a degree of anonymity they might not find under the intense media and fan scrutiny in Canada.

“If Brady (Tkachuk) walks down Elgin Street in Ottawa, everyone’s gonna know who he is,” Naraine said. “Brady Tkachuk could walk down the streets of Florida and no one is going to know who the heck he is.”

Taxes are clearly a factor, with multiple states charging an income tax rate of zero per cent, he noted, which makes states like New York or Illinois, Democratic states with higher taxes, a less appealing destination.

On the subject of taxes, Naraine said many players are “spooked” by Toronto Maple Leafs’ John Tavares’ court battle with the Canada Revenue Agency.

Tavares argues that the millions of dollars he received for signing with the team were legitimate signing bonuses designed to entice him to come to Canada and therefore deserve special tax treatment. The CRA counters that they were really just salary dressed up as bonuses, meaning the player would owe millions more in taxes.

Should the CRA win and limit teams’ ability to offer those bonuses, Naraine expects smaller-market Canadian teams like Ottawa, Vancouver and Winnipeg will “really struggle.”

While that May not be the case for Hellebuyck, Naraine said the Tavares situation could prompt more agents to advise their clients that “maybe now’s the time to strike while the iron’s hot and get out, make things even keel, get to a place where you feel more comfortable.”

Naraine also posited that what’s happening with American NHL players is akin to a shift that took place in the NBA following the 2008 Summer Olympics.

Bonds were forged as the best U.S. players came together to dominate on their way to a gold medal, and two years later LeBron James, Dwyane Wade and Chris Bosh reunited to form one of the NBA’s first super teams. Naraine thinks similar friendships were formed in the U.S. Olympic men’s team locker room.

“I wouldn’t be surprised if like three or four of these guys in a couple of years go, ‘look, let’s all go to Seattle, make bank, and live it up and just make a powerhouse squad’ or ‘let’s all go to L.A.’ or ‘let’s all go to Dallas,’” he said.

The CRA counters that they were really just salary dressed up as bonuses, meaning the player would owe millions more in taxes.
Should the CRA win and limit teams’ ability to offer those bonuses, Naraine expects smaller-market Canadian teams like Ottawa, Vancouver and Winnipeg will “really struggle.”

While that May not be the case for Hellebuyck, Naraine said the Tavares situation could prompt more agents to advise their clients that “maybe now’s the time to strike while the iron’s hot and get out, make things even keel, get to a place where you feel more comfortable.”
Naraine also posited that what’s happening with American NHL players is akin to a shift that took place in the NBA following the 2008 Summer Olympics.

Bonds were forged as the best U.S. players came together to dominate on their way to a gold medal, and two years later LeBron James, Dwyane Wade and Chris Bosh reunited to form one of the NBA’s first super teams. Naraine thinks similar friendships were formed in the U.S. Olympic men’s team locker room.

“I wouldn’t be surprised if like three or four of these guys in a couple of years go, ‘look, let’s all go to Seattle, make bank, and live it up and just make a powerhouse squad’ or ‘let’s all go to L.A.’ or ‘let’s all go to Dallas,’” he said.

content_blocks.text: Hockey has entered into the Canada-U.S. trade war again. Not over tariffs on hockey sticks or President Donald Trump’s AI-generated meme of himself knocking down Prime Minister Mark Carney on the ice, but as part of the conversation surrounding the departure of American-born players from Canadian teams.

There hasn’t been a flood of players leaving, and plenty of players from the U.S. joined Canadian clubs in the off-season, but when elite players are involved — including three who played for this year’s Olympic gold-medal-winning Team USA — the moves are subject to extra scrutiny.

Asked to weigh in on the apparent American exodus in a pre-season interview aired by Sportsnet this week, the Edmonton Oilers ’ Connor McDavid said he hopes it’s not because they don’t want to be in Canada.
content_blocks.html: Asked to weigh in on the apparent American exodus in a pre-season interview aired by Sportsnet this week, the Edmonton Oilers’ Connor McDavid said he hopes it’s not because they don’t want to be in Canada.

content_blocks.text: “Canada and the U.S. has had a great relationship for years and years and years, and I hope that continues for a long time,” he said.

Without specifying any players who have left or want to, the Oilers captain reasoned it could be that players simply “don’t see the opportunity to win on that specific team.” He highlighted his organization signing Ryan Shea, from Massachusetts, and St. Louis native Trent Frederic this season.
“Americans still want to play in Canada,” he said. “At least, that’s the sense that I get. They want to play for teams where they see a future.”

Late last month, Michigan-born Winnipeg Jets goaltender Connor Hellebuyck made public his desire to waive a no-movement clause and be traded from the organization after only two years of a seven-year, US$59.5 million contract signed in 2023.

The three-time Vezina Trophy winner who is the league’s best goalie didn’t specifically say he wants out of Canada for a U.S. destination, nor did he provide a list of teams where he’d be willing to move, but NHL insiders believe he’s bound to land with a U.S. club.

content_blocks.text: After the Jets failed to make the playoffs last season, he made it clear he wants to compete for a Stanley Cup.

“That’s my goal, and that’s all I have left, and that’s what I want on my resumé,” Hellebuyck said in April, according to TSN. “I don’t play this game for the money. I don’t play it for the fame. I do it for my own personal fun and, you know, part of that is winning a Cup. So for me, I’m just looking at how I can get that. How can I get there?”

Should the Jets receive an acceptable offer for Hellebuyck from one of the league’s 25 U.S. teams, he’ll join Brady Tkachuk as the second player from the Team USA squad to be traded from a Canadian club to an American in recent months.

The Ottawa Senators sent their Arizona-born captain to the Florida Panthers on June 21, one of four teams the four-time All-Star submitted as destinations when he made it clear to management that he would not extend his contract before it expired in 2028, according to Sportsnet. The trade came less than two months after he said he was “fully committed” to the Senators and questions about his contract were becoming a “distraction,” Reuters reported.

content_blocks.text: Michael Naraine, associate professor of sport management at Brock University, said NHL players May be drawn to certain U.S. clubs — the Panthers, Tampa Bay Lightning, Vegas Golden Knights, or Dallas Stars, for example — for a “multitude” of reasons unrelated to the trade war.

At the same time, for NHL players, moving to an American market affords them a degree of anonymity they might not find under the intense media and fan scrutiny in Canada.

stories.title: 'There's Been A Tragedy': The untold history of Canada's 9/11 response
stories.summary: Exclusive book excerpt: A minute-by-minute investigation of how senior leaders scrambled -- and fretted -- as the U.S. diverted its planes.
stories.author: Special to National Post
stories.content:
This is an excerpt from Ash and Honor: The Untold 368 Minutes of 9/11, by American author Jeffrey Robinson. The book tells the story of the official response to 9/11 by North American authorities. This excerpt, drawn from multiple chapters, focuses on senior Canadian officials.

Jean Chrétien, the 67-year-old Canadian prime minister who’d led his Liberal Party to a parliamentary victory in 1993, lived at 24 Sussex Drive in Ottawa, Canada’s equivalent of the White House. Built in 1866, the 35-room mansion was set on four acres in the fashionable New Edinburgh neighborhood, overlooking the Ottawa River.

With Parliament in recess, and all of his ministers out of town, he was working from home that morning.

Having suffered Bell’s palsy at the age of 12, making the left side of his face weaker than the right side, Chrétien spoke in a very distinct lopsided way out of the left side of his mouth, with a heavy accent in both French and English. It gave him a quality of being authentic, a tough, straightforward yet self-deprecating man who didn’t put on the airs of the intellectual lawyer and avid reader that he actually was.

He was also a man with deep political instincts. For example, he dealt with President Clinton by playing golf. And he dealt with President Bush by talking about baseball.

Coming downstairs from the residence just before 8:30 a.m., he walked into the ground-floor living room to greet the new premier of Saskatchewan, Lorne Calvert. They’d never met and were scheduled to talk about farm aid. But after the usual pleasantries, their meeting was cut short by an aide coming into the room to tell Chrétien that a plane had just crashed into the World Trade Center in New York.

Like so many people that morning, Chrétien thought, it must have been a small plane flown by a pilot who didn’t know what he was doing.

Then the second plane hit.

Calvert made his exit and Chrétien went to his ground-floor office to assess the situation. He and his aides sat and watched CNN, until he decided he was going to phone George Bush to express Canada’s sympathy and support.

His aides talked him out of it.

They convinced Chrétien there would be time for that tomorrow.

Right now, they said, the president is busy. Your call will only get in the way.

Chrétien agreed and, instead, tried to reach the U.S. ambassador to Canada, Paul Cellucci. He’d been governor of Massachusetts when George Bush sent him to Ottawa. But that morning, Cellucci was on a plane heading back to Ottawa from Winnipeg.

The prime minister eventually got the deputy chief of mission on the phone and assured him that Canada was prepared to do whatever needed to be done.

The American diplomat was grateful.

When they hung up, Chrétien admitted that while the offer stood, there actually wasn’t much Canada could do.

Little did he know.

Reaching his cabinet wasn’t easy. They were spread out across the country, with some outside the country, in an era when email and smartphones weren’t plentiful.

Chrétien and his staff had mobile phones, clumsy early versions that, they often complained, didn’t work very well. So for the rest of the morning they stayed where they were, contacting the few people they could while watching on television as events unfolded in the States.

The one constant interruption was his Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) security detail. They kept trying to convince Chrétien to leave the residence and go to a safer place.

They tried again a little while later.

He refused a second time, and then a third.

The Mounties pressed him whenever they could, genuinely concerned that he might not be safe. After all, no one knew if the terrorists were heading north of the border.

Or, worse, if they were already in Canada.

What Chrétien didn’t mention to his security detail, or anyone else at the time, was that he worried about the same thing.

One terrorist in particular concerned him greatly.

Now he began phoning everyone he could think of to ask if anyone knew about any possible ties between the terrorists in New York and the one that worried him, Ahmed Ressam.

If it turned out that Ressam had somehow been involved, this would not just be Jean Chrétien’s worst nightmare, it could be Canada’s as well.

David Collenette, Canada’s minister of transport, got up that morning at five o’clock to fly with two members of his staff from Toronto to Montreal, where he was giving the welcome address to a conference held by Airports Council International.

This was the international trade group for all the world’s airport managers, which meant that everybody who was anybody in the airport business — more than 2,000 people from all over the world — would be there.

That included the airport managers from Montreal, Toronto, Vancouver, Winnipeg, Calgary, Gander, Goose Bay, Halifax, St. John’s, Moncton, Charlottetown, Thunder Bay, Sault Ste. Marie, and smaller airports all over Canada. All of whom would soon be needed home. Most of whom would not be able to get there.

Collenette was introduced to the crowd in the Palais de Congrès just after 8:30 and had only spoken for six minutes before he became aware of murmuring at the back of the auditorium.

He thought, am I that bad a speaker or are these guys just rude?

The best thing, he knew from experience, was to ignore them.

But the murmuring increased and began to spread throughout the audience. That’s when one of his officials came up to him, ON stage — which visibly ticked him off — and put a note in front of him with eight words written in large caps: Wind UP Your Speech There’s Been A Tragedy.

Not knowing anything more than that, he excused himself and quickly left the stage.

One of the organizers replaced him at the microphone to announce they were suspending proceedings because there’d been an aviation incident.

Backstage, Collenette was met by his two aides, who tried to fill him in on what they knew, plus a press scrum demanding comments about what had happened in New York.

After nearly 18 years in Parliament, and having served three of those years as defense minister before coming to this post, he had considerable experience with press scrums. He was known, and appreciated by the media, as someone who would always speak his mind. This morning, though, he’d been caught off guard and the best he could come up with was, a small plane has crashed into the North Tower of the World Trade Center in New York. That’s all I know.

He did not say what he suspected. This sounded to him like a terrorist incident.

His aides tried to get him out of the building and into a car for the airport. They rushed him down an escalator. Reporters followed on his heels.

One of his aides, ON the phone with their office in Ottawa, informed him there was a second plane and that the South Tower had been hit.

Worried that they might not be able to fly back, Collenette announced, we’ll drive.

The 125-mile trip would take over two hours.

He and his aides hurried into one of his department’s black vans. He told the driver, we’ve got to get back to Ottawa right away.

But the driver didn’t speak English.

The driver explained in French, I don’t know how to get to Ottawa.

Collenette wrote out the directions for him.

On the way, his deputy minister, Margaret Bloodworth, called to say that all U.S. airspace had been shut down. That the secretary of transportation, Norman Mineta, had closed America’s skies.

But no one had bothered to tell the Canadians.

Long before Collenette’s car reached the Ontario border, he’d checked with his department’s lawyer and was told that he had the authority to do what he wanted to do, which was to close Canada’s skies.

So he pushed that button and now air traffic in both countries was turned off.

For Collenette, that was the easiest part of the trip home.

Much tougher was figuring out, what the hell are we going to do with all the planes that can’t land in the States and are being dumped into Canada?

He didn’t know it then, but the final total would be 239 flights diverted to 17 Canadian airports with an estimated 33,000 displaced and sometimes very unhappy passengers.

What he did know was that, however many planes and passengers were on their way, they’d have to land somewhere. But all the airport managers Collenette needed to help make this happen were stuck inside the Palais de Congrès in Montreal and could be for days.

Sitting in the rear seat of that van, with a driver who didn’t know the way to Ottawa, David Collenette realized he didn’t have much time to figure this out.

John Manley, Canada’s minister of foreign affairs, was returning from a conference, flying with a small staff from Frankfurt, Germany, to Ottawa in the upstairs first-class cabin of an Air Canada 747.

Happy to be coming home, he was reading a book when one of the flight attendants approached him and asked that he follow her into the rear galley. Once they were out of earshot of the other passengers, she told him what little she knew about planes hitting the World Trade Center.

Manley asked if he could speak to the pilot. She escorted him to the flight deck, where, given a headset, he listened to a live broadcast by Britain’s BBC World Service Radio.

The more he listened, the more queasy he became.

Sitting there, hearing what was happening in the United States, the name that kept running through his mind was Ahmed Ressam.

Richard Clarke had been warning of an al-Qaeda attack for years.

He told President Clinton in December 1998 that al-Qaeda was preparing several attacks against America, which included hijacking aircraft. He claimed the attacks were being orchestrated by Osama bin Laden and his second-in-command, Ayman Al-Zawahiri.

He predicted that the attacks would happen around the millennium.

The Central Intelligence Agency concurred, separately and in unison, that bin Laden was turning his attention to the United States.

With the millennium in mind, an attack was planned against Los Angeles International Airport. Mistakenly believing that the millennium began on January 1, 2000 — in fact, the actual date was one year later — an Algerian-born, al-Qaeda-trained militant set in motion a plan to blow up the airport on New Year’s Eve 1999.

He came to be known as the Millennium Bomber.

Arriving in Montreal in 1994 with a counterfeit French passport, he sought political asylum, was awarded the right to remain in Canada, committed benefit fraud, got thrown out, and came back and stayed illegally, committing petty crimes unhindered to finance himself while he plotted the attack. He flew to Vancouver, loaded a rental car with explosives, and, ON December 14, 1999, took the ferry from Victoria, British Columbia, to Port Angeles, Washington.

He was stopped there by a keenly alert U.S. customs inspector, Diana Dean, who didn’t like the fact that the man seemed unusually nervous. He avoided eye contact with her, and when she asked what he was doing there and where he was going, his answers were evasive and inconsistent.

She ordered him into secondary inspection and found his trunk packed with explosives. And when he tried to escape, he was stopped.

In May 2001, he pleaded guilty to conspiracy to bomb a U.S. airport, possession of explosives, and membership in al-Qaeda.

After agreeing to cooperate with the government, he received a sentence of 22 years. When his cooperation suddenly stopped, that was increased to 37 years.

Dean was the hero who foiled the plot. But, unbeknownst to her, such an attack had been on the Cia’s radar for years.

Concerned about the idea that al-Qaeda was planning a series of attacks against U.S. targets, the agency’s Counterterrorism Center had frequently sent out alerts calling for heightened vigilance.

Based on those warnings, former agency managers maintain that several attacks had been thwarted. But one constant concern — reinforced by what they came to know about the Millennium Bomber — was just how long and undefended the U.S.–Canada border was.

The Millennium Bomber’s name was Ahmed Ressam.

At 24 Sussex Drive, Jean Chrétien’s security detail, made up of specially trained officers from the RCMP, wanted to move him to a secure secret location.

Eventually, he spoke with the head of the RCMP, Commissioner Giuliano Zaccardelli.

For the man widely known simply as Zac, this was an extremely busy time, shifting the RCMP from a national policing agency to becoming the primary source of national security.

It was Zac who raised the national threat posture and oversaw RCMP headquarters’ coordination with provincial divisions and other police forces, in addition to establishing an intelligence liaison with the FBI, the CIA, and other U.S. law enforcement.

At the same time, he strengthened the Mounties’ presence at Parliament Hill, the U.S. embassy in Ottawa, and the seven U.S. consulates spread out across the country. He helped to secure nuclear facilities, military bases, key bridges, tunnels, and the nation’s energy infrastructure.

Chrétien told him the Mounties wanted him to leave the residence.

Zac agreed it would be prudent.

Chrétien restated that he would not be moving.

After a while, he asked Zac if he’d found any connection between the 9/11 hijackers and Ahmed Ressam.

Zac eventually came back to the PM to say no.

Chrétien spoke with John Manley as soon as he’d made his way home from Europe. What about Ahmed Ressam?

Manley said he couldn’t find a 9/11 connection.

He spoke with his justice minister, Anne McLellan.

What about Ressam?

He spoke with his solicitor general, Lawrence MacAulay.

One of the most experienced politicians in the world, Jean Chrétien didn’t have to be reminded that if a connection was found, the public response would be ugly.

Especially the response that would be coming from the Americans.

What’s more, even his staunchest denials of a connection would trigger calls of cover-ups.

Many people around Chrétien quickly rallied to his side.

In a classified cable to him from an overseas ambassador, he was warned that both the Canadian and American press would use the Ressam case to create a Canadian connection to 9/11, and that he had to get out in front of it.

The cable advised: Now is the time to put out quick, decisive messages to key U.S. media on the extensive network of cooperation that exists between Canadian and U.S. security, immigration, and customs authorities and the ways in which those already strong ties have been further reinforced since Ressam.

Even Chrétien’s Privy Council secretly warned that he needed to take control of the news cycles that were associating Canada with Ressam and the 9/11 hijackers. Not just in the States but also in Canada.

Chrétien knew that was necessary, but almost as soon as the second plane hit the South Tower, he also knew there would be politicians in the States, and the media in both nations, who would rush to link Canada, Ressam, and 9/11, no matter what the truth.

Representative Lamar Smith, the Republican chair of a House immigration subcommittee, labeled Canada a Club Med for terrorists.

Janet Napolitano, who would later serve as President Obama’s secretary of homeland security and was at the time U.S. attorney for the district of Arizona, implied that some terrorists were known to have entered the U.S. from Canada.

However, when she was specifically pressed about the 9/11 hijackers, she backed down, admitting that her previous comment was not correct.

But the worst of them was Senator John McCain, who would not back down.

In one of the greatest fabrications of 9/11 — of which there were all too many — he stated, categorically, that some of the 9/11 hijackers did come through Canada.

Leading the charge against McCain from Canada was none other than Giuliano Zaccardelli, who quickly became the public face of Canadian security cooperation with the United States. He openly, loudly, and categorically rejected any and all claims that some of the hijackers had entered the U.S. from Canada.

Adding insult to injury, when Chrétien finally got George Bush on the phone to express his condolences and offer any help Canada could give him, Bush didn’t bother to say thank you for taking in all those diverted planes and passengers.

Sitting in the back seat of the van racing back to Ottawa, David Collenette knew that if a jet crashed into the tallest building in New York, it was not an accident. That if a pilot was in trouble, he could either get back to an airport or ditch in the water surrounding the island of Manhattan. So for the next two hours, most of it on Highway 417, he was on his phone, understanding that he needed to make decisions that might put one part of his country in potential danger in order to protect the other part.

It was his deputy, Margaret Bloodworth, who announced the news to him that the FAA had halted all flight operations in the States. That they’d ordered all aircraft out of the sky.

That the Americans did this without consulting the Canadians, he couldn’t believe the disrespect.

That was a problem.

Bloodworth now suggested that all aircraft in Canadian airspace should also be ordered to land.

This had never been done before. It was never even an option in any emergency planning scenario. No one at Transport Canada knew how to manage this.

He dialed Chrétien to consult with him before he ordered the Canadian skies shut.

Chrétien told him that he didn’t need to be consulted; what Collenette was doing was absolutely right.

Collenette thought, maybe the Americans should have consulted with us before shutting everything down.

As far as he knew, the Americans had never done this before.

What’s more, he told himself, they almost certainly had no idea how to manage it. After all, it’s one thing to clear the skies of nearly 5,000 planes. It’s another thing to know where to land them. Especially planes coming across the Atlantic bound for U.S. cities.

He and Bloodworth were in agreement that in closing U.S. airspace, the FAA clearly hadn’t stopped to think what that meant to Canada.

Or to all those planes crossing the North Atlantic.

Or to all those passengers in those planes whose lives were going to be disrupted.

Or to the many airports in Canada that would have to figure out what to do with all these people.

That’s when he heard that a third hijacked plane had crashed into the Pentagon.

No one could say how many planes had been, or were about to be, hijacked. Nobody could say when the attacks might end.

The Americans ordered pilots in hundreds of planes over the North Atlantic, if they had the fuel, to turn around and go back to Europe.

But that still left something like 260 planes that didn’t have the fuel, or were already close to North American landfall.

They had to land somewhere. And with U.S. airspace closed — and the American authorities warning that any plane violating U.S. airspace could be shot down — Collenette realized they needed to land in Canada.

Compounding his worries, Collenette had no idea if any of those planes landing in Canada had been hijacked, or could be hijacked. He had no idea who was on any of those planes. He had no idea where a potential attack might be coming from.

He and Bloodworth decided they had to assume there were problems in at least some of the planes coming to Canada.

Throughout his drive back to Ottawa, David Collenette coordinated with his deputy Margaret Bloodworth.

They decided that the obvious spots for planes coming from Europe were East Coast airports, and that those planes needed to be grounded as quickly as possible. They also needed to keep planes away from Canada’s most populated areas, not just Montreal and Toronto but also the big cities of central Canada.

They agreed that after attacks in New York and Washington, other cities would be likely. That the terrorists wouldn’t go back to New York, they’d target other population centers, which could include Toronto and Montreal. Because they’d attacked Washington, it couldn’t be ruled out that they might target Ottawa.

Collenette worried that, even if Toronto and Montreal weren’t their targets, if a plane coming across the Atlantic and into Canadian airspace was carrying hijackers and they could somehow reach Toronto, it wasn’t very far in a large airliner from there to Rochester or Buffalo. Same for Montreal. From there, hijackers could get to Boston.

They decided they needed to put planes down as far away as they could and settled on Gander, St. John’s, Stephenville, and Goose Bay. Planes could also be brought into Halifax because the airport was far enough away from the city center.

But with that plan came a giant headache. There wasn’t much room at those smaller airports to park wide-bodied planes, and the runways would quickly turn into giant parking lots.

They calculated that 226 wide-bodied jets needed to land, and as big a landmass as Canada was, it just didn’t have enough runway and taxi room for all those planes.

But those were the cards they’d been dealt by the Americans, and those were the cards they had to play.

They had to figure out how to get enough customs and immigration officers to those airports, and maybe even medical people, because 33,000 unexpected guests were landing in Canada.

And they needed to be treated as guests. Even if nobody knew who those people actually were.

Collenette made the decision that once a plane landed in Canada, the passengers could not be let off. At least, not until they were properly screened. Then they’d have to leave their checked baggage on the plane. Once they were allowed off, if they were allowed off, they would be permitted to take one carry-on item.

After all, they didn’t know whether terrorists and hijackers were flying in. Collenette and Bloodworth had to believe that some people arriving on those planes might be.

And they had to be prepared for the real possibility that some of them were.

By the time Dave Collenette made it back to his office in Ottawa, Margaret Bloodworth had fully manned the SitCen — Situation Center — and it was busier than he’d ever seen it.

The ministry’s hub for managing emergencies and coordinating with airports, air traffic control centers, and other federal agencies during a transportation crisis was a windowless, secure room on the 14th floor of the ministry’s office block. On a normal day, there might be seven people manning the room.

Now 20, 30, sometimes 40 were in there.

The room consisted of six desks, each with multiple computer screens. At the back was the aviation desk, next to that the Marine desk, and then the land desk. In the middle of the room was the SitCen director’s desk. In front of him was the flight communications desk and the security communications desks.

Facing them, ON the front wall, were large screens showing flight tracking, other maps, real-time data, and news feeds.

Because there were so many people coming in and out, he and Bloodworth created a separate path system to control who could be there.

And it was still overcrowded.

It was the SitCen that coordinated airspace closures, worked on where diverted planes would be landed, and coordinated with agencies that were now vital for all this to happen, such as the RCMP, NAV Canada, and other federal ministries.

It was also, somewhere in the SitCen, where someone came up with a name for the diversion of those planes and the handling of those passengers.

They called it Operation Yellow Ribbon.

Jean Chrétien said he wanted to go to Parliament and address the Canadian people.

His staff agreed that would be a good idea and said they would work on a statement right away.

Chrétien said no, don’t worry, I know what I want to say.

He was not going to minimize what was happening in the States, but he felt his immediate role was to reassure Canadians. He had to be careful not to create any panic. That meant he wouldn’t say too much. That meant he would be measured and just right.

He went over it with his staff in the car to Parliament Hill.

When they got there, he was surprised to find it roped off.

A car with a package in the front seat was illegally parked and the police were going to blow it up.

Chrétien looked at it from far away and thought about the consequences of blowing it up — talk about sending a panic signal to the country — and felt intuitively that someone had made a mistake about parking.

The police insisted they needed to be prudent.

Chrétien said, leave it alone.

It turned out that he was right. A tourist had parked in the wrong place and the package in the front seat was a souvenir of Ottawa.

In his brief comments, Chrétien expressed condolences and sorrow; said that Canada stood with the United States; said that his government was working with communities to accommodate travelers stranded in Canada with food, shelter, and care; offered his full cooperation with America; and added that no one yet knew the identities of the attackers.

That last part wasn’t true. But there was so much uncertainty about what was happening in the States that even his staunchest political opponents let that one slide.

And while his political allies felt he’d gotten it just right, especially in his not wanting to spread any fears and worries, those opponents would say that his remarks were too brief and not substantial enough.

In the weeks to come, they were not about to give him a pass.

Especially if it involved Ahmed Ressam.

Media coverage would zero in on Ressam, using that to challenge Chrétien on immigration and refugee policies, and on national security.

How did Ressam get into the country with a false passport? How did he maintain his refugee status after getting arrested so many times for petty crimes? How did he get back into Canada after being thrown out? What about his associates who were still in Canada? What did Canadian intelligence and the Mounties and the local police in Montreal know, and when did they know it? What did they know now about other extremist networks in Canada? How vulnerable was Canada to foreign terror cells?

Ressam was in jail on 9/11 and had been for nearly two years.

But what about his association with any of the terrorists who’d blown up the United States?

Who else was still in Canada waiting to do the next 9/11?

Yellow Ribbon took off slowly.

David Collenette and Margaret Bloodworth had agreed that all the incoming planes would be sent to the most remote airports, landing them as quickly as possible and keeping them far away from Canada’s most populated areas, such as Montreal and Toronto, and the capital, Ottawa.

After all, if hijackers on planes coming to Canada assumed they’d lost their primary target in the United States, what was stopping them from finding a new target in Canada?

But landing all these diverted planes in remote airports was a double-edged sword.

The more remote the airport, the fewer people there to handle this influx of passengers. There weren’t enough customs agents to process 33,000 passengers spread out over eastern and northern Canada. Nor were there anywhere near enough immigration agents.

Without those people in place, they couldn’t let passengers off the planes.

Then, what about food? And personal items like medicines?

And clothes? If passengers couldn’t get their luggage, and they were stuck for several days, what were they going to do?

And what about accommodations? There weren’t enough hotels.

They all needed someplace to sleep. They needed cots and blankets. Many needed prescription drugs. Babies needed diapers and formula. They all needed food. And they would all want to use computers and cellphones to get in touch with loved ones.

Every airport would also eventually need enough fuel to get all those planes back in the air again and on their way home.

Then, what were these people stranded at these remote airports supposed to do all day? They weren’t prisoners. They needed to be treated like guests. Could the local authorities provide tours and entertainment and things to keep these people from going stir-crazy?

This was a nightmare in the making.

But the SitCen, together with the entirety of Transport Canada, Canadian Forces, Canada Customs, Canada Immigration, the RCMP, local law enforcement and emergency services, the prime minister’s office and his cabinet, hundreds of local airport officials, and literally hundreds of local community authorities all pulled together, working overtime to provide everything anyone imagined the passengers would need.

It all came down to this: How do you care for and feed 33,000 people from 238 planes when you don’t have enough resources already in place and those people don’t want to be where they are?

Operation Yellow Ribbon took off slowly, but once it began, it flew.

Canadians called what they did that day Operation Yellow Ribbon, evoking a welcoming sense of safety, care, and compassion.

Perhaps understandably, in Ottawa, both Jean Chrétien and David Collenette thought that at some point George Bush might publicly say thank you for stepping up, for taking in all those planes and caring for all those passengers.

It never happened.

That bothered Collenette.

The way he put it, when the world came calling on Canada, we opened our doors.
