For years the Army has been organized into four divisions primarily based on geography. The new structure, announced last year, takes effect Thursday and will see the Army reorganized into three divisions focused on foreign combat, home defence and infrastructure support.

Major-General Stéphane Masson, director-general of army capability development, said the restructuring is in response to a complex array of threats facing Canada − including competition among great powers − climate instability, technological advancements and lessons from allies at war.
“When you compile all that, we are at a pivoting point in Canada and for the defence of Canada,” Maj.-Gen. Masson said in a recent interview with The Globe and Mail.
The restructuring is part of a long-term effort by the Canadian Armed Forces to expand its ranks and prepare for the possibility of major conflict.

The pressure to shore up the military has increased over the past year and a half, as Ottawa works to make Canada less reliant on the United States for trade and defence in the face of U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade war and annexation rhetoric. Canada is ramping up its spending on military staffing and equipment to meet the higher defence investment targets agreed to last year by NATO members.

A Canadian Army Support Division in Kingston will be responsible for administrative support.
And finally, the Canadian Army Doctrine and Training Centre, also in Kingston, will lead training and professional military education.

stories.title: Ukraine's Zelenskyy to meet with Carney in Calgary, address cabinet in Banff
stories.summary: Calgary - Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is set to meet Prime Minister Mark Carney in Calgary this morning before addressing cabinet members gathered in Banff, Alta.
stories.author: Bill Graveland The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Calgary - Canada will work with Ukraine to produce millions of drones for the Canadian military, Prime Minister Mark Carney said Thursday in Calgary after meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

“I have to confess that our Armed Forces currently have but 2,000 drones in our inventory. In the years to come, we will need millions,” Carney said.

He also promised more air defence support for Ukraine, and the two nations signed joint statements on energy co-operation and defence.

“Canadians understand in our bones the importance of your struggle,” Carney told reporters, standing alongside Zelenskyy. “There is no qualification to our commitment. Because your cause — freedom, democracy, sovereignty — is our cause.”

The prime minister said the two countries finalized a $350-million agreement to deliver air defence interceptors through an American mechanism to help protect Ukraine from Russian airstrikes.

Carney also said Canada is launching a national drone marketplace for the Canadian Armed Forces and the Canadian Coast Guard. He said the marketplace will give Canada the capacity to produce “millions of drones within the next two years.”

“Today’s contracts will increase the number of drones available to the CAF tenfold,” he said.

“Importantly, one-third of all the drones we manufacture will go to support Ukraine’s defence of its homeland.”

Zelenskyy said on social media that the measures amount to more than $2 billion, including more than $1 billion for defence.

Carney said Ukrainian “ingenuity and courage” has led it to build drone companies that are world leaders, and those companies will teach Canadian firms. Ukraine will benefit from Canadian skills in manufacturing and artificial intelligence, he said.

“This is merely the first step toward our goal of ensuring Canadian industry has the capacity — the factories, supply chains, and key components — to produce millions of drones over the next two years,” his office added in a news release.

Zelenskyy said another drone deal with Canada should be finalized within weeks.

Russia launched its war on Ukraine in 2014 and expanded to a full-scale invasion in 2022.

Carney pointed out that “Ukraine had agreed to drastically reduce its arsenal in the wake of the breakup of the Soviet Union,” in exchange for an understanding that other countries would protect Ukraine from invasion.

He said Canada is also boosting its humanitarian support to help Ukraine meet its energy needs. Carney said the two countries have signed a “declaration for a 100-year partnership” that covers defence, trade, reconstruction and critical minerals.

Earlier, Zelenskyy told reporters he was thankful for the air-defence support.

“This is crucial. This is a big deficit in the world. We are thankful for this,” Zelenskyy said, praising Canada’s financial, diplomatic and moral support throughout the war.

“We are thankful that we have such strong partners as Canadians.”

Zelenskyy said he expects Moscow to intensify its attacks but insisted they won’t break Ukrainian resolve.

“Knowing Russia, when they hear that we have somewhere negotiations — with Europeans, with Canadians, with Americans — when they hear, they try to intensify attacks on us, just to break any kind of negotiations.”

Zelenskyy said his visit to Canada includes a discussion of preparations for winter, given the prospect of further Russian strikes on critical infrastructure. He was set later in the day to address federal cabinet members gathered in Banff, Alta.

Zelenskyy was also scheduled to travel to Toronto and North Bay, Ont. before departing Canada on Friday.

Carney noted the huge Ukrainian-Canadian population in Alberta and its contributions to many communities over decades.

“Ukrainians helped build this province, this country. And Canada will help rebuild Ukraine when peace comes,” Carney said.

Both nations also released a joint statement on liquefied natural gas, nuclear and green energy linking Ukraine’s recovery with Canadian economic growth.

The statement says the two countries “welcome dialogue with (the) Canadian private sector to facilitate long-term agreements on LNG supply from Canada to Ukraine.

“They note Ukraine’s significant underground gas storage capacity and its potential contribution to regional energy resilience.”

After answering questions from the media, Carney and Zelenskyy were given a drone demonstration from Ukrainian defence technology companies Airlogix and SkyFall.

Walking along gravel to a tented flatscreen TV outdoors, the two watched through the eyes of the drones.

“I wouldn’t mind if it were centred a little farther away from me,” Carney said with a laugh as the drones flew overhead.

The Kiel Institute, which measures global contributions to Ukraine, pegs Canada as the fourth most generous nation in raw dollars, and in 12th place based on gross domestic product. Canada’s donations include military aid, government financing and humanitarian support.

Ukraine has managed in recent months to hold back Russian advances and strike targets within Russia, including oil refineries and warehouses owned by Russia’s biggest online retailer.

Moscow has at times hinted at an end to the conflict, but Ukrainian and European officials have said the war should only end on terms that prevent Russia from rearming and attacking elsewhere.

Zelenskyy’s visit to Canada comes as European leaders argue Russia is widening its war through acts of sabotage, such as paying youths to vandalize railways. European airports have had to halt operations multiple times due to drone incursions attributed to Russia.

Across Europe, political parties once considered fringe over their support for Russia have seen their popularity increase as the continent tackles economic, environmental and migration crises.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 10, 2026.

— With files from Dylan Robertson in Ottawa

stories.title: Carney tells Zelenskyy Canada will help Ukraine rebuild
stories.summary: Calgary — Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy thanked Canada today for its support during the war with Russia.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
CALGARY — Canada will work with Ukraine to produce millions of drones for the Canadian military, Prime Minister Mark Carney said Thursday in Calgary after meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

“I have to confess that our Armed Forces currently have but 2,000 drones in our inventory. In the years to come, we will need millions,” Carney said.

He also promised more air defence support for Ukraine, and the two nations signed joint statements on energy co-operation and defence.

“Canadians understand in our bones the importance of your struggle,” Carney told reporters, standing alongside Zelenskyy. “There is no qualification to our commitment. Because your cause — freedom, democracy, sovereignty — is our cause.”

The prime minister said the two countries finalized a $350-million agreement to deliver air defence interceptors through an American mechanism to help protect Ukraine from Russian airstrikes.

Carney also said Canada is launching a national drone marketplace for the Canadian Armed Forces and the Canadian Coast Guard. He said the marketplace will give Canada the capacity to produce “millions of drones within the next two years.”

“Today’s contracts will increase the number of drones available to the CAF tenfold,” he said.

“Importantly, one-third of all the drones we manufacture will go to support Ukraine’s defence of its homeland.”

Zelenskyy said on social media that the measures amount to more than $2 billion, including more than $1 billion for defence.

Carney said Ukrainian “ingenuity and courage” has led it to build drone companies that are world leaders, and those companies will teach Canadian firms. Ukraine will benefit from Canadian skills in manufacturing and artificial intelligence, he said.

“This is merely the first step toward our goal of ensuring Canadian industry has the capacity — the factories, supply chains, and key components — to produce millions of drones over the next two years,” his office added in a news release.

Zelenskyy said another drone deal with Canada should be finalized within weeks.

Russia launched its war on Ukraine in 2014 and expanded to a full-scale invasion in 2022.

Carney pointed out that “Ukraine had agreed to drastically reduce its arsenal in the wake of the breakup of the Soviet Union,” in exchange for an understanding that other countries would protect Ukraine from invasion.

He said Canada is also boosting its humanitarian support to help Ukraine meet its energy needs. Carney said the two countries have signed a “declaration for a 100-year partnership” that covers defence, trade, reconstruction and critical minerals.

Earlier, Zelenskyy told reporters he was thankful for the air-defence support.

“This is crucial. This is a big deficit in the world. We are thankful for this,” Zelenskyy said, praising Canada’s financial, diplomatic and moral support throughout the war.

“We are thankful that we have such strong partners as Canadians.”

Zelenskyy said he expects Moscow to intensify its attacks but insisted they won’t break Ukrainian resolve.

“Knowing Russia, when they hear that we have somewhere negotiations — with Europeans, with Canadians, with Americans — when they hear, they try to intensify attacks on us, just to break any kind of negotiations.”

Zelenskyy said his visit to Canada includes a discussion of preparations for winter, given the prospect of further Russian strikes on critical infrastructure. He addressed federal cabinet members gathered in Banff, Alta., later in the day.

Zelenskyy was also scheduled to travel to Toronto and North Bay, Ont., before departing Canada on Friday.

Carney noted the huge Ukrainian-Canadian population in Alberta and its contributions to many communities over decades.

“Ukrainians helped build this province, this country. And Canada will help rebuild Ukraine when peace comes,” Carney said.

Both nations also released a joint statement on liquefied natural gas, nuclear and green energy linking Ukraine’s recovery with Canadian economic growth.

The statement says the two countries “welcome dialogue with (the) Canadian private sector to facilitate long-term agreements on LNG supply from Canada to Ukraine.

“They note Ukraine’s significant underground gas storage capacity and its potential contribution to regional energy resilience.”

After answering questions from the media, Carney and Zelenskyy were given a drone demonstration from Ukrainian defence technology companies Airlogix and SkyFall.

Walking along gravel to a tented flatscreen TV outdoors, the two watched through the eyes of the drones.

“I wouldn’t mind if it were centred a little farther away from me,” Carney said with a laugh as the drones flew overhead.

The Kiel Institute, which measures global contributions to Ukraine, pegs Canada as the fourth most generous nation in raw dollars, and in 12th place based on gross domestic product. Canada’s donations include military aid, government financing and humanitarian support.

Ukraine has managed in recent months to hold back Russian advances and strike targets within Russia, including oil refineries and warehouses owned by Russia’s biggest online retailer.

Moscow has at times hinted at an end to the conflict, but Ukrainian and European officials have said the war should only end on terms that prevent Russia from rearming and attacking elsewhere.

Zelenskyy’s visit to Canada comes as European leaders argue Russia is widening its war through acts of sabotage, such as paying youths to vandalize railways. European airports have had to halt operations multiple times due to drone incursions attributed to Russia.

Across Europe, political parties once considered fringe over their support for Russia have seen their popularity increase as the continent tackles economic, environmental and migration crises.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 10, 2026.

— With files from Dylan Robertson in Ottawa

Bill Graveland and Dayne Patterson, The Canadian Press

SDV[](http://www.thestar.com/news/canada/nova-scotia/n-s-mother-continues-son-s-fight-for-added-financial-help-for-people-living-in-tents/article_b2aa2467-f657-5429-b076-d8bea6a2eccb.html)

By Lyndsay Armstrong The Canadian Press

Jackie Lowe’s son, Bradley Lowe, died in 2023, years before he won a legal case on Aug. 5 that found that people living in tents were eligible for the enhanced provincial government support.

The Nova Scotia government responded to the Nova Scotia Court of Appeal ruling by changing the definition of housing to exclude people who live in tents, as was the case for Bradley Lowe.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Who’s downloading photos of your kid at dance competitions?

Image 9Image 10

But his mother said the government response was cruel and she is urging the province to reverse its decision and respect the ruling in her son’s case.

“He was fighting for change, because he saw others around him experiencing the same things he was,” Jackie Lowe said Wednesday.

The August ruling overturned a Nova Scotia Supreme Court decision last year that found Bradley Lowe did not meet the eligibility requirements for enhanced income assistance because he lived in a tent.

Jackie Lowe said her son would have celebrated the August decision, adding that he was someone who was always fighting for the underdog. The family pursued the case after he died with human rights lawyer Vince Calderhead.

Lowe spoke to reporters at a press conference held by the Opposition NDP on Wednesday.

The party introduced three bills related to housing, including one that they called “Bradley’s law.” NDP Leader Claudia Chender said Bradley’s law would overturn the province’s regulation change to allow those living in tents to access the enhanced assistance.

The government introduced the regulatory change to the definition of housing through an order-in-council filed about three weeks after the August court decision. The amended regulations remove the term “accommodation” and substitute it with “lives in a home.”

It also repeals the prior definition for “home” and defines it as a self-contained unit someone rents or owns, a room in a lodging house or a single-occupancy room in a building.

Calderhead, the human rights lawyer, said the province later made further changes to income assistance rules to make people with disabilities living in tents ineligible for a disability supplement.

An order-in-council, signed Sept. 3, changed the eligibility for this supplement to require that the person with a disability receiving the support “must live in a home or board.”

Calderhead said he asked the Nova Scotia Human Rights Commission to investigate this “discriminatory” action.

“This move sends a clear message that people with disabilities living in these very vulnerable circumstances are not as worthy, indeed, are not equal in consideration; in other words: they are not really people — at least not equal in terms of dignity and respect,” Calderhead said in an email Tuesday.

Susan Corkum-Greek, minister of opportunities and social development, said the department was making changes to regulations to provide more clarity in its language so the program can be administered consistently.

Lowe asked members of Premier Tim Houston’s Progressive Conservative government to put themselves in the shoes of someone who is homeless and living in a tent and consider how they would survive on her son’s income assistance rate — which was $380 a month.

The new base income assistance rate has since risen to $410 per month.

Corkum-Greek said she heard about Lowe’s remarks on Wednesday and has reached out in hopes of speaking with her.

“I won’t know until I meet her, but I think we would have a lot of shared space. Because I do want to get the supports that people need, I want to get them access to those supports,” the minister said in an interview Wednesday.

She added that raising the rates of income assistance is a “constant” conversation in her department.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 10, 2026.

The Canadian Press

By Lyndsay Armstrong The Canadian Press
Jackie Lowe’s son, Bradley Lowe, died in 2023, years before he won a legal case on Aug. 5 that found that people living in tents were eligible for the enhanced provincial government support.
The Nova Scotia government responded to the Nova Scotia Court of Appeal ruling by changing the definition of housing to exclude people who live in tents, as was the case for Bradley Lowe.
ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW
Who’s downloading photos of your kid at dance competitions?
Image 9Image 10
But his mother said the government response was cruel and she is urging the province to reverse its decision and respect the ruling in her son’s case.
“He was fighting for change, because he saw others around him experiencing the same things he was,” Jackie Lowe said Wednesday.

The August ruling overturned a Nova Scotia Supreme Court decision last year that found Bradley Lowe did not meet the eligibility requirements for enhanced income assistance because he lived in a tent.

Jackie Lowe said her son would have celebrated the August decision, adding that he was someone who was always fighting for the underdog. The family pursued the case after he died with human rights lawyer Vince Calderhead.
Lowe spoke to reporters at a press conference held by the Opposition NDP on Wednesday.

The party introduced three bills related to housing, including one that they called “Bradley’s law.” NDP Leader Claudia Chender said Bradley’s law would overturn the province’s regulation change to allow those living in tents to access the enhanced assistance.

The government introduced the regulatory change to the definition of housing through an order-in-council filed about three weeks after the August court decision. The amended regulations remove the term “accommodation” and substitute it with “lives in a home.”
It also repeals the prior definition for “home” and defines it as a self-contained unit someone rents or owns, a room in a lodging house or a single-occupancy room in a building.
Calderhead, the human rights lawyer, said the province later made further changes to income assistance rules to make people with disabilities living in tents ineligible for a disability supplement.
An order-in-council, signed Sept. 3, changed the eligibility for this supplement to require that the person with a disability receiving the support “must live in a home or board.”
Calderhead said he asked the Nova Scotia Human Rights Commission to investigate this “discriminatory” action.

“This move sends a clear message that people with disabilities living in these very vulnerable circumstances are not as worthy, indeed, are not equal in consideration; in other words: they are not really people — at least not equal in terms of dignity and respect,” Calderhead said in an email Tuesday.

Susan Corkum-Greek, minister of opportunities and social development, said the department was making changes to regulations to provide more clarity in its language so the program can be administered consistently.

Lowe asked members of Premier Tim Houston’s Progressive Conservative government to put themselves in the shoes of someone who is homeless and living in a tent and consider how they would survive on her son’s income assistance rate — which was $380 a month.
The new base income assistance rate has since risen to $410 per month.
Corkum-Greek said she heard about Lowe’s remarks on Wednesday and has reached out in hopes of speaking with her.

“I won’t know until I meet her, but I think we would have a lot of shared space. Because I do want to get the supports that people need, I want to get them access to those supports,” the minister said in an interview Wednesday.
She added that raising the rates of income assistance is a “constant” conversation in her department.

stories.title: Distilleries to bear brunt of U.S. ban on Canadian booze: experts
stories.summary: Distilleries and spirit makers are likely to be the hardest hit among Canadian alcohol producers as the United States proposes a broad ban on Canadian booze starting later this month.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Distilleries and spirit makers are likely to be the hardest hit among Canadian alcohol producers as the United States proposes a broad ban on Canadian booze starting later this month.

Craig Johnston, chief economist at Farm Credit Canada, said distilleries ship more than half of their overall product across the border.

“If you think about different categories of the alcohol industry — distilleries, wineries and breweries — it’s really distilleries which have significant exposure to the U.S. market,” he said.

Johnston said it will be challenging for many distilleries that sell stateside to find alternative homes for their products domestically, in Europe or elsewhere.

Canada’s retaliatory duties earlier this week prompted U.S. President Donald Trump to ban most imports of Canadian alcohol, among a long list of other items, starting Sept. 29.

Canadian whisky and liqueur in bottles larger than four litres will be exempt from the ban; however, Cal Bricker of trade association Spirits Canada said there are not many four-litre bottles that get sold anyway.

“For all intents and purposes, it’s more or less a ban on Canadian whisky,” he said in an interview.

Spirits Canada represents manufacturers, marketers and exporters in the industry.

The solution for distilleries is not as easy as moving production south of the border, because of legal agreements and intertwined supply chains, Bricker said.

“You can only make Canadian whisky in Canada. You can only make American whiskey bourbon in the U.S. And you can make tequila in Mexico,” he said.

That’s true for alcohol producers like Diageo, for instance, which makes Crown Royal domestically, Bulleit Bourbon in the United States and Don Julio tequila in Mexico.

“A hundred years ago, you could identify a company in a country and target it and hit it specifically and hurt it,” Bricker said.

“You can’t really do that now because the supply chain is so integrated that if you’re trying to retaliate against Diageo in the United States, well, it’s one balance sheet that manages the whole business.”

So far, Bricker said he hasn’t heard from any of the 11 distilleries and spirit makers represented by the association about moving production south of the border.

Andrew Oland, chief executive of Moosehead Breweries, said he wasn’t surprised but still “very disappointed” to see alcohol further dragged into the latest trade escalation.

Oland, who heads the Saint John, N.B.-based brewery, said 15 per cent of its beverages get shipped south and are already facing steep duties after trade negotiations between the two countries fell apart last month.

The brewery is currently absorbing the cost of 50 per cent tariffs and focusing on shipping as much beer as possible over the next three weeks to preserve its shelf space and relationship with U.S. retailers.

“If our beer is not on the shelf in the United States, they’ll quickly put someone else’s beer on, and it can be really tough to regain that shelf space,” he said.

But Oland said he is more of a “beer glass half full” type of person and hopes the situation will resolve before the ban kicks in. At the same time, he said the brewery has been preparing for the long run and looking for marketing beyond the United States.

Robert Carter, a food industry analyst at the StratonHunter Group, said the threatened move has the potential to erase years of work for some smaller players with retail presence stateside.

“They’ve built pretty strong relationships with the U.S. distributors, restaurants and whatnot,” he said. “This is going to impact them more aggressively than some of the others.”

Between April 2024 and March 2025, Canada imported $1 billion in alcohol from the United States, down 5.4 per cent from the previous fiscal year, Statistics Canada data shows. Exports to south of the border totalled $1.4 billion, up 4.1 per cent year-over-year.

While some brewers could face challenging times ahead, Canadian beer is overwhelmingly a domestic industry, said Luke Chapman, vice-president of federal affairs at the trade association Beer Canada.

Last year, for instance, more than 90 per cent of all beer bought in Canada was brewed within the country with domestic ingredients, Chapman said.

“Canada’s brewing industry is far less dependent on the U.S. market than many other Canadian industries.”

Meanwhile, the wine industry is also expected to escape the worst effects of the potential ban, said Norman Beal, board chair of Ontario Craft Wineries, which represents more than 110 wineries in the province.

Beal said only about one per cent of all wine sales come from the United States.

“Canadian wine producers, we’re relatively small,” Beal said. “Most of our products are sold right here in Canada.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 10, 2026.

Ritika Dubey, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Netflix series ‘Below’ blends Newfoundland heart and Atlantic noir at Tiff
stories.summary: Toronto — In “Below,” an upcoming Newfoundland-set Netflix miniseries, the horrors under the sea are just the tip of the iceberg.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
By Sandra Ezekwesili, The Canadian Press

Posted September 10, 2026 4:00 am.

Last Updated September 10, 2026 5:30 am.

Toronto — In “Below,” an upcoming Newfoundland-set Netflix miniseries, the horrors under the sea are just the tip of the iceberg.

Jesse McKeown is the creator of the show, which falls into the North Atlantic noir sub-genre but also explores current-day issues such as communities losing their livelihoods, climate change and family displacement. It premieres at the Toronto International Film Festival on Thursday.

“Below” is set in Snook’s Arm, a close-knit town whose few remaining residents are debating whether to leave for good.

Newfoundland is special to McKeown. His wife is a Newfoundlander; they live there on and off, and he has felt a pull to write about it for 18 years.

“There are a number of reasons why I think I always wanted to make something there,” he said. “It was that kind of crazy contrast between how unforgiving and scary the landscape was, and just how warm and fun and inviting the people and the community were.”

Warm and inviting, like show protagonist Calvin Penney (played by Josh Hartnett) and his youngest son Wade (Charlie Heaton), running an Airbnb for mainland tourists.

McKeown compares Calvin to the iceberg: “You only see this much, but then he’s got a lot of stuff going on below the surface.” And it’s in watching Calvin that we gradually see the horror haunting the waters around Snook’s Arm.

“At its heart, ‘Below’ is about a fisherman who can’t fish because there’s no fish left, so he’s been forced to adapt,” said McKeown. “He’s had to figure out other ways of making a living on the water, and that’s when he starts to notice that there are strange things happening.”

Calvin’s life weaves across all the major themes of the show. Like the loss of fishing — first from overfishing, and then a decades-long moratorium meant to restore cod stocks. Calvin’s son Wade represents a generation that feels alienated from a true working-class identity — he tells their Airbnb guests he’s never fished in his life but considers himself a fisherman.

Ironically, melting glaciers have given Calvin a new living: selling ice to vodka makers. This substitute for fishing keeps him happy at sea yet brings him closer to the horrors below.

“Below” also explores two real-world provincial government programs: Resettlement and Come Home Year.

With resettlement – government-led in the 1950s to 1970s, and community-initiated in this century – residents receive financial support if they’re willing to relocate from isolated communities that are considered unsustainable.

The show opens with a family on a boat, towing their house behind them.

“So many families now are directly affected by resettlement,” McKeown said. “If you spend any time there, or if you grew up there, that image of the house floating on the ocean is a key image,” he said.

The screenwriter reflected on the power of the visual for him: “There’s something about that image of the house on the water and a family pulling everything, the whole world, sort of, ON their backs that really spoke to me. That’s why we open the show with that image.”

The real-life Snook’s Arm was resettled in 2018, when its last 10 people took the deal. But the Snook’s Arm of “Below” has held on for six years after that, because of dwindling holdouts. They include Calvin and his sister Ruth, played by Willow Kean, a Labradorian actor, novelist and playwright.

While resettlement moved some Newfoundlanders from their communities, Come Home Year is about bringing others back to the province. The show is set during a Come Home Year, with Calvin’s daughter Mary (Ruby Stokes) and son Jay (Rohan Campbell) visiting from the mainland, and Calvin contemplating a future where he gets them to stay.

McKeown is a seasoned screenwriter, recently serving as co-showrunner on Season 4 of Netflix’s “The Umbrella Academy,” but “Below” is his first time as showrunner on a series he created.

“This was the first thing that really felt like, OK, for better or worse, this is my show. I pitched it. It’s very personal to me. It’s not based on anything else, so love it or hate it, this is my thing.”

He says he leaned into this sense of ownership for the project. “In how I do my job day to day, it’s so much easier because it’s all coming from me. I can speak directly to the vision of the show and how I want it to go.”

Shot on location in St. John’s, the production leverages Newfoundland and Labrador’s deep bench of screen talent, ON both sides of the camera. Comedian and writer Mary Walsh, of “This Hour Has 22 Minutes” fame, plays the mayor.

“There is a small but really strong film and television community there. One of the best, strongest, and punching above its weight class, artistic communities in Canada is in St. John’s,” McKeown said.

But the Toronto-born screenwriter is also thrilled to return to the city for Tiff and see his project open the festival’s Primetime lineup.

‘’It feels like a weird kind of homecoming, like a full-circle kind of thing,” McKeown said, referring to a return to the festival where he premiered his first-ever short, two decades ago.

While “Below” is an authentic Newfoundland story, McKeown believes it connects through common themes felt across Canada and abroad.

Posted September 10, 2026 4:00 am.
Last Updated September 10, 2026 5:30 am.
Toronto — In “Below,” an upcoming Newfoundland-set Netflix miniseries, the horrors under the sea are just the tip of the iceberg.

Jesse McKeown is the creator of the show, which falls into the North Atlantic noir sub-genre but also explores current-day issues such as communities losing their livelihoods, climate change and family displacement. It premieres at the Toronto International Film Festival on Thursday.
“Below” is set in Snook’s Arm, a close-knit town whose few remaining residents are debating whether to leave for good.
Newfoundland is special to McKeown. His wife is a Newfoundlander; they live there on and off, and he has felt a pull to write about it for 18 years.

“There are a number of reasons why I think I always wanted to make something there,” he said. “It was that kind of crazy contrast between how unforgiving and scary the landscape was, and just how warm and fun and inviting the people and the community were.”
Warm and inviting, like show protagonist Calvin Penney (played by Josh Hartnett) and his youngest son Wade (Charlie Heaton), running an Airbnb for mainland tourists.

McKeown compares Calvin to the iceberg: “You only see this much, but then he’s got a lot of stuff going on below the surface.” And it’s in watching Calvin that we gradually see the horror haunting the waters around Snook’s Arm.

“At its heart, ‘Below’ is about a fisherman who can’t fish because there’s no fish left, so he’s been forced to adapt,” said McKeown. “He’s had to figure out other ways of making a living on the water, and that’s when he starts to notice that there are strange things happening.”

Calvin’s life weaves across all the major themes of the show. Like the loss of fishing — first from overfishing, and then a decades-long moratorium meant to restore cod stocks. Calvin’s son Wade represents a generation that feels alienated from a true working-class identity — he tells their Airbnb guests he’s never fished in his life but considers himself a fisherman.
Ironically, melting glaciers have given Calvin a new living: selling ice to vodka makers. This substitute for fishing keeps him happy at sea yet brings him closer to the horrors below.
“Below” also explores two real-world provincial government programs: Resettlement and Come Home Year.

With resettlement – government-led in the 1950s to 1970s, and community-initiated in this century – residents receive financial support if they’re willing to relocate from isolated communities that are considered unsustainable.
The show opens with a family on a boat, towing their house behind them.

“So many families now are directly affected by resettlement,” McKeown said. “If you spend any time there, or if you grew up there, that image of the house floating on the ocean is a key image,” he said.

The screenwriter reflected on the power of the visual for him: “There’s something about that image of the house on the water and a family pulling everything, the whole world, sort of, ON their backs that really spoke to me. That’s why we open the show with that image.”

The real-life Snook’s Arm was resettled in 2018, when its last 10 people took the deal. But the Snook’s Arm of “Below” has held on for six years after that, because of dwindling holdouts. They include Calvin and his sister Ruth, played by Willow Kean, a Labradorian actor, novelist and playwright.

While resettlement moved some Newfoundlanders from their communities, Come Home Year is about bringing others back to the province. The show is set during a Come Home Year, with Calvin’s daughter Mary (Ruby Stokes) and son Jay (Rohan Campbell) visiting from the mainland, and Calvin contemplating a future where he gets them to stay.
McKeown is a seasoned screenwriter, recently serving as co-showrunner on Season 4 of Netflix’s “The Umbrella Academy,” but “Below” is his first time as showrunner on a series he created.

“This was the first thing that really felt like, OK, for better or worse, this is my show. I pitched it. It’s very personal to me. It’s not based on anything else, so love it or hate it, this is my thing.”

He says he leaned into this sense of ownership for the project. “In how I do my job day to day, it’s so much easier because it’s all coming from me. I can speak directly to the vision of the show and how I want it to go.”

Shot on location in St. John’s, the production leverages Newfoundland and Labrador’s deep bench of screen talent, ON both sides of the camera. Comedian and writer Mary Walsh, of “This Hour Has 22 Minutes” fame, plays the mayor.

“There is a small but really strong film and television community there. One of the best, strongest, and punching above its weight class, artistic communities in Canada is in St. John’s,” McKeown said.
But the Toronto-born screenwriter is also thrilled to return to the city for Tiff and see his project open the festival’s Primetime lineup.
‘’It feels like a weird kind of homecoming, like a full-circle kind of thing,” McKeown said, referring to a return to the festival where he premiered his first-ever short, two decades ago.
While “Below” is an authentic Newfoundland story, McKeown believes it connects through common themes felt across Canada and abroad.
“I wanted to tap into a feeling we all have right now: that we’re sort of living on the precipice. That we’re all sort of living on the brink of something.”
For him, perhaps the true horror of “Below” is that there are “a lot of people like the Penney family who are living in very precarious situations.”
“Below” screens at Tiff on Thursday, Friday and Sept. 19, and streams globally on Netflix Oct. 8.

stories.title: Sept. 11 attack anniversary reminder of Canada-U.S. ties, St. Catharines mayor says
stories.summary: The lingering grief caused by 9/11 terror attacks is a reminder of strong ties between Canadian and American people despite the current political climate and trade tensions, said the mayor of St. Catharines, Ont., as the city expands its memorial for victims.
stories.author: Maan Alhmidi The Canadian Press
stories.content:
ST. CATHARINES - The lingering grief caused by the 9/11 terror attacks is a reminder of the strong ties between Canadian and American people even as political and economic tensions flare, the mayor of St. Catharines, Ont., said as the city marked an expansion of its Sept. 11 memorial walking trail on Thursday.

Sept. 10, 2026

By Maan Alhmidi The Canadian Press

Friday marks 25 years since nearly 3,000 people were killed when al-Qaida hijackers slammed planes into the World Trade Center towers in New York and crashed into the Pentagon and a Pennsylvania field.

The anniversary comes amid an escalating trade war between Canada and the United States, but Mayor Mat Siscoe said the relationship between the two countries’ people remains stronger than any trade conflict.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Who’s downloading photos of your kid at dance competitions?

Image 9Image 10

“At the end of the day, I think Canadians view American citizens as brothers, and cousins, and sisters,” Siscoe said in an interview.

“The words and the actions of our governments, I don’t think, will necessarily affect that.”

Siscoe and the U.S. consul general for Toronto, Baxter Hunt, along with other dignitaries, participated in a tree planting at the 9/11 memorial trail at Happy Rolph’s Animal Farm in St. Catharines’ north end, overlooking Lake Ontario.

Siscoe said the memorial trail, which opened in 2006, has trees honouring 24 Canadians and three U.S. citizens with family in Canada who were killed in the attacks. The city wanted to commemorate survivors and first responders by planting nine more trees this year.

“Each tree’s plaque honours one of those Canadians killed, providing a lasting memorial to their memory,” he said.

Siscoe said the plaques on the newly planted trees read: “In memory of all who lost their lives and in honour of the courage of survivors and responders dedicated on the 25th anniversary of Sept. 11, 2001.”

Hunt said Canada’s response to 9/11 attacks was spontaneous, generous and deeply human.

“It reminded us in our darkest hour that we were not alone. Canadians were there for us, and we will never forget that,” he said.

“Twenty-four Canadians lost their lives in those attacks, and I’m really grateful to be here today at the 9/11 Memorial Trail to recognize and honour them in solidarity with our Canadian friends and neighbours.”

Hunt said he was touched to see the care that city staff have provided to the memorial trees.

“Though 9/11 is a story of loss and tragedy, it is also a story of resilience, and the trees on this memorial walkway are a beautiful reminder not only of the lives lost, but also of all that we have overcome,” he said.

A Canadian flag permanently flies at half-mast at the memorial trail, which also has a “tree of peace.” The trees honouring the victims have plaques listing their names, ages, birthplaces and where they died that day.

“This is the most significant terrorist attack that’s taken place on ... North American soil,” Siscoe said.

“Given the Canadian connection and our proximity to the American border, we thought that it was an appropriate place to commemorate them.”

On the day of the attacks, more than 200 planes were diverted to Canadian airports, most notably in Gander, N.L., which famously took in 38 passenger planes carrying more than 6,500 travellers after U.S. airspace was closed.

Three days after the attack, 80,000 people crowded Parliament Hill for a national day of mourning, according to a police estimate reported by The Canadian Press that week.

The Canadian Red Cross sent 146 volunteers to help on the ground in New York and hundreds of Canadian firefighters and police officers went to support the survivors and assist in the recovery efforts.

Siscoe said he hopes the memory of the attacks brings the people on both sides of the border closer.

“I think this was a grief borne predominantly by residents of the United States, but it was a grief shared by Canadians, and so I think if nothing else, this is a recognition that the ties that bind our peoples are a lot stronger than any trade war,” he said.

“I hope that our memories of this are a reminder that we are still two of the closest nations in the history of the world, and we have a lot of shared history together.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 10, 2026.

A Canadian flag permanently flies at half-mast at the memorial trail, which also has a “tree of peace.” The trees honouring the victims have plaques listing their names, ages, birthplaces and where they died that day.
“This is the most significant terrorist attack that’s taken place on ... North American soil,” Siscoe said.
“Given the Canadian connection and our proximity to the American border, we thought that it was an appropriate place to commemorate them.”

On the day of the attacks, more than 200 planes were diverted to Canadian airports, most notably in Gander, N.L., which famously took in 38 passenger planes carrying more than 6,500 travellers after U.S. airspace was closed.
Three days after the attack, 80,000 people crowded Parliament Hill for a national day of mourning, according to a police estimate reported by The Canadian Press that week.

The Canadian Red Cross sent 146 volunteers to help on the ground in New York and hundreds of Canadian firefighters and police officers went to support the survivors and assist in the recovery efforts.
Siscoe said he hopes the memory of the attacks brings the people on both sides of the border closer.

“I think this was a grief borne predominantly by residents of the United States, but it was a grief shared by Canadians, and so I think if nothing else, this is a recognition that the ties that bind our peoples are a lot stronger than any trade war,” he said.
“I hope that our memories of this are a reminder that we are still two of the closest nations in the history of the world, and we have a lot of shared history together.”
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 10, 2026.

stories.title: Edmonton Oilers lose support of superfan 'Mama Stanley' after Formenton signing
stories.summary: Edmonton - The Edmonton Oilers announcement to sign a former Team Canada junior player acquitted of sexual assault last year has come as a massive bodycheck to one longtime superfan.
stories.author: Aaron Sousa The Canadian Press
stories.content:
EDMONTON - The Edmonton Oilers’ decision to sign a former Team Canada junior player acquitted of sexual assault last year has come as a massive body check to one longtime superfan.

Mary Loewen — affectionately known among Oilers fans as “Mama Stanley” for dressing as a sequined Stanley Cup during the playoffs — took to social media to say she’d no longer support the team.

The Oilers, meanwhile, are defending the signing in direct emails to fans who have complained about the decision.

“I am deeply disappointed by the Edmonton Oilers’ decision to sign Alex Formenton,” Loewen’s post Wednesday says.

“Although he was acquitted in court, I cannot ignore my conscience or what this decision represents to me.”

Loewen did not respond to a request for an interview.

The NHL team announced earlier Wednesday it had signed Formenton to a one-year contract worth US$850,000. He was one of five players from Canada’s 2018 world junior team accused of sexual assault.

The charges stemmed from an encounter with a woman after a Hockey Canada gala in London, Ont. All five players were acquitted following a trial last year. The NHL later reinstated them, allowing them to resume playing beginning Dec. 1, 2025.

After the signing, Formenton said he was grateful to join the team after what he called a “difficult road.”

A longtime hockey fan, Loewen caught Oiler fever during the team’s heyday in the mid-1980s, when the team won its first of five Stanley Cups.

In recent years, she developed the Mama Stanley persona and has been a regular fixture at Oilers games, with other team diehards posing for pictures with her.

Some of her fans live as far away as Germany and Australia.

Loewen’s post Wednesday says her decision to no longer support the Oilers isn’t tied to the team’s already-signed players, but to management’s decision to bring on Formenton.

She says she feels betrayed and that she’s lost a team she’s supported for most of her life.

“As a sexual assault survivor, I must stand by my morals and stand with the woman at the centre of this case,” she said.

“For that reason, as long as Formenton remains an Oiler, I CANNOT AND WILL NOT support or cheer for this team.”

The Oilers defended the signing by pointing to what they described as a “lengthy due diligence process,” Formenton’s acquittal and his reinstatement by the NHL and Hockey Canada.

In an email to a fan, the Oilers’ ticketing and customer service team said the organization reviewed the legal proceedings, the NHL and Hockey Canada processes and “all of the information available” before making its decision.

“The team also spoke directly to Alex and those close to the matter,” the email read.

The organization said it was “comfortable providing Alex with the opportunity to return to the NHL as a member of the Edmonton Oilers.”

“Alex is grateful for the opportunity and, like every Oilers player, he is expected to uphold the standards and expectations of our organization,” the team wrote. “The Edmonton Oilers remain committed to fostering a respectful, professional and positive environment for our players, staff and fans.”

The Oilers were eliminated from the first round of last season’s Stanley Cup playoffs after a 5-2 Game 6 loss to the Anaheim Ducks. The team fell in the final in both 2024 and 2025 to the Florida Panthers.

Loewen’s post did not state whether she’d back another team. She ended her post by saying she was still “Mama Stanley.”

“Mama Stanley belongs to ME — not the Edmonton Oilers organization,” she said.

“She represents BELIEVE, kindness, children, survivors and community. I will not abandon her or EVER compromise her values.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 9, 2026.

Note to readers:This is a corrected story. An earlier version of this story stated that sexual assault charges against Alex Formenton and four other former world junior hockey players were dropped. The five players were acquitted following a trial in 2025.

TD is, after 30 years, ending its scholarship program that awarded up to $70,000 to Canadian students who were leaders in making community change.

ByJanet Hurley Senior Writer

One of the richest corporate scholarships available to post-secondary students in Canada is coming to an end after 30 years.

TD announced this week that it is cancelling itsScholarships for Community Leadership program. The program provided up to $70,000 in tuition and living expenses over four years as well as an opportunity for paid summer employment to students who demonstrated outstanding commitment to their communities.

Ranked among the most generous undergraduate awards, it was surpassed only by the Schulich Leader Scholarships, worth up to $120,000, and the Loran Scholar Experience, valued at $150,000, both administered by private foundations and considered the most coveted of their kind.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Who’s downloading photos of your kid at dance competitions?

TD spokesperson Vandana Fatima Kattar told the Star that the bank is increasing its community giving to “programs that help young people build skills, gain experience and strengthen their confidence in the future,” citing barriers facing youth, “including access to meaningful employment opportunities.”

Kattar, who said the bank is proud of the scholarship’s legacy,did not say how much the program cost annually, or what specifically these “evolving” youth-focused investments will look like in practice, but TD did say, on its website, that it will honour all existing commitments to current scholars.

Stephanie Ikharia will be among the last cohort to receive the award.

The Markham student had a Grade 12 average in the mid-90s but it was her initiative and leadership that set her apart: She relaunched a Black Students’ Association at her high school, served as a Black youth liaison with the city and organized a Boys to Men event focused on mentoring youth through conversation and sport.

Ontario students say shifting OSAP from grants to loans is forcing them to defer degrees or drop out of school.

This week, the 17-year-old started her first year of study in integrated business and humanities at McMaster University, a decision her $70,000 scholarship made possible.

“It gave me a freedom of choice, just to really decide what was best for me, regardless of finances,” she said. “It was a huge relief for me and my family, but also I felt very proud of myself for having accomplished that.”

She has already met up with scholarship alumni at McMaster and understands that while there are reasons for TD’s decision, she “is sad the way things have turned out.”

The award cancellation comes as students face a tightening financial landscape. In Ontario, the government this year invested $6.4 billion in the post-secondary sector over four years, but it also overhauled OSAP, shifting financial aid from mostly nonrepayable grants to loans. The province also lifted a seven-year tuition freeze, allowing universities to raise domestic tuition by up to two per cent annually for three years.

The pressures extend beyond Ontario. In Quebec, out-of-province students at English-language universities have faced a significant tuition hike; meanwhile, students in Alberta are worried that recentchanges to the provincial loan programwill create “a financial barrier.”

A 2024 survey from TD Bank Group itself found 65 per cent of Canadian students “define themselves as financially unstable and nearly half are currently unable to adequately cover basic needs such as food and housing.”

Margaret de Leon, a PhD candidate at OISE whose research examines post-secondary financial aid policy, told the Star that the TD program was “particularly significant” because it combined financial aid with employment opportunities, mentorship and a national network.

“There are relatively few undergraduate awards in Canada that provide that level of sustained support,” she said, adding that the program “created a particular pathway for students whose accomplishments were demonstrated through service and leadership. Its disappearance, therefore, leaves a gap that cannot simply be filled by directing students toward another scholarship application.”

Since the program launched in 1995, 620 Canadians in their final year of high school or CEGEP have benefited. In May, TD announced the 20 recipients of its 2026 scholarships, including seven from Ontario, but gave no indication then that the program was ending.

TD posted a standout quarter among Canada’s six top banks.

At that time, Alicia Johnston, TD’s vice-president, public affairs, noted, “We are inspired by the passion, talent and heart that these students bring to their communities. TD is proud to champion the next generation of Canadian leaders, and we can’t wait to see what they do next.”

This article was updated from a previous version to note that following publication, TD clarified that all funds from the cancelled scholarship will be directed to support programs for youth to build skills and experience.

Janet Hurley is a Toronto Star journalist and senior writer covering culture, education and societal trends. She is based in Toronto. Reach her via email: jhurley@thestar.ca.

This week, the 17-year-old started her first year of study in integrated business and humanities at McMaster University, a decision her $70,000 scholarship made possible.

“It gave me a freedom of choice, just to really decide what was best for me, regardless of finances,” she said. “It was a huge relief for me and my family, but also I felt very proud of myself for having accomplished that.”
She has already met up with scholarship alumni at McMaster and understands that while there are reasons for TD’s decision, she “is sad the way things have turned out.”

The award cancellation comes as students face a tightening financial landscape. In Ontario, the government this year invested $6.4 billion in the post-secondary sector over four years, but it also overhauled OSAP, shifting financial aid from mostly nonrepayable grants to loans. The province also lifted a seven-year tuition freeze, allowing universities to raise domestic tuition by up to two per cent annually for three years.

The pressures extend beyond Ontario. In Quebec, out-of-province students at English-language universities have faced a significant tuition hike; meanwhile, students in Alberta are worried that recentchanges to the provincial loan programwill create “a financial barrier.”

A 2024 survey from TD Bank Group itself found 65 per cent of Canadian students “define themselves as financially unstable and nearly half are currently unable to adequately cover basic needs such as food and housing.”

Margaret de Leon, a PhD candidate at OISE whose research examines post-secondary financial aid policy, told the Star that the TD program was “particularly significant” because it combined financial aid with employment opportunities, mentorship and a national network.
The Star, simplified

“There are relatively few undergraduate awards in Canada that provide that level of sustained support,” she said, adding that the program “created a particular pathway for students whose accomplishments were demonstrated through service and leadership. Its disappearance, therefore, leaves a gap that cannot simply be filled by directing students toward another scholarship application.”

Since the program launched in 1995, 620 Canadians in their final year of high school or CEGEP have benefited. In May, TD announced the 20 recipients of its 2026 scholarships, including seven from Ontario, but gave no indication then that the program was ending.
TD posted a standout quarter among Canada’s six top banks.

At that time, Alicia Johnston, TD’s vice-president, public affairs, noted, “We are inspired by the passion, talent and heart that these students bring to their communities. TD is proud to champion the next generation of Canadian leaders, and we can’t wait to see what they do next.”

Nathan Denette/Canadian Press file photo [](http://www.thestar.com/news/canada/ontario-is-offering-universities-and-colleges-40-000-new-spots-here-s-how-they-were-allocated/article_cc6fd46e-1ea2-4214-807c-6da2d8207da3.html)

ByKristin Rushowy Senior Writer

Georgian College in Barrie had the support of a high-voltage transformer manufacturer for its trades program; an aerospace company liked the aviation offerings at Mohawk in Hamilton; and a tech innovator was behind Carleton University’s bids for funding for more STEM degree spots.

In what was akin to a post-secondary version of “Dragons’ Den”in anew process to allocate 40,000 new spaces— in high-needs areas such as science/technology, health, education and the trades— the province put out a call for proposals from universities and colleges that saw them collaborate with communities before submitting plans to be evaluated by a 40-person ministry team.

While concerns have been raised about the focus on science and technology over the humanities— and the transferable skills taught in those programs that many employers, especially in AI, have said they value— the government says the new priority growth plans are to address what students want as well as workforce needs.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Who’s downloading photos of your kid at dance competitions?

Image 10Image 11

“We wanted to ensure the institutions really understood that we want this to be driven by the local economy of the communities that these institutions serve,” Colleges and Universities Minister Nolan Quinn said in an interview on Wednesday, in advance of his Thursday morning announcement in Hamilton about the new spaces.

“It was a process of back-and-forth, there was a lot of engagement with different chambers of commerce to ensure that the institutions are meeting the needs not only for today but for the years ahead ... We really wanted to make sure that the schools were focusing on local economic needs.”

Quinn first announced the new process last spring, with the 40,000 spots coming on top of another 30,000 in the same areas but without the same competitive process.

Of the total 70,000 funded spaces, about 40,200 are in STEM (science/technology/engineering/math), 16,100 in health care, some 7,900 in education programs, 3,800 in the trades, and 3,000 in other areas.

Some 27,000 of the 40,000 spots have opened up for this fall, and another 13,000 are coming next fall.

The change is a part of the government’s $6.4 billion in funding for the post-secondary sectorover four years, announced in February, that also ended a tuition freeze and, controversially, reversed student aid to favour repayable loans instead of non-repayable grants.

Though schools often do confer with industry, the new process formalized it and was the first time consultations were required.

In the end, the ministry received about 1,000 letters of support from local chambers of commerce and businesses.

At the time he announced the new process, Quinn had said it would mean “more mechanical engineers for North Bay, more teachers for Windsor, more welders for Ottawa and more nurses for Toronto.”

Steve Orsini, president and CEO of the Council of Ontario Universities, said schools “have multiple industry partnerships that proved to be instrumental in supporting (their) applications but also tied to industries’ need for labour,” especially given the huge need for university grads in the coming years.

He noted that the spaces come amid a trade and tariff dispute between Canada and the U.S., and said these “priority fields will strengthen Ontario’s talent pipeline and economic competitiveness at a crucial time.”

The Star, simplified

Orsini said universities already do a lot of work to support a number of sectors through research— “They have wind tunnels. They have a lot of experimental technology. The nuclear energy industry has partnerships with a number of universities to train the engineers” needed, he added. “Those partnerships are vital.”

Maureen Adamson, president and CEO of Colleges Ontario, called the process “very focused on the major areas where we need graduates and that will support the economy ... But it’s really prioritizing— that’s what’s important here, prioritizing the extra 40,000 seats in a way to move the economy.”

Kristin Rushowy is a Toronto-based senior writer covering education for the Star. Follow her on Twitter: @krushowy.

stories.title: Colonel Talbot Road will close between Glanworth Drive and Tempo Road for MTO project
stories.summary: be closed between Glanworth Drive and Tempo Road from September 11 to November 27 as part of a Ministry of Transport
stories.content:
Colonel Talbot Road will be closed between Glanworth Drive and Tempo Road from September 11 to November 27 as part of a Ministry of Transportation (MTO) highway improvement project.

Expect delays on Colonel Talbot Road between Decker Drive and Orr Drive, northbound and southbound traffic will be reduced to one lane in each direction.

A signed detour will be in place via Glanworth Drive and Tempo Road. The Highway 401/Colonel Talbot Road interchange ramps are also currently closed and are expected to reopen when the Colonel Talbot Road closure ends.

The closure is needed to rebuild Colonel Talbot Road where it connects to the new Highway 401 ramps, including removing the existing section of road that passes underneath the highway and installing new traffic signals.

For more information and updates about the project and upcoming traffic changes:

Highway 401/Colonel Talbot Road project: Visit Hwy 401 Colonel Talbot project website for project information, construction updates and current traffic restrictions.

stories.title: Reminder - TVDSB Special Education Advisory Committee seeks membership nominations
stories.summary: General News
stories.author: - Sep
stories.content:
General News

All Notices and Updates

The Thames Valley District School Board invites local associations or organizations of parents that operate locally within the jurisdiction of the Board to apply to serve on its Special Education Advisory Committee (SEAC) for the period of November 15, 2026, to November 14, 2030.

The Committee will include up to 12 representatives selected from the nominations.

The local associations/organizations must be affiliated with associations or organizations that:

are incorporated;

operate throughout Ontario;

further the interests and well-being of one or more groups of exceptional children or adults; and,

do not represent professional educators.

Organizations with an interest in special education that do not fully meet the above criteria may apply as an additional member.

How to apply

Visit the SEAC page on our website to learn more and apply. Applications must be received by 4:00 p.m. September 18, 2026.

stories.title: Zelenskyy arrives in Calgary ahead of Carney meeting
stories.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and his wife, Olena Zelenska, are also set to visit Toronto and North Bay, Ont., before leaving Friday.
stories.author: Bill Graveland
stories.content:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy landed in Calgary on Wednesday night ahead of a scheduled meeting with Prime Minister Mark Carney.

They are set to meet in the city Thursday morning, and Zelenskyy is to later address a cabinet meeting in the nearby mountain resort town of Banff, Alta.

Carney said the visit will focus on the countries’ shared priorities, including deepening defence, economic and energy co-operation.

“It will also address the human cost of Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine and build on the strong people-to-people ties that connect our countries,” Carney said in a statement.

“Canada remains steadfast in our commitment to support Ukraine’s defence, recovery and reconstruction.”

Zelenskyy and his wife, Olena Zelenska, are also set to visit Toronto and North Bay, Ont., before leaving Friday.

It’s Zelenskyy’s first visit to Canada this year. He was in Halifax in December amid efforts to end the war that Russia started in 2014.

Carney visited Kyiv in August 2025, and his predecessor Justin Trudeau visited Ukraine each year after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Kyiv has suffered a barrage of Russian airstrikes in recent months, and Ukraine has pleaded for more air defence support from its allies.

Since 2022, Canada has pledged $6.5 billion in military assistance for Ukraine running through to 2029.

Members of Parliament across party lines have put Ukraine at the centre of their foreign policy platforms. In May, Canada joined an agreement to learn from Ukrainian drone producers.

Ottawa has made no new funding announcements for Ukraine since then.

The Kiel Institute, which measures global contributions to Ukraine, pegs Canada as the fourth most generous in raw dollars and in 12th place based on gross domestic product. Canada’s donations include military aid, government financing and humanitarian support.

Ukraine has managed in recent months to hold back Russian advances and strike targets within Russia, including oil refineries and warehouses owned by Russia’s biggest online retailer.

Moscow has at times hinted at an end to the conflict. But Ukrainian and European officials have said the war should only end on terms that prevent Russia from rearming and attacking elsewhere.

Zelenskyy’s visit comes as European leaders argue Russia is widening its war through acts of sabotage, including paying youths to vandalize railways. European airports have had to halt operations several times due to drones attributed to Russia.

Germany last week blamed Russia for what it called an attempted explosive drone attack near a Ukrainian cargo plane at the Leipzig airport.

Carney called it “an egregious attempt by Russia to weaken our resolve and our collective defence.”

Across Europe, political parties once considered fringe over their support for Russia have seen their popularity increase as the continent tackles economic, environmental and migration crises.

Zelenskyy’s visit also comes at a time of rising domestic pressure on his own government, which was elected in 2019 and cannot call elections due to a constitutional ban on votes during martial law.

In July, Zelenskyy fired both his defence minister and military chief after days of protests. Opponents have accused him in various corruption scandals.

Ukraine has increasingly relied on Canada to advocate for its sovereignty and a just end to the war in various international forums.

U.S. President Donald Trump is set to host world leaders in Miami for the G20 summit in December. There are signs he might allow Russian President Vladimir Putin to attend, despite Putin being subject to an arrest warrant issued by the International Criminal Court.

The warrant is based on Russia’s abduction of thousands of Ukrainian children in what the court says is a probable war crime.

Anita Anand, Canada’s foreign affairs minister, is to co-host a summit later this month in Toronto about the return of Ukrainian children and prisoners of war.

Members of Parliament across party lines have put Ukraine at the centre of their foreign policy platforms. In May, Canada joined an agreement to learn from Ukrainian drone producers.
Ottawa has made no new funding announcements for Ukraine since then.

The Kiel Institute, which measures global contributions to Ukraine, pegs Canada as the fourth most generous in raw dollars and in 12th place based on gross domestic product. Canada’s donations include military aid, government financing and humanitarian support.
Ukraine has managed in recent months to hold back Russian advances and strike targets within Russia, including oil refineries and warehouses owned by Russia’s biggest online retailer.
Moscow has at times hinted at an end to the conflict. But Ukrainian and European officials have said the war should only end on terms that prevent Russia from rearming and attacking elsewhere.

Zelenskyy’s visit comes as European leaders argue Russia is widening its war through acts of sabotage, including paying youths to vandalize railways. European airports have had to halt operations several times due to drones attributed to Russia.
Germany last week blamed Russia for what it called an attempted explosive drone attack near a Ukrainian cargo plane at the Leipzig airport.
Carney called it “an egregious attempt by Russia to weaken our resolve and our collective defence.”
Across Europe, political parties once considered fringe over their support for Russia have seen their popularity increase as the continent tackles economic, environmental and migration crises.
Zelenskyy’s visit also comes at a time of rising domestic pressure on his own government, which was elected in 2019 and cannot call elections due to a constitutional ban on votes during martial law.
In July, Zelenskyy fired both his defence minister and military chief after days of protests. Opponents have accused him in various corruption scandals.
Ukraine has increasingly relied on Canada to advocate for its sovereignty and a just end to the war in various international forums.

U.S. President Donald Trump is set to host world leaders in Miami for the G20 summit in December. There are signs he might allow Russian President Vladimir Putin to attend, despite Putin being subject to an arrest warrant issued by the International Criminal Court.
The warrant is based on Russia’s abduction of thousands of Ukrainian children in what the court says is a probable war crime.
Anita Anand, Canada’s foreign affairs minister, is to co-host a summit later this month in Toronto about the return of Ukrainian children and prisoners of war.

stories.title: Grand Theatre celebrates 125 years of live performance
stories.summary: Wednesday was a show stopping night for The Grand Theatre, celebrating a major milestone.
stories.author: Lauren Stallone
stories.content:
Wednesday was a show stopping night for The Grand Theatre, celebrating a major milestone.

“Today we’re celebrating 125 years of live performance here at the Grand Theatre,” said Lyndee Hansen, executive director at The Grand Theatre.

To mark the occasion theatre buffs were invited to attend a “Backstage Bash.”

“It’s an open house sort of vibe,” said Hansen. “It’s a chance to wander around and look at all the things we have available for people to see.”

The main attraction was a display showcasing more than a century of history.

“We have this beautiful display that runs all the way through the building,” said Hansen. “It’s a great opportunity for Londoners to have a chance to see just how much impact this building and this theatre and this building has had for the past 125 years.”

The journey through The Grand’s history wouldn’t be complete without paying tribute to memorable fashion moments.

“I pulled pieces that correlate with the Backstage Bash,” said Lisa Wright, head of wardrobe at the theatre. “We’ve got looks from the 20’s, 30’s and 50’s.”

Visitors also got their chance to take centre stage.

“We really like this idea of people coming in through the stage door and getting an experience that the average theatre goer doesn’t get,” said Rachel Peake, artistic director at the Grand Theatre. “They stand on the stage and look out at the audience the way the actors do.”

Organizers said they are looking forward to 125 more years of live performance in London.

“We have our high school project coming up first which is School of Rock,” said Peake. “Then we start our main season in just a little over a month with Dracula.”

stories.title: Sports Notes: Kennington ready for Delaware, Knights to wrap up preseason, Mustangs prep for Windsor, HS Football starts Friday
stories.summary: DJ Kennington is always looking forward to racing at his home track. There is no doubt the #17 car will be in the hunt when Nascar Canada wraps up its season Saturday at Delaware Speedway.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
DJ Kennington is always looking forward to racing at his home track. There is no doubt the #17 car will be in the hunt when Nascar Canada wraps up its season Saturday at Delaware Speedway.

“A lot of family, friends and people you don’t get to see all year are going to be there to cheer us on, and hopefully we can turn things around,” said Kennington.

“It’s been an up and down season for us. It’s not the one that we wanted by any means, but hopefully we can end up strong here. And I always love going to Delaware”.

Sitting fourth in the points standings, Kennington has had just one top-five finish, and 10 more top 10’s.

“Every race, it seems like it’s been something different,” he added.

“We’ve had speed. We’ve had good equipment, good cars, just little things that I’ve never seen go wrong before have gone wrong this year. You can’t really get upset about it, it’s just racing,” said Kennington.

This past weekend he took the risk of running the entire race without a fuel stop at Canadian Motorsports Park. The race went to overtime, and his fuel ran one lap short. The gamble for a top-three finish didn’t work out.

“I hate it because I’m so competitive that it drives me nuts,” said Kennington.

“We want to win races, so hopefully we can get out there for Castrol and all of our family and friends this weekend at Delaware”.

Western mustangs prepare for windsor lancers

The Western Mustangs crushed York 78-7 in their season opener, but will face a much stiffer test in their second game. The Mustangs will travel to Windsor to face the Lancers who beat Laurier last weekend.

“We had a great first game but now it doesn’t matter anymore,” said quarterback Jerome Rancourt who had five touchdowns in the season opener.

“We were going on to the next one playing Windsor and on Saturday, and it’s going to be a good one to just come off a big win against Laurier. They’re more physical (than York) and they’re very aggressive on defense”. Western is a perfect 10-0 in their last ten meetings with Windsor dating back to 2016. They won a tight 15-6 defensive battle last October.

For Mustangs rookie captain Cyrus McGarrell, he’s excited to head back to his hometown this weekend.

“I’m excited to see all the guys again and play against them,” said the transfer from Northern Illinois in the Ncaa.

“I’ve always grew up watching the Windsor Lancers, so playing against them is going to be a definitely a great experience.” He was excited to step on the field in week one, and was surprised by the massive crowd.

“The atmosphere is crazy,” said McGarrell.

“About 30-45 minutes outside of kick off, I didn’t think there was many people going to be here. But when kickoff happened, all the fans and all the students came out. So great atmosphere.”

Knights to wrap up preseason vs sting

The Knights are ready to wrap up their preseason with a home game and home game with the Sarnia Sting starting Thursday at Canada Life Place.

“I can’t wait for the first game of the season”.

That first game will be Friday, Sept. 18 against the Windsor Spitfires.

The Knights have just returned from a two-game series out west against the Victoria Royals in British Columbia.

After getting whipped 7-1 in the first game, they bounced back with a 5-3 win in game two.

“We need to come out right at the opening whistle and that was the key to the second game that we played,” said Cover.

“Started off really well and just kept building off that. The first game, we didn’t start off so hot and a long plane ride probably didn’t help at all. I’d say the second game is more of who we are.”

Assistant coach Dylan Hunter said they made adjustments after the first game and changed up a few of their systems.

“We wanted to see how they would adjust to that and they did a good job kind of learning on the fly stuff you’re going to have to do throughout the year,” said Hunter.

“It was a good little test point for all our young guys”.

Hunter said the players had a chance to see the city on some down time and credited the Royals for “taking good care of us”.

High school football to play exhibtion games friday

The Lions – ranked 25 in the Ontario Coaches Poll to start the season will face St. Thomas Aquinas in the exhibition game.

“I’m so hyped and I don’t think I’ve ever been more excited,” said Lions safety Ben Ledger.

“The coaches make us put in that work and they prepare us to be the best we can be on and off the field.”

The Lions expect to have talent on both sides of the ball but offensively could be dangerous.

“We’ve got some underdogs here and they May not be names yet but they’ll come up,” said Izaiah Moxley, Lions running back.

“I’ve been waiting all summer for this game. Summer football is fun, but high school football is where it’s at.”

stories.title: Zelenskyy arrives in Calgary for multi-day visit to Canada
stories.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy arrived in Calgary on Wednesday night to kick off a multi-day visit to Canada.
stories.author: Denio Lourenco
stories.content:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy arrived in Calgary on Wednesday night to kick off a multi-day visit to Canada.

A statement issued by Prime Minister Mark Carney earlier that evening said the president’s visit “underscores Canada’s continued leadership in supporting Ukraine and reflects our unwavering commitment to a just and lasting peace.”

He was accompanied by his wife, Ukrainian First Lady, O’lena Zelenska, and was greeted by Canadian Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand.

They are slated to attend events in Calgary, Toronto, and North Bay. Zelenskyy will also address Cabinet members at the Cabinet Planning Forum in Banff, Alta.

The Prime Minister’s Office says the visit “will focus on shared priorities between Canada and Ukraine, including deepening defence, economic, and energy cooperation” and “address the human cost of Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine.”
