stories.title: Zelensky arrives in Calgary ahead of Carney meeting
stories.summary: Meeting expected to focus on defence, economic and energy co-operation
stories.author: Bill Graveland
stories.content:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky landed in Calgary on Wednesday night ahead of a scheduled meeting with Prime Minister Mark Carney .

They are set to meet in the city Thursday morning, and Zelensky is to later address a cabinet meeting in the nearby mountain resort town of Banff, Alta.

Carney said the visit will focus on the countries’ shared priorities, including deepening defence, economic and energy co-operation.

“It will also address the human cost of Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine and build on the strong people-to-people ties that connect our countries,” Carney said in a statement.

“Canada remains steadfast in our commitment to support Ukraine’s defence, recovery and reconstruction.”

Zelensky and his wife, Olena Zelenska, are also set to visit Toronto and North Bay, Ont., before leaving Friday.

It’s Zelensky’s first visit to Canada this year. He was in Halifax in December amid efforts to end the war that Russia started in 2014.

Carney visited Kyiv in August 2025, and his predecessor Justin Trudeau visited Ukraine each year after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Kyiv has suffered a barrage of Russian air strikes in recent months, and Ukraine has pleaded for more air defence support from its allies.

Since 2022, Canada has pledged $6.5 billion in military assistance for Ukraine running through to 2029.

Members of Parliament across party lines have put Ukraine at the centre of their foreign policy platforms. In May, Canada joined an agreement to learn from Ukrainian drone producers.

Ottawa has made no new funding announcements for Ukraine since then.

The Kiel Institute, which measures global contributions to Ukraine, pegs Canada as the fourth most generous in raw dollars and in 12th place based on gross domestic product. Canada’s donations include military aid, government financing and humanitarian support.

Ukraine has managed in recent months to hold back Russian advances and strike targets within Russia, including oil refineries and warehouses owned by Russia’s biggest online retailer.

Moscow has at times hinted at an end to the conflict. But Ukrainian and European officials have said the war should only end on terms that prevent Russia from rearming and attacking elsewhere.

Zelensky’s visit comes as European leaders argue Russia is widening its war through acts of sabotage, including paying youths to vandalize railways. European airports have had to halt operations several times due to drones attributed to Russia.

Germany last week blamed Russia for what it called an attempted explosive drone attack near a Ukrainian cargo plane at the Leipzig airport.

Carney called it “an egregious attempt by Russia to weaken our resolve and our collective defence.”

Across Europe, political parties once considered fringe over their support for Russia have seen their popularity increase as the continent tackles economic, environmental and migration crises.

Zelensky’s visit also comes at a time of rising domestic pressure on his own government, which was elected in 2019 and cannot call elections due to a constitutional ban on votes during martial law.

In July, Zelensky fired both his defence minister and military chief after days of protests. Opponents have accused him in various corruption scandals.

Ukraine has increasingly relied on Canada to advocate for its sovereignty and a just end to the war in various international forums.

U.S. President Donald Trump is set to host world leaders in Miami for the G20 summit in December. There are signs he might allow Russian President Vladimir Putin to attend, despite Putin being subject to an arrest warrant issued by the International Criminal Court.

The warrant is based on Russia’s abduction of thousands of Ukrainian children in what the court says is a probable war crime.

Anita Anand, Canada’s foreign affairs minister, is to co-host a summit later this month in Toronto about the return of Ukrainian children and prisoners of war.

stories.title: London civic election: Ward 12 all-candidates debate
stories.summary: The candidates in London's Ward 12 attended a debate at the London Public Library's Jalna branch on Wednesday night, believed to be the first of what will be many such events leading up to the Oct. 26 election.
stories.author: Ryan Goodison
stories.content:
The candidates in London’s Ward 12 attended a debate at the London Public Library’s Jalna branch on Wednesday night, believed to be the first of what will be many such events across the city in the lead-up to London’s municipal election on Oct. 26. LFP reporter Ryan Goodison was there and has full coverage:

Elizabeth Peloza (incumbent)

Age: 46

Occupation: Ward 12 city councillor.

Top three priorities: Community safety and wellbeing, infrastructure and transportation, and accountable and accessible leadership.

Age: 19

Occupation: Civil engineering student at Western University and entrepreneur.

Top three priorities: Housing and affordability, economic opportunity and fiscal responsibility and modernizing municipal services and infrastructure.

Age: 52

Occupation: Business owner.

Top three priorities: Community safety, affordability and enforcement.

In her opening statement, Peloza says she has been knocking on doors across Ward 12, hearing about residents’ priorities and the areas in need of improvement across the city.

If Peloza is re-elected, it will be her third straight term as Ward 12 councillor, having first been elected in 2018. In 2022, Peloza won by a landslide, taking 77 per cent of the vote. Peloza was also the council’s budget chief this term and an ally of Mayor Josh Morgan – she recently attended his campaign launch .

The 46-year-old was diagnosed with cancer earlier this year, and gave residents an update on her treatment at the debate. She said her chemotherapy treatment has wrapped up, while radiation treatment will conclude on Friday.

Zebian, the youngest candidate by a wide margin, said his campaign has focused on making sure city hall is working for the people, and not the other way around. Zebian first gained attention in high school when he built a wooden electric vehicle, and has since turned his attention to designing and building small modular homes.

Main said in his opening statement that he believes city hall has become disconnected from the challenges people face every day. Main also ran for Ward 12 councillor in 2022, finishing third with roughly 10 per cent of the vote (466 votes in total).

In a rather quiet evening, the three candidates addressed topics ranging from community safety to the recent councillor pay increase in front of a crowd of around 30 residents at the library on Jalna Boulevard.

In a question written by an audience member, candidates were asked how much of an impact the 35 per cent base salary increase would have on councillors and residents’ taxes when in kicks in next term.

Zebian called the pay raise insulting to the general public. In his opening statement, he promised that, if elected, he would put the extra pay toward scholarships for students in the London area.

Main said the optics surrounding the situation are awful and that “city hall has become disconnected from the very people it represents.”

Peloza responded by saying the job of a city councillor was examined through an independent review task force, which determined it was going from a part-time job to full-time job. She said the wage reflects that being a city councillor is a full-time position.

Candidates also tackled a question about rising crime in the White Oaks area, as well as open drug use across the ward and on buses. Main said that, if elected, he would push for greater enforcement against open-air drug use across the city.

Peloza agreed, saying “open-air drug use needs to come to an end,” and that she recently met with members of the London police to discuss, among the things, public safety.

Voters will head to the polls to elect their next city council on Oct. 26. There are more than 100 people running for London mayor and the 14 ward councillor positions – read what most of them have to say, in their own words, right here .

stories.title: Calgary’s mayor says ‘fiscal discipline’ will guide council through tough budget decisions
stories.summary: Calgary mayor Jeromy Farkas said the city's $50 billion infrastructure deficit "won't dissapear" in a single budget or council term, but noted council must chip away at it.
stories.author: Adam MacVicar
stories.content:
Despite his optimism about the city’s future, Calgary’s mayor isn’t shying away from tough decisions in the upcoming city budget, including the need for a multi-billion-dollar infrastructure investment.

Mayor Jeromy Farkas said Wednesday that the “bill is now coming due” for decades of deferred decisions from all orders of government in the form of a $50-billion infrastructure deficit over the next 10 years.

“Right now, we face incredibly serious challenges,” Farkas said during a State of the City address to the Rotary Club of Calgary Downtown. “Affordability, public safety, economic uncertainty, rapid growth, and infrastructure that hasn’t kept pace with the city that we have become.”

The mayor said the city must invest in its transportation network, water system and recreation facilities to meet population growth, as well as the needs of the city when it reaches two million people.

Farkas told the luncheon crowd that the issue is evidenced by the Dec. 30 rupture of the Bearspaw feeder main as well as the fast-tracked project in the city’s northwest to replace the failing water line by the end of this year.

The $50-billion deficit “won’t disappear” in a single budget or council term, Farkas said, but council “can stop making it worse” by chipping away at the issue in the upcoming four-year budget in November.

However, Farkas said the situation doesn’t give city hall permission “to spend without discipline.”

“Fiscal discipline does not mean refusing to invest, it means knowing the difference between what we need and what we want,” the mayor said. “It means finding savings before asking taxpayers for more.”

How much of an increase Calgarians could see on their property tax bills has been top of mind at city hall after Global News obtained confidential preliminary budget documents showing property tax revenue would need to increase by 20.2 per cent in 2027 to fund all the funding requests in front of council.

Those documents also show city administration has begun whittling down those requests to prepare a preliminary budget scenario with a potential 15 per cent property tax increase for consideration during a closed-door session later this month.

Farkas made no mention of the confidential documents during Wednesday’s address, or the special meeting of council held Tuesday to discuss potential ramifications for Ward 14 Coun. Landon Johnston; the councillor who claimed to have leaked confidential documents.

“I think he’s trying to shift the narrative or change the channel away from controversy towards forward thinking and planning,” said Lori Williams, an associate professor of policy studies at Mount Royal University. “One of the things that’s relatively new in municipal budgeting is trying to plan for infrastructure failure; in other words, investing in something that’s been left off the list.”

Farkas’ address came on the same day a pair of funding requests were in front of the city’s Infrastructure and Planning Committee for consideration during the upcoming four-year budget.

Those requests, which will require a final say from council as a whole, include $37 million annually for sidewalk renewal as well as $13.5 million per year for the public tree canopy.

Ward 10 Coun. Andre Chabot said questioned how council is expected to fund everything over the next four years.

“Is it millrate support like as in property taxes? Or is there other funding mechanisms we can look at to minimize a tax increase,” Chabot said. “We could look at debt financing some of the capital infrastructure that has a long life expectancy, which would lessen the burden today on immediate taxpayers.”

Farkas said just because something falls on the “city hall wishlist,” doesn’t mean it will receive funding.

He told the crowd of Rotarians that council must demand value from city administration and have the “discipline to say no.”

“We have to choose water before wants, safety before nice-to-haves, and core infrastructure before projects that can wait,” Farkas said. “That is how we protect taxpayers, while still preparing Calgary for the future.”

The four-year budget will be made public in early November, three weeks ahead of deliberations.

stories.title: First Nation plans to flout Alberta law that restricts gender-affirming care for transgender youth
stories.summary: Asserting treaty rights, Saddle Lake Cree Nation says it will establish safe haven for the treatment on reserved lands
stories.author: Alanna Smith
stories.content:
A First Nation in Alberta says it will defy a provincial law that restricts access to gender-affirming care for transgender youth, arguing these health services are protected under treaty rights.

The Saddle Lake Cree Nation, roughly 180 kilometres northeast of Edmonton, announced during a news conference on Wednesday that it is asserting its jurisdiction to provide Albertans access to gender-affirming treatment that is currently banned by the province.

The First Nation cited the “medicine chest” clause of Treaty No. 6, which states that “a medicine chest shall be kept at the house of each Indian Agent for the use and benefit of the Indians at the direction of such agent.” Indigenous leaders interpret this as a legal obligation for the federal government to provide health care on a continuing basis.

James Makokis, a Nehiyô (Plains Cree) two-spirit family physician from Saddle Lake, said the violence and harms faced by two-spirit and transgender people has to stop, stressing that the denial of care significantly increases mental-health risks.

He described Alberta’s legislation as “anti-trans” and said it is a profound violation of the treaty.

“The Saddle Lake Cree Nation categorically rejects these attacks on all gender diverse peoples, including Tastawiyiniwak – our two-spirit relatives – ensuring that life-affirming health care remains accessible, safe and protected from external political interference,” Dr. Makokis said in a subsequent statement.

Alberta’s trio of laws regarding transgender and gender-diverse youth are the most restrictive of any province in Canada. The legislation bans participation in certain sports divisions and regulates pronouns in schools, in addition to limiting gender-affirming care.

Last November, Alberta invoked the notwithstanding clause to shield the bills from being overturned by legal action. The clause – historically viewed to be a last resort – allows governments to override certain sections of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms for up to five years.

Legal challenges against the province are still before the courts.

Under the law restricting gender-affirming care, doctors are prohibited from prescribing puberty blockers and hormone therapies for those under 16. Additionally, physicians are banned from performing gender-reassignment surgeries on minors (those under 18), which was already a rare occurrence in the province.

Saddle Lake said the three laws are an “assault on gender diverse people” and that it will establish a safe haven for gender-affirming care on reserved lands. The nation said it will create a new health law, welcome Canadian-trained physicians to practise and work with health regulators to ensure there are no licensing barriers for these clinicians.

Heather Jenkins, press secretary to Alberta Justice Minister Mickey Amery, did not directly address the First Nation’s plans to offer gender-affirming care.

She said the laws “preserve the choices of children and youth,” strengthen the role of parents and “ensure fairness and safety” in amateur sports. “Alberta’s United Conservative government will be unapologetic in our commitment to these principles,” said Ms. Jenkins.

The Tastawiyiniwak, which roughly translates to the “in-between” people, also known as two-spirit, have always been recognized and included by the Cree people. Saddle Lake said it must protect these individuals against “continued assault” as a growing number of jurisdictions implement policies that limit care for gender-diverse people.

Standing behind speakers at Wednesday’s news conference were people wearing shirts with the transgender flag and holding signs in support of the Lgbtq+ community. One read: “As long as the sun shines, the grass grows and the river flows, tastawiyiniwak will exist.”

Chief Dale Steinhauer of the Saddle Lake Cree Nation said Alberta’s law is “dehumanizing” and the nation will not stand by as basic human rights and vital health care services are denied.

“Have the colonial governments not learned enough from their own history? Today, Saddle Lake Cree Nation reminds them again to stay in their boat,” said Ms. Steinhauer.

“When we were being stolen from our parents and experienced genocide in Indian Residential Schools, we wondered ‘Who are the people that will help us?’ Today, we are those people. Today we offer our help, support and jurisdiction to override these dehumanizing laws,” she said in a subsequent statement.

Representatives from the Canadian Medical Association and the Indigenous Physicians Association of Canada, who joined the news conference, voiced their support for Saddle Lake.

stories.title: Susan Stevenson kicks off election campaign, promising safety and accountability
stories.summary: Susan Stevenson kicks off election campaign, promising safety and accountability CBC
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: Incumbent Ward 4 Coun. Susan Stevenson has officially launched her campaign for mayor, promising to focus on neighbourhood safety, support for small businesses and greater transparency at City Hall.
· Posted: Sep 09, 2026 9:33 PM EDT | Last Updated: 44 minutes ago

Incumbent London Coun. Susan Stevenson has officially launched her campaign for mayor, promising changes to how the city approaches public drug use, spends taxpayer money and works with the community.

At a campaign launch at her new downtown office Wednesday night, Stevenson unveiled her six-part platform that includes neighbourhood safety, support for small businesses and greater accountability at City Hall.
"I'm most excited for change and giving the people what I believe they want," Stevenson said in an interview with CBC News.

"I do believe I represent the silent majority and when that's proven to be true, I'm very excited about being able to give Londoners what I think they're so desperate for, in terms of change in leadership in the city."

More than 100 people attended Stevenson's launch event, where she spoke about her history in the city and outlined the pillars of her campaign. She said she plans to release more specific proposals in the coming weeks.
"I believe in London. I believe in the people who keep this city going every day. And I believe we can build a city hall that matches their effort, their care and their ambition," she told the crowd.
London Mayor Josh Morgan launches re-election campaign with 4-part platform
Coun. Susan Stevenson enters race to become London's next mayor
Stevenson is one of 11 candidates running for mayor, including incumbent Mayor Josh Morgan.
Morgan launched his platform Monday, where he revealed his campaign will be focused on housing, transit, economic growth and public safety.

Other mayoral candidates have released platforms—in varying levels of detail—on their campaign websites, includingKirsten Krose,Mustafa Zebuun,John Feher, Lawrence-Zachary Howe,Bronagh Joyce Morgan, Jeff Yam and Tariq Khan.
Stevenson has sat on city council since 2022, representing Ward 4, which previously included Old East Village.
She said issues she has raised as a councillor will remain central to her mayoral campaign, including the city's response to drug use and homelessness.

"We need to reject the harm reduction model that is currently endorsed by council and choose the recovery model that the province went with in the spring of 2024, and create pathways for recovery for people so that there's a way out of the trap of addiction and the life that they're living on the street," she said.
The Ontario government announced in 2024 that it would close 10 supervised consumption and treatment sites and replace them with a new model focused on treatment and recovery.
Morgan has also made public drug use and community safety issues in his campaign platform. Stevenson, however, said she sees a fundamental difference between the two approaches.
"I think Londoners have a clear decision point this election and that is enabling drug use or saying we're gonna stop public drug use," she said.
London's youngest mayoral candidate aims to reach voters through viral videos and social media
As nominations open for city council, Josh Morgan already has a challenger for mayor
Stevenson said she is confident city council will support her approach if she is elected mayor.
"I'm not concerned about that at all. A council will follow along once I'm elected on a clear mandate and they'll give the people what they ask for," she said.

Stevenson also said she has plans to create a more financially transparent City Hall, with more publicly available information about spending on items such as the bus rapid transit system and homelessness.

"Londoners, especially given the affordability crisis that we're in, expect us to be reviewing the financials and to be their eyes on their taxpayer dollars and how they're being used. And currently that's not the case," she said.
When asked how she would make that information public, Stevenson said it would start with requesting more reports from city staff.
"It's simply asking for the reports and getting staff to do them. Currently, when I bring forward those motions, there isn't an appetite on council at the moment to get those details."
Got a minute? Tell us what changes you want to see in London, Ont., and area this election

Stevenson said her campaign will also focus on improving transportation around the city, strengthening partnerships with other organizations and levels of government, and showing up for the community.
Londoners will take to the polls to vote for mayor and 14 council seats on Oct. 26.

stories.title: Okanagan wine producers brace for U.S. ban on Canadian alcohol imports
stories.summary: B.C. wine producers are bracing for the latest blow to cross-border alcohol sales, with the United States set to ban most Canadian alcohol imports later this month.
stories.author: Klaudia Van Emmerik
stories.content:
B.C. wine producers are bracing for the latest blow to cross-border alcohol sales, with the United States set to ban most Canadian alcohol imports later this month.

At Lightning Rock Winery in Summerland, the impact is expected to be significant.

“It seems that wine and booze in general in Canada and the U.S. is the punching bag for everything,” said Ron Kubek, owner of Lightning Rock Winery. “If I had known this, I wouldn’t have gone into the business.”

Kubek is bracing for the looming U.S. ban and the potential loss of roughly 500 cases of his wine sold in the United States each year.

“That’s about $120,000 to $150,000 a year,” he said.

At Painted Rock Estate Winery in Penticton, the direct financial hit is expected to be less significant, but the winery says losing access to the U.S. market could still have an important impact.

“It’s really important in terms of brand building. It’s something that we use to be able to get in front of important reviewers, in front of important influencers, and competitions,” said Lauren Skinner-Buksevics, the winery’s managing director.

B.C. wine producers were first hit with a 50 per cent tariff.

Now, the U.S. is going a step further by moving to ban most Canadian alcohol imports entirely.

Jeff Guignard, president and CEO of the Wine Growers of British Columbia, says the consequences will be felt on both sides of the border.

“It’s going to hurt businesses on both sides of the border,” Guignard said. “When this ban comes in, it’s going to be Canadian producers, American importers, distributors, retailers, hospitality businesses who are going to be hurt by this.”

But Guignard says the broader implications of what he describes as a form of prohibition could be even more significant.

“I think it’s a really dangerous precedent that’s being set right here. It is showing us that the United States is a completely unreliable trading partner,” he said.

The latest development is prompting renewed calls for Canada to eliminate interprovincial trade barriers that make it difficult for Canadian wineries to sell across the country.

“This is the time to solve interprovincial trade barriers and this is the time to allow Canadian businesses to build their brand here at home,” Skinner-Buksevics said.

Kubek agrees, saying governments need to do more to support Canadian-made wine, including prioritizing domestic products in government-run liquor stores.

“The B.C. LDB (B.C. Liquor Distribution Branch) is promoting a South African winery, ‘win a car.’ They’re promoting an Italian winery, wine region, ‘win a trip in France.’ You know, the Penticton liquor store, the Penticton B.C. liquor store has 12 rows devoted to foreign wines and only two to B.C.,” Kubek said.

“We need to look in the mirror and fix our own problems first. Then we can deal with the U.S.,” he added.

The ban is set to take effect on Sept. 29.

stories.title: Dawson families urge Ottawa to strengthen gun laws ahead of 20th anniversary of college shooting
stories.summary: Families of Dawson College shooting victims are urging Ottawa to strengthen gun laws ahead of the attack's 20th anniversary, saying key firearms-control measures remain unfinished.
stories.author: Alessia Simona Maratta
stories.content:
Families and survivors of the Dawson College shooting are calling on Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government to strengthen firearms laws, saying key gun-control measures promised in the wake of mass shootings remain unfinished nearly 20 years after the deadly attack.

In an open letter released Wednesday, the advocacy group Dawson Families for Gun Control urged the federal government to take action on what it describes as three outstanding priorities: completing the ban on assault-style firearms, closing loopholes involving large-capacity magazines and strengthening oversight of exemptions to Canada’s handgun freeze.

The letter comes ahead of the 20th anniversary of the Sept. 13, 2006 shooting at Montreal’s Dawson College, when a gunman opened fire with legally acquired firearms, killing 18-year-old Anastasia De Sousa and wounding 19 others.

“Since that terrible day, survivors and families of Anastasia and those injured or traumatized have urged successive governments to fix the laws that enabled a troubled and angry young man to legally obtain firearms and accessories capable of causing mass casualties,” the letter states.

While acknowledging progress, including the prohibition of many assault-style firearms and the federal handgun freeze, the families argue significant gaps remain.

They say many prohibited firearms are still in civilian hands because of an ongoing amnesty period tied to the federal buyback program. The group is also calling for regulations to ban magazines that can be modified to hold more rounds than legally permitted and wants stricter national standards governing exemptions for Olympic and Paralympic sport shooters.

The families say Ottawa should move forward on those measures without further consultation.

The letter is signed by relatives of victims and survivors connected to the Dawson College shooting.

Louise Hevey De Sousa, whose daughter Anastasia was killed in the attack, said families have been waiting too long for governments to act.

“I think action really needs to be taken now. It’s enough,” she told Global News. “It’s been 20 years since Dawson and even longer since Polytechnique, so I don’t think it’s really acceptable.”

Hevey De Sousa also pointed to Montreal’s recent incident of gun violence this past June as evidence that stronger measures are needed .

In a statement to Global News, a spokesperson for Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree said the upcoming anniversary is “a solemn reminder of the devastating consequences of gun violence and of our shared responsibility to keep communities safe.”

The federal government said it remains committed to its firearm-control agenda, including the Assault-Style Firearms Compensation Program.

According to the minister’s office, more than 142,000 assault-style firearms have been declared, collected or destroyed through the program to date.

The government also highlighted broader efforts to combat gun violence, including investments in border security, additional Canada Border Services Agency and RCMP personnel, and funding aimed at disrupting organized crime networks involved in firearms trafficking.

“Altogether, these measures reflect our comprehensive approach: removing dangerous firearms from communities, strengthening our borders, supporting law enforcement, and disrupting the organized criminal networks that fuel gun violence,” the statement said.

Dawson College will hold a commemorative ceremony Friday to mark the 20th anniversary of the shooting.

On Sunday, the anniversary of the attack, members of Anastasia De Sousa’s family will gather at her gravesite, continuing a tradition they have observed each year since her death to honour the life she never had the chance to complete.

stories.title: Two Second World War air training bases in Huron County marked by historical society
stories.summary: Overlooking the mighty Maitland River, Huron County history buffs gathered to mark the lives lost at two military training bases, used more than 85 years ago.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
Overlooking the mighty Maitland River, Huron County history buffs gathered to mark the lives lost at two military training bases, used more than 85 years ago.

“During the Second World War, two air bases along the coast of Lake Huron, Port Albert, and here at Sky Harbor in Goderich, were hives of activity as they trained thousands of pilots for aerial combat and overseas missions in Europe,” said Huron County historian, David Yates.

From 1939 to 1945, at the height of Second World War, pilots from across the Commonwealth came to Huron County to learn how to fly combat missions overseas. Thousands made it to the frontlines, but some didn’t.

“65 of those who trained here lost their lives while in training. They never made it back to their homes. And 17 of them we are going to commemorate next year with an official statue, for the first time, an official memorial for the 17 that lost their lives over Lake Huron, and their remains were never recovered,” said Yates.

A plaque along the Guelph to Goderich Trail, not far from the former air training base in Goderich, now marks those 65 lives lost at the British Commonwealth Air Training and Navigations Schools in Port Albert and Goderich.

Two bases overshadowed by the air base near Clinton, now Vanastra, that operated in secret for decades.

“Vanastra was part of the Clinton base where the focus was on radar, and it was a huge secret at the time. Of course, they didn’t want the information getting into the wrong hands during the Second World War,” said Huron Historical Society President, David Armstrong.

In all, four air training bases were situated in Huron County during the Second World War, making the area an important part of the war effort.

“It was a frenzy of activity here for just under five years where they came, and then they went, after the war was over. And we take it for granted, because we won, and our way of life continued,” said Yates.

“We need to, as a society, remember our past because without remembering our history, heaven knows we’re bound to repeat it,” said Armstrong.

stories.title: Mother of slain children opposes Guy Turcotte’s release
stories.summary: Turcotte was sentenced to 17 years in prison without parole eligibility for murdering his children, who were five and three years old.
stories.author: Alessia Simona Maratta, Dan Spector
stories.content:
Warning: This story contains details that May be disturbing to some readers. Discretion advised.

The mother of two children murdered by their father says she is not ready to face the man who killed them, but plans to do so later this month when he appears before the Parole Board of Canada.

Isabelle Gaston, whose children, Olivier and Anne-Sophie, were stabbed to death by her ex-husband, former cardiologist Guy Turcotte , in 2009, announced in an emotional post on social media that she will deliver a victim impact statement at Turcotte’s parole hearing on Sept. 22.

“I knew this day would come and I’ve been trying to prepare myself for it for a long time,” Gaston wrote. “I truly do not feel ready to face it.”

Turcotte was sentenced in 2016 to 17 years in prison without parole eligibility for murdering the children, who were aged five and three. He is now seeking permission for supervised temporary absences outside prison.

Gaston says she is reliving years of trauma to explain to parole board members why she believes Turcotte should not be granted any additional freedom.

“This is like the second nightmare of judicial proceedings starting for her,” said victims’ rights advocate Darlene Ryan.

Ryan says parole hearings can force families to revisit some of the most painful moments of their lives. Her stepdaughter, Brigitte Serre, was murdered in 2006, and Ryan has delivered victim impact statements during proceedings involving her killer.

“You do have to delve deep down and relive everything. And then you have to put it into words,” Ryan said.

Criminal lawyer Eric Sutton says supervised absences can be an important step in the correctional process.

“If these absences went well, then they’d be more inclined to give an offender parole,” Sutton said.

The Parole Board of Canada told Global News it will not publicly disclose whether it grants Turcotte’s request.

Sutton noted that, given the high-profile nature of the case, authorities could also consider any potential risks to Turcotte’s safety should he be allowed into the community.

“That’s a concern they could validly have,” he said.

Victims’ rights advocate Pierre-Hugues Boisvenu, whose daughter was murdered in 2002, argues Turcotte should not be granted supervised visits. Boisvenu said he believes withholding information about parole decisions offers more protection to offenders than to the public.

“He killed two kids, and keeping all information secret means we have more protection for criminals than for society,” Boisvenu said.

Boisvenu, who appeared before the parole board in 2025 to oppose the release of his daughter’s killer, said allowing supervised absences in Turcotte’s case would send the wrong message.

“That sends a strong message to society that killing kids is not a serious crime,” he said.

Sutton, however, noted that seeking temporary releases as a parole eligibility date approaches is a normal part of the corrections system.

“He’s subject to a 17-year parole ineligibility period, which is substantial. As that period approaches expiry, it’s perfectly normal that the offender will seek some form of temporary release,” Sutton said.

Gaston declined Global News’ request for an interview, citing concerns that public comments could interfere with the process. Ryan and Boisvenu say they have both reached out to offer their support.

“You just have to follow your heart and do the best that you can to defend your loved one’s memory,” Ryan said.

It remains possible that Turcotte’s request for supervised absences will be denied following the hearing later this month.

stories.title: Endocrine Society publishes research roadmap for advancing obesity science in the era of GLP-1s
stories.summary: Led by Canadian scientist Daniel Drucker the research will chart a path toward improved health, optimized treatments and better understanding of obesity
stories.author: Jennifer Yang
stories.content:
Why are some people “super responders” to GLP-1 drugs, while others barely shed any weight? Should women stop weight-loss therapies if they want to get pregnant, and if so, when? And what are the most pressing safety concerns as millions more people start taking these powerful medicines?

These are just a sample of the dozens of questions raised by a new research priority statement issued by the Endocrine Society, the world’s largest organization of endocrinologists and clinicians who treat hormone-related conditions.

The statement was published in the journal Endocrine Reviews on Wednesday, when the society also launched its Center on Obesity , a new global hub for the latest in obesity science, resources and advocacy.

Led by Daniel Drucker , the Canadian scientist renowned for his pioneering GLP-1 research, a team of eight scientists reviewed more than 200 studies to compile a research roadmap for advancing obesity science in the era of weight-loss drugs such as Wegovy and Zepbound.

Throughout history, transformational discoveries such as penicillin and vaccines have reshaped our understanding of the diseases they aim to treat, the statement said – and obesity drugs are no different.

So the time is ripe for scientists to “seize the moment” with thoughtful research that can chart a path toward improved health, optimized treatments and a better understanding of obesity, the society said.

“There are literally hundreds of questions that are now very germane and very relevant to the clinic that we never even had to worry about before, because we never had medical therapies that could achieve what these medicines do,” Dr. Drucker said in an interview.

“We wanted to put it all together to say, what should the priorities be? And how should we think about this field going forward, beyond the question of just how much weight do I need to lose?”

“We’re now in a position to transform our understanding of obesity.”

Obesity is one of the most “urgent health issues of our time,” affecting one in eight people worldwide, said Amy Rothberg , a University of Michigan professor and chair of the society’s Obesity Strategy Initiative Member Task Force, addressing reporters Wednesday at a virtual press conference.

But in the last few years, GLP-1s have dramatically transformed the treatment landscape. Today, this class of medicines – which include brand names such as Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro and Zepbound – have become Canada’s top-selling drugs, generating about $2.4-billion in sales during the first half of 2026 alone.

Doctors are now prescribing GLP-1 medications not just for diabetes and obesity, but also cardiovascular diseases, obstructive sleep apnea and weight-related liver disease . Researchers around the world are studying these drugs as potential treatments for a growing list of conditions, including Parkinson’s disease, drug addiction and some forms of cancer.

The widespread use of GLP-1s is also revealing new phenomena, including the existence of “super responders” – people who lose 25 per cent of their body weight or more on GLP-1s.

Meanwhile, other patients taking the same drug might barely respond to the treatment at all, he said. Scientists didn’t know before about this type of variation between people, “because we never had medicines that would allow us to achieve this kind of weight loss,” Dr. Drucker said.

“There are so many things we need to understand about individualized outcomes and how to achieve them,” Dr. Drucker said.

“And there are 100 or more investigational medicines that seek to bring new innovations into the clinic based on these GLP-1 medicines. So we’re going to have these ask all of these questions over and over again, repeatedly.”

So the time is ripe for scientists to “seize the moment” with thoughtful research that can chart a path toward improved health, optimized treatments and a better understanding of obesity, the society said.

stories.title: Eight-storey Sarnia Road apartment plan advances despite neighbour pushback
stories.summary: The site was approved for a six-storey building last year, but a taller proposal is now moving forward.
stories.author: Jack Moulton
stories.content:
Proposed by Kimko Inc. and 20223388 Holdings Inc. is an eight-storey apartment building containing 204 units at 299-307 Sarnia Rd ., between Western Road and Wonderland Road North, ON the site of what is now two single-family homes.

What was an issue for ward councillor Sam Trosow and many neighbours in the Sherwood Forest and Orchard Park neighbourhoods, however, was the fact the same site has already seen two previous planning applications.

“One of the things that really bothers me with this is whatever the decision is going to be – there has to be some closure,” said Trosow, who is not a committee member.

“It’s just a serial set of applications, there seems to be no end to them.”

The planning and environment committee voted 4-1 to endorse the proposal, which would also include 188 underground parking spaces and 225 bike parking spaces. Coun. Susan Stevenson, who appeared virtually and did not speak, was the sole opposition vote.

The building would be eight storeys directly fronting Sarnia Road and step down to six and five storeys to the rear, with the latter two sections both having one storey below grade. Several courtyards are also baked into the design.

While city staff recommend approval of the project, it would be subject to a holding provision until the nearby sewer network is upgraded – meaning development can’t start. They also recommend improving the facade to make it look less “institutional” and more residential.

Katelyn Crowley, an associate planner at planning firm Zelinka Priamo, presented to politicians, acknowledging staff’s feedback and residents’ concerns, but noting eight storeys is allowed as of right on that section of Sarnia Road under recently increased height limits.

“From a planning perspective, the fundamental question is not whether residential development and intensification should occur here, the city planning framework already identifies this type of location as appropriate,” she said. “The question is how that intensification should be designed, and that is where the city’s recommended provisions are particularly important.”

Council chambers saw 11 speakers either opposed to or raising concerns about the proposal, along with 13 letters submitted in opposition to the project, including one from a lawyer representing a nearby household.

City council ignores its own height limits, OKs 8-storey apartment building

Proposed 10-storey Sarnia Road apartment too tall: Committee

Of particular concern to neighbours was the fact that the site had gone through two previous development iterations, including a six-storey building approved by council last year and a four-storey townhome development before that.

“How we perceive our neighbourhood is going to change dramatically with this development,” said neighbour Doug Anglin-Bodrug.

“When we looked at some of the original designs, yeah we weren’t that happy with it but it’s like OK, we can learn to live with this, but then suddenly we’re looking at eight storeys.”

Some councillors were sympathetic, with Ward 3 Coun. Peter Cuddy saying he shared some of the concerns about the application before saying he would further consult with Trosow.

“I have a problem with this application at eight storeys, this is a beautiful and pristine neighbourhood,” he said. “There’s really not a lot about this application that is appealing, if anything at all.”

However, deputy mayor Shawn Lewis, vice-chair of the committee, pushed back on concerns about the planned student housing and traffic. He explained council cannot dictate who lives in new developments and said Sarnia Road already sees 24,000 vehicles a day, adding the trips generated by the building would not be significant.

Council will make its final decision on the application at its Sept. 22 meeting.

Now that city hall is allowing wider driveways, politicians are interested in studying incentives for Londoners to make those driveways more permeable.

Proposed by Ward 11 Coun. Skylar Franke and tabled by committee members Shawn Lewis and Peter Cuddy, the planning and environment committee unanimously agreed to have city staff study amending city driveway regulations to include definitions of permeable materials, incentives for their use and the impact on the city’s stormwater network.

Earlier this year, council approved returning to a one-parking-space-per-unit regulation for higher-density developments and loosened regulations around driveway width, something Franke said inspired her to consider permeable surfaces.

“I know that one larger driveway in a neighbourhood isn’t causing a flood, but we’re talking about potentially thousands of properties across a growing city,” she said of driveway water runoff. “The question is more about if there are more cost-efficient ways of managing that runoff before it even enters our system.”

Permeable driveway surfaces allow water to absorb directly into the ground through porous asphalt and concrete, or lattice-style driveways with gravel or grass in between.

A clause in the motion asking staff to study requirements for permeable driveways was struck, with some expressing a hesitant or tepid response to the idea.

“In my mind, there is value in getting more information back on this, but I want to be very clear that I’m not looking to incentivize the materials people put on their driveways,” said Corrine Rahman, who is not a committee member.

Council will make its final vote on the idea at its Sept. 22 meeting.

stories.title: Lewis and Lehman: Extend road construction hours to get major projects done sooner
stories.summary: On Wednesday, Ward 2 candidate Shawn Lewis and Ward 8 candidate Steve Lehman made a joint campaign announcement on Wellington Road next to ongoing roadwork to build the bus rapid transit (BRT) system.
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
A pair of incumbent candidates are pitching a strategy that they believe could significantly shorten traffic disruptions caused by major roadwork in London.

On Wednesday, Ward 2 candidate Shawn Lewis and Ward 8 candidate Steve Lehman made a joint campaign announcement on Wellington Road next to ongoing roadwork to build the bus rapid transit (BRT) system.

“The commitment we are making is about major streets, allowing construction to run until 11 p.m. and also allowing it to extend into Saturdays,” Lewis explained.

Both candidates emphasized that the longer construction hours would only be permitted on major roadways.

“We’re not intending this to be anywhere near residential neighborhoods at all. We don’t want them to be impacted,” Lehman assured. “We’ve got big city challenges with infrastructure and traffic. We need big city solutions.”

A local industry leader says it could significantly shorten the number of days required to complete major projects.

“You can actually open (the site) up for 16 hours (each day) and then close it up, or even improve the phasing because a lot more work is going to get done each day. You (could) do a bigger chunk, take off a bigger bite,” explained Ryan Aarts, CEO of J-AAR.

Aarts says running two-shifts could also cut down on lost days by still bringing in the second shift even if the first is disrupted by bad weather.

“We average a 50-hour workweek right now, but we lose on average 8 to 10 hours a week just because of weather or other conditions.”

Lewis acknowledged that the initiative would likely require changes to city hall’s procurement policy, as well as consultation with construction unions.

“If we get to work on it right away at City Hall after the election, then I think by 2028 we could at least see this being tried at a couple of projects that summer. Then see how things go, and hopefully expand from there,” he said.

“It’s one of our shared (platform) planks in our campaigns,” Lehman said. ”We hear a lot about traffic problems in this city. London has experienced tremendous growth, but with that growth comes infrastructure projects.”

Last year’s annual satisfaction survey conducted for city hall found “traffic and road congestion” at 23 per cent and “road maintenance” at 16 per cent among the four most commonly identified “Top of Mind” by Londoners.

“Sure, residents will still have to deal with some tie-ups, but less. Anything we can do to get this city moving faster we have to consider,” committed Lehman.

“If we can get (roadwork) done faster, that’s less headaches for the residents of the area and less headaches for London commuters,” said Lewis.

Also running in Ward 2 are Alexandria Hames, Zachary Ramsey, and Steve Reed.

Also running in Ward 8 are Osam Ali and Coralia Tudor.

Election Day is Oct. 26.

stories.title: ‘First thing I thought of was the truck,’ says $44M Saskatchewan lotto winner
stories.summary: A tailgate was thrown to celebrate Doug Putland, a Prince Albert man who won $44 million. Now that he has his dream truck, he said the rest of cash is for his family.
stories.author: Tavi Dhillon
stories.content:
A tailgate was thrown in Saskatoon to honour Saskatchewan’s newest multimillionaire, Doug Putland, who won a $44-million lottery jackpot.

Putland won the Aug. 8 Lotto 6/49 Gold Ball jackpot, Sask Lotteries announced at Wednesday’s celebration in Saskatoon – more than 140 kilometres from his home in Prince Albert.

Putland bought his ticket in Rosthern, Sask., while en route to cheer on his beloved Saskatchewan Roughriders. Upon confirming that his ticket was the winner after the early-August draw, he said he “dropped the f-bomb and said, ‘holy smokes this is crazy.’”

“The amazing part is the very first thing I thought of was the truck,” he said at his tailgate, adding that his dream vehicle, a GMC Denali Ultimate, is now his.

Pultand also plans on sharing the money with his family, as well as donating some of it to charity, he said.

“Coming from a very big family, there was 14 of us in the family, and we had nothing. So, it’s kind of overwhelming in a way to know that I can set up my daughters and generations to come,” the winner added.

Putland has three daughters and nine grandchildren.

“They are never, ever going to experience having schooling debts and stuff like that. It gives them a start in life that everybody deserves, and not many get,” he said.

After being handed his $44-million cheque, Putland was also gifted a new, personalized Riders jersey with his surname and an autograph from quarterback Trevor Harris on the back.

“I’m going to wear this to all the games now,” Putland said, adding that he plans on tailgating Roughriders’ games in his new Denali, which came equipped with an incredible sound system.

Putland’s prize is the largest Saskatchewan has seen since 2022, the Western Canada Lottery Corporation (Wclc) said in a news release, noting that sums as large as $70 million were handed out that year.

stories.title: London woman killed in crash remembered as longtime gymnastics coach, dedicated mother
stories.summary: London woman killed in crash remembered as longtime gymnastics coach, dedicated mother CBC
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: Friends have identified a pedestrian struck by a vehicle in London's northwest end on Sept. 2 as Felicia Aves. The 41-year-old later died in hospital, leaving behind three children.
· Posted: Sep 09, 2026 6:32 PM EDT | Last Updated: 11 hours ago
Friends have identified 41-year-old Felicia Aves as the pedestrian struck by a vehicle in northwest London on Sept. 2.(Felicia Aves/ Facebook)
A 41-year-old London mother is being remembered for her "bubbly" personality and longtime dedication to coaching gymnastics, after she was struck by a vehicle in the city's northwest last week.

Emergency crews were called to the area of Sarnia Road and Chapman Court around 11:20 p.m. on Sept. 2, according to London police. A pedestrian was taken to hospital with life-threatening injuries and later died, police said.
Friends have identified the victim as Londoner Felicia Aves.
Pedestrian dies of injuries after collision in northwest London Wednesday night
"You don't expect it. There was no plan for this to happen," said Jamie Matte, a longtime friend of Aves. "It really is just a tragic thing that happened so quickly."
Matte, who is a director at London Gymnastics Academy, met Aves more than 30 years ago when they started gymnastics classes at the academy.
Felicia Aves, 41, is being remembered as a single mother of three and longtime gymnastics coach. (Felicia Aves/ Facebook)

"I remember her walking in the first day. She was so bubbly and the most naturally talented person you would ever meet," Matte said. "She could do anything first or second try, which drove us all nuts, but she was the sweetest and could get us out of any funk."

Both women eventually became coaches at the academy, with Aves teaching a mix of competitive and recreational tumbling, cirque and cheer classes. Matte estimates Aves coached thousands of kids over her 20-year career.
"Her energy and the way she coached showed her love of kids and her love of the sport," she said. "She would give her kids everything she had."
Matte said she doesn't know why Aves was out the night of the crash, but added that it would not be unusual for the lifelong athlete to go for a run at that hour.

"I think anyone in north London would know exactly who she is if you just described her because she ran that often," she said, adding that Aves would run for recreation, mental health and to complete errands.
Felicia Aves with her daughter Nigea at a gymnastics practice. (Supplied)
London police say they are are still investigating the cause of the crash.
Aves was also a single mother to three children, aged 18, 17 and 12.
"Those kids were her life," Matte said. "As a single mom, she tried to do everything they could so she could provide a life for them where they would excel with what they had."
Matte has launched a GoFundMe campaign to support the family with funeral costs, final expenses and the children's future.
"We're trying to pick up the pieces and we're trying to come together for these children as much as we can."

stories.title: U.S. to ban imports of some Canadian products as trade war escalates
stories.summary: Most Canadian-made liquor and some dairy products will be banned, but dozens of other products get tariff reprieve
stories.author: The Canadian Press staff
stories.content:
U.S. President Donald Trump plans to ban a range of Canadian exports and shuffle tariffs on others as Ottawa and Washington trade accusations over which side is responsible for the escalating trade war.

Most imports of Canadian-made liquor and a handful of dairy products will be banned from the United States at the end of September, but dozens of other products are getting a tariff reprieve.

Trump on Tuesday signed new executive orders ramping up retaliation after Canada imposed its latest set of counter tariffs on the United States.

The five new orders, which take effect later this month, will completely bar imports of certain Canadian goods, including motorcycles, some dairy products like whey and cheese, and molasses.

Alcoholic products from Canada, including beer, wine, rye and vodka, are also facing a ban.

But the orders also exempt from tariffs some Canadian products, including toilet paper, road salt, cement and fishing rods. Canadian whiskey and liqueur in bottles larger than four litres will also be exempt.

With these exports set for exemptions, new products with a similar dollar value have been substituted on the U.S. tariff list.

The product bans will go into place Sept. 29, while the additions and removals of other tariffs take effect Sept. 15.

Much like Canada was pressured by domestic companies and provincial leaders to back off of seafood tariffs, there has been pressure on the White House from state representatives and American companies about the economic impacts of certain tariffs.

In a statement posted on X Tuesday, Maine Sen. Susan Collins said she appreciated the Trump administration’s flexibility as she continued to press for a trade resolution with Canada.

“I mentioned in a letter to the Administration that Frenchville, a small Maine town on the Canadian border, would incur $10,000 in extra costs for road salt, threatening the town’s ability to provide municipal services,” wrote Collins, a Republican.

“These additional exemptions follow Canada’s announcement that it will carve out American seafood and fish products from its retaliatory tariff list, which would have caused significant harm to Maine’s lobstermen.”

Collins said tariffs on forest products were still in place and would lead to higher costs in Maine.

“I urge the Administration to continue to work to de-escalate this conflict,” she said.

The escalating U.S.-Canada trade war 'widens the divide between our two great countries,' an Ontario regional economic development and tourism official said.

The Associated Press

U.S. Republican Senator Jerry Moran said on social media that the Trump administration’s decision to exempt salt from tariffs on Canadian imports is “welcome news” for Kansas businesses and taxpayers.

He said salt is a critical commodity in his state, with local governments utilizing it to remove ice and keep Kansans “safe on the roads.”

“When these tariffs were proposed, I urged the U.S. Trade Representative to consider the impact on Kansas taxpayers and local businesses, including Morton Salt and Compass Minerals, both headquartered in Overland Park, which own and operate Canadian mines and bring salt into the United States for distribution,” he said.

BMO chief economist Doug Porter said the “reshuffling” of U.S. tariffs will have no new net effect on Canada’s economy. New import bans, while potentially consequential to the industries themselves, are also expected to have a marginal impact on the wider economy.

Porter said by swapping out tariffs on key inputs such as cement, the Trump administration could be trying to avoid further inflaming the inflationary pressures dogging the U.S. economy.

In a statement issued Tuesday, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer blamed Canada for Washington’s decision to escalate the trade war.

Fuel prices tend to ease off around this time of year, but one industry expert says drivers should expect no such relief this time as geopolitical tensions push crude oil prices higher.

The Canadian Press

Greer said the escalation was a “natural consequence” of Canada discriminating against American exports and choosing “senseless retaliation” over an almost final trade deal.

“President Trump will continue to leverage the tools at his disposal to defend the interests of American workers and exporters, and restore reciprocity in our bilateral trade relationships,” Greer said in a statement.

Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne said Ottawa is not ramping up the trade war when he spoke to reporters in Edmonton on Wednesday.

“This is not a trade conflict that we chose. We certainly did not escalate,” Champagne said. “The counter-measures that we have announced were proportionate, were strategic and were targeted.”

Canada’s retaliatory tariffs targeted the same value of goods hit by the U.S. on Aug. 22, and the products affected were drawn from those the U.S. targeted as well.

Speaking at an event hosted by the Edmonton Chamber of Commerce earlier in the day, Champagne recounted his conversation with U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on the sidelines of the G20 finance ministers meetings in North Carolina last week.

Champagne said he was “serious” and “firm” in the discussion. He said Canada’s counter-tariffs were about giving Canadian firms a “level playing field.”

B.C. Premier David Eby says the trade dispute with the United States has entered a new phase with the introduction of Canadian retaliatory tariffs. He warns British Columbians of job losses, but says his government will work with Ottawa to reduce the impact.

“If you’re going to put tariffs on Canadian companies who want to sell in the United States, if I don’t react, then I give an unfair advantage to U.S. companies wanting to come into Canada,” he told the crowd.

Trump’s Section 338 tariffs, imposed on a range of Canadian goods starting Aug. 22, hit some five per cent of Canada’s exports to the United States with a dollar value of around $28-billion.

Canada’s tariffs target a similar dollar value of U.S. exports but at duty rates of 15 to 50 per cent.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has said that Canada’s pivot away from the United States will come at a cost, but the alternative would be far worse.

Stephen Brown, chief North America economist at Capital Economics, said in a note to clients Wednesday that the items removed from the U.S. tariff list are valued at roughly US$1.7 billion, and the new targets are worth about the same amount.

He estimated that Trump’s new import bans will apply to 0.25 per cent of Canada’s exports to the United States, or 0.03 per cent of total U.S. imports.

Brown said the U.S. import bans will have “little effect on either economy.”

“Nonetheless, the escalation raises the risk that the 50 per cent tariffs will remain in place for longer than the month or so that we assumed for our forecasts, therefore dealing the Canadian economy a larger blow,” he said.

Most imports of Canadian-made liquor and a handful of dairy products will be banned from the United States at the end of September, but dozens of other products are getting a tariff reprieve.
Trump on Tuesday signed new executive orders ramping up retaliation after Canada imposed its latest set of counter tariffs on the United States.
The five new orders, which take effect later this month, will completely bar imports of certain Canadian goods, including motorcycles, some dairy products like whey and cheese, and molasses.
Alcoholic products from Canada, including beer, wine, rye and vodka, are also facing a ban.

But the orders also exempt from tariffs some Canadian products, including toilet paper, road salt, cement and fishing rods. Canadian whiskey and liqueur in bottles larger than four litres will also be exempt.
With these exports set for exemptions, new products with a similar dollar value have been substituted on the U.S. tariff list.
The product bans will go into place Sept. 29, while the additions and removals of other tariffs take effect Sept. 15.

Much like Canada was pressured by domestic companies and provincial leaders to back off of seafood tariffs, there has been pressure on the White House from state representatives and American companies about the economic impacts of certain tariffs.
In a statement posted on X Tuesday, Maine Sen. Susan Collins said she appreciated the Trump administration’s flexibility as she continued to press for a trade resolution with Canada.

“I mentioned in a letter to the Administration that Frenchville, a small Maine town on the Canadian border, would incur $10,000 in extra costs for road salt, threatening the town’s ability to provide municipal services,” wrote Collins, a Republican.

“These additional exemptions follow Canada’s announcement that it will carve out American seafood and fish products from its retaliatory tariff list, which would have caused significant harm to Maine’s lobstermen.”
Collins said tariffs on forest products were still in place and would lead to higher costs in Maine.
“I urge the Administration to continue to work to de-escalate this conflict,” she said.

stories.title: Moe says latest U.S. trade move would have minor impact on Saskatchewan
stories.summary: Trump's orders are set to take effect later this month and would also ban imports of certain Canadian goods, including motorcycles, some dairy products and alcoholic beverages.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe says the latest trade war escalation from the United States would have a minor impact on his province.

He says U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariffs remain on some key Saskatchewan exports, including honey and wooden furniture, but his executive orders signed Tuesday would drop tariffs on other exports, like road salt and electrical panels.

Trump’s orders are set to take effect later this month and would also ban imports of certain Canadian goods, including motorcycles, some dairy products and alcoholic beverages.

Moe says even with the new orders, about 94 per cent of Saskatchewan’s exports remain tariff free.

He says the goal should be to have no tariffs across the board, as they hurt both Canadian and American businesses and workers.

Moe says his government would continue working with businesses feeling the brunt of the trade dispute while also advocating for Saskatchewan.

stories.title: Think there’s nowhere to buy gifts downtown? This man found 60-plus stores
stories.summary: Kristan Smith says he wanted to spotlight downtown businesses and encourage Londoners to support them.
stories.author: Allison Young
stories.content:
Who says there’s nowhere to shop downtown? One man put that notion to the test.

London resident Kristan Smith found more than 60 places where he could buy a gift.

His search began with a post in the London Downtown Neighbours Network Facebook group asking what was going into the former Rock Universe store on Dundas Street. Smith also mentioned several new and longtime shops he enjoys visiting downtown.

Smith, 53, said the post “went crazy,” reaching about 25,000 views.

“(People commenting) just loved positive news about downtown,” Smith said. “I didn’t really say anything negative. It was just, ‘Hey, there’s new stuff. We should go check this out.’ And they really seemed to appreciate that.”

Smith said the response stuck with him.

Over the long weekend, he decided to see how many shops he could find during a walk around downtown, photographing storefronts where shoppers could buy a gift. He left out restaurants, spas, tattoo shops and other businesses that didn’t meet his criteria. Covent Garden Market was also not included because it was closed.

His search lead him from shops like Attic Books, a staple of the downtown community that opened in 1976, to The Crones Cave Metaphysical Shop, For You Consignment, Grooves and many more featured in what Smith called the unofficial downtown London shopping wall in a second Facebook post.

“I was actually personally surprised how many actual shops there were. I didn’t expect to get up to 50, but lo and behold, right?” Smith said.

“The collection was really impressive to me and I do think that with the number of local shops that we have downtown, it really does make a shopping afternoon of browsing and getting a bite to eat really worthwhile, even if there’s not a festival going on.”

Downtown bookstore owner reflects on 50-year run, and the chapters still ahead

New cafe brings taste of family's Colombia coffee farm to downtown London

Smith said it’s important to fight back against negativity about downtown by celebrating the good things.

“Narration is such a part of helping people create their perception. You can either tell a nice story or a bad story,” Smith said. “I think it’s time we start telling more nice stories.”

Several downtown shop owners reached out to Smith to thank him for shining a spotlight on their stores, including Alex Rupert, owner of Whim and Wonder, a stationery shop that opened on Dundas Street in July.

“It’s great to have a positive voice in the community because it’s so easy for people to be really negative, especially about downtown,” Rupert said.

“I’m not going to sugarcoat it, there are issues downtown for sure. Sometimes people don’t wanna bring their family out or they don’t feel safe being downtown and it’s really nice to have a voice that’s like, ‘Hey, it’s not as bad as people make it out to be. Maybe you just need to get out there and see what’s out there for yourself before making that judgment.’”

Rupert said she always tries to engage with positive posts about downtown London.

“There’s so much to do down here. It’s just getting people to come down and do it,” she said.

stories.title: Think there’s nowhere to buy gifts downtown? One man found 60-plus stores
stories.summary: Kristan Smith says he wanted to spotlight downtown businesses and encourage Londoners to support them.
stories.author: Allison Young
stories.content:
Who says there’s nowhere to shop downtown? One man put that notion to the test.

London resident Kristan Smith found more than 60 places where he could buy a gift.

His search began with a post in the London Downtown Neighbours Network Facebook group asking what was going into the former Rock Universe store on Dundas Street. Smith also mentioned several new and longtime shops he enjoys visiting downtown.

Smith, 53, said the post “went crazy,” reaching about 25,000 views.

“(People commenting) just loved positive news about downtown,” Smith said. “I didn’t really say anything negative. It was just, ‘Hey, there’s new stuff. We should go check this out.’ And they really seemed to appreciate that.”

Smith said the response stuck with him.

Over the long weekend, he decided to see how many shops he could find during a walk around downtown, photographing storefronts where shoppers could buy a gift. He left out restaurants, spas, tattoo shops and other businesses that didn’t meet his criteria. Covent Garden Market was also not included because it was closed.

His search lead him from shops like Attic Books, a staple of the downtown community that opened in 1976, to The Crones Cave Metaphysical Shop, For You Consignment, Grooves and many more featured in what Smith called the unofficial downtown London shopping wall in a second Facebook post.

“I was actually personally surprised how many actual shops there were. I didn’t expect to get up to 50, but lo and behold, right?” Smith said.

“The collection was really impressive to me and I do think that with the number of local shops that we have downtown, it really does make a shopping afternoon of browsing and getting a bite to eat really worthwhile, even if there’s not a festival going on.”

Smith said it’s important to fight back against negativity about downtown by celebrating the good things.

“Narration is such a part of helping people create their perception. You can either tell a nice story or a bad story,” Smith said. “I think it’s time we start telling more nice stories.”

Several downtown shop owners reached out to Smith to thank him for shining a spotlight on their stores, including Alex Rupert, owner of Whim and Wonder, a stationery shop that opened on Dundas Street in July.

“It’s great to have a positive voice in the community because it’s so easy for people to be really negative, especially about downtown,” Rupert said.

“I’m not going to sugarcoat it, there are issues downtown for sure. Sometimes people don’t wanna bring their family out or they don’t feel safe being downtown and it’s really nice to have a voice that’s like, ‘Hey, it’s not as bad as people make it out to be. Maybe you just need to get out there and see what’s out there for yourself before making that judgment.’”

Rupert said she always tries to engage with positive posts about downtown London.

“There’s so much to do down here. It’s just getting people to come down and do it,” she said.

stories.title: B.C. court certifies wheelchair users' class-action lawsuit against Air Canada
stories.summary: Vancouver - The B.C. Supreme Court has certified a class-action lawsuit filed against Air Canada by passengers who use wheelchairs and other mobility aids.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
VANCOUVER - The B.C. Supreme Court has certified a class-action lawsuit filed against Air Canada by passengers who use wheelchairs and other mobility aids.

Sept. 9, 2026

Updated at 5:20 p.m.

New subscriber benefit!

Copied to clipboard

A gifted article has been claimed.

Out of gifts for the month

Unfortunately you've used all of your gifts this month. Your counter will reset on the first day of next month.

GAC[](http://www.thestar.com/news/canada/british-columbia/b-c-court-certifies-wheelchair-users-class-action-lawsuit-against-air-canada/article_c699d426-3b0e-536f-a064-19126fff338d.html)

By The Canadian Press

Lead plaintiff Rodney Hodgins, who has spastic cerebral palsy, claims he had to “physically drag himself” down an aisle after Air Canada staff didn’t help him off a flight in 2023.

The court certified Hodgins’ lawsuit on Tuesday, and the class includes passengers who travelled with Air Canada between January 2021 and June 2023 who require a wheelchair getting to and from an aircraft and assistance with steps and seating.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Who’s downloading photos of your kid at dance competitions?

Image 9Image 10Image 11Image 12

The lawsuit alleges the airline breached contractual obligations to help passengers who rely on mobility aids and to “assist with physically moving passengers safely and with dignity.”

The ruling says Hodgins alleges Air Canada has a “systemic” issue and a “culture of apathy and indifference” toward passengers who need mobility-related assistance.

The ruling says Air Canada tried to argue Hodgins’ claims would be better adjudicated by the Canadian Transportation Agency, but the judge found the agency’s process would deprive Hodgins and class members “of the specific remedy they seek,” and deny “substantive access to justice.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 9, 2026.

stories.title: ‘Motorists have to adapt’: City unveils first stretch of centre-running bus lanes
stories.summary: A London Transit Express Route 90 bus travels uninterrupted between Masonville and White Oaks on a small section of Wellington Road.
stories.author: Bryan Bicknell
stories.content:
A London Transit Express Route 90 bus travels uninterrupted between Masonville and White Oaks on a small section of Wellington Road. It moves along a deep red centre lane reserved for buses. This is the first look at what’s to come for the city’s Bus Rapid Transit network under construction across various parts of the city.

Driver, Al Henderson sees progress down the road. “I think it’s going to be good when it’s finished,” he told CTV News. This week, London Transit began using the first completed section of centre running bus lanes. It stretches along Wellington Road between Simcoe Street and Grand Avenue.

The idea is buses can continue moving through busy areas while drivers have fewer buses coming in and out of their lanes. One of the biggest changes for drivers is there are no direct left turns into driveways or some side-streets.

That means advancing to the next light, then making a U-turn. Road users who have traversed this small stretch agree it’s going to take some getting used to. “Traffic flows. I like the left-hand turns they got. I enjoy it,” added Henderson.

The centre lanes are equipped with new protected platforms in the middle of the road for bus riders, along with signal crossings. With Wellington Road so wide now to accommodate BRT, resident Harsha Perera wishes there were more pedestrian crossings all the way up and down the road.

“When they want to cross, it’s difficult. I didn’t find many pedestrians’ crossings everywhere. So. Kind of a hassle,” he said. In the meantime, after several years of heavy construction on his corner at Wellington and Simcoe, business owner Ryan Alnajjar of Car Tech is hoping customers find their way back.

“It’s better right now. But the thing is that, because construction is still going on on the street, so people are trying to avoid going through Wellington Street. But at least it’s better than the construction, where it was front of us,” Alnajjar explained.

The new centre running lanes are part of the Wellington Gateway project of BRT, scheduled to begin full operations in 2029. “Motorists have to adapt to that concept of having the buses in the middle lanes,” said car passenger Chris Ginty.

“I notice there isn’t any bike lanes on either side. I know they have extended sidewalks. But the emphasis is on bus rapid transit. So, it should clear up the congestion, and help commuters get from point A to point B,” he said.
