By Ashley Joannou The Canadian Press

Justin and David Cho said in a statement on Wednesday that they are “struggling to understand how something so senseless could happen” and are appealing to anyone with information about the shooting to come forward.

“We are devastated by the tragic loss of our father, Chang Yong Cho. Our father was a man of deep Christian faith, gentle spirit, and unwavering kindness. To lose him in such a shocking way has shattered our hearts,” the brothers said in a statement released by the province’s Integrated Homicide Investigation Team.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Who’s downloading photos of your kid at dance competitions?

Chang Yong Cho was found dead in his apartment around 4 p.m. on Sunday, Aug. 30, more than 14 hours after police responded to reports of shots being fired about a block away.

It is the latest in dozens of cases where people have died or been injured by stray bullets in Canada in the last 30 years or so.

The brothers said their father was born in Korea in 1940, before building a life in Canada “grounded in faith, integrity, and service to others.”

“He loved golfing, dancing, sharing meals with friends, and spending time with his family. The greatest joy of his life began when he married our mother, Keum Soon Lee, in 1971,” the statement said.

After his wife’s death in 2012 the family said Cho “carried his grief quietly and faithfully.”

“He found comfort in time spent with family, friends, his church and community. We take solace in knowing that he is now reunited with our mother in eternal rest,” they said.

His funeral is scheduled for Sept. 14 in Burnaby.

Police said Tuesday that a group of young people, all aged under 18, were believed to have been involved in a personal dispute that led to the shooting and know police want to talk to them.

In the statement the brothers urge the youth and their parents to “to do the right thing” and turn themselves in to police.

“We are struggling to understand how something so senseless could happen to a man who lived with such gentleness and grace,” the brothers said.

“From his sisters, daughters-in-law, grandchildren, nieces and nephews, great nieces and nephews, extended family and friends — his loss is being deeply felt by all who had the pleasure of knowing him.”

Police want anyone with information about the incident, in which shots were fired near 18th and Humphries avenues, to contact IHIT. They also want to speak to anyone with dashcam or security footage from the area between 12:30 a.m. and 2 a.m. on Aug. 30.

While police on Tuesday called the case “highly unusual,” there have been at least 30 instances of people being killed or wounded by stray bullets in Canada since 1996.

At least 16 people have died, with multiple high-profile cases involving children and adults killed in public spaces as well as their homes.

In 2018, 15-year-old Alfred Wong was in the back seat of a vehicle with his family as they drove home from dinner in Vancouver when he was hit by a bullet as they drove past a shootout between gang rivals on the busy Broadway thoroughfare.

Kane Carter was sentenced in July to two life terms for second-degree murder, for killing Wong and an alleged gangster who died in the same shootout.

Other victims in stray-bullet shootings have included eight-year-old JahVai Roy, who died after being hit by a bullet in bed in Toronto in August last year, 21-year-old Indian student Harsimrat Randhawa, who died in April 2025 after being shot while waiting for a bus in Hamilton, Ont., and Dante Andreatta Marroquin, 12, killed in Toronto in 2020 when two men sprayed dozens of rounds from a moving vehicle.

Five-year-old Ethan Yellowbird died in 2011 after being struck by a bullet while he slept on the Samson Cree reserve south of Edmonton, while in 2007, 11-year-old Ephraim Brown was attending a birthday party outside a Toronto housing complex when he was struck in the neck by a bullet and died.

Laurie Tinga survived after being shot in the head in 2005 by a stray bullet while watching TV in her home in Port Moody, B.C., in what police called a gang shootout.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 9, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: ‘Dynacare sucks,’ Kinew says, as company orders striking employees back to work
stories.summary: Manitoba Premier says he May de-privatize lab testing after his NDP government intervened to end the strike
stories.author: Ian Bickis
stories.content:
Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew, a day after his government intervened to end a medical workers strike, called out their employer and suggested he may de-privatize lab testing.

“Dynacare sucks. Dynacare sucks,” Kinew repeated numerous times Wednesday when asked by reporters about the one-day walkout by 350 Dynacare lab technicians and technologists.

“The workers are frustrated. Absolutely they’re frustrated (and) rightfully so,” the premier added.

“Dynacare, get back to the (bargaining) table and give these people a raise.”

Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew, a day after his NDP government intervened to end a strike by medical workers, questioned their employer and suggested he may de-privatize lab testing.

The Canadian Press

The workers walked off the job Tuesday morning, shuttering 22 Dynacare lab locations across the province and stopping the collection of thousands of tests, including blood work, urinalysis and prenatal checks.

Hours later, Kinew’s government successfully argued to the Manitoba Labour Board that Dynacare work is vital to the health system. By day’s end, the board ordered the workers back.

The union, the Manitoba Association of Health Care Professionals, complied and the employees were back on the job Wednesday morning.

The union and Dynacare didn’t have an essential workers agreement in place in case of a strike.

Kinew lambasted Dynacare for “making a mess of the situation” and said his government had no choice but to intervene, because it has a higher responsibility to keep the health system running.

“Nobody should be using the results of a cancer test as leverage in a negotiation. Nobody,” the premier said.

The strike centred around wages. The union said its workers earn as much as 20 to 50 per cent less than counterparts in the public system.

Dynacare said in a statement that it shares Kinew’s commitment to maintaining reliable lab services and that’s why it’s pushing for a “sustainable” collective agreement.

“We acknowledge that this has been a difficult situation for patients and for the province, and we share the premier’s desire for a resolution,” the company said.

It said it has offered a substantial pay increase and has proposed arbitration as the fastest path to a fair resolution.

Union president Jason Linklater said workers are determined to close the wage gap and aren’t prepared to risk that in arbitration.

He said the premier has the power to fix the problem, including by adding a wage agreement to the existing contract, and making more of the contract public.

Linklater said he wants to know why Kinew renewed the contract last year without better wage supports for workers and has now cut off the union’s ability to strike.

“Government intervened; they totally took away the single piece of leverage,” he said.

“There’s a whole bunch of anger right now, and people who feel betrayed. But I have to remain hopeful that there’s still a solution.”

He pushed back on the province’s perspective that critical testing would be lost, noting that Shared Health had said essential services would be maintained through government labs.

Kinew said fault also lies with the former Progressive Conservative government for contracting out all non-hospital testing to Dynacare – a private operator.

He said his NDP government is considering de-privatizing the testing but acknowledged it’s a tall, very expensive decision.

“The PCs privatized this system,” Kinew said. “Once you privatize something and it goes to the private sector, it becomes extraordinarily costly to bring it back into public hands.”

Asked for a response to Kinew, Progressive Conservative labour critic Josh Guenter, in a statement, said, “Under the NDP, we have seen wait times continue to go up across all sectors of our health-care system.

Guenter added, “We saw, once again, this premier – who ran on fixing health care – choosing conflict over care.”

stories.title: Ryan Brown’s bagpipe talent strikes a chord with London Knights
stories.summary: The Dallas Stars prospect showed off an unexpected skill during the Knights’ trip to Victoria, B.C.
stories.author: Ryan Pyette
stories.content:
Every hockey team with a lot of new faces needs something fun to break the ice.

The London Knights used their trip to Victoria, B.C., for that purpose. Little did they know they would share a moment over bagpipes.

“We were walking to dinner and there was a guy on the street just playing,” veteran forward Ryan Brown said. “I went up to him and asked if I could play a song and do the notes for him.

“He let me.”

As the whole team watched, the Dallas Stars prospect displayed a hidden skill he had honed since Grade 7 at St. Andrew’s College in Aurora. The bagpipes are notorious for requiring patience and discipline to learn properly.

“They have a world-renowned piping class and program there,” the 18-year-old Newmarket native said, “so I thought it was pretty unique to start and learn it. I loved the sound of it and kept it going.”

Brown hasn’t performed much in public, but he did play at a funeral once and occasionally piped his lacrosse team onto the field at school – right before taking part in the game.

Would he play the national anthem at Canada Life Place in uniform before a Knights game if GM Mark Hunter asked?

“If he wants me to, I would,” Brown quipped. “I’ve got my own (set) just to keep it up and practice, to have the music in shape and my memorization of everything.”

Every once in a while, he plays for his billet family.

“They think it’s pretty cool,” the 2023 Sarnia Sting first-rounder said. “They’re loud, though. I think if I played them every day, they would get tired of it sometimes.”

Brown went to SAC with Senators first-rounder Jaxon Cover, one of the Knights stars this season, for a couple of years. Did his teammate from the Cayman Islands join him in the woodwind section?

“I don’t think he played any instrument,” Brown said. “He was pretty good at soccer, though.”

STING ON DECK: The Knights’ older players are scattering for NHL rookie and training camps this week. So it will be a younger crew that dresses in the final pre-season tune-ups Thursday (7 p.m. at Canada Life Place) and Friday in Sarnia (7:05 p.m.) against the Sting.

The Knights don’t expect to see new import signee Marcus Nordmark, the Ducks first-rounder, until he is done trying out for Anaheim. For many, this week is the last chance to crack an increasingly competitive roster.

“The pre-season has been a good test to see our team together,” Brown said. “Victoria is a good team and it was cool to play against a full group of new faces. It’ll be good for the younger guys to get some time in against Sarnia and we’ll be ready when everyone comes back.”

Brown didn’t communicate much with Dallas ahead of the NHL draft and was pleasantly surprised to hear his name called while he watched from home. The 6-foot, 192-pounder exploded offensively after being acquired from Sarnia for fellow forward Logan Hawery – with 16 goals and 40 points in 33 games, then three goals and five points in five playoff tilts against Sault Ste. Marie.

“Being a late (birth date), guys my age got to go to camps and play rookie tournaments last year,” he said, “so being able to experience it will be super cool and a good learning experience to play with older players.

“I’m happy with how my year went and I think this one will be even better. In London, we need to make a little bit of a deeper run in the playoffs this year, which is the goal.”

There will be some challenges along the way, of course.

But it probably won’t be as difficult as trying to master the bagpipes.

stories.title: Trump’s latest trade threat weighs on Canadian firms with U.S. contracts
stories.summary: Shares of Canadian companies doing business with the U.S. fell following Trump’s threat to products being sold to federal contractors.
stories.author: Bloomberg News
stories.content:
Shares of Canadian companies that do business with the U.S. government fell following President Donald Trump’s threat to bar Canadian-origin products from being sold to federal contractors.

“From now on, NO Reciprocity – NO Access!” Trump said in a social media post Tuesday afternoon, saying Canadian and provincial governments ban U.S. firms from winning contracts in the country.

He directed the U.S. General Services Administration to work with the U.S. Trade Representative to “take all necessary steps to Remove Canadian-origin products from Gsa’s Multiple Award Schedules unless Canada restores full and fair reciprocity for American Farmers and Companies.”

Share prices for IT consulting company CGI Inc., engineering firms WSP Global Inc., AtkinsRealis Group Inc. and Stantec Inc., and construction firm Aecon Group Inc. had all dropped by more than 2 per cent in Toronto as of Wednesday afternoon.

It’s not yet clear how “Canadian-origin products” are defined, and whether the directive includes services or parent companies of U.S. subsidiaries.

CGI has “relatively material exposure” to U.S. government contracts, National Bank of Canada analyst Doug Taylor wrote in a client note. “We estimate U.S. government revenue could represent between 15 per cent to 20 per cent of Cgi’s total revenue.”

But the company primarily sells services, not goods, in the U.S., which means CGI May be “potentially more insulated than the current scope of the language implies,” Taylor said. “Risk would become more meaningful if restrictions instead apply based on Canadian (parent) ownership, e.g., if U.S.-based subsidiaries of Canadian companies are also included.”

CGI said in an emailed statement that CGI Federal, which serves U.S. federal agencies, is a “U.S.-based, wholly-owned operating subsidiary,” and that it employs over 8,000 people “who live and work across 60 U.S. locations.”

Trump strikes back with executive orders banning Canadian goods, including alcohol and dairy

Trump targets Bombardier, Canadian dollar in Truth Social blitz ahead of tariff deadline

“CGI Federal is proud to provide U.S.-originated technology services and core business platforms under a wide range of contract vehicles to support the federal government’s mission-critical objectives,” it added.

Following the first round of U.S. tariffs in 2025, the Canadian government introduced a policy that favours local businesses in federal procurement and prioritizes Canadian materials in major construction and defence projects. The move came alongside a push to make Canada more self-sufficient and sovereign in digital capabilities.

Provinces have also announced limits to U.S. procurement. For example, the Quebec government said this week that it will reserve certain calls for tenders for Canadian firms, and Ontario has a policy that greatly restricts procurement from U.S. businesses while preferring local firms.

stories.title: AI minister says solutions exist after Anthropic researcher quits over safety fears
stories.summary: The federal artificial intelligence minister said the government is closely following the situation at Anthropic after a researcher who resigned from the company Tuesday said people in the industry fear AI could “kill us all.”'
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — The federal artificial intelligence minister said the government is closely following the situation at Anthropic after a researcher who resigned from the company Tuesday said people in the industry fear AI could “kill us all.”

Evan Solomon also told reporters Wednesday such warnings aren’t new and that there are both regulatory and technical solutions to the dangers posed by AI.

He pointed to the Liberal government’s efforts to introduce privacy legislation. “We’re establishing a new regulator that will have the power to hold these big companies to account,” he said.

Solomon also said the government is investing in AI safety and noted ongoing work by Canadian AI pioneer Yoshua Bengio on safe AI. Solomon added the government is also working with other countries on ways to protect citizens.

He said there are “real concerns” about the negative consequences of AI.

On Tuesday, researcher Jacob Coxon, who worked at both OpenAI and Anthropic, said in a post on X that neither “company is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.”

I resigned from Anthropic today. I spent the last three years doing pretraining research at both OpenAI and Anthropic. Neither company is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives. More thoughts below. — Jacob Coxon (@hilbertspaess) September 9, 2026

He said those who are building AI “earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.”

Adding that this is “not a marketing stunt,” Coxon said that many in the industry will use more measured phrasing when speaking publicly, even as they express fear in private.

Solomon made the comments in Edmonton, where he announced the launch of a new initiative to boost AI literacy among Canadians.

That initiative includes “AI essentials” courses for students, educators and Canadians in general. The government is partnering with the Alberta Machine Intelligence Institute, one of Canada’s three national AI institutes.

“We’ll invest $13 million to launch this course, to expand AI literacy for every single Canadian,” Solomon said.

Last week, he announced new voluntary principles for building data centres in Canada in response to growing backlash against data centres across the country.

The federal government won’t be enforcing the guidelines. Solomon told reporters last week decisions on data centres fall under provincial and municipal jurisdiction.

In response to a question about whether the government will monitor compliance, Solomon said the agreement will provide reliable and verifiable information on the standards that were set.

“Those are going to be enforced by the municipalities or the provinces,” he said.

The framework says data centres must “create lasting local benefits,” can’t shift electricity costs to Canadians, and must minimize water use and their impact on the environment. It also calls for transparency on local impacts and says data centres have to “bring strategic value to Canada.”

The list of signatories includes Amazon, Google, Meta, Microsoft, Bell, Telus and Anthropic.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 9, 2026.

Anja Karadeglija, The Canadian Press

stories.title: New Toronto condo will feature porcelain tile handpicked in Italy
stories.summary: Summerhill-Rosedale project possesses the same DNA as many other Woodcliffe developments
stories.author: Dave LeBlanc
stories.content:
Joseph Notarfonzo has been cutting the hair of investment bankers, real estate moguls, creative types (such as this columnist), fellow Yonge Street retailers and office stiffs since 1961. If you were to ask, he’d likely be able to tell you how many times the floor tiles have been replaced at his little barbershop at 1204 Yonge St., or give you an accurate estimate how long a pair of shoes lasts for someone who spends all day on his feet. A good storyteller and a sharp wit, the octogenarian might also tell you he’s ready to retire.

But it’s not true, said Eve Lewis, CEO of Woodcliffe Landmark Properties: “Paul [Oberman] bought the building, and we’d always worked together, but I had never worked with the tenants, so I introduced myself to Joe and he said, ‘Well, you know, I am thinking of retiring’. That was 15 years ago,” she says with a laugh.

Like barbers or architects or artists, real estate developers never really retire. Had it not been for the 2011 plane crash that took his life, Mr. Oberman would be standing beside his wife, Ms. Lewis, at Yonge Street and Birch Avenue, admiring the enormous poster promoting “The Summerhill,” a boutique condominium that, once construction begins, might be the only thing to part Mr. Notarfonzo from his scissors.

For the company that gifted the city, in the first decade of this century, the restoration of Canadian-Pacific’s North Toronto Station (1915, now home to an Lcbo) and the beloved shops known as “The Five Thieves” (1892) – both across the street and both sold in 2016 – it’s a fitting location for Woodcliffe to build again.

But, unlike the slapdash condominium towers that dot the city, this one will be special, even on the outside, thanks to a shipload of Italian porcelain and architect Peter Clewes, who has “designed every single inch of this building,” said Ms. Lewis.

“We went to Modena, in Italy, with Peter in June,” said Woodcliffe VP of investments and corporate strategy Stratton Townley. “That’s where 90 per cent of Italian porcelain comes from. You go to these factories, and they show you not only the materials and how they manufacture it … but they also show you the mounting systems that they recommend.”

Mr. Clewes, principal/owner at architectsAlliance, could, at this stage of his career, pull a Frank Gehry and scribble a few things onto a cocktail napkin and let a gang of underlings decipher his chicken-scratches. But that, he said, would just add to the commodification that has plagued residential high-rise design for the past decade.

“It’s less about beautiful buildings and well-proportioned living spaces, and more about the number of investment units that can be packed into buildings with massing and program dictated by tall building guidelines,” said Mr. Clewes. “This project represents an opportunity to return to my roots as a designer, to create something compelling, beautiful, contextual … to think deeply about how the building meets grade, about materiality; above all else, about creating a beautiful place to live.”

Clad in that scrumptious imported porcelain intersected by bits of champagne-coloured metal and featuring acres and acres of glass, it will be beautiful indeed. Plus, with the heritage restoration of the stores along the Yonge Street sidewalk, the project possesses the same DNA as so many other Woodcliffe developments: “Paul loved retail restoration, office, more than he liked residential,” said Ms. Lewis.

“We’ve shifted our focus to mixed-use,” said Mr. Townley. “We still love doing office and retail, but we’ve added the residential component.”

At the sales office down the road, Brodie Townley of Market Vision fires up a full-wall video screen. With the push of a button, he can place potential owners on any of the building’s 33 storeys. On floors with only two units, he can demonstrate how one can, literally, trace the path of the sun.

“Do you love morning or evening light?” he asks as he dials up 6:50 a.m. in June. “This is on the 28th floor, and you can just feel the expansiveness of where our views in this building are protected.” Lower down, and North Toronto Station’s clock tower – inspired by the Campanile in St. Mark’s Square in Venice – seems so close one could reach out and touch it.

Mr. Clewes’s sashless corner windows and staggered balconies, which eliminate that annoying roof overhead, means each unit enjoys a feast of sky, clouds, the trees of north Rosedale, and the mighty asphalt river of Yonge Street, which effortlessly divides the city into east and west.

“It was a real challenge to design that building because it has such a small floor plate,” said Ms. Lewis. “But the opportunities it created is that for 1,800 square feet, you can still have three sides of glass, which is unheard of.”

Interiors come courtesy of Brian Gluckstein, and, while minimal, landscaping is from the imaginative minds at Claude Cormier’s CCxA (the firm that gave Toronto the dog fountain and Berczy Park) and will feature a horse: “So, at [the grocery store] Harvest Wagon, there’s a wagon outside that Paul and I put there,” Ms. Lewis said with a smile. “So, this is the horse that got away from the wagon.”

And speaking of horses, the one Toronto rode during the condo boom has left the barn: the market has crashed and most developers have switched to building rental buildings. But Summerhill-Rosedale is a horse of a different colour and snack bracket, said Ms. Lewis: “The upper end of the market is a market that has the opportunity to be able to make choices for themselves, so our plan is that we could probably be under construction in 12 to 18 months.”

As to where all those movers and shakers are going to get a haircut, well, that’s another story.

stories.title: SIU charges London police officer after man injured at hospital
stories.summary: The constable faces an assault causing bodily harm charge stemming from a March incident.
stories.author: Dale Carruthers
stories.content:
The constable faces an assault causing bodily harm charge stemming from a March incident.

Last updated 28 minutes ago[](http://lfpress.com/news/local-news/SIU-charges-London-police-officer-after-man-injured-at-hospital#comments-area)

Special Investigations Unit. (File photo/Postmedia Network)

Ontario’s police watchdog has charged a London police constable after a man was injured during an interaction with an officer at Victoria Hospital.

Police arrested and apprehended a man under the Mental Health Act – legislation allowing a person to be apprehended and taken for psychiatric examination – on March 18, the Special Investigations Unit (SIU) said on Wednesday.

The man, whose name and age weren’t released, was taken to Victoria Hospital, where he was seriously injured during an interaction with an officer, the SIU said.

Const. Stephen Farrand is charged with one count of assault causing bodily harm. He is scheduled to appear in court on Sept. 22.

“As the matter is before the courts, and in consideration of the fair trial interests of the accused, the SIU will not provide further comment on the investigation,” the agency said in a statement.

London police issued a media release one day after the incident, saying the SIU had invoked its mandate and providing additional details.

Police responded around 11 a.m. to a report of a man who refused to stop at an east-end intersection that was closed for a traffic investigation, police said at the time.

Officers located the man in his vehicle. He was in distress and officers broke a window to remove him, police said.

The man was apprehended and taken to hospital. He suffered an injury requiring medical attention, police said.

The SIU investigates cases involving serious injury, death, gunshots and allegations of sexual assault involving police officers.

stories.title: Western prof develops post-concussion resources to support teens
stories.summary: Western prof Heather Shepherd developed a framework and peer support program to help students safely return to school, sports after concussion
stories.author: Special to Western News
stories.content:
Professor Heather Shepherd knows the dangers of concussion well. During her first two years of high school, she sustained four concussions, three of them within a six-month span. After the third concussion, she was taken out of school for the remainder of the academic year.

“I spent months recovering, isolated in a dark room. Not only was it a change in my routine and physical activity, but I lost a lot of the social relationships that came with sport and school.”

And she wasn’t the only one. Speaking to other adolescents who had sustained a concussion, she realized their journeys often echoed her own; one in four adolescents will sustain a concussion by the age of 18.

Despite this alarming number, many Canadian schools don’t have a plan to welcome students back to class gradually and safely.

Although legislation and policies like Rowan’s Law and Memorandum 158 exist to promote student safety surrounding concussion, they only exist in Ontario. Even there, these laws and policies are not always known or followed. They also fail to address the personal challenges many teens face when returning to the classroom.

Now a professor in Western’s School of Occupational Therapy , Shepherd is building on her previous work to help address this gap.

The sweet spot is a gradual return, according to Shepherd. Evidence shows that progressively returning to activity is the best approach for adolescents’ recovery and wellbeing.

“But that’s not what we see happening,” she said worriedly.

“Schools and teachers often don’t have the space, personnel or time resources to provide supports post-concussion. It’s not that they don’t want to support students – they are limited in what they can feasibly provide.” – Heather Shepherd, occupational therapy professor

While working as a school-based occupational therapist, Shepherd saw firsthand how the accommodations recommended for students after a concussion were difficult for educators to implement given resource constraints. Spotting this challenge, she wanted to address the gap in a way that would help students get back to their routine safely, while still being reasonable for educators and schools to implement.

Shepherd said it was like opening pandora’s box.

“What started as a small project has really shed light on a challenge so many are facing.”

Shepherd devised the Return to School Framework as a PhD student at University of Calgary. Created in collaboration with the school community, including students, caregivers and educators, as well as her fellow investigators, the framework offers schools a bundle of feasible, practical and accessible strategies to support recovering students.

“It’s leveraging the existing resources to make a change, not reinventing the wheel,” she said.

One of these supports is the Buddy Program, something Shepherd and her team designed after hearing students request extra social support during when returning after a concussion. The Buddy Program pairs recovering students with a peer, ensuring they have a friend to rely on at school – whether providing encouragement or taking class notes. Ensuring children aren’t losing social connections in their formative years was a crucial addition to Shepherd’s return-to-school protocol.

The framework also offers guidance and strategies that school boards and teachers can follow once a student endures a concussion. It includes details that often get lost or overlooked – like how schools can best communicate with caregivers.

With Shepherd’s framework, it’s no longer left to under-resourced teachers to figure out how to welcome a student back to school after a concussion; educators would have a guide they can use, developed in collaboration with school communities, to help students with the tools already at hand.

Now, working as a researcher in the Faculty of Health Sciences at Western, Shepherd wants to determine how the Return to School Framework could be implemented in schoolboards across Ontario, and ultimately, nation-wide.

“In 10 years, I hope students who sustain concussions will have the support of their teachers, guidance counselors and other adults to help guide them back to school in a supportive way that aligns with the supports they need, given their symptoms, while ensuring we’re not putting undue hardship on the school. There’s an opportunity to make a big difference over the next few years.”

And for Shepherd, collaborating with the people who will be using these programs is fundamental. Partnering with educators and connecting with students as part of her research, she’s learned both of the challenges and possibilities ahead.

“By engaging the people who have lived the experience, we end up with solutions that are more realistic, more practical and more relevant to what their needs are,” she said. “That’s what keeps me motivated as a researcher.”

Learn more about how Western is optimizing health for all .

stories.title: ‘Potentially catastrophic fire code violations’: Trail’s End Market closure necessary to protect the public, states fire dept
stories.summary: A popular weekend destination just outside of London has been ordered closed for fire safety violations, according to the Thames Centre Fire Dept.
stories.author: Sean Irvine
stories.content:
A popular weekend destination just outside of London has been ordered closed for fire safety violations, according to the Thames Centre Fire Dept.

Trail’s End Farmers Market must remain shut until multiple requirements are met, leaving its operators, vendors and visitors in limbo.

For decades, the market, between London and Thamesford, has been a southwestern Ontario weekend tradition.

But – at least for the short-term – all outings here have been put on hold.

With police standing by, fire chief Nick Dorken posted closure notices on the market buildings due to what he calls serious concerns.

“There are a number of potentially catastrophic fire code violations and deficiencies with that building that led us down to this path.”

The road down the path began last spring when a fire inspector, acting on a public complaint, visited Trail’s End.

“We were looking at blocked exits at that time,” he confirmed to CTV News London.

Over the next several months, additional inspections were carried out with multiple agencies assisting.

At one point, indoor cooking facilities were ordered shut – a move Dorken states the business owner complied with.

But shortly afterwards more concerns were noted.

“And as the list grew, we reached out to our advisors with the office of the fire marshal, who then attended themselves,” said Dorken.

After a two-day inspection, the closure order was posted. Those inside the buildings will now require the approval of the fire dept.

Dorken says the decision was not taken lightly given the number of people who rely on Trail’s End for employment, food and services.

He said the operator will determine the next step.

“The ball is in their court right now to be able to come back to us with suggestions on how to make the building safe. And then we have the authority to decide whether that is the case or not.”

Part of the concern, Dorken added, relates to a 1993 fire. That year, a large blaze destroyed most of the property. It was later rebuilt.

“We do not want to be in the situation where we have another structure fire, especially given the amount of people that attend that location, especially on the weekends.”

CTV News London reached out to representatives from Trail’s End for comment but we have not yet received a reply.

stories.title: D.J. Kennington sees shades of 2012 in Marc-Antoine Camirand’s dominance
stories.summary: The St. Thomas native says Camirand’s dominant season rivals his own remarkable 2012 championship run.
stories.author: Ryan Pyette
stories.content:
D.J. Kennington’s all-time great NASCAR Canada Series run in 2012 has company.

The 49-year-old St. Thomas native won seven races and had eight podium finishes in 12 starts at the height of his dominance. Marc-Antoine Camirand, the current king, already has seven wins and hopes to add a historic eighth in the finale Saturday (6 p.m.) at Delaware Speedway.

Camirand, a 47-year-old from Saint-Léonard-d’Aston, Que., has 10 podiums in 13 races and has wrapped up his third consecutive points title and fourth in five years. It takes some of the suspense out of the final tour stop.

“It’s better for the fans and the racers (if it’s not decided), but he had such a good year,” Kennington, the series Ironman, said. “He locked it up and you have to give him credit. It’s 100 per cent (comparable) to my 2012 season.”

Sixteen years ago, Kennington simply had to take the green flag and start the last race – then at Kawartha Speedway – to win the crown. That was the peak of an eight-year stretch in which the local speedster finished in the top three in points every season.

The driver of the No. 17 Castrol Edge Dodge was second overall a year ago and is currently fifth in the standings, two points behind Andrew Ranger.

“It’s part of the game,” he said. “They (the Camirand team) earned it. They kicked our butts all year. They’re the champs and we now go to work and figure out how the hell we stop it from happening next year.”

For now, Kennington’s team will pull out all the stops to get a victory at its home track.

“It’s been an up-and-down season for us,” he said. “We’re aiming to end it on a strong note and try to get a checkered flag at Delaware. I grew up racing here and it’s always fun. We have to reset the tone here and have our car run as top notch as we can.”

Kennington went with a bold strategy last weekend in the WeatherTech 200 at Canadian Tire Motorsport Park in Bowmanville and came up a half-lap short of a memorable finish before running out of fuel. It was the first time he tried that in this series.

D.J. Kennington shrugs off tough luck as season reaches halfway point

Hot Stuff: At family-friendly Delaware Speedway, high speeds, lots of history

“There are no reserves, no gauges, no nothing,” he said. “It’s all by calculations before the race starts and it depends how many caution laps you get and how hard you’re pushing the car. We went nine laps further than anyone else has ever gone there on fuel. We gambled and needed one more caution in the middle of the race, which we didn’t get. Our races are usually pretty planned that you know you’re going to get fuel, but track position was so key there with 39 cars.

“It sucks, but we weren’t in a championship points situation so we were trying for a win.”

Will they be as daring this weekend in front of family and friends during the NASCAR Canada Championship 200?

There is absolutely nothing to lose.

“The way I look at it, my wife plays like that all the time with her van,” Kennington joked. “Every time I get in, it’s on empty and she has a fuel gauge. It’s one of those things. We tried it. We just rolled the dice, needed sixes and rolled fives.

“It’s important to win. We want to finish strong at home.”

stories.title: Maine Senator lobbies, saves Canadian rock salt and cement from import tariff list
stories.summary: Maine's senator told the administration that road salt and cement are crucial to the state and would be severely affected by the tariffs.
stories.author: Stewart Lewis
stories.content:
The Trump administration agreed to swap these items for new duties on all-terrain vehicles, certain cheeses, and motorboats

The Trump administration has announced that Canadian road salt and cement will be removed from import tariffs as of Sept. 15., earning the gratitude of Maine’s Republican senator, Susan Collins.

U.S. communities that share the border with Canada rely heavily on Canadian rock salt to keep winter roads safe, according to Maine TV news station Wabi .

Collins, a five-term incumbent, says exempting those two items was something she lobbied for, reports the news outlet.

“I appreciate the Administration’s announcement that it will exempt road salt and cement from U.S. tariffs. In my communication with (U.S. Trade Representative Jamison) Greer and (Commerce Secretary Howard) Lutnick, I focused on road salt and cement as two products crucial to Maine that would be severely affected by these tariffs,” she said.

Collins explained that Frenchville, a small Maine town on the Canadian border, would incur U.S.$10,000 in extra costs for road salt. And one Maine cement company owner would pay U.S.$150,000 each month because of the tariff.

The Trump administration agreed to swap Canadian rock salt and cement for new duties on all-terrain vehicles, certain cheeses, and motorboats, reports Wabi.

Meanwhile, in an August 27 statement , Collins expressed her appreciation for Canada’s decision to remove seafood and fish products from its retaliatory tariff list. “These tariffs would have caused tremendous harm to Maine’s lobstermen, disrupting one of their most important markets during the fall fishing season,” she said.

She also advocated for improved trade relations with Canada, based on the two countries’ historic ties: “Canada is not China. Canada is one of our closest allies and largest trading partners. Our economies are inextricably linked, especially in the border regions. Continuing with these tariffs will harm Maine families, small businesses, municipalities, manufacturers, and farmers.”

This past weekend in an interview with Politico , Collins said the White House doesn’t understand how the trade war with Canada is affecting Maine.

“I think the administration has very much underestimated the impact on Maine families, ON small manufacturers, ON our agricultural products,” Collins said in an interview. “And that’s what I’m trying my best to educate them about. They look at this issue as a macro issue. And in fact, the micro impact on a state like Maine is considerable.”

Collins has been an ongoing critic of the tariffs on Canada, reports Politico , noting that she had spoken on the Senate floor about the close economic relationship between Maine and Canada ahead of a symbolic vote against earlier tariffs last year . And she, with other Maine Republicans, was quick to push back on Trump’s decision to impose 50 percent tariffs on Canada in July.

Canada is Maine’s largest trade and investment partner , according to the Maine International Trade Center (Mitc), a public-private partnership between the state government and private sector. Roughly 40 percent of all Maine’s goods exports go to Canada, Mitc estimates. That includes agricultural goods and pulp and paper, but these businesses are expecting a severe drop in demand.

Meanwhile, this shift on rock salt and cement May serve to boost Collins’ chances at reelection in the U.S. fall mid-term elections.

National Post previously reported that pollsters and analysts have speculated her political fortunes could fade in the wake of the ongoing trade war.

The Democrats have been framing the race in Maine around affordability — a major issue across the board for all voters —and in Maine and other border states, Trump’s tariff policies could have an adverse effect on Republican efforts to similarly frame the issue.

stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
A new analysis of Ontario’s municipal elections suggests some modest improvements in competition, with fewer uncontested races but only sparse gains in the share of female candidates.

By The Canadian Press

With 414 municipalities holding elections next month, the Association of Municipalities of Ontario says the trends are encouraging but they are no reason to relax efforts to strengthen local democracy.

Nearly one in four mayors, reeves and other heads of council have been acclaimed, down from the previous two election years.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Who’s downloading photos of your kid at dance competitions?

Image 9Image 10Image 11

Across Ontario, 400 candidates ran unopposed, also down from recent elections.

This year, 68 per cent of all candidates have never been in municipal office, a two-point increase over 2022.

The number of female candidates across Ontario ticked up by just one point compared to 2022, to 32 per cent.

“This year’s numbers show that Ontarians continue to step forward to serve their communities, with more than two-thirds of candidates new to the municipal election process,” Lindsay Jones, executive director of AMO, said in a statement.

“Strong municipal government depends on people being willing to put their names forward, compete in elections and take on the responsibility of representing their communities.”

There are 444 municipal governments in Ontario but only 414 hold elections, since some upper-tier municipalities are populated by lower-tier elections. Plus, in 19 municipalities the entire council was acclaimed.

The smallest of those is Township of Brethour, population 105, and the largest is the Town of Kapuskasing, home to 8,057.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 9, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Welcome back, Western: Back-to-school season hits campus
stories.summary: Western University welcomes 5,200 first-year students moving onto campus and welcomes back thousands of returning students.
stories.author: Western Communications
stories.content:
Western’s campus is bustling and vibrant as the newest cohort of incoming students start their university journeys, joining thousands of others returning after the summer term.

There are telltale signs of a new academic year.

“September is one of my favourite times on campus – you can feel the energy and excitement for the year ahead and the sense of community as we welcome our newest students,” said Western P resident Alan Shepard. “I want to thank everyone involved in creating a welcoming and supportive environment for all our students, regardless of where they are in their academic journey. Best wishes to all for a successful year.”

From karaoke and food trucks to bumper cars to a late-night arcade in the Mustang Lounge, Orientation Week – known as OWeek – is in full swing with a full lineup of activities to help break the ice and share “purple and proud” traditions with Western’s incoming students.

More than 5,200 first-year students moved into Western residence buildings over the weekend, greeted by upper-year Sophs and new classmates.International and graduate students also returned to campus for a new academic year, finding support and connection through Western’s suite of programming.

Students, staff, faculty, alumni and their families filled the stands at Alumni Stadium as the Western Mustangs football team kicked off their season against York University on Sunday, defeating the Lions 78 to 7.

OWeek also helps students connect with their new community, starting with volunteering alongside London, Ont. organizations, including the Muslim Resource Centre and Indigenous employment and education centre Nokee Kwe, through OServes. Students can contribute through hands-on activities such as making cards for pediatric patients or preparing welcome kits for vulnerable high school students.

Western provides a range of programming and student support during OWeek, including Care Hubs, help stations in high-traffic areas where volunteers answer questions and provide water, snacks and other necessary supplies. Mental health counsellors are also available in the Care Hubs.

Staff, faculty and Sophs pose outside of a Care Hub during OWeek 2026. Students can approach a brightly marked Care Hub at any time for help, support or to access resources. (Steve Anderson/Western Communications)

Student support continues well beyond OWeek. Western’s Student Experience unit offers an array of services for new and returning students, including transition-to-university resources, peer mentorship as well as learning and writing assistance.

Whether walking, cycling or driving to Western in the coming days, a little extra travel time is recommended. Ongoing construction projects across campus – and city infrastructure upgrades around it – will affect some travel routes. T here are also intermittent road clos ur es to support OWeek celebrations.

Western’s campus improvements are designed to keep services strong and make way for new long-term projects such as buildings and infrastructure that are important investments in Western’s future. They support the university’s strategic growth, renew infrastructure, improve campus facilities and create spaces that enhance teaching, learning and research.

The City of London is upgrading Western Road and Philip Aziz to enhance safety and accessibility for pedestrians, cyclists and drivers, while supporting future growth in the area. Western road is reduced to a single lane this week, and Philip Aziz Avenue remains closed.

Learn more about how Western is preparing future leaders and global citizens.

stories.title: How will counter-tariffs impact Canadians? Here's the potential cost
stories.summary: Carney has warned that the trade conflict with the U.S. "will come at a cost." Here's what experts are saying about what that cost could be.
stories.author: Ellie Hutchings
stories.content:
He made the comments the same day that Canadian counter-tariffs on $28 billion worth of U.S. imports came into effect, with the new levies of between 15 and 50 per cent impacting a long list of U.S.-made products from toilet paper and cutlery to motorcycles and refrigerators.

These tariffs are a response to U.S. President Donald Trump’s 50 per cent tariff on $28 billion worth of Canadian goods imposed on Aug. 22, after trade talks between Canada and the U.S. broke down last month.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre called on the prime minister on Tuesday to share what the impact of the counter-tariffs on Canadian consumers would be, saying in a video shared to social media : “Every single mother, small business owner, and senior should know what they will pay in these new counter-tariffs.”

Here’s what economic experts are saying about the potential cost.

Trevor Tombe, an economist at the University of Calgary, estimated in an analysis published by The Hub that Canada’s counter-tariffs carry a $4 billion hit to Canadian consumers, which will fall hardest on lowest-income households.

His report suggests that households earning under $30,000 a year will lose more than 0.5 per cent of their disposable income as a result of retaliatory tariffs, which is three times larger than the hit on households earning above $150,000. Meanwhile, he says families with kids face costs of roughly $250 per year from the tariffs while those without kids face costs of less than $170.

Rob Breakenridge: Carney must be honest about the cost of counter-tariffs

Carney says he's not 'escalating the conflict' as Canada hits U.S. with retaliatory tariffs

“Ultimately this is a tax on a purchase decision that a Canadian has made, either a Canadian household or individual, or a business buying an import from the U.S.,” he said. “And that means that, for the most part, tariffs are paid by Canadians, not Americans.”

Joseph Steinberg, professor of economics at University of Toronto, said that estimating the impact of the new counter-tariffs starts by looking back at March last year, when Canada imposed 25 per cent tariffs on $30 billion of U.S. goods.

Steinberg told National Post that those tariffs, which remained in place until September 2025, were focused on consumer products, meaning they visibly raised prices for Canadian consumers. Despite this, he said, that is a way of doing tariffs “that is going to cause the least economic harm for our economy.”

“The best estimates indicate that those measures increased the inflation rate here in Canada by about half a percentage point during the period in which those tariffs were in force,” he added.

However, the latest counter tariffs are instead focused on “intermediary inputs,” such as insulated conductors, construction machinery parts, and freight trailers, to name a few. What this means is that the cost of production for Canadian firms will increase.

“These companies respond by raising the prices of the products that they sell here at home, and in some cases by laying off workers or shrinking how much they produce. It’s going to hurt the economy more than tariffing consumer products will,” Steinberg said.

A Bank of Canada report published in May looked at how retailers adjusted prices during the six months Canada imposed 25 per cent counter tariffs on U.S. products last year. It found that prices for goods that were subject to counter-tariffs increased by about 6 per cent more than those of non-tariffed goods — or roughly one-quarter of the 25 per cent counter-tariff — adding roughly 0.3 percentage points to consumer price inflation.

The challenge, he added, “is that tariffs on some impacted products could be much higher, reaching up to 50 per cent in certain categories.” The impact will also be more concentrated, he said, in categories including health and beauty and paper.

“Consumers will not see prices rise in the short term,” Steinberg said of this round of counter-tariffs. “This is going to be a slower burn.”

Both Steinberg and Tombe agree that it is Canadian businesses, rather than consumers, that will feel the effects of the counter-tariffs first. In fact, a Canadian Federation of Independent Business (Cfib) survey found that 49 per cent of business owners are affected by the Canadian counter-tariffs, with 28 per cent reporting major negative impacts.

Affected importers estimated the median monthly financial impact of both the U.S. and Canadian tariffs to be $55,000, with 40 per cent saying they will absorb most of the tariff-related costs.

And 11 per cent of importers affected by the Canada-U.S. trade war said they would stop being financially viable if the trade war lasts three months or more.

Tombe previously put Canadian job losses as a result of U.S. 50 per cent tariffs at an estimated 87,200, while Steinberg said he expects Canada’s retaliatory measures to be “at least as harmful as that.”

Tombe previously told National Post that his estimate amounts to roughly 4 per cent of total employment, which is “not a recession-scale shock, but certainly for the individuals involved, a pretty significant cost to be borne.”

At the same time as the counter tariffs were announced, Ottawa also unveiled a $7.5 billion aid package for firms and workers impacted by the trade war.

Tombe previously told National Post: “If we’re not paying for that through taxes, then we’ll be paying for it through higher levels of public debt.”

Unlike the counter-tariffs Canada imposed last year, economic experts agree that it will take longer for Canadian consumers to feel the effects of the current retaliation.

Tombe said that the immediate hit is felt by businesses instead of consumers “because about 75 per cent of the affected trade will be in the form of industrial supplies and capital goods.”

Steinberg agreed. “The hit to prices will be slower to build, because it’s going to have to work its way through the entire Canadian supply chain,” he said.

“But eventually it will be larger because it will affect not only imported products but domestically produced products too.”

content_blocks.text: These tariffs are a response to U.S. President Donald Trump’s 50 per cent tariff on $28 billion worth of Canadian goods imposed on Aug. 22, after trade talks between Canada and the U.S. broke down last month.

content_blocks.text: His report suggests that households earning under $30,000 a year will lose more than 0.5 per cent of their disposable income as a result of retaliatory tariffs, which is three times larger than the hit on households earning above $150,000. stories.title: Quebec police watchdog investigating the death of a motorcyclist east of Montreal
stories.summary: Montreal - Quebec's police watchdog has launched an investigation after a motorcyclist died while fleeing police in the Eastern Townships.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The Bureau des enquêtes indépendantes says Quebec provincial police officers witnessed the cyclist potentially breaking traffic laws at around 9:15 p.m. on Tuesday near Waterville, Que.

A summary of events provided by the watchdog says police tried to intercept the motorcyclist, who fled and crashed into a guardrail.

Montreal police have been called in to help with the investigation.

TAKE NOTICE that the Council of the County of Middlesex passed amending development charges By-law No. 7428") on the 8th day of September, 2026 under section 2(1) of the Development Charges Act, 1997, S.O., 1997 c. 27, as amended;

The amending by-law, which came into effect on the 8th day of September, 2026 has the effect of striking out and removing “and shall not include self-storage or mini-storage facilities” from the definition of Industrial Use.

The amending by-law does not change the schedule of development charge rates as set out in By-law No. 7291.

No key map has been provided as the by-law applies to all lands located within Middlesex County.

A copy of the amending by-law is available for examination at the Middlesex County offices, 399 Ridout St. North, London, Ontario N6A 2P1 during regular business hours (weekdays from 8:30 AM to 4:30 PM) excluding statutory holidays.

DATED at the Middlesex County offices, London, Ontario, this 9th day of September, 2026.

Marci Ivanic

The amending by-law, which came into effect on the 8th day of September, 2026 has the effect of striking out and removing “and shall not include self-storage or mini-storage facilities” from the definition of Industrial Use.
The amending by-law does not change the schedule of development charge rates as set out in By-law No. 7291.
No key map has been provided as the by-law applies to all lands located within Middlesex County.

A copy of the amending by-law is available for examination at the Middlesex County offices, 399 Ridout St. North, London, Ontario N6A 2P1 during regular business hours (weekdays from 8:30 AM to 4:30 PM) excluding statutory holidays.

stories.title: Ontario's new high school grading scheme 'a lot more pressure' for students, teens say
stories.summary: High school students in Ontario are going into the first year of the province's education policy changes, which include mandatory final exams and attendance grading.
stories.author: Kendra Seguin
paragraphs: London·Video
High school students in Ontario are going into the first year of the province's education policy changes, which include mandatory final exams and attendance grading.
· Posted: Sep 09, 2026 5:22 AM EDT | Last Updated: 39 minutes ago

Expectations are changing for high school students in Ontario, who will be the first group to go through the province's new grading scheme, which puts more emphasis on attendance and final evaluations.
Education Minister Paul Calandra announced the changes earlier this year, saying then that the ministry has "heard constantly" from teachers that they need better control of classrooms
"We've been hearing about it all day," said grade 11 student Rowynn Whaley, who attends H.B. Beal Secondary School in London, Ont. "They're making it such a big deal."
Back to school: Everything you need to know about Ontario's education policy changes
Ontario has unveiled mandatory changes for schools, starting this fall. Here's what you need to know
Starting this year, students in grades 9 and 10 will be graded on 65 per cent of class work, 20 per cent on final evaluations and 15 per cent on attendance and participation.
Grade 11 and 12 students will be marked on 65 per cent of class work, 25 per cent on final evaluations and 10 per cent on attendance and participation.
What are students saying about Ontario's new grade breakdown?

"I'm not too happy about it. I don't think any of us are," Whaley said about the new attendance marks. "Not that I skip class a lot, but I just feel like as long as I'm getting my work done and things are getting handed in, showing up shouldn't really matter that much."

According to the province's website, students who miss two classes or fewer and consistently participate in class will receive 80 to 100 per cent of their participation marks. Those who miss more than nine classes and don't participate at all will receive less than 50 per cent of the mark.
Attendance for high schoolers, elementary students is plummeting in Ontario: data
Ontario education minister urges parents not to pull kids from school for sports
Excused absences such as illness or cultural days will not negatively affect a students' marks, the website says.
"It's fair because some people are skipping and don't come to school," said Catholic Central Secondary School student Jana Ibrahim. "I think that it's better."
Several students told CBC News the increased focus on final exams is anxiety-inducing and raises the expectations for high schoolers across the province.
"It's a lot more pressure in that aspect. It's good, but I'm kind of nervous," said Margarita Balbin, who is starting Grade 11 at Catholic Central.
New high school student Bailey Becker said she's staying positive as she starts the next chapter of schooling amid the new changes.
"I feel like some of the changes are a little bit too much, but I think I'll be OK."
Other teenagers said there should be more support for students preparing for exams this year, considering the raised stakes.

"Some teachers ... expect you to put all your focus into their lessons, but they're not accommodating if you need help and I think it's kind of ridiculous that they're going to make our exams 25 per cent," said Grade 12 Beal student Charli Lockhart.
Ragad Ibrahim, who attends Catholic Central, said she thinks final exams should be open book going forward.
"25 [per cent] is a really big number," she said.
However, Grade 12 student Sarina Haghighatnama said she thinks students can succeed with the new grading scheme, so long as they put in the effort.

"I think if you study, you can get a high mark," she said. "If you're just skipping and don't care, then absolutely you'll fail, but if you just focus, [go to] class and do everything, you're going to absolutely get a good mark."

stories.title: London constable charged with assault causing bodily harm: SIU
stories.summary: London constable charged with assault causing bodily harm: SIU CBC
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: Ontario's police watchdog has charged a London police constable with assault causing bodily harm in connection with an incident in March that left a man with serious injuries.
· Posted: Sep 09, 2026 2:07 PM EDT | Last Updated: 3 hours ago
Const. Farrant is required to appear before the Ontario Court of Justice in London on Sept. 22, the SIU said.(Yvon Theriault/CBC/Radio-Canada)
The Special Investigations Unit announced the charge against Const. Stephen Farrand on Wednesday, saying the alleged incident dates to March 18, 2026 at Victoria Hospital.
According to the agency, the man had been taken to the hospital after being arrested and apprehended under the Mental Health Act.
"At the hospital, there was an interaction with an officer that resulted in the man suffering serious injuries," the SIU said. No further detail is provided.
Farrant is required to appear before the Ontario Court of Justice in London on Sept. 22, the agency said.
"As the matter is before the courts, and in consideration of the fair trial interests of the accused, the SIU will not provide further comment on the investigation."
In a statement provided after publication, a London police spokesperson said Farrand has been with the service for nine years and remains on active duty pending the outcome of the case.
"As the matter is before the court, we cannot comment further," said Const. Gavin Dell.
"At the conclusion of the criminal court process, the London Police Service will conduct an investigation in accordance with Section 81 of the Community Safety and Policing Act.”
Retired London cop charged with sexually assaulting woman who says she tried for years to get help
It's the second time a London police officer, active or retired, has been criminally charged by the SIU in the last two years.
In February 2025, the agency announced it had charged a former officer, Edward Lane, with two sexual assault counts stemming from allegations dating to the 1980s and early 1990s.
The case remains before the courts.

stories.title: MLA calls for review after Surrey police involved in multiple collisions
stories.summary: In the last 12 months, six people have died or been seriously injured in collisions involving the Surrey Police Service, prompting a local MLA to ask for a review.
stories.author: Amy Judd, Angela Jung
stories.content:
In the last 12 months, six people have died or been seriously injured in collisions involving the Surrey Police Service, prompting a local MLA to call on the Solicitor General to launch a review.

The latest incident happened on Labour Day at 3 a.m.

Surrey Police Service says it was attempting to stop the driver of a black Chevrolet Avalanche near the intersection of King George Boulevard and 96 Avenue.

The two vehicles collided and investigators say the truck driver failed to stop.

Authorities say the truck driver later crashed into a concrete SkyTrain barrier and a pedestrian was left with life-threatening injuries.

The police watchdog is now looking into the incident.

But beyond the investigation by the Independent Investigations Office (IIO), Surrey-Cloverdale MLA Elenore Sturko would like to see the province conduct its own review.

“I think that there needs to be a review and that the minister should, you know, really take up this cause and if they find nothing, they find nothing,” she said. “But this, you know, we can’t just let this go as a bad coincidence or a series of unlucky circumstances.

“We need to ensure that you know, with every opportunity that we have here, that there isn’t something more we could address to improve safety for the officers in the public.”

The Ministry of Public Safety and the Solicitor General say it is awaiting the outcome of the IIO investigations before determining if further steps are necessary.

stories.title: Saskatchewan manufacturers re-evaluating imports as counter-tariffs kick in
stories.summary: Manufacturers in Saskatchewan say they are watching their bottom lines and evaluating their options as Canada's counter-tariffs kick in.
stories.author: Vanessa Tiberio
stories.content:
The president and chief executive officer of a Saskatoon-based mining equipment manufacturer says his company spent the last two weeks buying more American steel used in its products as Canada’s counter-tariffs kick in Tuesday.

“To make sure we had enough in stock to be able to ride out this kind of effect for as long a period as we could,” says Scott Bahr of Bit Service Company.

Canada’s counter-tariffs are in response to recent trade war escalations by U.S. President Donald Trump and equal $27.6 billion in imports from the U.S. across a variety of sectors, including steel and dairy, as well as electronics.

Bahr says his company is more affected by Canadian reciprocal tariffs than by the tariffs initially imposed by the United States because it imports more raw steel components for its manufacturing processes than it exports to the country. Now, Bahr says his company is closely watching its bottom line.

“For the short term, obviously it affects our margins, but long term it is something that does affect our competitiveness from a pricing standpoint with our clients,” he said.

For many Saskatchewan manufacturers, pivoting to Canadian or alternative sources for raw materials is not a simple solution. Bahr cites the well-regarded reputation of American products and the time-consuming nature of supply chain changes as reasons for not adapting right away.

“It’s something again that we would not take lightly, and we would have to do from a very long-term lens, but it would have to be something that we either look to support or potentially replace existing suppliers,” he said.

One Saskatoon business association executive director says there is great potential in businesses turning to Canada amid its supply chain challenges, but also recognizes the associated challenges.

“If they can source anything local, that would be a great opportunity for us to build our own economy locally. But of course, some things are not available here in the local marketplace,” said Keith Moen, executive director of the Nsba.

Moen says small- and medium-sized enterprises are most likely to bear the brunt of counter-tariffs in Saskatoon, with uncertainties plaguing business decisions from inventory and staffing to cost and expense control.

“The concern right now is if there will be further counter-to-counter tariffs that will be applied, and I think the expectation is that there likely will,” he said.

The federal government announced additional support for Prairie small- and medium-sized businesses impacted by tariffs Tuesday, offering up to $3 million in non-repayable support through its Regional Tariff Response Initiative (Rtri) by PrairiesCan.

Allan Wiens is the CEO of farm equipment supplier SeedMaster, which is receiving more than $596,000 in federal government Rtri funding to accelerate its expansion into Australia.

Wiens says the newly imposed counter-tariffs have hit his company on the supply chain side, with about 30 per cent of his company’s materials coming from the U.S.

“I’ve had better nights of sleep, let’s put it that way,” he said.

Wiens says the uncertainty in the trade talks is the biggest impact his company is feeling so far this year. When it comes to purchasing farm equipment, Wiens says it’s an investment farmers are “not willing to make when there is so much uncertainty in the market,” ultimately impacting his company’s bottom line even if his products were not previously subject to tariffs.

“So we look at ways that we can expand as simply as possible so it doesn’t require a major redesign of our equipment,” he said.

Despite the uncertainties, manufacturers remain optimistic in their responses, drawing on past experiences to help them weather the storm.

“I would say we’re slightly, I don’t wanna say less worried, but we have a bit of practice from the effects that we went through last year,” Bahr said.

Bahr says his company is more affected by Canadian reciprocal tariffs than by the tariffs initially imposed by the United States because it imports more raw steel components for its manufacturing processes than it exports to the country. Now, Bahr says his company is closely watching its bottom line.
“For the short term, obviously it affects our margins, but long term it is something that does affect our competitiveness from a pricing standpoint with our clients,” he said.

For many Saskatchewan manufacturers, pivoting to Canadian or alternative sources for raw materials is not a simple solution. Bahr cites the well-regarded reputation of American products and the time-consuming nature of supply chain changes as reasons for not adapting right away.

“It’s something again that we would not take lightly, and we would have to do from a very long-term lens, but it would have to be something that we either look to support or potentially replace existing suppliers,” he said.
One Saskatoon business association executive director says there is great potential in businesses turning to Canada amid its supply chain challenges, but also recognizes the associated challenges.

“If they can source anything local, that would be a great opportunity for us to build our own economy locally. But of course, some things are not available here in the local marketplace,” said Keith Moen, executive director of the Nsba.

Moen says small- and medium-sized enterprises are most likely to bear the brunt of counter-tariffs in Saskatoon, with uncertainties plaguing business decisions from inventory and staffing to cost and expense control.
“The concern right now is if there will be further counter-to-counter tariffs that will be applied, and I think the expectation is that there likely will,” he said.

The federal government announced additional support for Prairie small- and medium-sized businesses impacted by tariffs Tuesday, offering up to $3 million in non-repayable support through its Regional Tariff Response Initiative (Rtri) by PrairiesCan.
Allan Wiens is the CEO of farm equipment supplier SeedMaster, which is receiving more than $596,000 in federal government Rtri funding to accelerate its expansion into Australia.
Wiens says the newly imposed counter-tariffs have hit his company on the supply chain side, with about 30 per cent of his company’s materials coming from the U.S.
“I’ve had better nights of sleep, let’s put it that way,” he said.

Wiens says the uncertainty in the trade talks is the biggest impact his company is feeling so far this year. When it comes to purchasing farm equipment, Wiens says it’s an investment farmers are “not willing to make when there is so much uncertainty in the market,” ultimately impacting his company’s bottom line even if his products were not previously subject to tariffs.
“So we look at ways that we can expand as simply as possible so it doesn’t require a major redesign of our equipment,” he said.
Despite the uncertainties, manufacturers remain optimistic in their responses, drawing on past experiences to help them weather the storm.
“I would say we’re slightly, I don’t wanna say less worried, but we have a bit of practice from the effects that we went through last year,” Bahr said.

stories.title: Two Cape Breton counties lift states of emergency as flood recovery continues
stories.summary: Slow-moving storm dropped more than 200 mm of rain on some parts of the Nova Scotia island in less than two days
stories.content:
Two Cape Breton counties have lifted their local states of emergency while another kept its travel restrictions in place Wednesday following widespread flooding over the weekend.

A slow-moving storm dropped more than 200 millimetres of rain on some parts of the Nova Scotia island in less than two days. It washed out roads and culverts, damaged bridges and temporarily left some people stranded in their neighbourhoods.

Victoria and Inverness counties lifted states of local emergency Tuesday evening, but Richmond County remained in a state of local emergency, which meant unnecessary travel was prohibited. Schools remained closed as a result.

The county’s warden said the decision to maintain the state of emergency would allow for further assessment of roads and infrastructure in the hardest-hit areas.

“Our issues today are twofold: continuing those recovery, repair and reconstruction efforts, but also to do the last of the assessments we need to have confidence in the existing infrastructure,” Lois Landry said in an interview Wednesday.

Landry said Route 4 between the towns of Port Hawkesbury and St. Peter’s was badly damaged, as were spots in the River Bourgeois area. She said repair work has been done, and the roads will be in good shape once they receive a new layer of asphalt.

The warden said there were bigger infrastructure concerns in the area around the St. Georges Channel and The Points West Bay areas at the western end of Bras d’Or Lake.

Temporary fixes have been made, but permanent repairs will likely come with significant detours, she said.

Still, Landry said it appeared that everybody in the county was able to remain in their homes safely and had access to local roads.

Meanwhile, the provincial Department of Public Works said in an e-mail that 21 of the 120 roads damaged in the flooding were still being repaired. As well, it said four of 12 damaged bridges must be replaced, while the others have since reopened to traffic.

The department says repairs will be prioritized based on safety. The cost of repairs remains unknown.

stories.title: Beverette, Duncan-Busby, Harris take CFL honours
stories.summary: Montreal's Tyrice Beverette and Saskatchewan teammates Dhel Duncan-Busby and Trevor Harris were named CFL players of the week on Wednesday.
stories.author: n The Canadian Pressn
stories.content:
By The Canadian Press The Canadian Press

Posted September 9, 2026 1:44 pm

TORONTO – Montreal’s Tyrice Beverette and Saskatchewan teammates Dhel Duncan-Busby and Trevor Harris were named CFL players of the week on Wednesday.

Harris threw for 362 yards in Saskatchewan’s 32-26 overtime win over the Winnipeg Blue Bombers last weekend. He had three completions of at least 30 yards and moved into 10th place in league history with 41,590 career passing yards.

Duncan-Busby caught 10 passes for a career-high 148 yards in the victory. Six of those receptions came in the fourth quarter and overtime.

Alouettes linebacker Tyrice Beverette had a 57-yard interception return for a touchdown in Montreal’s 37-30 victory over the B.C. Lions. He also had six defensive tackles and one special-teams tackle.

The three players were chosen by a panel composed of representatives from the CFL’s football operations, player and game statistics, and content departments.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 9, 2026.

stories.title: Pedestrian killed in London collision was mom-of-3 out for jog: Friend
stories.summary: "She just had so much joy and happiness in her. She was just bubbly, always willing to help out anyone."
stories.author: Brian Williams
stories.content:
Family and friends are mourning the loss of a mother-of-three who died after she was struck by a vehicle in northwest London.

London police have said emergency crews were called to a collision shortly before 11:30 p.m. on Sept. 2, last Wednesday, in the area of Sarnia Road and Chapman Court, just west of Wonderland Road North. The pedestrian involved died after being taken to hospital, police have said, adding the driver remained at the scene.

Contacted on Tuesday, police said the investigation into the collision is ongoing.

The pedestrian killed was 41-year-old Felicia Aves, said Jamie Matte, a friend for roughly 30 years. Aves was out for a jog and heading to a store when the collision happened, Matte said, adding exercise was something Aves did often to relieve stress and boost her mental health.

Matte remembered her longtime friend as someone who was “always smiling” in life.

“She was the most energetic person you’ve ever met in your entire life,” Matte said. “She just had so much joy and happiness in her. She was just bubbly, always willing to help out anyone.”

Aves was athletically gifted and “just naturally very talented,” Matte said.

A single mother of three, Aves leaves behind two daughters, Nigea, 18, and Leila, 17, and 12-year-old son DJ, Matte said, noting her children have been taken in by their grandmother. Aves would always do anything for her children, Matte said.

“She loved them so much,” Matte said. “Her whole purpose in life was the three children.”

Aves and Matte met decades ago when they were training in competitive gymnastics, a passion they both turned into careers as coaches. A gymnastics teacher who mentored students for 20 years, Aves also provided circus training and ran dance fitness classes, Matte said, adding her friend believed staying active was key to maintaining good mental health.

Matte has launched a GoFundMe fundraising campaign to help cover memorial costs and to support the three children. As of Wednesday morning, it had raised more than $10,000 toward its goal of $14,000.

“We are asking for your help to support Nigea, Leila, and DJ and their family during this incredibly difficult time,” the GoFundMe page states. “Funds raised will help with Felicia’s funeral and final expenses, as well as provide financial support for her children as they navigate life without their mom.

“Felicia’s life was far too short, but the love, laughter, lessons and memories she gave to so many will live on through her children, her family, her students and everyone who had the privilege of knowing her.”
