Aves and Matte met decades ago when they were training in competitive gymnastics, a passion they both turned into careers as coaches. A gymnastics teacher who mentored students for 20 years, Aves also provided circus training and ran dance fitness classes, Matte said, adding her friend believed staying active was key to maintaining good mental health.
Matte has launched a GoFundMe fundraising campaign to help cover memorial costs and to support the three children. As of Wednesday morning, it had raised more than $10,000 toward its goal of $14,000.

“We are asking for your help to support Nigea, Leila, and DJ and their family during this incredibly difficult time,” the GoFundMe page states. “Funds raised will help with Felicia’s funeral and final expenses, as well as provide financial support for her children as they navigate life without their mom.

“Felicia’s life was far too short, but the love, laughter, lessons and memories she gave to so many will live on through her children, her family, her students and everyone who had the privilege of knowing her.”

stories.title: B.C. forestry industry says it’s at ‘breaking point’ in letter to Eby
stories.summary: The letter asks Eby to take swift action to form a crisis group with a mandate to cut costs, remove regulatory barriers and get economically viable wood moving.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
British Columbia forestry groups have written to Premier David Eby saying the industry is at a “breaking point” and calling for urgent action to address challenges ranging from provincial permitting delays to U.S. tariffs.

The letter is co-authored by groups representing contractors, manufacturers, unions and others dependent on forestry, including the BC Council of Forest Industries, BC First Nations Forestry Council and the Truck Loggers Association.

The groups acknowledge that international trade pressures are beyond the premier’s control, but say many challenges are “homegrown.”

The letter asks Eby to take swift action to form a crisis group with a mandate to cut costs, remove regulatory barriers and get economically viable wood moving.

The groups say the group should be led by Eby’s office and bring together senior government decision makers and representatives from across the sector.

The letter also asks Eby to increase B.C.’s economically viable harvest to 45 million cubic metres annually, up from a current projection of 29 million cubic metres.

The province had issued an update on Aug. 27 saying it was exploring what it described as a working forest landscape model and identify areas where logging will be prioritized with the aim of reaching the target of 45 million cubic metres.

B.C. has seen mill closures in recent years, with Domtar announcing last month it was shuttering its Howe Sound pulp mill along with a chipping facility in the region.

“B.C. companies cannot control U.S. trade policy. But British Columbia can control many of the costs, regulations, policies, permitting processes and fibre-access decisions that determine whether those companies survive it,” the letter says.

“While international trade pressures are beyond the province’s direct control, many of the conditions determining whether B.C. companies can continue operating are not.”

stories.title: SIU charges London police constable with assault causing bodily harm
stories.summary: Ontario’s police watchdog has charged a London Police Service officer in connection with serious injuries suffered by a man following an interaction at a local hospital earlier this year.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
Ontario’s police watchdog has charged a London Police Service officer in connection with serious injuries suffered by a man following an interaction at a local hospital earlier this year.

The Special Investigations Unit (SIU) said it has reasonable grounds to believe an officer committed a criminal offence related to the incident from March 18.

According to the SIU, a man was arrested and apprehended under the Mental Health Act and transported to Victoria Hospital in London. While at the hospital, the man was involved in an interaction with a police officer that resulted in serious injuries.

Following an investigation, Const. Stephen Farrand has been charged with one count of assault causing bodily harm.

Farrand is scheduled to appear in London court on Sept. 22.

The SIU said it will not provide further details on the investigation because the matter is now before the courts.

The SIU is an independent civilian agency that investigates incidents involving police in which there has been death, serious injury, the discharge of a firearm or allegations of sexual assault.

VANCOUVER - British Columbia forestry groups have written to Premier David Eby saying the industry is at a “breaking point” and calling for urgent action to address challenges ranging from slow-moving provincial processes to steep U.S. tariffs.

DD[](http://www.thestar.com/news/canada/british-columbia/b-c-forestry-sector-says-industry-at-breaking-point-in-letter-to-premier-david-eby/article_4a595aa4-18bc-57bd-ae24-13be3b295379.html)

By Brenna Owen The Canadian Press

The letter dated Sept. 4 said the entire industry is at risk, from logging and transportation to pulp and paper and value-added manufacturing.

“We are in the middle of a major international trade crisis. Government must respond with the urgency that crisis demands,” said the letter from groups representing contractors, manufacturers, unions and others linked to the sector.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Who’s downloading photos of your kid at dance competitions?

The letter pointed to new U.S. tariffs on a broader range of forest products on top of those already applied to Canadian softwood lumber and acknowledged that international trade pressures are beyond the premier’s control.

But other challenges are “homegrown,” it said. The province “can control many of the costs, regulations, policies, permitting processes and fibre-access decisions that determine whether those companies survive it,” the letter said.

“Every day without stable, predictable access to economically viable wood increases the risk to B.C. businesses, workers, families and forest-dependent communities,” it said.

The letter asked Eby to take swift action to form a “forestry crisis action group” with a mandate to cut costs, remove regulatory barriers and get timber moving.

The group should be led by the premier’s office and bring together senior government decision makers and representatives from across the sector, it said.

The BC Council of Forest Industries, BC First Nations Forestry Council, BC Community Forest Association, BC Pulp & Paper Coalition, Truck Loggers Association, Independent Lumber Manufacturers’ Association and United Steelworkers are among the signatories of the letter released Wednesday.

Forests Minister Ravi Parmar later addressed reporters, saying U.S. tariffs and low pulp prices were part of a “perfect storm” battering the industry.

“Clearly we are in arguably the most challenging period in forestry’s history,” he said.

Parmar said he’d seen the letter and he and the premier were committed to charting a path forward that helps stabilize the sector and ensures its future.

The minister said he and Eby would meet with the signatories of the letter “in the next little while” to listen to their concerns and work on solutions.

“The path forward for forestry must be moving us away from a boom and bust cycle to one that is structurally sound and stable,” he said.

B.C. has seen numerous mill closures in recent years, with Domtar announcing last month it was shuttering a pulp mill in the Howe Sound region. The idling followed news that forestry giant Canfor was closing a mill in Prince George, B.C., in July.

Eddie Petryshen, conservation specialist with the advocacy group Wildsight, based in B.C.‘s Kootenay region, said the downturn or “falldown” of the province’s forest industry has been predicted — and ignored — for decades.

“We’ve been talking about getting more jobs per tree for a very long time but we haven’t effectively moved the needle on that,” he said in an interview.

Petryshen said B.C. has an “alarming history” of miscalculating the level of logging its forests can sustain, resulting in overcutting that has caught up with the sector.

The situation has been made worse by the destruction wrought by worsening wildfires and the historic mountain pine beetle epidemic, he added.

Petryshen said the letter from industry groups, which asked B.C. to speed up permitting and increase access to areas for logging, doesn’t buck the trend.

“What’s the actual plan for long-term sector sustainability and not just liquidating the forest and biodiversity values in the short term?” he said.

“We can extract the remaining economical old and primary forests … and not get any more jobs than we have today.”

B.C.‘s forest-dependent communities will be “left with the scraps” if the province and the industry don’t change their approach, he said.

The industry letter asked the B.C. government to increase the province’s economically viable harvest to 45 million cubic metres annually, up from a current projection of 29 million cubic metres, a figure linked to the price of lumber.

Parmar said he was committed to finding ways to hit the higher target. But it was “next to impossible to do that” given the punishing U.S. tariffs, he said.

Petryshen, meanwhile, said volume does not necessarily equate to jobs, especially if the sector remained slanted toward “high-volume and low-value” forestry.

Logging in B.C. has often targeted the most ecologically productive sites that support the biggest trees, which are highly sought by the industry, he said.

“I’m not sure how you can get to this theoretical 45 million cubic metres and not impact existing protections or things like what the industry might consider constraints — old-growth management areas, wildlife habitat areas.”

B.C. needs a biodiversity crisis action group, he added.

“I’ve watched as seven southern caribou herds have been locally extirpated in the last two decades and I see their habitat moving down the highway on the back of logging trucks,” said Petryshen, who lives in Kimberley, B.C.

Parmar highlighted the province’s plan to shift to a “working forest” model, saying Wednesday that it would address concerns the industry has been raising.

The new approach would eliminate what the minister described as a “cutblock by cutblock” approach to permitting, a shift he said would cut costs, speed up harvesting timelines and provide certainty for the industry.

The province has outlined the model, saying it includes three zones: the working forest where the priority is commercial logging, a multiple-use zone with stewardship efforts alongside “carefully managed” forestry activities, and a conservation zone aimed at preserving habitat, biodiversity and ecosystem health.

An update last month said the province would work with First Nations to identify “early candidate areas” set to be announced this fall for testing the approach.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 9, 2026.

The Canadian Press

Council Highlights is an informal summary of selected actions taken by Middlesex County Council or Committee of the Whole at business meetings. The Council Highlights are not an official record of County Council proceedings. To view official agendas and minutes, please visit Council Meetings and Minutes .

2025 Audit Report highlights strong financial stewardship

County Council received the 2025 Independent Auditor’s Report completed by Kpmg. The report found that the County’s financial statements are presented fairly and in accordance with Canadian public sector accounting standards. The audit found no uncorrected misstatements, no matters requiring special reporting, and no major issues related to fraud, financial reporting, or going-concern risks. Auditors reviewed 100 per cent of the County’s assets and revenues, including operations of the Middlesex London Paramedic Service and the Middlesex County Library Board. Total revenues increased to $188.6 million, while total assets grew to $332.5 million.

To learn more, read the Kpmg Audit Findings Report for the Year Ended December 31, 2025 .

Western Ontario Wardens’ Caucus visits County Council

The Committee of the Whole received a delegation from the Western Ontario Wardens’ Caucus (Wowc) highlighting the organization’s recent advocacy efforts. Wowc represents 15 upper tier and single tier municipalities in the region and advocates for shared priorities.

Recent Wowc accomplishments include securing regional pilot project funding, advocating successfully to protect farm lot severance policies, and supporting improved processing times for vulnerable sector checks. Wowc has been active in engaging with the federal and provincial governments, including hosting a Queen’s Park Day and at the AMO Conference in August. Looking ahead, Wowc will continue focusing on its priorities, including infrastructure to support local growth, homelessness prevention, and rural transit.

For more information, see the Western Ontario Wardens’ Caucus presentation .

Council receives Middlesex Archives Feasibility Study

The Committee of the Whole received the results of the Middlesex County Archives Feasibility Study examining options for a county archives service. The report, completed by TCI Management Consultants in partnership with The Information Management Specialists, provided information to support future Council decision-making. It outlines five potential service models ranging from a fully centralized county archives to partnerships with existing heritage organizations, a digital archives approach, enhanced coordination among current providers, or maintaining the status quo.

While the report identifies significant financial considerations, it also highlights opportunities for collaboration, shared services, external funding, and improved access to historical resources. Staff were directed to include details on how to further explore the options presented in the upcoming budget.

Read the Middlesex County Archives Feasibility Study report for more information.

Middlesex County Connect sees success in first half of 2026

The Committee of the Whole received an update on Middlesex County Connect, the County's inter-community transit service, including recent route enhancements, ridership trends, and long-term funding support. Since launching in 2020, Middlesex County Connect has expanded to four routes connecting rural communities with London, St. Thomas, Woodstock, Strathroy, and Sarnia.

Service improvements took effect on August 17, 2026, following a review of ridership data, third-party analysis, and customer feedback. Enhancements include new stops in several communities, improved access to destinations such as Victoria Hospital and Fanshawe College, expanded weekend service on Route 4 to Sarnia, improved schedule coordination, and additional fare and trip-booking options.

Ridership is projected to reach between 16,000 and 18,000 passenger trips in 2026, supported by the addition of Route 4 and anticipated growth from post-secondary students this fall. County staff will continue efforts to build ridership through new marketing initiatives, outreach to major employers and educational institutions, and more affordable monthly transit passes designed to encourage regular use of the service.

For more information, read the Middlesex County Connect – 2026 Mid-Year Update report .

Recommendations made by the Committee of the Whole at the September 8, 2026, meeting will be considered by County Council at its next regular meeting on September 22, 2026. The Legislative Services Department maintains the official record for all County government proceedings.

stories.title: Live Nation hands Toronto engineering report on Rogers Stadium damage
stories.summary: A "100-year storm" battered Toronto last week, leaving bleachers strewn across Rogers Stadium, which, in the aftermath, also appeared to have partially collapsed grandstands.
stories.author: Isaac Callan
stories.content:
The City of Toronto says Live Nation has sent it an engineering report on the damage Rogers Stadium suffered during last week’s massive rain and hail storm.

The “100-year storm” that battered Toronto left bleachers strewn across Rogers Stadium, which, in the aftermath, also appeared to have partially collapsed grandstands.

City inspectors slapped Live Nation with a violation notice after, ordering them to close the site down, retain an engineer to inspect the venue and urgently work on repairs.

On Wednesday, a spokesperson for the City of Toronto said the engineer’s report had been received by officials and was under review.

“The City will continue working with the owner throughout this process,” they wrote in a statement.

Retaining an engineer, however, is only one of the steps Live Nation has to take if it wants to host AC/DC at Rogers Stadium on Sept. 16.

Live Nation had until Sept. 8 to share its findings and solutions with the city, a deadline it met.

The order issued last week then said Live Nation must follow all the steps suggested by the engineer and update the city no later than Sept. 11 on what it’s been able to do.

Reconstruction work, the city said, will require a building permit.

Live Nation did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Global News.

Previously, the promoter said it would continue working with Toronto’s technical teams.

“Wednesday’s storm was a severe and significant weather event that City officials have deemed a ‘100-year storm,’” a statement on Sept. 4 read .

“The inspection, assessment and remediation of structures affected by significant weather events, like a red-level storm of this nature, is a standard process, and we remain engaged with the City as that work continues.”

stories.title: Montreal West parents say temporary return of crossing guard ‘short-lived victory’
stories.summary: Three students have been injured at the intersection in the past two years but a crossing guard put in place last school year was only temporary.
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
Parents and students at a Montreal West school are celebrating after a crossing guard has returned to a troubled intersection, though they’re saying it’s a “short-lived victory.”

The return of that crossing guard at the corner of Ainslie Road and Westminster Avenue follows a safety campaign by parents of Royal West Academy students during the summer after that guard’s job ended in June.

“Very much a short-lived victory but we’re happy to get anything down here,” said Eric Lamoureaux, former governing board chair at Royal West Academy. “We’ve been trying for two years to bring change to this corner.”

In the past two years, three students from the school have been struck by vehicles and injured at the intersection.

Back in April, Montreal police stationed a crossing guard at the roadway. It was in place until the end of the school year.

The guard was temporarily assigned with the expectation the municipality of Montreal West would be making changes, including reducing the number of lanes to two from four, according to the subcommittee. The work was to take place during this past summer, along with road changes at the nearby level train crossing.

By last week, that work had not taken place year though a pilot project was underway to narrow the roadway and remove left-hand turns to make the area safer.

When the school year ended, the guard was no longer in place, but the subcommittee went to the Montreal Agglomeration Council to ask for the crossing guard to return this school year.

Twice a day, an Spvm crossing guard will be stationed at the intersection — but much like the previous school year, it’s only temporary.

After October, there will again be no crossing guard.

Last week, Montreal West Mayor Jonathan Cha told Global News he’s hopeful the work set to be done will make things safer.

“With these improvements, we really think that this will be some kind of calming measures and that there will be more space for kids to cross safely,” said Montreal West Mayor Jonathan Cha.

But Lamoureux said there’s still concerns about what happens after the work is done.

“To my mind, the road changes, narrowing down the lanes, I think that will cause more frustration for the drivers, potentially even more people driving more recklessly towards the (Highway) 20, we need a physical presence here,” he said.

Reconfiguration of the intersection was expected to begin on Sept. 22 and expected to be completed by the end of October.

Even if road changes come into place, Lamoureaux said parents would still like to see a crossing guard be permanent to protect vulnerable pedestrians, like students.

“The situation keeps demanding action,” he said.

— with files from Global News’ Brayden Jagger Haines

By The Canadian Press

MONTREAL - A Quebec-based recreational vehicle manufacturer is among the Canadian companies facing the impact of the latest U.S. trade measures as the Canada-U.S. trade war escalates.

The measure is part of a new round of trade restrictions announced by U.S. President Donald Trump on Tuesday targeting Canadian goods.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Image 9Image 10Image 11Image 12

BRP says it expects the immediate financial impact to be limited because the majority of production and shipments for the current season have already been completed.

The move comes as other Quebec manufacturers are being drawn deeper into the trade dispute.

On Monday, Trump threatened to bar Quebec-based Bombardier from selling its aircraft in the United States unless the company manufactures them there.

In a statement, Bombardier cited the thousands of people it employs at more than 20 locations across the United States.

In 2003, Bombardier sold its recreational products division, which became the independent company known as BRP.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 9, 2026.

— with files by Kelly Geraldine Malone in Washington

stories.title: Record number of Western scholars join Royal Society of Canada
stories.summary: University scholars were elected to Royal Society of Canada as Fellows and Members of the College.
stories.author: Lauren daSilva
stories.content:
A record-breaking number of Western researchers across eight different faculties have been elected Fellows of the Royal Society of Canada (RSC), with another three scholars elected to the College of New Scholars, Artists and Scientists.

The RSC is Canada’s national academy, recognizing distinguished scholars, scientists, researchers and artists to promote academic and research excellence. Membership in the RSC is one of the country’s highest honours.

“Western’s record recognition by the Royal Society of Canada reflects the tremendous depth, creativity and impact of researchers across disciplines,” said Penny Pexman, Western’s vice-president (research). “Having nine Fellows and three College members honoured in a single year is a powerful testament to the talent, ambition and global influence of our research community.”

Western’s long-standing connection to the RSC includes more than 100 all-time scholars elected as Fellows and members of the College, beginning in 1958.

RSC president Françoise Baylis, MA’84, PhD’89, an internationally renowned bioethicist, is a Western alum.

“Today, we are pleased to welcome the newest Fellows and College Members of the Royal Society of Canada. Their work spans breakthroughs in medicine, technology and climate research, contributions in the arts and literature, leadership in reconciliation, and efforts to build a more inclusive future,” Baylis said during the announcement of the Rsc’s 2026 cohort on Sept. 9.

“These individuals are shaping Canadian society through their scholarship, creativity, and impact – today and into the years ahead.”

RSC Fellows are distinguished Canadians who have made significant contributions to Canadian society. Fellows are elected to one of three academies: The Academy of the Arts and Humanities, The Academy of Social Sciences or The Academy of Science.

Nine Western scholars – June Cotte, Corey Dyck, Hesham El Naggar, Ingrid Johnsrude, Lorelei Lingard, Valeri Oosterveld, Sharon Sliwinski, Shannon Stewart and Xianbin Wang – were elected by the Rsc’s existing Fellows.

Ivey Business School professor June Cotte is an expert on consumer behavior in Canada. She introduced important research on how time influences behavior, the role of family in consumption and behaviors like ethical and sustainable consumption.

With a global teaching career spanning multiple countries, Cotte’s work has been featured in publications such as the Journal of Consumer Research, MIT Sloan Management Review , and The Wall Street Journal.

Corey Dyck is a leading authority on eighteenth-century German philosophy whose groundbreaking work has redefined understanding of Kant and the German Enlightenment.

He pioneered the recovery of historical items made by women and other equity-deserving groups. His work is shaping how scholars and audiences view the Enlightenment.

An internationally recognized scholar in geotechnical engineering, H esham El Naggar has helped shape the design of resilient and sustainable infrastructure worldwide.

His work on soil dynamics, foundations and earthquake engineering has led to new analysis and design tools in the field. His research is incorporated into guidelines used globally.

Ingrid Johnsrude , professor of neuroscience and head of the department of psychology, is a leading researcher in knowledge-guided perception of speech and sound.

Her area of focus is on how the brain is organized to support perception. She is a highly awarded member of the Canadian Academy of Health Sciences.

Lorelei Lingard is a leading researcher in health professions education whose work has helped reshape how communication and teamwork are taught in medical training.

Her findings have informed medical education policies, curriculum and assessment across Canada. Her work on research methods and scientific writing has strengthened knowledge sharing in the field internationally.

Valerie Oosterveld is a global expert on gender-based crimes in armed conflict and the conceptualization of gender in international criminal law.

Her scholarship has made crucial contributions to addressing gendered forms of genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes. Her research is widely cited by courts, directly influencing international prosecutorial policy and practice.

Sharon Sliwinski is celebrated internationally for her expansive and interdisciplinary research bridging visual studies, cultural history, human rights and psychosocial studies.

Chair of the creative arts and production program in the Faculty of Information and Media Studies, her work spans photography, human rights and the social imaginary. She is the creator of the Museum of Dreams , a research hub dedicated to exploring the social and political significance of dream life.

Shannon Stewart is a professor and psychologist within the Faculty of Education. She is a Canadian Academy of Health Sciences Fellow and associate scientist at the Children’s Health Research Institute.

Stewart is known for her global contributions related to the development of the interRAI Child and Youth assessment-to-intervention system – designed to improve outcomes for vulnerable children and youth in ongoing psychological care.

Xianbin Wang is a Tier 1 Canada Research Chair who has transformed wireless communications.

With 700 publications and 35 patents, his pioneering work established new foundations for secure communications across interconnected consumer, defence and mission-critical industrial systems.

The College of New Scholars, Artists and Scientists elects mid-career leaders in their fields with interdisciplinary scholarship and diverse perspectives to benefit Canadian society.

Scholars are elected to a seven-year term where they will attend and host RSC events, serve on committees, work with other scholars across the country, participate in programming and provide advice to government and the public.

Western scholars Jackson Leween, Yanping Li and Ryan Stevenson have been recognized for their work advancing societies and navigating new realities; a major honour for Canadian researchers.

Jackson Leween, 2bears, professor of visual arts and Indigenous studies, is the Canada Research Chair in Indigenous Arts Research & Technology and director of the Otekhnòtshera Ratirihwisaks Etho:onhwentsyáke (Otekh) Lab.

Two Bears is recognized globally for research-creation work connecting Haudenosaunee knowledge with emerging technologies grounded in place, responsibility and community governance.

Yanping Li , professor of Earth sciences, is a leading emerging scholar in climate dynamics and climate-risk science.

She developed an innovative crop-wetland-climate framework that informs national adaptation strategies. Her interdisciplinary work, national climate-assessment contributions and partnerships spanning agriculture, conservation and Indigenous communities have enhanced Canada’s capacity for climate-resilience planning.

Ryan Stevenson , professor of psychology and recipient of a Dorothy Killam Fellowship , has established himself as a world leader in neurodevelopmental cognitive neuroscience.

Stevenson’s internationally funded research program pioneered work with important mpacts on understanding sense perception in brain development, particularly in neurodiverse brains.

stories.title: Bank CEOs maintain positive credit outlook despite Canada-U.S. trade war escalations
stories.summary: Toronto — Canadian bank CEOs say their credit outlooks are still generally positive despite an escalating trade war, but they're taking some precautions.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
TORONTO — Canadian bank CEOs say their credit outlooks are still generally positive despite Canada-U.S. trade tensions ratcheting up, though they’re taking some precautions.

“I’m a little cautious because of the escalation of the trade war right now, but what we’re seeing outside of that, consumer, commercial, U.S. commercial is getting better,” RBC president and CEO Dave McKay said on Wednesday at the Scotiabank Financials Summit in Toronto.

However, he says tariff-impacted sectors are facing a significant degree of uncertainty and the bank is maintaining a robust capital buffer to absorb potential losses.

Scotiabank president and CEO Scott Thomson says he doesn’t think tariffs will have a large effect on the lender’s credit performance.

“A relatively small amount of trade is tariffed, and so I don’t think that’s going to have a huge impact on the credit performance, but obviously we’ll have to stay tuned for what transpires over the next year or so from a macro perspective and the relationship with the U.S. will be important,” Thomson said.

He said that the bank’s commercial, small business and automotive segments don’t appear to have any significant issues so far.

TD chief executive Raymond Chun said he is seeing resiliency in both Canada and the U.S. on the credit front.

Though, he said the bank has also set aside $500 million of reserves for tariff-related uncertainties.

The trade war entered a new chapter on Tuesday as the Canadian government introduced retaliatory tariff measures in response to U.S. tariffs introduced in August. In response to Canada’s retaliatory tariffs, U.S. President Donald Trump signed new executive orders to completely bar imports of certain Canadian goods.

Shortly after the U.S. imposed its initial round of duties, Canada’s major banks reported third-quarter earnings that were largely positive, with the lenders pointing to a resilient economy while saying the trade tensions were manageable.

The banks are also navigating a recent change to the country’s domestic stability buffer, which was announced by the federal banking regulator in June.

OSFI lowered the domestic stability buffer to three per cent from 3.5 per cent, saying the change would give the country’s six largest banks greater flexibility to deploy capital. The buffer is part of the amount of money Canada’s big banks must keep on hand in case of economic shock.

Speaking at the summit, Peter Routledge, OSFI’s superintendent, said the risk environment in Canada has “fundamentally changed.”

“The benefit is we’re sending a clear and unambiguous message to the banking system that you have capital planning certainty and more capital flexibility yourself to make commercial decisions,” Routledge said on the regulator’s decision to lower the buffer.

The summit also comes as the big banks face increasing competition from smaller digital platforms.

McKay said competition in the sector is “great” and acknowledged some customers are being swayed by improvements in customer experience offered by some of the smaller platforms.

“We need to improve our overall customer experience. I think that is the most important, and we’ve underinvested in a couple of our platforms. So we’re all over that, and you’ll see a relaunch and a rebranding of our approach to that,” he said.

McKay said he is optimistic RBC can win back customers that have left banks for alternative lenders.

As competition rises in Canada’s banking sector, BMO InvestorLine announced Wednesday it is offering commission-free trading on all stocks and exchange-traded funds in a bid to grow its digital self-directed investing platform.

BMO says it’s the first direct investing brokerage owned by one of Canada’s five big banks to eliminate commissions on stock and ETF trades.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 9, 2026.

Companies in this story: (TSX: RY, TSX: BNS, TSX: TD)

Daniel Johnson, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Penélope Cruz, John Malkovich, Michelle Yeoh among stars expected to attend Tiff
stories.summary: Toronto — Stars including Penélope Cruz, Michelle Yeoh and John Malkovich are set to attend the Toronto International Film Festival.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
TORONTO — Stars including Penélope Cruz, Michelle Yeoh and John Malkovich are set to attend the Toronto International Film Festival.

TIFF announced its list of 800 expected guests on Wednesday, a day before the 51st edition of the festival was set to get underway.

Cruz is on deck for the films “Bunker” and “La Bola Negra,” and was also tapped to receive a Tribute Award at a TIFF fundraising event on Sunday, while Yeoh stars in the film “The Surgeon.”

Malkovich, meanwhile, stars in Martin McDonagh’s CIA black comedy “Wild Horse Nine” alongside Sam Rockwell and Steve Buscemi, who are also both due to walk the red carpet.

Canadian stars attending the festival include Seth Rogen, who features in his wife Lauren Miller Rogen’s film “Babies,” and Rush bandmates Alex Lifeson and Geddy Lee for the documentary “Neil Peart: No One’s Disciple,” about the late drummer.

Also expected are Sebastian Stan, who’s in “Fjord;” Cynthia Erivo, who’s in “Prima Facie;” Jesse Eisenberg, who directed “The Debut” and Fan Bingbing, who is in “Diary of a Mad Old Man” and is also receiving a Tribute Award.

So too are sisters Kate and Rooney Mara, who star as twins in Werner Herzog’s “Bucking Fastard.”

Absent from the list of attendees is Mark Ruffalo, who stars in opening night film “Being Heumann,” but who has been at the centre of a dispute with Paramount in recent weeks after criticizing its merger with Warner Bros.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 9, 2026.

Nicole Thompson, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Olivia Chow maintains double-digit lead in Toronto mayoral race, new poll finds
stories.summary: A new study from Liaison Strategies, conducted at the start of the Labour Day long weekend, puts Chow at 50 per cent among decided and leaning voters.
stories.author: Isaac Callan
stories.content:
Incumbent Olivia Chow maintains a double-digit lead in the Toronto mayoral race, according to a new poll, which shows Brad Bradford in second place.

A new study from Liaison Strategies, conducted at the start of the Labour Day long weekend, puts Chow at 50 per cent among decided and leaning voters, with Bradford at 39 per cent and Chris Alexander in third at 11 per cent.

“The mayoral ballot is stable, but it has settled in a better place for Olivia Chow than for her challengers,” David Valentin, principal at Liaison, said in a statement.

“The regional picture is still the key to the race. Chow leads downtown 60 per cent to 30 per cent, in North York 53 per cent to 36 per cent, and in Scarborough 51 per cent to 38 per cent. Bradford’s best region is Etobicoke, where he leads Chow 56 per cent to 33 per cent.”

The poll comes on the eve of Chow’s official campaign launch, although she has made her intention to run again public for months, while Bradford declared his plan to launch a campaign almost a year ago.

The Liaison study also shows residents are split on whether or not the city is heading in the right direction.

Forty-seven per cent said they thought the city was heading in the right direction, while 48 per cent said it was the wrong direction. Five per cent were unsure.

The same poll found 34 per cent want to see property tax frozen or reduced, even at the cost of cutting services.

Twenty per cent said they should increase at less than the rate of inflation.

The election will be held on Oct. 26.

stories.title: Oilers sign acquitted 2018 World Juniors player Alex Formenton
stories.summary: Formenton, a 26-year-old native of Barrie, Ont., spent three seasons over the last four years with HC Ambri-Piotta in Switzerland.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
The Edmonton Oilers have signed forward Alex Formenton to a one-year contract worth US$850,000, the NHL team said Wednesday.

Formenton was one of five players from Canada’s 2018 world junior team who were acquitted last year on sexual assault charges stemming from an encounter with a woman known as “E.M.” after a Hockey Canada gala that year in London, Ont.

The NHL a year ago reinstated all five players, allowing them to play beginning Dec. 1, 2025.

Carter Hart signed with Vegas and backstopped the Golden Knights to the Stanley Cup final last spring before losing to the Carolina Hurricanes in six games. Dillon Dube, a forward, signed with the St. Louis Blues in July.

The 26-year-old Formenton didn’t shy away from questions about the case after his first Oilers practice on Wednesday.

“It was a difficult road, it was tough on my family and me personally ,” Formenton said.

“Throughout the whole process it’s been pretty transparent, you know, everyone is obviously aware of the outcome. It was definitely a difficult time but I’m very grateful and thankful to be here today,” said Fermonton.

An independent appeal board ruled last month that the players breached the Hockey Canada code of conduct, but Formenton was the only one eligible for immediate reinstatement from suspension from Hockey Canada-sanctioned programs.

The board recommended continued bans for Hart, Dube, Cal Foote and Michael McLeod.

The NHL is seperate from Hockey Canada and last year reinstated all five players.

“I think he’s gone through a process, he’s been transparent through the process and that process has led him here today,” Oilers Captain Connor McDavid said of his new teammate. “It’s a great opportunity for him.”

The Formenton signing is also sparking concerns outside the arena, however.

“The Edmonton Oilers’ decision to sign Alex Formenton will have a significant impact on fans, survivors, and the broader Edmonton community,” the Sexual Assault Centre of Edmonton said in a statement to Global News.

Fans also weighed in on Formenton’s signing.

However other fans said they feel Formenton should be able to get on with his life as he sees hit. Formenton said he’s looking the Oilers signing as a fresh start and says he’s a different person today.

stories.title: Tiff tipples and tasting menus offer up a food spectacle, with a $8,888 meal on the menu
stories.summary: An eye-catching feast for six attracts visitors seeking luxury, plus delicious pairings highlight local wines
stories.author: Christopher Waters
stories.content:
The excitement surrounding the 51st annual Toronto International Film Festival extends to the city’s restaurants looking to enhance their dining experiences. In preparation for the influx of tourists and industry guests over the 11-day event, sommeliers have been stocking up noteworthy wines from classic regions as well as top-notch Canadian producers.

In a bid to create an eye-catching menu that matched the spectacle of TIFF, Lai Wah Heen’s culinary team conjured up The Treasure of Fortune, a $8,888 five-course meal featuring reimagined classic Cantonese dishes, designed for six people. Peony Cen, Lai Wah Heen’s sommelier and talent director, says the special festival offering draws its inspiration from the extravagant banquets held by Cantonese merchants in what is now the Liwan district in Guangzhou, China, in the 18 th and 19 th centuries when it was one of the world’s wealthiest trading hubs.

“I thought it would be fitting to offer something that offered luxury with a bit of drama,” she says. The centrepiece of the meal is a goose dish, stuffed with prized ingredients including Italian white truffle, dried abalone and wild Yunnan black tiger paw mushroom, which requires a three-day advance order to prepare.

There’s also the option to pair it with a bottle of Château Margaux 1989, which sells for $3,888 on their wine list.

Cen says she considered recommending the 1982 Lafite Rothschild, a red wine from a legendary Bordeaux estate with a famous film tie-in, after being featured in Chow Yun-Fat’s classic 1989 action film, God of Gamblers . However, she explains that she selected the celebrated vintage of Margaux based on an article by Chinese Master of Wine, Jeannie Cho Lee. She wrote about planning a dinner that served Château Margaux’s wines with classic Cantonese dishes, where the synergy between the 1989 and a savoury beef and mushroom dish made it the highlight of the night.

Beyond the celebratory aspect of the festival, which increases demand for popular Champagne brands and other well-known French labels, TIFF also attracts tourists who are looking to try local products. Ashleigh Forster, head sommelier and assistant general manager at Don Alfonso 1890, believes that the restaurant’s view from the 38 th floor of the Westin Harbour Castle, overlooking the CN Tower, the Rogers Centre and other landmarks, helps to create interest in what the region has to offer.

“It’s fun to help open up the minds and palates of those who haven’t had the opportunity to taste what we can do here,” says Forster, who was the Michelin Guide’s Toronto Sommelier of the Year in 2024.

Forster features Ontario wines from Cave Spring Vineyard, Stratus Vineyards and others on special pairing menus. She said she’s excited to pour local favourites, such as Cloudsley Cellars Hanck Pinot Noir 2021 and Leaning Post Grimsby Hillside Chardonnay 2021, alongside classic bottles from Burgundy, France: Domaine Michel Arcelain Pommard 2017 and Daniel-Etienne Defaix Vaillon Chablis 2014.

“I’m lucky to work with such a large cellar and have the opportunity to bring in special wines for our by-the-glass and pairing programs,” Forster says. “With the temperature of relationship between Canada and the U.S. right now, I have seen a shift in people’s mindset about Canadian wine. They are letting go of past pretenses.”

Across town at Prime Seafood Palace on Queen Street West, head sommelier Matthew Landry has just unpacked deliveries of older vintages from Ontario wineries Hidden Bench, Pearl Morissette and Stratus to pour during TIFF. The combined star power of celebrity chef owner Matty Matheson and culinary director Coulson Armstrong, winner of Top Chef Canada Season 12, mean that the restaurant is gearing up for one of its busiest periods of the year, he says.

“Locals generally aren’t looking for Ontario wine when they come to a place like Prime Seafood Palace, but people from out-of-town are curious, so I want to show off what I consider to be the top-tier wineries,” says Landry, who moved back to Toronto this past October after working at Restaurant Pearl Morissette in Jordan Station, Ont.

“I want to have the best examples of Ontario wine to offer, especially to anyone visiting whose only idea of Canadian wine is icewine.”

Here are my reviews of three wine recommendations from Toronto sommeliers.

13th Street Gamay 2025 (Canada), $19.95

A bright and berry-flavoured red wine like this gamay isn’t an obvious pairing for seafood dishes, which is why Peony Cen likes to surprise guests at Lai Wah Heen. “A lot of our dishes use fermented and rich sauces with flavours that really complement red wine,” she says. The vibrant character of this gamay makes it enjoyable with a wide assortment of Cantonese dishes. This has 12 per alcohol by volume and 3 grams a litre residual sugar. Drink now to 2029. Available in Ontario.

Cave Spring Adam Steps Riesling 2024 (Canada), $27.95

Ashleigh Forster stocks an assortment of rieslings made by Cave Spring, including this off-dry table wine from the namesake Cave Spring Vineyard in Beamsville, Ont. Its mix of citrus and plum flavours and balanced sweetness makes for a versatile wine to pair with a variety of dishes, which is why it’s become a staple on the by the glass listing at Don Alfonso. This has 10 per cent ABV and 30 g/litre r.s. Drink now to 2034. Available direct, cavespring.ca

Tornatore Etna Rosso 2023 (Italy), $24.95

The pretty fragrance and lively character of this distinctive red wine from the north slope of Mount Etna makes it a summertime favourite for Prime Seafood Palace sommelier Matthew Landry. A blend of nerello mascalese and nerello cappuccio grapes with herbal and floral notes results in an elegant and expressive wine. For best enjoyment, serve slightly chilled. This has 14 per cent ABV and 3 g/litre r.s. Drink now to 2029. Available at the above price in Ontario, various prices in Alberta, $32.78 in New Brunswick.

content_blocks.text: Across town at Prime Seafood Palace on Queen Street West, head sommelier Matthew Landry has just unpacked deliveries of older vintages from Ontario wineries Hidden Bench, Pearl Morissette and Stratus to pour during TIFF. The combined star power of celebrity chef owner Matty Matheson and culinary director Coulson Armstrong, winner of Top Chef Canada Season 12, mean that the restaurant is gearing up for one of its busiest periods of the year, he says.

“Locals generally aren’t looking for Ontario wine when they come to a place like Prime Seafood Palace, but people from out-of-town are curious, so I want to show off what I consider to be the top-tier wineries,” says Landry, who moved back to Toronto this past October after working at Restaurant Pearl Morissette in Jordan Station, Ont.
“I want to have the best examples of Ontario wine to offer, especially to anyone visiting whose only idea of Canadian wine is icewine.”

stories.title: More than 2,100 charges laid by West Region OPP during Labour Day traffic campaign
stories.summary: OPP in the West Region laid more than 2,100 charges during this year’s Labour Day long weekend traffic campaign
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
OPP in the West Region laid more than 2,100 charges during this year’s Labour Day long weekend traffic campaign, with speeding accounting for nearly half of all offences.

Police say officers conducted 2,330 traffic stops between Sept. 4 and Sept. 7, resulting in 2,142 charges, up from 1,601 charges laid during the same campaign in 2025.

The annual enforcement and education initiative focused on the “Big Four” risky driving behaviours: aggressive driving, failure to wear a seatbelt, distracted driving and impaired driving.

Speeding violations led the list of offences, with officers laying 1,004 charges compared with 814 during last year’s campaign.

Police also laid 37 stunt driving charges, up from 27 in 2025, while seatbelt-related offences increased to 172 from 123. Officers issued 11 distracted driving charges, more than double the five laid during the previous Labour Day campaign.

Meanwhile, impaired driving charges remained relatively steady, with 52 charges laid this year compared with 50 last year.

stories.title: Social media brings new crowds to Clovermead
stories.summary: Clovermead Adventure Farm in Aymer, Ont. is going viral because content creators have been sharing viral videos showcasing all the attractions the farm has to offer.
stories.author: Lauren Stallone
stories.content:
Clovermead Adventure Farm in Aymer, Ont. is going viral because content creators have been sharing viral videos showcasing all the attractions the farm has to offer.

There are over 65 family-friendly activities including a splash pad, zip lines, wagon rides, and an opportunity to get up close with farm animals.

“It’s been incredible because we are getting people from other areas that we generally can’t get from Toronto, Kitchener, and even from Windsor,” said owner Christy Hiemstra. “When they see these videos of what it’s like to be at the farm at Clovermead they just have to bring their kids.”

Hiemstra said they invite local influencers to come out and promote the farm.

“We go with influencers that have a vision similar to what we have,” said Hiemstra. “We invite them through our administrator.”

With the fall season approaching, Hiemstra said “pumpkin season” is right around the corner at Clovermead.

“Pumpkin festivals are every Saturday starting September 19 and throughout the week we do some canon shows as well,” said Hiemstra. “We put some pumpkins in canons and try to hit some targets.”

stories.title: Jamieson Greer blames Canada for U.S. hitting back over counter-tariffs
stories.summary: Canada forced the United States' hand in delivering its latest trade war escalation, according to U.S. President Donald Trump's trade czar.
stories.author: Ariel Rabinovitch
stories.content:
Canada forced the United States’ hand in delivering its latest trade war escalation , according to U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade czar.

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer issued a statement late Tuesday shortly after Trump signed five executive orders that banned most imports of Canadian dairy and alcohol products, as well as motorcycles.

“After weeks of good faith and intensive efforts between U.S. and Canadian negotiators, Canada walked away from a near-final trade deal that offered better treatment than any other trading partner, and instead Canada chose to embark on senseless retaliation against the United States,” said Greer.

Prime Minister Mark Carney pulled the plug on trade negotiations in August saying Canada was “walking away from a bad deal,” and cited three key sticking points that led the talks to collapse.

One of the issues related to automotive tariffs, and what Carney referred to as “the treatment of Canadian content” in some motor vehicles. The proposed deal only offered tariff relief for cars, while medium or heavy vehicles like trucks were excluded, which Carney said would severely impact Canada’s automotive manufacturing sector.

Another issue Carney described was that the United States wanted to include terms in the deal that would put limits on the trade deals Canada was able to seek with other countries.

Finally, Carney said there were disagreements over French language rules, with few details of exactly where the two sides had disagreed but suggested it related, in particular, to French and said those rules would have amounted to a broader attack on Canada.

Canada’s minister responsible for U.S. trade, Dominic LeBlanc, issued a statement on social media late Tuesday in response, and said he is “in contact” with Greer.

“When the US is ready to engage, our government will work in good faith and constructively towards a more secure mutually beneficial trading relationship that fully respects Canadian sovereignty,” said LeBlanc.

“The Government of Canada is assessing the latest tariff measures from the United States. As has been the case for the last 18 months, our first priority remains on protecting and supporting Canadian workers, farmers, families, and businesses from these unjustified actions.… — Dominic LeBlanc (@DLeBlancNB) September 9, 2026

An earlier statement from LeBlanc’s press secretary on Tuesday said, “Canadian and American officials have maintained ongoing discussions on a range of issues, although formal trade negotiations are not taking place at this stage.”

The latest trade war escalation by the U.S. followed Canada implementing dollar-for-dollar counter tariff measures on U.S. goods on Tuesday, and after tariffs of 50 per cent were imposed on hundreds of Canadian products last month.

Trump last month used Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 to hit Canada with 50 per cent tariffs, accusing Canada of treating the U.S. unfairly.

Tuesday’s executive orders justified Trump’s latest move by saying Canada didn’t stop its discrimination against U.S. autos, dairy and vehicles so now they are able to block the import of certain products because it is “consistent with the interests of the United States and the public interests.”

Speaking in a video posted on social media prior to Trump’s latest escalation, and after implementing counter-tariff measures on the U.S., Carney said, “in the spring of last year, I warned that America is trying to break us so they can own us. And I promised that that will never, ever happen.”

Carney also warned Canadians that “this won’t be easy, and I won’t pretend otherwise,” adding that the alternative would be far worse.

– with files from Global News’ Isaac Callan and The Canadian Press.

stories.title: Woman taken to hospital after Toronto crash involving cyclist and driver
stories.summary: Toronto police said they were called to the area of Sheppard Avenue East and McCowan Road around 9:20 a.m. to respond to the collision.
stories.author: Isaac Callan
stories.content:
A female cyclist has been taken to hospital after a crash with a vehicle on Wednesday morning.

Toronto police said they were called to the area of Sheppard Avenue East and McCowan Road around 9:20 a.m. to respond to the collision.

Investigators said the cyclist and the driver collided, and the driver remained at the scene.

Paramedics said the woman was taken to hospital with serious but not life-threatening injuries.

Westbound lanes on Sheppard Avenue East were briefly closed after the collision but have reopened.

stories.title: Oilers sign forward Formenton to one-year deal
stories.summary: The Edmonton Oilers have signed forward Alex Formenton to a one-year contract worth US$850,000, the NHL team said Wednesday.
stories.author: n The Canadian Pressn
stories.content:
Edmonton – The Edmonton Oilers have signed forward Alex Formenton to a one-year contract worth US$850,000, the NHL team said Wednesday.

Formenton was one of five players from Canada’s 2018 world junior team who were acquitted last year on sexual assault charges stemming from an encounter with a woman known as “E.M.” after a Hockey Canada gala that year in London, Ont.

The NHL a year ago reinstated all five players, allowing them to play beginning Dec. 1, 2025.

Carter Hart signed with Vegas and backstopped the Golden Knights to the Stanley Cup final last spring before losing to the Carolina Hurricanes in six games. Dillon Dube, a forward, signed with the St. Louis Blues in July.

An independent appeal board ruled last month that the players breached the Hockey Canada code of conduct, but Formenton was the only one eligible for immediate reinstatement from suspension from Hockey Canada-sanctioned programs.

The board recommended continued bans for Hart, Dube, Cal Foote and Michael McLeod.

McLeod will not be eligible for reinstatement until Nov. 10, 2030. Foote will be eligible on Nov. 10, while Hart and Dube will be eligible on that day in 2027 and 2028, respectively.

Formenton, a 26-year-old native of Barrie, Ont., was selected by Ottawa in the second round of the 2017 NHL Draft. He recorded 23 goals and 16 assists over 109 career games with the Senators.

Formenton spent three of the past four seasons playing in Switzerland (for HC Ambri-Piotta) and the other not in hockey at all.

McLeod, meanwhile, is under contract in the KHL.

Foote played last season with the American Hockey League’s Chicago Wolves and recently had a one-year contract with Farjestad BK rescinded when the Swedish club received criticism for the signing.

With files from The Associated Press.

stories.title: Feds 'open' to loosening rules banning nicotine pouch sales at convenience stores
stories.summary: The federal government is considering loosening some of its rules around the sale of nicotine pouches.
stories.author: Christopher Nardi
stories.content:
Ottawa — The federal government is considering loosening some of its rules around the sale of nicotine pouches that could see the increasingly popular product sold in Canadian convenience stores, National Post has learned.

One senior federal government source told National Post that the “openness” to change existing regulations comes amid pressures from certain provinces as well as the convenience store industry.

“There is interest on our end” to loosen regulations and allow the products to be sold in convenience stores again, said the source who was granted anonymity in order to discuss private deliberations openly.

But the source insisted that no decision has been taken yet and that the file isn’t a priority for Ottawa, comments confirmed by two other federal or provincial government sources.

Nicotine pouches like Zonnic and Zyn, which are placed between the lip and gum and gradually release nicotine, are a controversial product that has been strictly regulated since 2024.

Currently, Imperial Tobacco Canada’s Zonnic is the only nicotine pouch product approved by Health Canada for sale in the country.

The ministerial regulations established under then prime minister Justin Trudeau capped the products’ concentration at 4 mg of nicotine per pouch and limited flavours to mint and menthol. They also barred any packaging design that could make the product appealing to minors.

The regulations further required the products to only be sold behind the counter at pharmacies, whereas they could previously be sold where tobacco products are available, such as convenience stores.

The Liberal government argued at the time that the strict regulations were necessary because the products potentially presented “a risk of injury to health” and should not appeal to young people.

A cross-country road trip uncovered a booming illicit nicotine pouch market

'Free the Zyn': Why nicotine pouches are all the buzz on Canada's right

But some or all of that could change if the federal government bows to pressure from Alberta, Ontario as well as convenience store giant Alimentation Couche-Tard.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith has been a vocal proponent for Ottawa to ease up its restrictions on nicotine pouch products. In March, she wrote to Prime Minister Mark Carney asking why nicotine pouches were subject to more restrictive sales models than other nicotine pouches or cigarettes.

But in the background, the Ontario government has also lobbied the Carney government to loosen the 2024 regulations on nicotine pouches to allow them to be sold in convenience stores, National Post has learned.

One government source described it as “very quiet diplomacy” and said Ontario Health Minister Sylvia Jones had brought it up during a meeting with her federal counterpart in recent months.

They noted it isn’t a priority for Ontario, but said that there could be an economic opportunity for the province should a foreign pouch maker decide to start manufacturing their products in Canada if the 2024 regulations are loosened.

Behind the scenes, Quebec-based global convenience store giant Couche-Tard — which owns the eponymous chain in Quebec as well as brands Circle K, Mac’s and Statoil in Canada, the U.S. and Europe — has also lobbied the government hard to allow their stores to resume selling nicotine pouches.

According to lobbying records, company lobbyist Marie-Hélène Labrie met with Carney’s chief of staff Marc-André Blanchard and two other PMO advisors on March 13,2026. It also notes that top bureaucrat Michael Sabia also attended on invitation from PMO.

The federal lobbying registry states Labrie met them to discuss health issues linked to the “flexibility, coherence, and predictability of the federal regulatory framework concerning certain goods sold in convenience stores (and grocery stores) in Canada.”

But one source also noted that chain founder Alain Bouchard has met directly with Carney as well as Blanchard in recent months to make the same pitch.

Prime Minister’s Office spokesperson Sofia Ouslis said Blanchard was not available for an interview. She did not deny that the meeting had occurred.

Tobacco companies and their representatives argue that nicotine pouches represent the new era of tobacco cessation products to help smokers kick the habits.

But critics and health advocates argue that they are simply a new way to get people hooked on to nicotine and are designed to attract young consumers. A 2025 paper from researchers at the Ottawa Heart Institute concluded that such products May help reduce the number of cigarettes smoked in a day, but do not appear to increase quit rates.

Part of the argument to loosen regulations is that current rules encourage an unchecked “black market” of nicotine pouches being sold outside of pharmacies — an argument also pushed by tobacco companies who produce such products.

Health Canada said “illegal” products are a “serious concern” but denied any link between the rules mandating nicotine pouches be sold behind pharmacy counters and black market product sold elsewhere.

“Current illicit sales appear to be driven primarily by unauthorized products approved as recreational items in other jurisdictions and by illegal cross‑border importation,” Health Canada spokesperson Karine LeBlanc said in a statement.

Alimentation Couche-Tard did not respond to multiple emailed requests for comment.

Popular nicotine pouches like Zyn have become a political flashpoint in recent years. The Conservative party promised during last year’s election to “free the Zyn” by legalizing the sale of nicotine pouches at stores.

Ontario MP Jamil Jivani has been an especially visible advocate of loosening restrictions, notably signing Zyn canisters during a recent tour of college campuses.

National Post, with files from Rahim Mohamed cnardi@postmedia.com

stories.title: Krose launches mayoral campaign to win, not play spoiler
stories.summary: Surrounded by almost 100 supporters, mayoral candidate Kirsten Krose shared her vision for London at an event in downtown London to officially launch her campaign.
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
Surrounded by almost 100 supporters, mayoral candidate Kirsten Krose shared her vision for London at an event in downtown London to officially launch her campaign.

“I want to do this for the people who live in London,” Krose told the enthusiastic crowd. “I have gained knowledge and experience over 20 years working in government and politics.

I see how a city can be run. I see how levels of government can come together. I see how results can be delivered and I want to do that for Londoners.”

She highlighted the four pillars in her platform:

A city that feels safe for all

Services that work

Traffic that moves

The taxpayer is respected

Following her remarks to supporters, she was interviewed by CTV News.

Krose pushed back when asked if her campaign might play the role of spoiler on election night, asserting that she’s running to bring her vision to the mayor’s office.

“I’ve never heard of a spoiler campaign in my 20 years in (public affairs), I’m running for me and what my vision is. I’m running for what people are telling me,” she responded.

Krose added, “This is for the City of London. This is for the people I just want to represent. What I’m hearing from people and make sure that we get the change that they’re asking for.”

Krose’ campaign platform also proposes several new initiatives at city hall including:

One city hall experience - Residents and businesses should not have to navigate multiple departments to get an answer. Common interactions will be reviewed to reduce unnecessary hand-offs and create clearer responsibility for resolving a resident’s issue.

Traffic bottleneck program - Identifies, ranks and publicly reports London’s most problematic intersections and corridors and then targets practical improvements where they will have the greatest impact

Risk-rank London’s school zones - Prioritize physical safety improvements where speeding, collision history and pedestrian risks are greatest.

London performance dashboard – Display major spending commitments, project status, expected outcomes and significant cost overruns.

Annual taxpayer value report - Straightforward annual account of what City Hall spent, what programs were reviewed, what savings or efficiencies were identified, which major projects stayed on budget and what needs to improve next.

Also running for mayor are Josh Morgan (incumbent), Susan Stevenson, John Feher, Lawrence-Zachary Howe, Barry Douglas Jacklin, Tariq Khan, Dan Lenart, Bronagh Joyce Morgan, Christine Rosehart, Jeff Yam, and Mustafa Zeboon.

Election Day is Oct. 26.

stories.title: Person wearing Cat in the Hat costume chased teen: West Kelowna RCMP
stories.summary: West Kelowna RCMP are investigating after a teenage girl who was out for a walk was reportedly chased by a person dressed in a Cat in the Hat costume.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
West Kelowna RCMP are investigating after a teenage girl who was out for a walk was reportedly chased by a person dressed in a Cat in the Hat costume.

The RCMP said Tuesday the incident occurred on Aug. 24 near the 2000 block of Shamrock Drive. Around 9 p.m. that day, a teenage girl was out for a walk when she was reportedly chased by a person wearing a costume resembling the popular children’s book character.

She was able to make it home safely, police said.

“Regardless of whether the individual intended the behaviour as a joke, following a young person and causing them to fear for their safety is extremely concerning,” said Cpl. Devon Gerrits in a news release.

“People should understand that behaviour intended as a prank can have serious consequences when it causes another person to reasonably fear for their safety.”

Police said those consequences could include criminal harassment if a person being pursued fears for their safety. Other potential offences like assault, uttering threats or intimidation, May also be considered if evidence supports them.

The RCMP is reminding parents and youth that if they believe they are being followed or pursued, they should move toward a safe, populated location, contact a trusted adult and call 911 if they are in immediate danger.

Several incidents involving the Cat in the Hat are emerging across the globe as part of a social media trend.

That trend features a sinister version of the Dr. Seuss character appearing to lurk outside homes and schools, the New York Times reported earlier this month . Some posts appear to have been generated by artificial intelligence.

The Times reported cases in Ireland and in several U.S. states.

Furthermore, the Caledonia Courier reported on Sunday the trend hit Fort St. James, a small community in northern B.C.

stories.title: 25 years ago Canada went to war. It was a war that changed everything.
stories.summary: A quarter of a century ago, the terror attacks of Sept. 11, 2001 forced Canadians to quickly wake up to a world that had changed overnight — and to confront a new war which would change everything for Canada’s military.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — A quarter of a century ago, the terror attacks of Sept. 11, 2001 forced Canadians to quickly wake up to a world that had changed overnight — and to confront a new war which would change everything for Canada’s military.

The Afghanistan war, Canada’s longest armed conflict, taught harsh lessons — some that Canada learned, others it did not.

Soon after the attacks on the Twin Towers and the Pentagon, Canada stepped out of the quiet decade after the Cold War into the global fight on terror, and soon found itself at war with a Taliban insurgency halfway around the world.

“Who would have dreamt the day prior to that, Canadian troops in their thousands would be serving in Afghanistan — Afghanistan, for God’s sake, of all places. It was a dramatic change,” said retired general Rick Hillier, who led a multinational force of Nato nations in Kabul and would become Canada’s best-known chief of defence staff.

“It was a shift in our understanding of how the world functioned. We no longer operated, if you will, as a country isolated from all that upheaval and turmoil and hatred and violence.”

Canada’s ambassador to Nato moved for the alliance to, for the first time ever, invoke Article Five — the clause in the Nato treaty that says an attack on one member country constitutes an attack on all.

Canada went to war with its allies to support the United States and overthrow the Taliban regime which was harbouring the terror group led by Osama bin Laden that was behind the 9-11 attacks.

That alliance spirit is harder to detect today, with Canada’s relationship with the U.S. tanking over a trade war and President Donald Trump threatening to tear up the Nato alliance and pull more troops out of Europe.

In the immediate aftermath of the terror attacks, no one knew that more than 40,000 Canadians would serve in the 12-year Afghanistan war and 159 Canadian military members would lose their lives there.

Eugene Lang, a former chief of staff to two defence ministers, said Ottawa thought at the time it was entering a short-term conflict.

“Nobody was really anticipating what we got into, and we weren’t really prepared for it, in terms of the severity of the situation, the complexity of the situation and the duration,” he said.

Military doctrine had to change on the fly as Canadians learned to fight an insurgency and the Canadian Forces scrambled to find Pashto speakers to help soldiers talk to locals.

The operational tempo was fast and the military entered the war short of necessary equipment and personnel after its budget had been slashed over the 1990s.

“We had a Canadian Forces that was under-strength, under-budget, under-equipped and not ready for operations quite literally anywhere in the world,” Hillier said. “While we were trying to rebuild the basis for an armed forces, we were also getting ready to go to war, and those two things were demanding in a way that was quite incredible.”

Hillier said while Canadians rose to the challenge, the lesson of Afghanistan is that countries can’t afford to take a decade to prepare their armed forces for the next war.

When Canadian troops arrived in Afghanistan, they were the only ones to show up in green uniforms. The military also had wound down its tank fleets and would need to acquire new ones to deal with the proliferation of roadside bombs.

While Canada went into Afghanistan believing Nato allies would cover any equipment shortfalls, Canadian troops often ended up last in line to use any equipment that could be spared — and often did without.

Canada didn’t have helicopters suitable to deploy at the outset, making operations more risky. That’s when Ottawa bought the air force’s Chinook transport helicopters.

Another key lesson from Afghanistan, Hillier said, is that fighting a modern war takes an enormous number of people. The size of the regular force contracted by tens of thousands after the end of the Cold War, and numbered around 60,000 by the time the Afghan war began.

Even now, he said, Canada does not have a large enough military.

“The numbers are so far down as to be sort of frightening and we’ve got to rebuild those numbers,” Hillier said. “I hope that we have learned that lesson and that we’re getting back to it.”

Justin Massie, professor of political science at the Université du Québec à Montréal, said he teaches his students the same lesson about Canada post-9-11 as he does when discussing the Korean War — that Canada entered the conflict with allies, was caught unprepared, scrambled to mobilize, then demobilized after the shooting stopped.

“The Canadian Armed Forces weren’t equipped to wage a combat mission abroad to the likes of what we faced against the Taliban, and so the first victims were Canadian soldiers from improvised explosive devices because they didn’t have armoured vehicles, didn’t have helicopters to move from one village to another, didn’t have the right camouflage gear,” he said.

“There are consequences when you start a war unprepared, and I’m not convinced that we are now prepared to face an adversary such as Russia in eastern Europe.”

He said the current government tends to talk about defence policy more as a way to create jobs than to build a capable military.

Lang said the government has learned that getting into such conflicts can happen very quickly and it can be “very difficult to get out once you’re in.”

He also said the Canadian Armed Forces seems to be on a better footing now than when it entered Afghanistan, thanks to rising defence spending, improving recruitment numbers and aircraft fleets being recapitalized.

“I’m not sure you’re ever really prepared for (war) because you don’t know exactly what it’s going to be and how you’re going to be implicated in it,” he said.

Retired Canadian Armed Forces corporal Bruce Moncur still remembers being told to pack his kit and being given 72 hours notice to move after the 2001 terror attacks.

Moncur, who grew up in the U.S., signed up for the military just months before the event that would change the course of his life.

“I wanted to deploy after those attacks. I was immensely affected,” he said. “I had family, I had friends, I lived there.”

Moncur never knew a peacetime military. He missed the “decade of darkness” after the Cold War — when the defence budget was slashed — and joined up just as the Canadian Forces were getting bigger budgets, better exercises and bigger missions.

He would deploy five years later and take part with about a thousand other Canadian troops in Nato’s largest-ever land battle, known as Operation Medusa. Canadians saw some of the most vicious fighting there against the Taliban at the height of the conflict in September 2006.

Canada’s complex legacy from that war snapped into focus for many this year, but not because of 20- or 25-year anniversaries. In January, President Trump publicly cast doubt on Nato’s contributions and claimed allied troops “stayed a little back, a little off the front lines.”

That offhand comment deeply hurt people who fought in Afghanistan — including Moncur, who was shot three times by an American A-10 Warthog that mistakenly strafed his position.

“When Mr. Trump said the Nato forces weren’t on the front lines, that cut deep because I had friends that lost limbs and died and killed themselves over what they saw on the front line,” he said. “That was really hard on me mentally because I almost died for that — going to the defence of my neighbours to the south and to hear that was very, very distressing.”

Since the war, Moncur has become an outspoken advocate for Canadian Afghanistan veterans. He’s led the charge to get the government to reconsider awarding veterans Canada’s top military honour, the Victoria Cross — something Ottawa recently promised to review.

Lang said that as Canadians look back on the war, they must not let it become something like Canada’s Vietnam — a war that everyone avoids talking about.

“We don’t really want to talk about it much as a country because it wasn’t successful in the end. We sacrificed a lot,” he said. “The main thing for me is that we don’t forget about it. We owe that to the people that served there, if nothing else.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 9, 2026.

Kyle Duggan, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Popular farmers market a fire risk, ordered to close: Fire department
stories.summary: Trails End Farmers' Market on Dundas Street has been ordered to close after multiple inspections by fire officials
stories.author: Brian Williams
stories.content:
A London-area farmers market has been ordered to close until “serious . . . safety deficiencies” are fixed, a local fire department says.

Trails End Farmers’ Market – located about 1.5 kilometres east of London at 4370 Dundas St. – has been served an order to close after multiple inspections by fire officials and other regulatory safety agencies, the Thames Centre fire department said in a statement posted on the municipality’s website. The department said the order was approved by the Ontario fire marshal’s office.
