stories.title: Rights advocate barbara findlay used the law to fight for equity for Lgbtq people
stories.summary: Setting out to serve the queer and trans community, she slowly helped build up case law that advanced their rights
stories.author: Gordon Bowness
stories.content:
As a teenager in the 1960s, barbara findlay was institutionalized against her will for being a lesbian. She transformed that bewildering experience of betrayal and erasure into fuel that powered a 50-year legal career dedicated to serving underdogs and outsiders. findlay (who wrote her name in lower-case letters and eschewed honorifics) is considered one of the most influential jurists in Canada, playing an outsized role in advancing queer and trans rights in this country.

Outside the courtroom, findlay conducted countless anti-oppression workshops, energized numerous advocacy and equity groups and was a generous mentor to scores of law students and young lawyers, efforts that continued well after her retirement in 2019. A breast cancer survivor, findlay struggled in recent years with myalgic encephalomyelitis and other chronic conditions. She died with medical assistance on Aug. 22 in Vancouver. She was 77.

Long-time Vancouver Centre MP Hedy Fry remembers findlay as a woman of steely determination and formidable intellect. “I think her biggest achievement was getting justice and human rights for people who were vulnerable, especially beginning with the 2S-Lgbtq community,” Ms. Fry says. “But also she worked very strongly with Indigenous peoples and Indigenous women. She was just a fighter for justice.”

“She was way ahead of her time,” past president of the Canadian Bar Association Steeves Bujold says. “What she thought was right was at least two, three decades before it became mainstream. She was a visionary.”

Born May 4, 1949 in Regina, findlay was raised in a working-class, Presbyterian family. According to the 2015 documentary In Particular, findlay was a precocious straight-A student. Elsewhere she described her young self as socially awkward and desperately lonely. At the age of 17, she moved to Kingston, Ont., to attend university. That’s when she was institutionalized.

“I said to my psychiatrist, ‘Either there’s something wrong with me or there’s something wrong with the world. And I’m hoping it’s me, because that’d be easier to fix’,” findlay told CBC Radio in 2016. “I was wrong; it was the world.”

So findlay set out to change the world.

After graduating from Queen’s University, findlay moved to Vancouver in 1970 to pursue a graduate degree in sociology at the University of British Columbia. It was a heady time of youthful revolt and critical thinking. findlay described her study of radical feminist thought as foundational to her emerging understanding of the world and how to make it more equitable. Anti-racism work soon expanded that understanding.

“I came to the law on purpose,” findlay said on a CBA podcast in 2023. “I had discovered feminism in 1970 … and I looked around for something that would enable me to have power to make change. And I picked law for that reason.”

At first findlay practised labour law and worked for legal aid in Vancouver for 10 years, working closely with the Native Programs department, trying to advance Indigenous access to the law and support the development of Indigenous-led legal policies.

Following a short stint on the law faculty at UBC, she set up her own private practice in 1992 with the explicit aim of serving the queer and trans community.

“When I opened my legal practice in 1992 the law relating to queers was a desert. There was, for example, no family law regime relating to queers at all, period. We were invisible.”

findlay began to green the desert, slowly building up case law that advanced the rights of queers, trans folk and others. In 2001, for example, arguing before the B.C. Human Rights Tribunal, findlay secured the right of two lesbian moms to appear on their child’s birth certificate. Other breakthroughs would follow including the legal recognition that families can have more than two parents.

“She was very invested in access to reproductive health care, not just in the early abortion battles, but in access to IVF, which is the way that many queer families are made,” says friend and lawyer Adrienne Smith. “barbara’s work making a legal regime clarifying parentage for people who have had assisted reproduction is amazing. She really wrote the model for a parenting agreement involving more than two parents. It was a tremendous advance in family law.”

Arguably her most famous case was one that ended in defeat, but findlay refused to see it that way.

In 1995, Kimberly Nixon filed a human rights complaint against Vancouver Rape Relief Service for denying her employment opportunities because she was a trans woman. findlay took up the case two years later, embarking on an epic 10-year legal battle that went all the way to the Supreme Court of Canada. The B.C. Human Rights Tribunal ruled in Ms. Nixon’s favour in 2002, but then she lost subsequent appeals. In 2007, the Supreme Court dismissed Ms. Nixon’s final appeal on narrow grounds.

In findlay’s view, with her focus on community engagement and media exposure, they had lost the battle but won the war. Ms. Nixon agrees.

“I could see in the early days the media was like a sideshow or circus,” Ms. Nixon says. “Then over time the media evolved: They believed me, they trusted me and they supported me. On a societal level it was really interesting to see that evolution of support.

“The greatest honour to me is that, now, 90 per cent of women’s organizations are trans-inclusive because of barbara and I,” Ms. Nixon says. “They could see that everything I did was based on truth. That’s stronger than the law. It really means so much more to me, that they changed, not because they had to but because it was the right thing to do.”

findlay was an intelligent and passionate lawyer. And she could be scrappy. “She’s fierce,” Ms. Nixon says. “You did not want to be on her wrong side.” Ms. Nixon laughs as she recounts one of her favourite stories about findlay involving an encounter with a reporter who was trying to cast doubt on Ms. Nixon’s gender. “barbara just fired back, ‘Well, Kimberly’s birth certificate has an F, so F you.’ That’s my all-time classic.”

Perhaps as influential as findlay’s case law work was her activism inside the legal profession. In 1992, when there were scarce few out lawyers, findlay founded Sogic (Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity Community) within the B.C. chapter of the Canadian Bar Association, bringing together Lgbtq lawyers to raise their visibility among their colleagues and to share strategies and support in their fight to advance queer and trans rights in the courts. She co-founded a national group in 1996. Sogic-affiliated lawyers brought forth a series of landmark cases en route to securing marriage equality first through the courts in Ontario in 2002 and B.C. in 2003 and then federally through legislation in 2005.

“It’s very, very difficult to convey the suffocating silence of being queer in the legal profession, and in the law, in the early 90s,” findlay told The Every Lawyer podcast in 2024. “Our initial Sogic meetings in Vancouver were accessible by a back entrance, so that people wouldn’t be identified as queer for coming to the meetings.”

Currently, the national queer and trans CBA group, now known as Sadga (Sexual and Gender Diversity Alliance), has hundreds of members across the country – the group’s vice-chair just happens to be the child of the two lesbian moms findlay represented back in 2001.

Co-founding Lawyers Against Transphobia in 2019, findlay has been sounding the alarm on trans rights in recent years. She was particularly concerned with the rising use of the notwithstanding clause in the Charter of Rights to override equality protections, as happened in Saskatchewan and Alberta.

“The wave of right-wing hatred from the United States is splashing over into Canada,” findlay said in 2024. “The dangers to trans folks cannot be overstated.” To findlay, trans rights are the proverbial canary in the coal mine. If using the notwithstanding clause to override trans rights becomes normalized, findlay argued, then everyone’s rights are in jeopardy. findlay’s long history of community organizing speaks to this moment.

“There’s an entire generation now of lawyers and judges steeped in the Charter and the values of the Charter,” findlay said. “That is an amazing protective factor in the face of transphobic attack.”

Both inside and out of the legal profession, findlay had a special gift for connecting people, reaching across differences of identity, experience or understanding that often divide us. Smith, who does not use honorifics and goes by they/them, fondly remembers how findlay befriended them while they were still in law school. “She decided we would be friends and that wasn’t optional. She just called and scheduled lunch, and then, you know, 15 years went by.” They marvel at how many people they know through findlay’s community-building efforts. Ms. Nixon, too, says findlay was more than her lawyer, she was a friend. “She loves each one of those she represented,” Ms. Nixon says.

findlay’s community building was animated by what she called “cultural humility,” a unique combination of joy and skepticism. Her 2023 comments about becoming a trans advocate exemplify this. “One of the things that I find so fascinating about learning about trans stuff is how exciting it is to learn that things I took for granted were in error, and learning to see the world differently, entirely differently than it was taught to me. There’s no greater intellectual fun as far as I’m concerned than to find and unearth and set aside the assumptions that I was educated on.”

barbara findlay leaves her partner of 35 years, Sheila Gilhooly, her chosen family and a community across the country who call her friend. That community – sprawling, diverse, raucous and passionate about social justice – is perhaps findlay’s greatest legacy.

You can find more obituaries from The Globe and Mail here .

To submit a memory about someone we have recently profiled on the Obituaries page, e-mail us at obit@globeandmail.com .

Her 2023 comments about becoming a trans advocate exemplify this. “One of the things that I find so fascinating about learning about trans stuff is how exciting it is to learn that things I took for granted were in error, and learning to see the world differently, entirely differently than it was taught to me. There’s no greater intellectual fun as far as I’m concerned than to find and unearth and set aside the assumptions that I was educated on.”

barbara findlay leaves her partner of 35 years, Sheila Gilhooly, her chosen family and a community across the country who call her friend. That community – sprawling, diverse, raucous and passionate about social justice – is perhaps findlay’s greatest legacy.

content_blocks.text: As a teenager in the 1960s, barbara findlay was institutionalized against her will for being a lesbian. She transformed that bewildering experience of betrayal and erasure into fuel that powered a 50-year legal career dedicated to serving underdogs and outsiders. findlay (who wrote her name in lower-case letters and eschewed honorifics) is considered one of the most influential jurists in Canada, playing an outsized role in advancing queer and trans rights in this country.

content_blocks.text: Born May 4, 1949 in Regina, findlay was raised in a working-class, Presbyterian family. According to the 2015 documentary In Particular, findlay was a precocious straight-A student. Elsewhere she described her young self as socially awkward and desperately lonely. At the age of 17, she moved to Kingston, Ont., to attend university. That’s when she was institutionalized.

content_blocks.text: Perhaps as influential as findlay’s case law work was her activism inside the legal profession. In 1992, when there were scarce few out lawyers, findlay founded Sogic (Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity Community) within the B.C. chapter of the Canadian Bar Association, bringing together Lgbtq lawyers to raise their visibility among their colleagues and to share strategies and support in their fight to advance queer and trans rights in the courts. stories.title: Hundreds of UK flights delayed, cancelled due to Heathrow Airport air traffic control technical issue
stories.summary: Nats, the provider of air traffic control services at Heathrow, first reported the problem around 9 a.m. ET and resolved the issue hours later
stories.author: Dilshad Burman
stories.content:
All flights going in and out of Heathrow Airport in London were cancelled or delayed Tuesday due to technical difficulties with their air traffic control service that lasted several hours.

The issue had ripple effects across the world, including at Toronto Pearson International Airport where a number of flights arriving from and departing for Heathrow were cancelled.

NATS, the provider of air traffic control services at Heathrow, first reported the problem around 9 a.m. ET, saying on X that they were investigating a technical issue “which is causing some disruption to flight departures.”

A few hours later, Heathrow Airport staff posted on X that both arriving and departing flights were affected by the issue. Travellers were advised to check with their airlines for the latest information on their flights and only travel to the airport if their flight was confirmed.

Around 2:30 p.m. ET, NATS officials said the technical issue took longer than anticipated to fix, but was resolved. They said they were working hard to clear the backlog of flights.

More to come

stories.title: B.C. man killed by stray bullet while at home, RCMP say
stories.summary: Chang Yong Cho, 85, found dead shortly after reports of shots fired about a block away
stories.content:
Homicide investigators say an 85-year-old man was killed in his Burnaby, B.C., home by a stray bullet from a shooting a block away, and are appealing to a group of youth believed to be involved to “do the right thing” and come forward.

Sgt. Freda Fong with the Integrated Homicide Investigation Team said investigators believed a personal dispute among the teenagers may have led to the death of Chang Yong Cho in a “heartbreaking and tragic” case.

The homicide team said Cho was found dead in his home around 4 p.m. on Sunday, Aug. 30, more than 14 hours after police responded to reports of shots being fired.

Fong told reporters at a briefing in Burnaby that the group of young people believed to have been involved know police want to talk to them.

“We have been making efforts to locate the youth and to identify their exact involvement in the shooting,” she said, while also urging their parents to come forward.

“They’re young individuals, maybe they somehow got access to guns, but we do believe someone will have the heart to do the right thing for the sake of Mr. Cho’s family and to give them some answers. Maybe it was a mistake,” said Fong.

It was unclear about how many youth were involved in the incident, but Fong said they were from the Lower Mainland, including one person from Burnaby.

She said she did not want to go further in identifying them “so as not to compromise their rights in the future.”

Fong declined to say how many bullets were fired, where exactly Cho had been in the apartment or if he was asleep when he was shot.

She said any time young people are involved in a case, police need to exhibit care in what they tell the public, in case the investigation is compromised.

“They know who we’re talking about, and we’re appealing to them and their parents to do the right thing, right now,” Fong said of the suspects, adding that the crime was not believed to be gang-related or linked to the drug trade.

Fong said Burnaby RCMP officers had responded to the initial report of shots near 18th and Humphries avenues at around 1:30 a.m. on Sunday.

A vehicle thought to be linked to the shooting had fled before police arrived and the initial investigation did not locate any injured victims, the homicide team said in a statement.

It was not until Sunday afternoon that RCMP received a request for a wellness check in an apartment complex in the 7400 block of Kingsway, where officers located Cho with a gunshot wound. He was subsequently pronounced dead.

“Preliminary findings led investigators to believe the deceased was an innocent victim who was struck by a stray bullet from the earlier shots-fired incident,” the statement said.

There was no visible indication of the shooting at the apartments on Tuesday.

Fong called the case “highly unusual” and the complexities of the scene led police to delay the “shocking” preliminary findings.

Cpl. Mike Kalanj with Burnaby RCMP said he believed Cho lived alone.

“We’re doing everything we can to find the people responsible for this,” he said, adding that Cho was known in the community as “a lovely individual.”

The homicide unit said it was identifying the victim in an effort to advance the investigation.

“This is a heartbreaking and tragic loss of life,” Fong said. “Mr. Cho was simply in his home when his life was suddenly taken, leaving behind a grieving family and loved ones.”

Fong said the source of the gun would be part of the investigation.

“What’s important here is that this is a stark reminder that any time there is gun violence in our communities, someone innocent can be at risk. And this was someone’s grandpa, this was someone’s dad who leaves behind a grieving and loving family,” said Fong.

Kalanj said the shooting was every first responder’s “nightmare.”

Homicide investigators want to speak to witnesses and anyone with dashcam or security footage from the area near the scene in Burnaby between 12:30 a.m. and 2 a.m. on August 30.

Fong said “the Cho family deserves answers.”

“At that age, you would expect that they pass peacefully, surrounded by their loved ones,” she said. “He didn’t have that opportunity, and you need to do the right thing and take some accountability for yours or your children’s actions, and we’re pleading for you to come forward to help our investigation.”

stories.title: Here’s where Canada’s counter-tariffs will hit Canadian wallets the hardest
stories.summary: Canadian consumers are likely to face higher prices as a result of new counter-tariffs of up to 50 per cent on hundreds of U.S. goods — even for Canadian products.
stories.author: Ariel Rabinovitch
stories.content:
Canadian consumers are likely to face higher prices, even for some Canadian products, as a result of new counter-tariffs of up to 50 per cent on hundreds of U.S. goods worth about $28 billion.

Tariffs are taxes or duties applied for importing certain goods, and as businesses generally face heightened costs, including from these new counter-tariff measures, experts say they may choose to pass them along to consumers by raising sticker prices.

“Eventually, the costs of domestic products are going to start to rise, the cost of doing business for Canadian firms goes up, [and] eventually, some of them are going to have no choice but to raise their own costs, and so we’re going to see the prices of Canadian products go up,” says economics professor Joseph Steinberg at the University of Toronto.

These latest counter-tariff measures come as a response to U.S. President Donald Trump imposing 50 per cent tariffs on hundreds of Canadian products last month, especially those within the dairy, alcohol and automotive sectors.

Although the U.S. tariffs are mainly felt by American businesses and consumers, at least in the near term, some experts say Canada’s counter-tariff measures in response could soon lead to higher prices for Canadian consumers.

“Food and beverage would be at the top of that list. Ingredients going into food and beverages products, we know dairy products are on the list, both the lists of both countries in that case,” says John Boscariol, partner at McCarthy Tétrault and co-head of the international trade and investment law group .

“Secondly, I’d look at appliances, home appliances are on that list and we can expect that that could also be an area of a potential expansion to the extent that we’re going to see further retaliation on each side.”

Boscariol also says some agricultural products will likely get hit by these counter-tariffs, which could eventually result in higher prices for food and beverages in Canada.

Among the hundreds of U.S. items facing these new counter-tariffs, there are consumer focused goods ranging from U.S. dairy products to seafood, some furniture products made of wood, beauty and makeup items ranging from perfume to sunscreen, as well as clothing and textiles including men’s suits, t-shirts and dresses, track suits and ski suits, even hazardous material suits and other protective clothing.

Beyond consumer goods hit by these new counter-tariffs, there are also many items Steinberg refers to as “intermediate” goods. This means items that consumers may not regularly see or purchase, but are often required as part of a manufacturing process or supply chain that ultimately could mean higher prices for a wider variety of goods — even if they’re made in Canada.

For example, tariffs of 15 or 25 per cent are being applied to U.S. tower cranes, jacks and hoists, forklift trucks and lawn mowers, rail locomotives, train parts and railway maintenance vehicles, among many others. There are also smaller components that go into making machinery and other equipment, including pumps, compressors, fans, insulating conductors and networking components.

U.S. steel, aluminum and copper products are also being hit with a 50 per cent counter-tariff, up from 25 per cent. This includes steel rods, bars and sheets, along with prefabricated items such as bridges, towers, scaffolding and door and window frames, and aluminum products such as wires, bars, rods and foil.

“These are what I would call ‘intermediate’ inputs that manufacturers and agricultural businesses in Canada need to conduct their business,” says Steinberg.

“You and I don’t buy construction machinery parts or insulated conductors, but the Canadian businesses that operate here, many of them do. And so that’s going to raise the cost of doing business for lots of different types of Canadian firms, manufacturers, and agricultural firms in particular.”

“The longer this goes on, the longer that increased cost of business is kind of with us, the more it’s going to reduce our economy overall.”

Steinberg also says that because Canadian businesses are going to see their costs increase, that also could mean Canadian-made products are likely going to go up in price.

Consumer patriotism has been on the rise in Canada ever since the U.S. launched its trade war with the world last year, and especially with Trump’s repeated threats on Canada’s sovereignty and that it should become the “ 51st state.”

2:10 Buy Canadian app sees spike in popularity

Canadian products that consumers were prioritizing may become more expensive as a result of these counter-tariffs.

“The products at the grocery store that are made in Canada, their prices are going to go up as a result of these retaliatory tariffs, and eventually what that’s going to do is it’s going to make it harder or at least more costly for Canadians to double down on ‘buying Canadian,” says Steinberg.

But the majority of Canadians may be willing to endure some higher prices amid the latest trade war escalations, as suggested by a new Angus Reid Institute poll released Tuesday, which polled roughly 1,500 Canadian adults from Sept. 3 to Sept 4.

Three-in-five (60 per cent) of respondents said they are willing to stay the course on Canada’s current negotiating strategy even if it means paying 10 or 20 per cent more for household expenses, including groceries and clothing.

“No one wants to see continuing rounds of additional duties or additional trade measures being taken that harm consumers on both sides of the border. It’s counterproductive for consumers, processors and manufacturers, and it’s in the best interests of both parties to now come to the negotiation table and hammer something out,” says Boscariol.

“Consumers are going to be pretty conservative over these next days and weeks when they think about their spending, knowing that all signs point to increasing costs, unfortunately.”

stories.title: N.S. tables bill to increase protection for some workers
stories.summary: The new protections in the proposed legislation would not apply to some workers, including people working in the construction and agriculture sectors.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
The Nova Scotia government has tabled legislation that would increase protections for some workers.

The bill tabled by Labour Minister Nolan Young would reduce the overtime threshold from 48 hours per week to 44 hours and give the government new tools to recover unpaid earnings owed to workers.

The proposed legislation would also expand overtime eligibility to ensure overtime pay is offered when extra hours are voluntary, not just when overtime work is required by an employer.

The new protections in the proposed legislation would not apply to some workers, including people working in the construction and agriculture sectors.

Another amendment in the newly tabled bill would guard against tip theft, ensuring gratuities are paid to those who earn the tips.

The legislation proposes to implement the changes to overtime and tip protection rules on April 1, while wage recovery measures would come into effect through separate regulations.

stories.title: Toronto police and mayor outline safety plans for upcoming Jewish High Holy Days
stories.summary: Chief Demkiw said police presence "both visible and covert" will take place through holidays and the anniversary of the October 7 attacks.
stories.author: Chris Knight
stories.content:
Toronto Chief of Police Myron Demkiw and Mayor Olivia Chow have provided an update on safety plans for the Jewish High Holy Days, with the police chief outlining a host of measures that will be in place this year.

In a press conference Tuesday afternoon at Toronto Police Headquarters, Demkiw said the Toronto police would have “an increased presence, both visible and covert, in strategic areas to help keep people safe.”

This includes embedding Toronto police officers with the Jewish Security Network , an independent, professional agency launched in 2024 by the United Jewish Appeal of Greater Toronto. There will also be command posts set up, including one at Bathurst and Sheppard.

“We have seen an alarming increase in hate-motivated incidents targeting the Jewish communities in Toronto and indeed in cities around the world,” Demkiw said.

He added that, since Oct. 7, 2023, Toronto police have made 573 arrests and laid 1,398 charges “in connection with demonstrations, protests and hate-motivated offences.”

After the High Holy Days, he continued, “we will maintain an enhanced presence throughout the anniversary of the October 7 terrorist attacks, to help ensure the safety of our communities.”

In her remarks, Chow said: “Jewish Torontonians should not need police presence to go to a synagogue or a community centre or simply to live proudly Jewish in our city. But they do.”

She continued: “In this moment of emboldened antisemitism, Jews, Jewish institutions and even Jewish neighbourhoods are being targeted. It is despicable.”

Toronto man charged with terrorism following anti-Israel protests: police

Chow added: “The Toronto police have also increased the number of officers in the hate-crime unit to investigate major incidents like the cowardly overnight shooting at North York synagogues, and to find those responsible and bring them to justice.”

Jewish holidays begin at sundown on the date in question. This year, Rosh Hashanah (the Jewish New Year) starts on Friday, Sept. 11, through nightfall on Sunday, Sept. 13. This is followed by the Fast of Gedaliah on Monday, Sept. 14.

Yom Kippur (the Day of Atonement) begins on Sunday, Sept. 20, through nightfall on Monday, Sept. 21.

Sukkot (Feast of Tabernacles) starts on Friday, Sept. 25 and runs through nightfall on Friday, Oct. 2.

The Toronto Police announcement follows similar remarks on Friday by the Montreal police (Spvm) . They too said they were closely monitoring the upcoming High Holidays and events marking the third anniversary of the October 7 attacks in Israel, and that they will adjust operations as needed based on available information.

The Spvm said Friday that “there is currently no indication of a specific or heightened threat,” and described the measures being taken as part of the department’s “usual practices around major gatherings, religious holidays and other significant events.”

Jewish institutions in Montreal and Toronto have been targeted in several attacks since the outbreak of the Israel-Hamas war in October 2023, including shootings at Jewish schools, and firebombings targeting synagogues and community centres.

stories.title: Telus sues former employee, alleges they charged $1.1M to company credit card
stories.summary: The company says the total value of the items reached almost $1.1 million, with some allegedly re-sold by the accused on Amazon and other online storefronts.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
Telus is suing a former employee for more than $1 million, alleging he purchased thousands of items including household appliances using company credit cards.

It says the man it employed in 2015 was in a position with “significant authority and discretion” over company procurement, equipment acquisitions and budgets.

Telus Communications alleges he began directing employees to make purchases using an Amazon business account linked to a company credit card starting in 2020, buying more than 2,500 identified items including home theatre equipment, a refrigerator, a dishwasher, cameras and consumer electronics.

The company says the total value of the items reached almost $1.1 million, with some allegedly re-sold by the accused on Amazon and other online storefronts.

None of the allegations in a notice of civil claim filed with the Supreme Court of British Columbia last week have been proven in court.

Telus says the man was terminated with cause on Aug. 13 after the alleged misappropriation was discovered, and the company is seeking the amount used to buy the items, costs and general and punitive damages.

A Canadian comedian is generating buzz with his new documentary on Silicon Valley fraudster Elizabeth Holmes.

Nathan Fielder’s “You Can See Everything” had its world premiere at the Telluride Film Festival in Colorado over the weekend, quickly becoming one of the season’s most talked-about films.

Holmes was convicted of fraud in 2022, after her startup Theranos was shown to have exaggerated the results it could garner from a device it developed to detect hundreds of diseases with just a few drops of blood.

About a month before she went to jail in 2023, Fielder moved into her Southern California rental home and started chronicling her preparations for incarceration in Texas.

Media outlets reported fans waited hours for a chance to attend the Telluride screening and those who made it inside were urged not to divulge some of the movie’s juiciest twists. However, early reviews of the film say Fielder and co-director Lance Oppenheim received unprecedented access to Holmes and her partner Billy Evans.

Vancouver-bred Fielder is best known for blending comedy and reality in projects that blur the lines between truth and fiction.

His docu-comedy TV series “The Rehearsal” explores how far people will go to reduce the unpredictability of their lives. With the help of actors and construction crews, he directs elaborately staged rehearsals meant to help people prepare for big life moments.

He got his start on CBC’s “This Hour Has 22 Minutes,” where he starred in segments called Nathan on Your Side. In them, Fielder took on the role of an absurdist TV reporter offering consumers advice around buying products such as winter tires, or interviewing kids about holiday wish lists.

Fielder is not the first to delve into the Holmes story.

Theranos’ unravelling was also explored in “The Dropout,” a TV series starring Amanda Seyfried; “The Inventor: Out for Blood in Silicon Valley,” a documentary from Alex Gibney; and “Bad Blood: Secrets and Lies in a Silicon Valley Startup,” a novel from investigative journalist John Carreyrou.

However, a short trailer distributor A24 released in tandem with the Telluride screening revealed Fielder’s take on the failed entrepreneur may be the most intense yet. It’s set for release in October.

The teaser features a close-up of Holmes and Fielder staring intently at one another while Holmes asserts that she’s being truthful. She says, “Why would I deceive you? There’s no — there’s no reason for me to do that.”

Fielder replies, “You’re being real right now?”

Holmes, still not breaking her gaze, says, “I am always being real,” before the camera pans out, showing her baby bouncing in a seat behind her.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 8, 2026.

Tara Deschamps, The Canadian Press

stories.title: London man charged after witness reports firearm pointed at vehicle
stories.summary: Police seized two replica firearms, drugs and identity documents belonging to other people Monday evening.
stories.author: Ryan Goodison
stories.content:
Police seized two replica firearms, drugs and identity documents belonging to other people Monday evening.

Last updated 29 minutes ago[](http://lfpress.com/news/local-news/London-man-charged-after-witness-reports-firearm-pointed-at-vehicle#comments-area)

London Police headquarters. (Free Press file photo)

A 46-year-old London man is facing multiple charges after police seized two replica firearms, drugs and identity documents belonging to other people Monday evening.

Shortly after 5:45 p.m., London police received a report from a witness who saw a man point what appeared to be a firearm toward the passenger side of his vehicle in the area of Belfield Street.

Officers located and arrested the suspect a short distance away within minutes of the report, police said.

During a search following the arrest, police seized two replica firearms, multiple bank and identification cards belonging to other people, approximately 0.3 grams of suspected crystal methamphetamine and drug paraphernalia.

Police said one of the imitation firearms matched the description provided by the witness.

The accused is charged with pointing a firearm, possession of an identity document, possession of an imitation weapon, breach of probation and possession of a Schedule I substance.

He remains in custody and is expected to appear in London court Tuesday.

Anyone with information is asked to contact London police at 519-661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-8477.

A 41-year-old London man is facing multiple charges, including impaired driving, after a single-vehicle collision with a hydro pole in Thames Centre.

Ontario Provincial Police responded at 1:16 a.m. Saturday to a report of a vehicle that left the roadway and struck a hydro pole on Gore Road.

Police said a passenger fled on foot before officers arrived. Members of the OPP canine and emergency response teams searched for the passenger, who was found and taken to hospital as a precaution.

The driver was arrested and taken to the Middlesex OPP detachment.

He is charged with operation while impaired by alcohol, dangerous operation and communicating with anyone for the purpose of obtaining sexual services.

He was released from police custody and is scheduled to appear in London court on Oct. 7.

stories.title: London doctor urges action after Ontario lowers colorectal cancer screening age
stories.summary: The LHSC specialist says too many people wait for symptoms before getting checked.
stories.author: Brian Williams
stories.content:
A London Health Sciences Centre doctor is encouraging eligible adults to get checked for colorectal cancer after a provincial health agency lowered the screening age for the deadly disease to 45.

LHSC gastroenterologist Michael Sey said Ontario Health’s decision in July to lower the minimum screening age for colorectal cancer from 50 to 45 comes as cases of the potentially fatal disease rise among younger adults.

“A lot of research has come out over the last five (to) 10 years, which indicate that we’re seeing colon cancer more often in younger people, people younger than 50, mostly people in their 40s,” Sey explained. “That was the reason behind the drop in the age.”

Although colorectal cancer is highly treatable when detected early, Sey said one of the biggest problems is that there are often no symptoms in the early stages. He noted patients diagnosed at stage one have a five-year survival rate of 92 per cent.

Symptoms including abdominal pain, blood in the stool and iron-deficiency anemia tend to appear when colorectal cancer has advanced, at which point survival outcomes drop significantly, Sey said. He noted the five-year survival rate falls to 10 per cent for patients at stage four.

“Some people can get even blockages like vomiting, but again, these are generally fairly advanced signs that we don’t want to wait for symptoms,” he said. “That’s the point of screening is you get it at such an early stage that you don’t even have symptoms.”

The move to lower the age for colorectal cancer screening was welcomed by the Canadian Cancer Society.

The organization called the decision a “critical step” that reflects growing momentum across Canada to detect cancer earlier and save more lives. In a May news release, it noted Ontario became the second province to adopt the policy in response to rising colorectal cancer rates among younger adults.

“The move comes on the heels of Prince Edward Island’s March 30 announcement and in the wake of mounting calls from CCS and other organizations to adapt screening programs to respond to changing needs,” the Canadian Cancer Society stated, urging the remaining provinces and territories to follow suit.

Colorectal cancer is the fourth most commonly diagnosed cancer and the second leading cause of cancer-related death in Canada, according to the Canadian Cancer Society. The organization says rates are “climbing among people younger than 50,” with younger people now two to 2.5 times more likely to be diagnosed than previous generations at the same age.

It isn’t clear why colorectal cancer is affecting younger adults more often than in previous generations, but Sey said dietary changes, such as eating more red meat and animal fats and fewer leafy greens, have been associated with a higher risk.

Sey, who recently turned 45, has been screened for colorectal cancer himself and said the process was easy.

He visited his family doctor and received a screening kit with instructions about a week later.

“Just follow the instructions, it’s really easy, and then you just put it back in that prepaid envelope, it’s already pre-addressed,” he said. “Just drop it off in a mailbox. You can also drop it off at any Rexall.”

For people without a family doctor, Sey said they can call 811 to arrange screening.

“I would say don’t delay,” Sey urged. “Go get screened today. . . (it’s) big for your health.”

stories.title: B.C. Premier David Eby to speak as Canada’s counter-tariffs now in effect
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney vowed to match Trump’s recently imposed 50 per cent tariffs “dollar-for-dollar,” and trade negotiations fell apart last month.
stories.author: Amy Judd
stories.content:
B.C. Premier David Eby slammed U.S. President Donald Trump on Tuesday afternoon as Canada’s counter-tariffs went into effect on billions of dollars’ worth of U.S. goods.

“In just three days, we mark the 25th anniversary of the September 11th attacks,” Eby said.

“Now, these horrific attacks represented a day of unimaginable tragedy for so many. Our closest friend and neighbour was under direct attack, and in that moment of fear and uncertainty, Canadians stepped forward.”

Eby said on that day, 8,500 passengers were diverted to Vancouver’s International Airport.

“Now, before smartphones and instant messaging, they found out when they landed about what was going on,” Eby added.

“And in that moment, airport workers, volunteers stepped up at a moment’s notice. People opened up their homes in Vancouver, Richmond, Delta, Squamish, Abbotsford and beyond, and they also opened up their hearts.”

Eby said now, 25 years later, Trump has “hurled insults, unfair tariffs and continues to threaten our independence as a country.”

“And if, after all of the president’s bad behavior, after everything that he’s done, if Americans ever had to face the same kind of horrors that they did on Sep. 11, would Canadians step up in the same way?

“You bet your ass we would.”

Eby said the government will continue to work with Mark Carney’s government to make sure small businesses in the province are supported when they are hit by tariffs.

He urged everyone to buy local or buy Canadian and choose local businesses to fill jobs or product needs.

Eby said the government will soon be re-launching its Buy BC program to include more products.

“On top of continuing our ban on U.S. alcohol products on B.C. liquor store shelves, we will continue to stand up for British Columbia and British Columbians and defend our economy against these unfair attacks,” he added.

“Twenty-five years ago, when fear and uncertainty came to our doorstep, Canada answered with generosity and compassion. Those values have not changed. We are still the country that opens its doors when others are in need.

“We are still the country that stands by its friends, and we are still the country that stands up for itself on our own two feet.”

Carney vowed to match Trump’s recently imposed 50 per cent tariffs “dollar-for-dollar,” and trade negotiations fell apart last month.

As the country pivots away from the United States, Carney is warning Canadians that “this won’t be easy, and I won’t pretend otherwise.” He added that the alternative would be far worse.

-with files from Ariel Rabinovitch

stories.title: Warm conditions across southwestern Ontario ahead of showers, thunderstorms
stories.summary: Southwestern Ontario is enjoying warm, sunny weather to start the school year, but forecasters say a cold front will bring an increased chance of showers and thunderstorms on Wednesday.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
Southwestern Ontario is enjoying warm, sunny weather to start the school year, but forecasters say a cold front will bring an increased chance of showers and thunderstorms on Wednesday.

Temperatures reached the mid-to-high 20s across the region Tuesday, with London climbing to about 26 C and warmer conditions near Windsor.

“It was a beautiful start to the back-to-school season across southern Ontario,” said CTV News meteorologist Julie Atchison.

Cloud cover is expected to increase overnight, with a slight chance of showers in parts of Midwestern Ontario, including Grey, Bruce and Perth counties. Overnight temperatures are expected to remain mild, near 20 C.

A cold front moving in from the northwest is expected to arrive Wednesday afternoon, bringing scattered showers and the possibility of thunderstorms.

“This is not shaping up to be an all-day rain event,” Atchison said. “It’s a frontal system that will bring the chance of showers later in the day for London and Windsor, while areas in midwestern Ontario could see rainfall earlier.”

Despite the unsettled weather, temperatures are expected to remain warm, reaching between 22 C and 26 C. Humidity levels will also increase ahead of the front before cooler conditions move in Wednesday evening.

stories.title: Canadian man killed while volunteering as a drone mechanic in Ukrainian army
stories.summary: Jessy Bourgeois of Nanaimo, B.C., gave his life in the defence of Ukraine, despite not having any formal ties to the country.
stories.author: Kenn Oliver
stories.content:
A Canadian father with no formal ties to Ukraine who left his life and family in B.C. to help the war-torn nation defend against Russia’s illegal invasion was killed in action on the front lines last month.

“I want him to be remembered as a hero,” his mother, Valery Simonds, told Victoria-based Chek News after a memorial prayer service for her 46-year-old son Jessy Noel Bourgeois was held at a church in Nanaimo on Saturday.

Dawn Bourgeois, his stepmother, said a celebration of life will take place when Jessy is repatriated, something they’re still waiting on despite him dying under unknown circumstances in the Donetsk region on Aug. 18 while serving as an aerial drone crew mechanic in Ukraine’s army.

“We’re still waiting to hear back from the embassy to make arrangements and get the information,” Dawn told National Post

The Embassy of Canada to Ukraine in the capital of Kyiv has been temporarily closed to in-person services since November 2024. Canadian Ambassador to Ukraine Natalka Tsmots recently told Ukrainian media outlet Ukrinform that there are currently 25 Canadians and Ukrainian staff there.

National Post has contacted Global Affairs Canada for more information.

Dawn attended Jessy’s service at the St. Michael the Archangel Ukrainian Catholic Church, where he was a congregant and where he fell in love with the Ukrainian community. She told National Post that being there to grieve with Jessy’s adopted community helped her and his father, James, understand his decision to risk his life in war.

“Going to the church and meeting the pastor and the people that were involved in Jesse’s life, at that point in time, we realized how committed he was to the cause and how he wanted to support them and how much he loved the Ukrainian community and the people.”

At least 20 combatants from Canada have been killed in action on the front lines of Ukraine

Ukraine on the brink: A Canadian journalist's blunt warning about the war-torn country

A friend introduced him to the church community, she said, and Jessy soon began learning Ukrainian. When he told his language instructor about his desire to fight in Ukraine, she and others in the congregation — some of whom have lost loved ones to the war — warned him of the danger, but were unsuccessful in talking him out of it.

“There was a lot of profound sadness and devastation with the people of the church as well,” she told National Post, her voice breaking. “Yes, they wanted him to support the cause, but I don’t think they were prepared for him to go over and fight the way he did.”

Prior to departing, he had no military or drone experience, she said.

In Ukraine, Dawn said Jessy’s call sign was “Skoden,” Indigenous slang for “let’s go,” a nod to his Metis roots.

“I just look at his picture, and I just see this is what he wanted to do,” she said. “It makes me feel warm.”

Jessy leaves to mourn two children, Maya, 11, and Elliot, 9, with whom his stepmother said he maintained contact while in Ukraine.

The kids’ mom and his ex-wife, Adrianne Cafariello, told Chek they were all “very proud” of him.

“He loved these kids,” Adrianne Cafariello. “He just loved to watch them be the selfless, amazing children that they are, and I want people to remember that yes, he’s a hero for the Ukraine, but he’s also a hero to these children. And that’s the memory that we hold dear in our hearts for him.”

His stepmother said everyone’s focus is now on those kids and “their health and well-being.”

Jessy is predeceased by his brother Jimmy (May 14, 2024).

“Two of my brothers are now at rest. May you both light up the stars together,” his sister, Tanya Larsen, wrote on Facebook , also sharing a photo of Jessy in military fatigues, holding a drone above his head.

“His sacrifice is a testament to the fact that freedom, dignity, and humanity know no borders,” they wrote.

“Jessy was remembered not only for his service in Ukraine but for his meaningful presence within the parish community, his participation in Ukrainian language classes, his genuine love for Ukrainian culture, his willingness to help, and his kindness toward children,” added the Association of Ukrainian Canadian Veterans.

Global Affairs Canada told National Post in February that while it does not track the number of Canadians who travel to Ukraine to fight or those killed in combat, it was aware of 27 Canadian citizens who have died in Ukraine from all causes since the war started. Jessy’s death would bring that to 28.

stories.title: Toddler found safe after hours-long search during storm in Oxford County
stories.summary: A toddler from the Township of Blandford-Blenheim was found safe after being reported missing during a major storm last week in Oxford County.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
A toddler from the Township of Blandford-Blenheim was found safe after being reported missing during a major storm last week in Oxford County.

According to police, ON Sept. around 1 p.m., the toddler was outside playing with family when they went missing.

Thanks to the prompt call to OPP, resources were quickly deployed, including canine.

At approximately 9 p.m., after hours of searching in adverse weather conditions, the toddler was located safe.

Oxford OPP would like to thank everyone who assisted in the search.

No injuries were reported. Police said no further details will be released and the investigation is complete.

stories.title: First of three new TVDSB elementary schools opens in London
stories.summary: The Thames Valley District School Board has debuted one of three new elementary schools it will open this year: Jackson Meadows Public School.
stories.author: Sean Irvine
stories.content:
The Thames Valley District School Board (TVDSB) has debuted one of three new elementary schools it will open this year: Jackson Meadows Public School.

The nearly $30-million Jackson Meadows Public School, sits in the expanded Summerside neighbourhood in London’s southeast end.

While many scenes from the first day of classes mirrored those across our region, there were a few more butterflies here as students and staff came together for the first time to form a new school community.

“I’m a little nervous and excited”, said Yuvrha Bahia, a grade four student.

Teachers themselves suffering from first-day jitters, worked to calm fears as classes formed outside for the first time.

“I know there will be changes from what they’re used to. We’re going to do things differently than their other schools. But hopefully everybody is on board and positive and just keeping an open mind,” said Jessica Bowering, a grade 7/ 8 educator.

While ready on day one, finishing touches on the gym and the library will take another week or two.

Still, parents told CTV News London they’re impressed with the design and technology found inside and outside of the building.

“It’s going to be a great opportunity for kids. They’ve got a state-of-the-art facility for all the students to learn,” said parent Tyler Erdie.

The school has a capacity for 655 students but is opening with about 460.

That is good news for parents moving their children from crowded schools nearby, said Kyle Trudell as he dropped his children off.

“It’s awesome. They were going to Summerside school, but it was overpopulated,” he added.

Still, with new housing being constructed around the school site, it May not be long before classrooms fill up, acknowledged principal Ken Overeem.

“There’s lots of building going on in the area, so I anticipate within the next couple of years we May be at capacity, depending on how the building goes in the area.”

Jackson Meadows is the first of three new public elementary schools to open in the TVDSB this school year. The others are in Belmont and in Lucan.

There is more to come, said Dennis Wright, a TVDSB Superintendent. “London’s still one of the fastest-growing cities in Canada. And so, yeah, we’re on track to continue to build over the next few years. We’re looking at new applications to the ministry, even this year, with four or five new applications.”

stories.title: London man arrested after gun pointed at passing vehicle
stories.summary: London man arrested after gun pointed at passing vehicle CBC
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: London police arrested and charged a man with firearms offences after someone reported seeing a gun pointed at a passing car on Monday evening.
· Posted: Sep 08, 2026 2:16 PM EDT | Last Updated: 30 minutes ago
London police say the quick actions of a witness helped them catch a man suspected of pointing a gun at a passing vehicle.(London Police Service)
Officers also found meth, drug paraphernalia, and multiple bank cards, health cards, membership cards and a driver's license belonging to an individual other than the accused, police said.
The incident began at about 5:45 p.m. when someone called police to say they'd seen a man pointing a gun at their vehicle on Belfield Street, between Kipps Lane and Huron Street.
Offers stopped the suspect a short distance away and found two replica firearms in a backpack. One matched the description of the gun provided by the witness.
A 46-year-old man has been charged with pointing a firearm, breaching probation, possessing an imitation weapon, possession of drugs and possession of identity documents.
The man arrested by police remains in custody and is expected to appear in court Tuesday.

stories.title: Alberta business leaders' group urges voters to choose Canada in Oct. 19 referendum
stories.summary: Calgary - A group of Alberta business leaders is urging voters to choose Canada in next month's secession referendum but admits it's an issue fraught with tension on the front lines.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
EDMONTON - A group of Alberta business leaders is urging voters to choose Canada in next month’s secession referendum but admits it’s an issue fraught with tension on the front lines.

The Business Council of Alberta is composed of more than 130 chief executives representing investment firms, retailers, construction companies and more.

Council president Adam Legge said Tuesday they’re adding their voice to the chorus of other business groups who warn a vote on Oct. 19 to quit Canada will create massive uncertainty and put jobs and the economy at risk.

Legge said member companies want to speak with a unified voice but some hesitate to speak out individually as they may have employees and customers leaning towards separation.

“They don’t want to upset employees and pit employees against each other or have tension within the workplace — or tension within their customer base,” he told reporters at a virtual news conference from Calgary.

October’s ballot will ask Albertans to vote on whether to remain a province of Canada or to begin the process of holding a second, binding referendum on separation.

Forty-two days out from the referendum, Legge said now is the time for the business sector to do what it can to help combat voter apathy, including sharing practical information for voters.

He said there’s optimism among business leaders that the separatist push will fail, but there is no guarantee, especially in the event of a low voter turnout.

The Canadian Chamber of Commerce, the Alberta Chambers of Commerce, and their counterparts representing member businesses in the province’s two biggest cities have all officially staked their position on the pro-Canada side of the debate.

Meanwhile, Premier Danielle Smith’s government has tasked the University of Calgary’s School of Public Policy with compiling the costs of the province going it alone.

That report, commissioned in June, is expected in the coming weeks.

Smith said earlier this summer it could cost up to $400 billion to begin the transition to an independent province.

Last week, the Canada West Foundation, a Calgary-based think tank, estimated in a report Alberta separation could carry a set-up cost of $200 billion, with ongoing costs of more than $50 billion every year. It added the move could also shrink Alberta’s economy.

Legge contributed to that report.

He said Tuesday Alberta ought to continue to push for fair treatment from the federal government but said a vote to separate would leave too much beyond Alberta’s control — from export market access to cross-border travel, currency and interest rates.

“The notion that a separate Alberta would be a master of its own destiny is a fiction,” he said.

“There is a potential that your job may not be there the next day.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 8, 2026.

stories.title: Alberta landowners challenge ‘chronic underfunding’ for orphan well cleanup
stories.summary: Landowners are going to court over what they allege is the Alberta Energy Regulator's failure to fund the cleanup of oil and gas sites with no company responsible for them.
stories.author: Lauren Krugel
stories.content:
Alberta landowners are going to court over what they allege is the provincial energy regulator’s failure to properly fund the cleanup of oil and gas sites that have no company legally responsible for them.

Lawyers at environmental law charity Ecojustice are representing landowners Dwight Popowich and Teresa Patry, as well as the Polluter Pay Federation and the Alberta Surface Rights Federation.

Their judicial review application in the Court of King’s Bench challenges what they call the Alberta Energy Regulator’s “chronic underfunding” of the Orphan Well Levy.

The regulator deems oil and gas wells “orphans” when an energy company becomes insolvent, defunct or unable to meet its obligations to safely and responsibly close its sites.

Cleanup is managed through the non-profit Orphan Well Association and is funded through an industry fee, the amount of which the AER recommends to the Alberta government every year.

The Orphan Well Levy for the 2026-27 fiscal year is $154.56 million, up from $144.45 million the previous year, though the well association has pegged total cleanup costs of its inventory at $1.66 billion.

Such wells can come with “significant risks,” the applicants argue in their lawsuit.

“Orphan wells can leak contaminants into the soil, the air and the water, putting Albertans’ health at risk and causing irreversible damage to the environment,” they said in the court document, adding orphan wells can also affect property values and land use and also come with big unpaid bills to municipalities and landowners.

“Oil and gas corporations with closure liabilities that exceed the value of their remaining assets often do not pay their bills, causing economic damage — and taxpayer funds are used to cover these shortfalls.”

The application alleges the AER is in violation of part of the Oil and Gas Conservation Act that says it alone is responsible for determining the amount of the levy, which must be “sufficient to cover, among other things, a number of costs associated with orphan oil and gas wells in the current fiscal year, as well as deficiencies arising from the previous fiscal year.”

The claim also alleges that the regulator has improperly delegated its legal responsibility to set the levy rates to Alberta’s political executive and allows for too much industry influence.

It further accuses the regulator of improperly taking into account factors like commodity prices and the health of the industry when setting the levy.

Among other things, the applicants are asking the court to declare the 2026-27 levy “unreasonable” and order it to be recalculated.

The latest monthly numbers from the Orphan Well Association include an inventory of 7,370 wells in need of decommissioning, which involves permanently dismantling equipment so that the site is safe.

Another 9,151 are in need of reclamation, which means restoring the land so it’s similar to its original state.

In the 2025-26 fiscal year, the average cost of decommissioning a well was $28,800 and for reclaiming a site, it was $27,700.

An inactive well on Popowich’s property in Two Hills, Alta., was designated an orphan in 2025 after eight years of effort on his part, the claim stated.

He was then informed by the Orphan Well Association that it would take 10 to 12 years to reclaim it.

He told a news conference Tuesday that he’s tried to work through the proper channels, but his concerns have been dismissed while the problem keeps getting worse.

“This isn’t complicated. Even my grandkids know that if you make a mess, you clean it up,” Popowich said.

“Landowners have held up their end of the bargain. As Albertans, we understand the importance of resource development to our province, and we welcome that development in exchange for the promise that, when companies were finished producing, they would clean up after themselves.

“That promise to me and thousands of other Albertans has been broken over and over again.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "That promise to me and thousands of other Albertans has been broken over and over again."

Patry, who lives near Vermilion, Alta., told the news conference the issue goes beyond finances.

“For years my family has lived with uncertainty about what these sites mean for our home, our land, our health and our future. We’ve experienced unexplained health concerns in our family, worry about our animals and repeatedly tried to get answers from the Alberta Energy Regulator,” she said.

“Living with that uncertainty takes a real toll.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "Living with that uncertainty takes a real toll."

The complainants’ claims have not been tested in court.

The AER declined to comment on the legal challenge Tuesday. But a statement from the regulator noted that the most recent annual levy has increased by seven per cent from a year earlier.

“The increase provides additional funding to help the Orphan Well Association address the growing number of orphaned oil and gas sites across the province.”

Ecojustice lawyer Susanne Calabrese said she’s heard some compare steady increases to the levy to gradually paying down a mortgage.

“That does not make any sense when the amount of wells are just astronomically increasing at the Orphan Well Association,” she told reporters.

“It’s like you’re paying interest-only payments on a mortgage and your house is doubling in size and you’re buying 10 more houses.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "It's like you're paying interest-only payments on a mortgage and your house is doubling in size and you're buying 10 more houses."

The Orphan Well Levy for the 2026-27 fiscal year is $154.56 million, up from $144.45 million the previous year, though the well association has pegged total cleanup costs of its inventory at $1.66 billion.
Such wells can come with “significant risks,” the applicants argue in their lawsuit.

“Orphan wells can leak contaminants into the soil, the air and the water, putting Albertans’ health at risk and causing irreversible damage to the environment,” they said in the court document, adding orphan wells can also affect property values and land use and also come with big unpaid bills to municipalities and landowners.

“Oil and gas corporations with closure liabilities that exceed the value of their remaining assets often do not pay their bills, causing economic damage — and taxpayer funds are used to cover these shortfalls.”

The application alleges the AER is in violation of part of the Oil and Gas Conservation Act that says it alone is responsible for determining the amount of the levy, which must be “sufficient to cover, among other things, a number of costs associated with orphan oil and gas wells in the current fiscal year, as well as deficiencies arising from the previous fiscal year.”
The claim also alleges that the regulator has improperly delegated its legal responsibility to set the levy rates to Alberta’s political executive and allows for too much industry influence.
It further accuses the regulator of improperly taking into account factors like commodity prices and the health of the industry when setting the levy.
Among other things, the applicants are asking the court to declare the 2026-27 levy “unreasonable” and order it to be recalculated.
The latest monthly numbers from the Orphan Well Association include an inventory of 7,370 wells in need of decommissioning, which involves permanently dismantling equipment so that the site is safe.
Another 9,151 are in need of reclamation, which means restoring the land so it’s similar to its original state.
In the 2025-26 fiscal year, the average cost of decommissioning a well was $28,800 and for reclaiming a site, it was $27,700.
An inactive well on Popowich’s property in Two Hills, Alta., was designated an orphan in 2025 after eight years of effort on his part, the claim stated.
He was then informed by the Orphan Well Association that it would take 10 to 12 years to reclaim it.
He told a news conference Tuesday that he’s tried to work through the proper channels, but his concerns have been dismissed while the problem keeps getting worse.
“This isn’t complicated. Even my grandkids know that if you make a mess, you clean it up,” Popowich said.

“Landowners have held up their end of the bargain. As Albertans, we understand the importance of resource development to our province, and we welcome that development in exchange for the promise that, when companies were finished producing, they would clean up after themselves.

“That promise to me and thousands of other Albertans has been broken over and over again.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "That promise to me and thousands of other Albertans has been broken over and over again."
Patry, who lives near Vermilion, Alta., told the news conference the issue goes beyond finances.

“For years my family has lived with uncertainty about what these sites mean for our home, our land, our health and our future. We’ve experienced unexplained health concerns in our family, worry about our animals and repeatedly tried to get answers from the Alberta Energy Regulator,” she said.
“Living with that uncertainty takes a real toll.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "Living with that uncertainty takes a real toll."
The complainants’ claims have not been tested in court.
The AER declined to comment on the legal challenge Tuesday. But a statement from the regulator noted that the most recent annual levy has increased by seven per cent from a year earlier.
“The increase provides additional funding to help the Orphan Well Association address the growing number of orphaned oil and gas sites across the province.”
Ecojustice lawyer Susanne Calabrese said she’s heard some compare steady increases to the levy to gradually paying down a mortgage.
“That does not make any sense when the amount of wells are just astronomically increasing at the Orphan Well Association,” she told reporters.

“It’s like you’re paying interest-only payments on a mortgage and your house is doubling in size and you’re buying 10 more houses.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "It's like you're paying interest-only payments on a mortgage and your house is doubling in size and you're buying 10 more houses."

stories.title: London Majors, Welland Jackfish trading blows in one-run playoff series
stories.summary: London Majors manager Roop Chanderdat expects more drama as his team leads Welland 2-1.
stories.author: Ryan Pyette
stories.content:
It’s been captivating so far.

The London Majors and Welland Jackfish are providing great theatre through three games of their Canadian Baseball League semifinal. Each game has been decided by one run, with the opener lasting 11 innings, the Jackfish scoring three times late in a failed comeback bid in Game 2 and London’s five-run ninth inning falling just short of a miracle turnaround Sunday at Labatt Park.

“It’s been a battle,” London co-owner and manager Roop Chanderdat said. “Welland is the defending champion and they’re not going away quietly. Every game is going to be tight.

“It’s exciting.”

That’s nothing less than you would expect from two teams that finished with identical 31-17 regular-season records. The Majors used their three left-handed starters – Victor Payano, Travis Keys and Cesilio Pimentel – in the opening three games and are expected to turn to right-hander Luis Perez to try to grab a stranglehold on the series.

The 31-year-old Dominican pitched the 11th inning in the Game 1 win and surrendered two runs in two innings in London’s Game 2 victory.

“I used Perez out of the bullpen,” Chanderdat said, “but he has been a starter all year and with a long break for him, he needed some work. We knew that it would be a long series going in and I need all four starters. That will leave Payano for Game 5 in London (then Keys and Pimentel in the final two games, if necessary).”

Welland’s probable Wednesday starter Ben Abram, a left-hander, threw five innings of two-hit, one-run ball in the back half of Game 1, but was tagged with the loss.

There hasn’t been much offence generated against either team’s starters. Most of the bigger blows have come against bullpen arms.

“It’s been hard to get hits and string them together,” Chanderdat said. “We had some opportunities we wasted with first and third, less than two outs. We had a runner at second, one out, and couldn’t cash. You get a few and have to capitalize.”

London right-fielder Tucker Zdunich, a 26-year-old Albertan, is leading the charge with six hits in 12 at-bats through three games. Centre-fielder Jarrett Burney chipped in with the walk-off single in the opener.

“You need some guys to be consistent and some guys to be heroes,” Chanderdat said. “You need someone to step up. There’s no quit in these guys. Last game, we fought back in the ninth and knew we had a push in us. After it, everyone was upbeat. Welland has a great bullpen and closer. We wanted our guys to see them and they got some runs off them to get back in it.

“It’s a marathon, not a sprint.”

On Sunday, the Majors stranded Jaden Babiuk at third to end the stirring rally. Welland saved the game when second baseman Jonah Weisner snared Burney’s ground ball up the middle with two runners on and recorded a force out at second.

“Otherwise, the game is tied,” Chanderdat said. “They made a couple of great plays defensively. We came up one short. In the playoffs, the next game is always the biggest one. Welland isn’t an easy place to win, but we’ve had some success there.”

They’re going to need the best of Perez and more timely hits to stay ahead in the series.

rpyette@postmedia.com

Game 5: Friday, 7:05 p.m. at Labatt Park

stories.title: Online harms now top threat to Canadian children, new report says
stories.summary: Ottawa - A new report says online harms now constitute the top threat facing children in Canada, ahead of bullying, poverty and child abuse.
stories.author: Anja Karadeglija The Canadian Press
stories.content:
OTTAWA - Online harms now constitute the top threat facing children in Canada, ahead of bullying, poverty and child abuse, Children First Canada said Tuesday in a new report.

It is the first time online harms have been in the top 10 list of threats, the report said.

“We’ve seen how now it’s permeating the lives of every kid in Canada, from birth all the way through adolescence. This is no longer a conversation just about teens on social media,” said Sara Austin, CEO of Children First Canada.

“In the past year alone, we’ve seen particularly the rise of AI-amplified harms,” she added.

The report says kids are coming into contact with AI toys and algorithmic-driven content before they even learn to read. It cites multiple risks related to the online environment, including cyberbullying, child luring, sexual extortion, AI-facilitated abuse and mental health impacts.

Last year’s shooting in Tumbler Ridge, B.C. — which has led to dozens of lawsuits focused on the shooter’s use of ChatGPT — was a defining moment for the debate around online safety in Canada, the report says.

It notes that over the past decade, police-reported incidents of online child sexual abuse have increased by more than 300 per cent, while the Canadian Centre for Child Protection processes more than 100,000 reports of online child sexual abuse and exploitation each month.

“Meanwhile, the emergence of violent online networks such as 764 has prompted law enforcement agencies to warn that Canadian children are being actively targeted through gaming platforms, social media, and messaging apps,” the report says.

The federal government added 764 to its list of terror entities in December 2025. It described the group as a “decentralized transnational network of online nihilistic violent extremists.”

It said members of the group use social media and gaming platforms “to lure, groom, and extort youth to commit violent and sexual acts, including self-harm.”

The report argues Canada has regulations and safety standards in place for other children’s products, including food, medicine, pyjamas and toys — and that tech companies should not enjoy an exception.

Children First Canada is calling on the federal government to strengthen and pass the digital safety bill it introduced earlier this year. Bill C-34 would force social media platforms to at least temporarily block access for kids under 16 and regulate the companies behind social media platforms and AI chatbots by imposing on them a duty to act responsibly, among other measures.

“We’re very glad to see that it goes beyond social media to include AI chatbots, but we know that kids don’t just exist in these two platforms,” Austin said.

The group also would like to see the bill address gaming and live streaming platforms, as well as messaging apps.

Austin said the onus needs to be on tech companies to design safer products in the first place.

The group received financial support and subject matter expertise from the non-profit PolicyWise for Children & Families, the Hospital for Sick Children, and the Canadian Medical Association.

The report argues that online harms aren’t a stand-alone issue.

“They are amplifying many of the other threats facing children, contributing to declining physical activity and play, bullying, violence and child abuse, racism and discrimination through online hate, and even climate change through the growing environmental impacts of digital infrastructure and artificial intelligence,” it says.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 8, 2026.
