stories.title: Coffee, CEOs and celebrities: Western offers roster of cool courses
stories.summary: Western University is offering a host of unique and entertaining courses that go beyond the foundational engineering, history or media theory.
stories.author: Crystal Mackay
stories.content:
Examine the history of celebrity throughout the ages.

Learn about navigating change in the business world from the CEOs who have lived it.

Explore chemical engineering principles by experimenting with coffee.

Western is offering a host of unique and entertaining courses that go beyond the foundational engineering, history or media theory.

“We want to ignite potential in our students by daring to do things differently, and that includes innovative courses and curriculum,” said Western’s registrar Marisa Modeski.

### “We are focused on breaking down barriers between disciplines to create a transformative learning experience. Western’s diverse course offerings encourages students to think big, make meaningful connections across fields of study and develop the adaptability they will need to thrive in a complex, rapidly changing world.” – Marisa Modeski, Western registrar

From roasting beans to developing cold brew, Engineering Coffee helps chemical engineering students at Western combine their morning caffeination with academic coursework.

“I wanted to incorporate more experiential learning for my chemical engineering students – and make it fun. The students actually get to taste their experiments,” said engineering professor Lauren Tribe, who teaches the course.

The hands-on elective even includes a field trip to a local coffee shop. Tribe said she hopes the class illustrates how engineering is embedded in so many elements of everyday life.

Faculty of Information and Media Studies

Combining play and learning is the name of the game for students in The Story of Play: Why Games Matter.

The course probes the history of gaming, from ancient board games originating in Mesopotamia to modern, advanced video game consoles. Course instructor and Fims professor Luke Arnott reflected on how games are inextricable from the technologies that support them.

“Think about how different the experience was playing Super Mario Bros. on a Nintendo Entertainment System and CRT TV back in the 1980s versus playing the same game today on a Nintendo Switch 2 while, for example, flying on a plane,” Arnott said.

One of the main features of the course is in-class guided gameplay sessions, where students test and analyze a variety of analog and digital games. These include table-top role-playing games, retro arcade games, choose-your-own-adventure books, classic consoles and VR games.

Brescia School of Food and Nutritional Sciences

Through hands-on experiences cooking (and eating!) in the food lab, students explore the social and cultural factors that influence variations in food preparation and culinary techniques around the world, from Indigenous and Canadian cuisine to South American, Central European, Middle Eastern and more.

Brescia School of Food and Nutritional Sciences professor Brenda Hartman said students will come to understand food as an expression of what it means to be human.

“As one of our previous students wrote in her thesis, ‘food is not only biological, but social, political, philosophical and ecological.’”

We all love to talk about celebrities, but what is it about certain individuals that elevates them to star status?

A new course in the department of history taught by Aldona Sendzikas focuses on the idea that our fascination with certain celebrities reveals something about us.

“By examining evolving definitions of celebrity over time and comparing case studies of celebrities from various historical periods, students learn about how celebrities reflect the values, aspirations and circumstances of different societies and time periods.”

For example, students will explore what motivated Annie Edson Taylor in 1901 to become the first person to go over Niagara Falls in a barrel, and how her story compares with those of more recent celebrity daredevils, such as Evel Knievel or Johnny Knoxville.

This popular course focuses on the rich cultural history and performance traditions of drum music from Africa, Brazil, Cuba and the Middle East to help students better understand its roots and origins.

Students perform within small and large ensembles while learning correct playing procedures for a variety of percussion instruments including hand drums, bells and shakers. The course is open to all Western students with no prior musical training or percussion expertise.

Music professor Rob Larose has been running Drumming Across Cultures for eight years and said students can expect to learn about the musical integration and rich heritage of certain cultures, develop proper hand drumming skills and “have a great deal of creative fun!”

The course culminates in a final recital where participants share what they’ve learned with an audience of family and friends.

Ivey Business School

Ever wanted to hear great business minds share their secrets to success? Students at Ivey Business School have a chance to hear directly from CEOs and corporate leaders about the strategies they use to ensure transformational success in their fields.

Taught by Doug Murphy, Hba’85, Ivey lecturer and former president and CEO of Corus Entertainment, the course combines case-based learning with guest lectures, with each case directly tied to the visiting CEO.

### “The vision was that by having the CEO in the room we could bring the case to life. The students are always impressed with the genuine human before them, as opposed to some imagined CEO described in a case.” – Doug Murphy, Ivey Business School grad and lecturer

This year’s speakers include Ian Rosen, Hba’11, president and COO of luxury menswear retailer Harry Rosen; Mike Katchen, HBA ’09, founder and CEO of digital investing and financial services platform Wealthsimple; Linda Hasenfratz, BSc’89, Mba’97, Lld’19, executive chair of Linamar, a global advanced manufacturing and mobility solutions company; and Sukhinder Singh Cassidy, Hba’92, Lld’26, CEO of Xero, a global cloud-based accounting software platform for small businesses.

“I believe this class is so special because of students’ aspirational realization that these CEOs are people just like them,” said Murphy.

From gemstones to ceramics and ancient monuments, Earth, Art and Culture highlights the ways in which Earth sciences shapes our everyday lives and how Earth materials have been used over the history of human culture.

Designed primarily for non-science students, the course explores the use of minerals and rocks as jewelry, art media and construction materials, and how Earth processes and materials have inspired visual art, literature, mythology and other aspects of society.

Students have a chance to explore gemstones, fossils and minerals in the department’s collections and study the stone used in campus buildings to understand the characteristics of different rock types used in architecture.

Earth sciences professor Cam Tsujita believes it is the only course of its kind offered at a Canadian university.

Physics and Astronomy

Look up into the night sky at the millions of stars – each one has a story.

Students in Observing the Stars learn how astronomers uncover those stories by studying the light that reaches us from distant stars.

“From stellar birth and evolution to the dramatic final stages of stellar life, the course explores how stars reveal the physics of the universe and helps students understand some of the most fascinating objects in the night sky,” said course instructor and visiting physics professor Shahram Abassi.

Students also have a chance to conduct their own astronomical investigations using a global network of robotic telescopes. They select targets, obtain real observations, analyze astronomical images and use their results to explore the properties and evolution of stars.

Law and Morrissette Institute for Entrepreneurship

The Law and Entrepreneurship course is focused on lawyers as entrepreneurs.

The course, open to second- and third-year law students and grad students from across campus, brings successful entrepreneurs and business leaders into the classroom each week to share their journeys, the decisions that shaped their ventures and how their legal training informed their entrepreneurial success.

Students hear directly from Western law graduates who have built ventures, led organizations, founded companies and navigated entrepreneurial challenges. These alumni share not just their stories, but the lessons learned along the way – the risks they took, the decisions they made and how they began to think about problems differently.

Learn more about how Western is preparing future leaders and global citizens.

Learn about navigating change in the business world from the CEOs who have lived it.
Explore chemical engineering principles by experimenting with coffee.
Western is offering a host of unique and entertaining courses that go beyond the foundational engineering, history or media theory.
“We want to ignite potential in our students by daring to do things differently, and that includes innovative courses and curriculum,” said Western’s registrar Marisa Modeski.

### “We are focused on breaking down barriers between disciplines to create a transformative learning experience. Western’s diverse course offerings encourages students to think big, make meaningful connections across fields of study and develop the adaptability they will need to thrive in a complex, rapidly changing world.” – Marisa Modeski, Western registrar
From roasting beans to developing cold brew, Engineering Coffee helps chemical engineering students at Western combine their morning caffeination with academic coursework.

“I wanted to incorporate more experiential learning for my chemical engineering students – and make it fun. The students actually get to taste their experiments,” said engineering professor Lauren Tribe, who teaches the course.
The hands-on elective even includes a field trip to a local coffee shop. Tribe said she hopes the class illustrates how engineering is embedded in so many elements of everyday life.
Faculty of Information and Media Studies
Combining play and learning is the name of the game for students in The Story of Play: Why Games Matter.

The course probes the history of gaming, from ancient board games originating in Mesopotamia to modern, advanced video game consoles. Course instructor and Fims professor Luke Arnott reflected on how games are inextricable from the technologies that support them.

“Think about how different the experience was playing Super Mario Bros. on a Nintendo Entertainment System and CRT TV back in the 1980s versus playing the same game today on a Nintendo Switch 2 while, for example, flying on a plane,” Arnott said.

One of the main features of the course is in-class guided gameplay sessions, where students test and analyze a variety of analog and digital games. These include table-top role-playing games, retro arcade games, choose-your-own-adventure books, classic consoles and VR games.
Brescia School of Food and Nutritional Sciences

Through hands-on experiences cooking (and eating!) in the food lab, students explore the social and cultural factors that influence variations in food preparation and culinary techniques around the world, from Indigenous and Canadian cuisine to South American, Central European, Middle Eastern and more.
Brescia School of Food and Nutritional Sciences professor Brenda Hartman said students will come to understand food as an expression of what it means to be human.
“As one of our previous students wrote in her thesis, ‘food is not only biological, but social, political, philosophical and ecological.’”
We all love to talk about celebrities, but what is it about certain individuals that elevates them to star status?
A new course in the department of history taught by Aldona Sendzikas focuses on the idea that our fascination with certain celebrities reveals something about us.

“By examining evolving definitions of celebrity over time and comparing case studies of celebrities from various historical periods, students learn about how celebrities reflect the values, aspirations and circumstances of different societies and time periods.”

For example, students will explore what motivated Annie Edson Taylor in 1901 to become the first person to go over Niagara Falls in a barrel, and how her story compares with those of more recent celebrity daredevils, such as Evel Knievel or Johnny Knoxville.

This popular course focuses on the rich cultural history and performance traditions of drum music from Africa, Brazil, Cuba and the Middle East to help students better understand its roots and origins.

Students perform within small and large ensembles while learning correct playing procedures for a variety of percussion instruments including hand drums, bells and shakers. The course is open to all Western students with no prior musical training or percussion expertise.

Music professor Rob Larose has been running Drumming Across Cultures for eight years and said students can expect to learn about the musical integration and rich heritage of certain cultures, develop proper hand drumming skills and “have a great deal of creative fun!”
The course culminates in a final recital where participants share what they’ve learned with an audience of family and friends.
Ivey Business School

Ever wanted to hear great business minds share their secrets to success? Students at Ivey Business School have a chance to hear directly from CEOs and corporate leaders about the strategies they use to ensure transformational success in their fields.

Taught by Doug Murphy, Hba’85, Ivey lecturer and former president and CEO of Corus Entertainment, the course combines case-based learning with guest lectures, with each case directly tied to the visiting CEO.

### “The vision was that by having the CEO in the room we could bring the case to life. The students are always impressed with the genuine human before them, as opposed to some imagined CEO described in a case.” – Doug Murphy, Ivey Business School grad and lecturer

This year’s speakers include Ian Rosen, Hba’11, president and COO of luxury menswear retailer Harry Rosen; Mike Katchen, HBA ’09, founder and CEO of digital investing and financial services platform Wealthsimple; Linda Hasenfratz, BSc’89, Mba’97, Lld’19, executive chair of Linamar, a global advanced manufacturing and mobility solutions company; and Sukhinder Singh Cassidy, Hba’92, Lld’26, CEO of Xero, a global cloud-based accounting software platform for small businesses.

From gemstones to ceramics and ancient monuments, Earth, Art and Culture highlights the ways in which Earth sciences shapes our everyday lives and how Earth materials have been used over the history of human culture.

Designed primarily for non-science students, the course explores the use of minerals and rocks as jewelry, art media and construction materials, and how Earth processes and materials have inspired visual art, literature, mythology and other aspects of society.

Students have a chance to explore gemstones, fossils and minerals in the department’s collections and study the stone used in campus buildings to understand the characteristics of different rock types used in architecture.

stories.title: From sunscreen to dairy, these are the U.S. goods hit by Canada’s retaliatory tariffs
stories.summary: Canada is striking back with tariffs the government says are targeted at the sectors affected by the Trump administration's tariffs.
stories.author: Lucas Casaletto
stories.content:
By Sarah Ritchie, The Canadian Press

Posted September 8, 2026 9:10 am.

The trade war between Canada and the United States enters a new chapter Tuesday as the Canadian government introduces retaliatory tariff measures.

Canada is striking back at the U.S. trade war with tariffs the federal government says are targeted at the sectors most affected by the Trump administration’s tariffs.

Here’s a look at the new levies coming into effect:

A 50 per cent tariff is being applied to a variety of American dairy products.

They include milk and cream, including concentrated and sweetened varieties and powders. It also applies to whey and several milk and whey protein products.

A 25 per cent tariff applies to fresh cheese and curd, including grated, powdered and processed varieties. The list specifies types of cheese: Camembert, brie, blue cheese, cheddar, mozzarella, Swiss, Gruyère, Havarti and Parmesan, to name a few.

Under the Canada-U.S.-Mexico Agreement on trade, imports of U.S. dairy products are tariff-free until specific quotas are reached. Imports over the quotas are subject to tariff rates of upwards of 200 per cent.

These new 50 per cent tariffs apply to imports both below and above the quota rate, according to the Finance Department.

Canada initially announced plans to impose a 25 per cent tariff on a wide range of U.S. seafood.

It covered imports of many kinds of live, fresh, preserved and frozen seafood: salmon, halibut, cod, haddock, tilapia, lobster, crabs, shrimps and prawns, oysters and mollusks, swordfish, mackerel, and a variety of smaller fish such as herring, capelin, anchovies and sardines.

On Aug. 26, Ottawa reversed course on the planned seafood tariffs and removed them from the list of goods, citing feedback from the fishing and processing sectors.

Canada is targeting U.S. wood products with 25 per cent tariffs. The products include softwood such as pine, fir and spruce that have been sawed or sliced thicker than six millimetres.

Plywood and veneered panels made from a variety of different softwoods and hardwoods have been hit with a 50 per cent levy.

Tariffs of either 25 or 50 per cent now apply to products like toilet paper, facial tissue, napkins and similar sanitary products (the rate depends on specific import sizes).

A 50 per cent tariff applies to most types of paper and paperboard, envelopes, and corrugated boxes and cases, with a lower 25 per cent levy for some imports of kraft paper and bleached paper products under a certain weight.

Wooden furniture for household use is subject to a 50 per cent tariff, except for kitchen furniture items, which are tariffed at 25 per cent.

On Aug. 26, Ottawa added a 50 per cent tariff on imports of wood charcoal.

Multiple steel and aluminum products are being hit with a 50 per cent tariff, up from the current 25 per cent rate.

They include steel rods, bars and sheets, along with prefabricated items such as bridges, towers, scaffolding and door and window frames.

Aluminum products such as wires, bars, rods and foil are all subject to the 50 per cent tariff rate.

On Aug. 26, Ottawa added a 50 per cent tariff to various sizes of copper wire.

Canada imposed a 25 per cent tariff on American steel and aluminum products in March 2025 in retaliation for U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariffs on Canadian steel and aluminum. Trump raised the tariff on steel to 50 per cent in June.

Trump’s latest threat, posted to his online platform Truth Social, is to raise tariffs to 50 per cent on Canadian steel, aluminum and vehicles starting Jan. 1, 2027.

Some beauty products and makeup are now subject to 50 per cent tariffs.

They include perfumes and eau de toilette, sunscreen and suntan products, lip and eye makeup, manicure and pedicure preparations, and hair products.

Tariffs of 50 per cent are being applied to a long list of clothing items that range from men’s suits and overcoats to T-shirts and dresses, track suits and ski suits.

The tariff also applies to hazardous material suits and protective clothing.

A 25 per cent levy applies to handwoven rugs, tiles and carpets made of wool, animal hair and a range of other textile materials.

A 50 per cent tariff now hits smartphones.

The same rate applies to golf clubs and equipment, video game consoles, chandeliers and light fixtures, exercise equipment and fishing rods.

American natural honey and molasses are getting 50 per cent tariffs.

Tariffs of 50 per cent are being applied to plastic wall and ceiling coverings made with vinyl chloride.

Plastics, including bags, packaging, tableware and kitchenware, are subject to 50 per cent tariffs.

Most air conditioners are subject to 15 per cent tariffs.

A 25 per cent tariff is hitting appliances, including stoves and ranges, refrigerators and freezers, laundry machines and small appliances like rice cookers, bread makers, grills and cooking plates.

Tariffs of 15 or 25 per cent are going on tower cranes, jacks and hoists, forklift trucks and lawn mowers.

Rail locomotives, train parts and railway maintenance vehicles are being hit with 25 per cent tariffs.

A 50 per cent tariff applies to motorcycles. Trailers and semi-trailers are subject to 25 per cent tariffs.

A 15 per cent tariff now applies to moulds for metal, rubber and plastics.

stories.title: Canadian students reading and math scores decline in Oecd’s global assessment
stories.summary: Canadian high-school students scored in the top 10 internationally, but scores have significantly declined over past two decades
stories.author: Dave McGinn
stories.content:
Canadian high-school students are outperforming many of their international peers in science, math and reading, but their overall scores in these subjects are also declining, according to a new international ranking by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development.

Results for the OECD’s Program for International Student Assessment, released Tuesday, show Canada in the top 10 among 91 countries and economies that were evaluated.

The OECD conducts the assessment, which measures the performance of 15-year-olds in science, math and reading, every three years. Science was the main focus of this latest round of assessments. Math and reading were also tested, but there were fewer questions asked.

In 2025, about 24,600 students from across the 10 provinces participated in the assessment.

The results showed that Canada’s scores in science, math and reading have all been declining, a trend also seen in other countries.

In science, Canada’s mean performance dropped five points compared to 2022. Its math score dropped 12 points, while reading saw a drop of 17 points.

Most other countries saw similar, if not worse, declines.

“I would look at Canada as one of the success stories that we have, because academic outcomes remain strong,” Andreas Schleicher, the OECD’s director for education and skills, said in an interview. “Yes, they have declined, but they remain strong overall.”

Canadian students are faring well compared to the majority of OECD countries, but they are “near the top of a falling curve,” said Anna Stokke, a mathematics professor at the University of Winnipeg.

In math, 26 per cent of Canadian students performed below level 2, the baseline proficiency level the OECD says is required to participate fully and productively in society, while 11.1 per cent performed at levels 5 and 6, the highest levels.

In 2003, 10.1 per cent of students performed below level 2, while 20.3 per cent of students performed at levels 5 and 6.

The latest results showed that while 74 per cent of students in Canada were at level 2 or above in math, more than 85 per cent of students in China, Singapore, Japan, Estonia and Korea performed at or above that level.

When it comes to reading, 21.8 per cent of Canadian students performed below level 2 in 2025, compared to 9.5 per cent in 2003.

Only 9.4 per cent of students reached levels 5 and 6 in reading in 2025, compared to 12.6 per cent in 2003.

Performance in science saw a similar pattern: roughly 16 per cent of students performed below level 2, compared to 10 per cent in 2006, the earliest year for which data is available.

In 2025, 10.6 per cent of students reached levels 5 and 6, compared to 14.4 per cent in 2006.

At the provincial level, New Brunswick had the highest percentage of students who performed below level 2 in reading, at 33 per cent. Ontario had the lowest percentage, at 20.9 per cent, according to an assessment by the Council of Ministers of Education, Canada.

Alberta had the highest percentage of students reach levels 5 and 6 in reading, at 12.3 per cent. New Brunswick had the smallest percentage at levels 5 and 6, with 5.1 per cent.

The provinces that have scored highest should share best practices with others, said Paris Semansky, coexecutive director of People for Education, a Toronto-based charitable organization.

“What can the rest of the country learn that makes sense and is adaptable?” she said.

The declines in reading skills in Canada and around the world are especially concerning, Mr. Schleicher said.

It’s not just reading as a whole that has declined, he said. “We are seeing particularly drops [in] reading skills that are particularly important in today’s world.”

Students now have a harder time navigating complex texts and distinguishing fact from opinion, he said.

Declines in reading scores are likely due to several complex factors, including that students spend more time with technology and are less likely to read for pleasure, Mr. Schleicher said.

Strong reading skills, however, are needed in an age that will be dominated by artificial intelligence, he said.

Prof. Stokke echoed the sentiment. Canada’s worsening performance in math and reading need to be addressed immediately, she said.

“Reading and math are really the roots of all the other subjects,” she said.

The number of students who perform at levels 5 and 6 in math has flatlined, she said, adding that these are the students who are most likely to pursue careers in math-dominated fields.

“We need people like this for our economy to be globally competitive,” Prof. Stokke said.

Numerous studies point to how times of economic hardship can lead to increased domestic violence, financial abuse, and gender-based violence. The COVID-19 pandemic, followed quickly by inflation, and now a economic trade war, the last few years have increasingly proven difficult for couples and families experiencing financial vulnerability.

stories.title: Missing Canadian mountaineer is seasoned survivalist, B.C. politician says
stories.summary: A British Columbia legislature member who went to law school with missing mountaineer Kalie McCrystal says the woman’s family and friends are “sitting by the phone” as they await updates on the search in Italy.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
A British Columbia legislature member who went to law school with missing mountaineer Kalie McCrystal says the woman’s family and friends are “sitting by the phone” as they await updates on the search in Italy.

Penticton-Summerland MLA Amelia Boultbee says she’s known McCrystal for a long time and says she’s “not just your average hiker,” and her disappearance while attempting to break a mountain-running record on the Matterhorn last week remains a mystery.

Boultbee says she’s been in touch with McCrystal’s sister and mother who are in Italy and they’ve been working mostly with Italian authorities.

She says the decision to suspend the search has been “very upsetting,” and the last time she was spotted via telescope before going missing showed no signs of any troubles.

Boultbee says McCrystal has done the Matterhorn several times before and it’s unusual that she went missing given her physical condition and extensive experience.

She says her friends and family are holding out hope that McCrystal is found alive.

“Nobody understands why there’s been zero trace of Kalie,” she said. “We also just want her family to get some answers.”

stories.title: Carney warns of tough times ahead in national address as retaliatory tariffs kick in
stories.summary: Ottawa — Prime Minister Mark Carney is warning Canadians that the country's pivot away from the United States will come at a cost, but that the alternative would be far worse.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
By Nick Murray, The Canadian Press

Posted September 8, 2026 8:01 am.

Last Updated September 8, 2026 12:31 pm.

Ottawa — Prime Minister Mark Carney is warning Canadians the country’s pivot away from the United States will “come at a cost” — but insists the alternative would be far worse.

In a national video address released Tuesday — hours after Canada’s retaliatory tariffs kicked in — Carney discussed Canada’s plan to respond to the U.S. trade war by striking new trade deals with other countries.

“We have everything we need to pivot and prosper,” he said.

“That pivot will come at a cost. There’s always a cost to action. But it doesn’t come close to the cost of standing still.”

The video is the latest in a series Carney launched last spring to update Canadians on his government’s polices and its response to U.S. trade actions.

Carney said the goal of those policies is to make Canada stronger and more resilient so that “no country can ever hold us hostage, and that we can live how we want to live.”

Carney cut off trade talks with the United States last month. The two sides failed to reach a deal before U.S. President Donald Trump’s deadline for imposing new 50 per cent tariffs on nearly $28 billion in Canadian goods.

In his video address, Carney again accused the U.S. side of trying to introduce measures that would have restricted Canada’s ability to trade with other countries, and its ability to promote and protect the French language and culture.

Federal conservatives continued calling over the weekend for Carney to release the full details of the deal his government rejected, and for Parliament to be recalled earlier than the scheduled Sept. 21 return date.

“We’re asking for the prime minister to be straight-up. We know it’s not easy to negotiate with the U.S. president. But the best way to keep everyone united and rowing in the same direction is to be up front about the costs, the decisions and the plan going forward,” Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said at a news conference in Regina on Sunday.

“The only people who haven’t seen (the deal) are the Canadian people. They deserve to see it so they can judge what we are fighting for, and what we are fighting against.”

Responding to Carney’s video on Tuesday, Poilievre said Canadians already are struggling with the high cost of living.

“How much tougher can things get for the 2.2 million food bank users, the people defaulting on mortgages, the small businesses closing, and the people who can’t afford homes?” Poilievre said in a post on X.

“Open Parliament. Release the deal. Reveal costs to families and small business and save jobs and money for our struggling people.”

Former Alberta premier Jason Kenny praised Carney’s video address.

“I don’t agree with every policy approach (e.g. regarding China as a reliable trade partner) and believe the government is still falling far short on deregulation and fiscal reform,” Kenny posted on X.

“But this is such a positive contrast to what’s coming out of the White House.”

In his video address, Carney said Trump’s tariffs are designed to harm some Canadians more than others. The U.S. has consistently taken aim at Canada’s steel, aluminum, auto and lumber sectors; those tariffs have primarily affected workers in Ontario, Quebec and B.C., while workers in Alberta and Saskatchewan haven’t been affected as much.

“In the spring of last year, I warned that America is trying to break us so they can own us. And I promised that that will never, ever happen,” Carney said in his video address.

Trump has mused openly for nearly two years about turning Canada into a U.S. state and has repeatedly referred to the prime minister as “governor.”

In January 2025, before being sworn in for his second term, Trump ruled out using military force but said he would consider using “economic force” to make Canada part of the U.S.

Canada’s reciprocal tariffs took effect Tuesday in response to Trump’s latest round of 50 per cent tariffs targeting dozens of products, including honey, hockey sticks, milk and cheese.

Canada’s tariffs, ranging from 15 to 50 per cent, target only products that were on the U.S. list and match the dollar value of the exports — $27.8 billion.

“I don’t believe in escalating the conflict. That’s not constructive,” Carney said in his video address.

“But our tariffs are necessary to protect our workers, protect our companies and our communities. We can’t let American goods into Canada tariff-free while they charge our companies to export them.”

Carney also offered a history lesson in his video address. He mentioned the Benjamin Harrison administration in 1890 and the push to impose tariffs on Canada led by Ohio congressman William McKinley, who would later become president.

“It put 50 per cent tariffs on our exports to the U.S. Sound familiar?” Carney said.

“McKinley’s 50 per cent tariff was meant to pressure us into dependence and eventually annexation by the United States. In reality, it did just the opposite.

“Rather than getting weaker, Canada grew stronger. Instead of becoming more dependent, we diversified by changing who we did business with. At the same time, inflation rose in the United States. They had a financial crisis and a four-year economic depression.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 8, 2026.

stories.title: For first time, the Oscar race officially starts at Tiff – at least for student filmmakers
stories.summary: The Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences will hold its annual Student Academy Awards in Toronto to coincide with the festival
stories.author: Barry Hertz
stories.content:
Every September, the Oscar race unofficially kicks off at the Toronto International Film Festival , where the most prestige-flavoured movies get their first exposure to audiences who will determine their Academy Awards fates. But this year, the Oscars are coming directly, and officially, to TIFF.

For the first time, the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences will hold its annual Student Academy Awards, a kind of little sister to the big ceremony that is telecast every spring, in Toronto to coincide with the festival.

The annual event, which was established in 1972 to highlight the work of undergraduate and graduate student filmmakers, has historically been held in the Academy’s L.A. home base. But under the aegis of Bill Kramer, who was named chief executive of the Academy in 2022, the ceremony has broken containment from the Hollywood bubble, taking place in London in 2024 and New York in 2025.

The international shift is part of a larger strategy for the Academy when it comes to broadening its global impact and diversification of membership. Of the Academy’s current membership, which totals a little more than 11,000 people, roughly 22 per cent are based outside of the United States.

“We have a broader global initiative to make our organization more international, a mission supported by the board and aligned with our goal of serving a truly global community of artists,” Kramer says in an interview. “And Canada has probably our largest membership outside of the U.S., too.”

That expanded sense of geography is represented in the 16 winners set to be honoured in Toronto. Just three of the finalists are from the United States, with the remaining artists hailing from the Czech Republic, the Netherlands, France, Germany, the United Kingdom, Spain, Poland and Canada (the latter represented by Concordia student Antoine Boulanger).

Unlike the mainstage Oscars telecast, none of the finalists for the student ceremony will walk away empty-handed. Instead, across four categories – Alternative/Experimental, Animation, Documentary and Narrative filmmaking – three filmmaking teams will vie for gold, silver and bronze placements. Meanwhile, all the winning films will be automatically eligible to compete in the 2027 Oscars in the Animated Short Film, Live Action Short Film, or Documentary Short Film categories.

“The student awards really mirror the Oscars. We’ve had presenters like Jason Reitman and Jon M. Chu, and the awards are voted on by the same Academy members who judge the Oscars,” says Kramer.

The student ceremony, which will take place inside TIFF’s Lightbox hub on Sept. 14, also serves as a crucial pipeline for industry talent. Previous student winners include Spike Lee, Robert Zemeckis, and Pixar’s Pete Docter.

“Toronto provides such great access for the students to Academy members, and they will all receive incredible access to the creative community while at TIFF,” says Meredith Shea, the chief membership, impact and industry officer for the Academy. “They’ll be able to start building their careers.”

The initiative runs parallel to a deepening relationship between the Academy and TIFF’s leaders, including chief executive Cameron Bailey and chief programming officer Anita Lee.

Earlier this year, the Academy revised its long-standing eligibility rules for the Best International Feature Oscar. Previously, a non-English-language film could only qualify for the award if it was submitted by a country’s Academy-approved selection committee. For instance, Telefilm Canada could only choose one Canadian film – often a French-language title from Quebec given that the category requires a submission’s dialogue be more than 50 per cent non-English – which resulted in stiff competition between domestic titles.

Starting with the 2027 Academy Awards, though, a non-English-language film can also be nominated for Best International Feature if it wins the top prize at one of six major international film festivals. This includes the juried Platform Prize at TIFF, whose level of prestige the Academy has effectively placed on par with the Golden Lion in Venice and the Palme d’Or in Cannes.

“While that change is separate from the Student Academy Awards initiative, we’ve always had a great relationship with Cameron and Anita,” says Shea, adding that TIFF’s position in the fall calendar is also crucial to the momentum of the awards season, which stretches from the fall until the Academy announces its winners live onstage every spring.

About that stage, though: Starting in 2029, the Academy Awards will enter a new era that pushes their reach far further than Toronto, with YouTube set to livestream the ceremony worldwide, a marked shift from the Academy’s long-time partnership with U.S. television network ABC.

“It will be more than just the show, too. This partnership will create a year-round hub for Academy content, everything from museum programming to digitizing components of the Academy’s collection of more than 52 million film-related items,” adds Kramer. “There will be global reach.”

stories.title: 4 teens dead, 4 others sent to hospital after crash near Manitoba resort town
stories.summary: Mounties in Manitoba say four teens died and four other victims were taken to hospital after two vehicles crashed and landed in a ditch near a resort town over the weekend.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
By Staff The Canadian Press

Posted September 8, 2026 7:52 am

Mounties in Manitoba say four teens died and four other victims, including two children, were taken to hospital after two vehicles crashed and landed in a ditch near a resort town over the weekend.

RCMP say they responded just after 9 p.m. on Sunday to an intersection near the town of Winnipeg Beach, located about 80 kilometres north of Winnipeg.

Police say a car with four occupants was westbound on Highway 229, and was crossing Highway 8 when it was hit by a southbound van.

Both vehicles went into a ditch, with one of them rolling over on to its roof.

Police say the three 18-year-olds from Manitoba — including the female driver — and a 17-year-old from Ontario who were in the car died at the scene.

The four people from Winnipeg who were in the van, including the 49-year-old man who was driving, a woman and two children, were taken to hospital with minor injuries.

Mounties say in a news release that the intersection has stop signs, and a traffic reconstructionist is assisting in the investigation.

stories.title: Expert explainer: Why screen kids for math skills?
stories.summary: Western University expert Daniel Ansari says early numeracy screening helps identify learning gaps and supports children's math development.
stories.author: Jacquelyn Mitchell
stories.content:
Early childhood screening helps identify kids who are behind on foundational skills in literacy and math so efforts can be made to provide support before they fall behind.

After the Ontario Human Rights Commission’s Right to Read report was released in 2022, the provincial government mandated reading screening for children in senior kindergarten through Grade 2 .

Daniel Ansari, Western p rofessor of psychology and education and Canada Research Chair in Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience and Learning, says screening for math, or numeracy, is just as important. His team is developing a tool to help.

Ansari, who is also principal investigator with the Numerical Cognition Laboratory in the Faculty of Social Science, spoke with Western News to explain why numeracy skills are important and how caregivers can support their children’s learning.

Daniel Ansari (DA ): There are many ways you can engage your child in numerical and mathematical activities , including adding up or estimating the cost of groceries, playing games that involve numbers and drawing attention to numerical relationships in everyday situations such as cooking or buying groceries.

The second piece of advice is to be engaged with your child’s schoolwork. Ask what they are doing in math and then seek ways to practice what they are doing. It is important to ensure this continues to be fun for everyone. Frustrations and conflict around math at home can be harmful, so if you as parents don’t enjoy it, don’t force it.

There is lots of data to show just how important numerical skills are, so treat them the same way as you treat reading and literacy development.

DA: Children come to school with different levels of skill in fundamental domains such as literacy and numeracy. One child May already be able to add, while another does not yet understand that eight is numerically larger than five. The reasons driving differences between learners are multifaceted. A part of it is linked with the learning opportunities children are afforded outside of their school building, be that formal – like tutoring for example – or informal, such as a parent who reads to their child.

Screening is a way to recognize children who May need a bit of extra help. Schools in Ontario routinely carry out literacy screening. This allows educators and other professionals, such as speech and language pathologists, to recognize children who May not have all the building blocks in place and give them additional attention.

This makes screening one of many tools schools can use to enhance equity and ensure all learners can benefit from instruction. It can also be used to chart student progress. By screening multiple times a year, education professionals can see how individual students in their classrooms are growing and recognize students who are not benefitting. It is important to note that screening is not intended to identify students with learning difficulties. Its primary purpose is to provide rapid, yet rich data to inform educators about differences between students in their classroom. Educators then need to use this information to tailor their instruction to the needs of different learners in their classrooms.

DA: Children come to the classroom with a diversity of backgrounds, skills and knowledge in numeracy and early math. This has the potential to create inequitable schooling pathways as students who come to school equipped with fundamental pieces of knowledge and skills go on to experience a learning trajectory of continuous growth, while those students who lack those skills early on find it hard to latch onto the instruction and continue to fall behind.

Screening draws greater attention to students who have not yet learned fundamental skills and acquired foundational knowledge. Educators will have a good sense of the differences between students in their classrooms after a few weeks of instruction and screening can help to both confirm and refine their understanding.

DA: Literacy has been a subject of much attention from the media, policy makers and research funders, creating greater awareness of reading difficulties among the public as well as educators.

Numeracy screening hasn’t had the same amount of attention, but that’s starting to change. For example, in Australia there was a large numeracy screening project over the past few years that covered a large portion of the country and, in future years, will allow educators to compare their students’ performance to those who have been screened before. That gives them an opportunity to assess an individual student’s skills relative to a population of students who live in a similar area and have undergone similar schooling.

My team at the Numerical Cognition Laboratory has developed a numeracy screening tool that is available for free online . We are currently in the phase of gathering responses to be able to use it as a reference going forward.

DA: Much can be done! It’s important to build greater awareness of the importance of early numeracy skills. Secondly, we need more evidence-based programs in early numeracy education so teaching is aligned with what we know about how children learn best. Finally, we need to empower educators by ensuring they have ongoing training to give them the right tools and methods to help all children success in numeracy and early math.

stories.title: Population growth drives school-building boom across London region
stories.summary: Both London-area school boards are opening new schools and planning more as enrolment pressures reshape where students learn.
stories.author: Brian Williams
stories.content:
The two major London-based school boards, serving the city and several surrounding communities, are opening and building new schools to accommodate the region’s growing population. Here are some things to know as students head back to class.

As students return to classes for the 2026-27 school year, some will be attending brand-new or newly renovated schools.

The newest addition to the London District Catholic school board – which operates 44 elementary schools and nine high schools – is the new $54.3-million replacement Regina Mundi Catholic Colleg e in the city’s southeast end. The original school opened in 1963 as a seminary, according to the Catholic board’s website.

“That’s a replacement build, but it is our newest building,” said the Catholic board’s education director, Vince Romeo, noting the school has capacity for about 700 students.

For the Thames Valley District school board, the $28.2-million Jackson Meadows public school, which opens its doors in southeast London for the first time on Tuesday, is its newest school. Thames Valley oversees 135 elementary schools and 27 high schools.

A second school, the $24.2-million Belmont Meadows public school in Belmont, with capacity for roughly 500 pupils, is “expected to be completed” in January 2027, Thames Valley officials said in an email statement.

“All students currently attending South Dorchester PS will switch schools to attend Belmont Meadows PS when it opens in January 2027,” the board’s website said, adding South Dorchester will close thereafter.

Thames Valley said a third school, the nearly $25-million Clover public school in Lucan, is expected to be completed in March. With capacity for about 530 pupils, the new school will serve junior kindergarten to Grade 3, while Wilberforce public school will be converted to a Grade 4-to-8 school.

An anticipated 28,500 students are expected to attend classes Tuesday, Romeo said, pointing out the London District Catholic school board is the fastest-growing school board in Ontario.

“Of all 72 school boards in the province, we’re going into year six as the fastest growing at a rate of 30 per cent growth over the last five years,” he said.

Romeo said 1,900 positions have been filled, including board staff, classroom teachers and early childhood educators throughout the district to support growing enrolment. “And we’re looking at that hiring growth to continue into this school year.”

Romeo said the Catholic board is excited to welcome students as it receives substantial provincial investments for new schools and school renewals amid record growth.

While enrolment at the London District Catholic school board has reached record levels, enrolment at Thames Valley has dipped slightly: About 84,110 students were enrolled in Thames Valley schools during the 2024-25 school year, according to a July 2025 Free Press story. Figures on Thames Valley’s website indicate about 83,500 students were enrolled for the 2025-26 school year.

The board said enrolment data for the 2026-27 school year will not be finalized until later this fall.

The London District Catholic school board continues to experience growth hotspots across London, Romeo said. He described growth as “pretty well distributed” across the city, but identified northwest and southwest London as particularly active areas.

He also pointed to Middlesex and Elgin counties as communities where the Catholic board has been “seeing huge growth” recently.

“That’s being recognized by the ministry with the approval of a second St. Thomas secondary school that we are in the planning stages,” Romeo said. “We’re going to be replacing our elementary school in Lucan (too).”

Thames Valley directed The Free Press to its website, which indicates the board has planned several attendance-area reviews, including in southwest and northeast London, St. Thomas and Elgin County.

Earlier this year, the provincial government announced $1.6 billion in funding for schools across Ontario. Both Thames Valley and the London District Catholic school board received funding.

With enrolment numbers climbing, the Catholic board has several new schools in the works across the region.

Romeo named seven schools, including two scheduled to open within the next year.

“(In) Kilworth-Komoka, it is an elementary school that we are hoping to open next September . . . that is well into the planning stages, and we’re more than halfway through,” he said. “We are also, with the same timeline of September 2027, opening a northeast elementary school, sort of in the Highbury-Fanshawe Park Road area.”

Romeo said a new $100-million north London high school on Richmond Street north of Fanshawe Park Road will have capacity for roughly 2,000 students – one of the largest schools ever built by the Catholic board and one of its largest approvals from the Ministry of Education.

In London, Romeo said the southwest and southeast ends are being eyed for new elementary schools, along with a new high school in the south end. He also said construction on a new St. Thomas secondary school will begin shortly, while a replacement St. Patrick’s Catholic school in Lucan is in the planning stages to address growth there.

“We’re welcoming and needing more schools to complement the existing schools that we have now,” he said.

Thames Valley officials said that in addition to opening three new schools during the 2026-27 school year, the board is continuing work on “many other capital projects.”

Among them is a $43.6-million new high school for roughly 700 students in St. Thomas, for which the board is still seeking land, according to its website.

“It’s our first new high school in decades with the replacement of Arthur Voaden secondary school in St. Thomas,” Thames Valley said.

Thames Valley said it is also designing and building new schools in Talbotville, Thamesford and several locations across London. The board is also eyeing additions at Parkview public school in Komoka and Nissouri public school in Thorndale.

As students return to classes for the 2026-27 school year, some will be attending brand-new or newly renovated schools.

The newest addition to the London District Catholic school board – which operates 44 elementary schools and nine high schools – is the new $54.3-million replacement Regina Mundi Catholic Colleg e in the city’s southeast end. The original school opened in 1963 as a seminary, according to the Catholic board’s website.
“That’s a replacement build, but it is our newest building,” said the Catholic board’s education director, Vince Romeo, noting the school has capacity for about 700 students.

For the Thames Valley District school board, the $28.2-million Jackson Meadows public school, which opens its doors in southeast London for the first time on Tuesday, is its newest school. Thames Valley oversees 135 elementary schools and 27 high schools.

A second school, the $24.2-million Belmont Meadows public school in Belmont, with capacity for roughly 500 pupils, is “expected to be completed” in January 2027, Thames Valley officials said in an email statement.

“All students currently attending South Dorchester PS will switch schools to attend Belmont Meadows PS when it opens in January 2027,” the board’s website said, adding South Dorchester will close thereafter.

Thames Valley said a third school, the nearly $25-million Clover public school in Lucan, is expected to be completed in March. With capacity for about 530 pupils, the new school will serve junior kindergarten to Grade 3, while Wilberforce public school will be converted to a Grade 4-to-8 school.

stories.title: In the age of artificial intelligence, professors try to make cheating hard again
stories.summary: Students at one Canadian university have assignments ranging from hand-written essays to generative AI free-for-alls
stories.author: Kelly Grant
stories.content:
As the fall semester begins at universities across Canada, professors are grappling with a fundamental challenge of the artificial-intelligence era: How do you assess students when cheating has never been simpler?

Research essays and other take-home written assignments can be conjured from thin air with a prompt to Claude or ChatGPT.

And ferreting out such subterfuge is hard because many Canadian universities forbid or discourage professors from using AI-detection software, said Mark Daley, the chief AI officer at Western University in London.

“We ban the use of AI detectors as unethical because they’re not 100 per cent accurate,” Prof. Daley explained, referring to Western’s policy.

When cheating is easy and cheaters can’t easily be caught, instructors must get creative. Here is how four professors in different fields at one university are remaking their assignments for the new AI reality.

For the past few years, Western University philosophy professor David Bourget tried to assign essays that were AI-resistant. He asked narrow questions and picked obscure readings that, as far as he knows, stumped early versions of ChatGPT.

But as large language models (LLMs) improved, “all of these techniques stopped working,” Prof. Bourget said. “Then I had to turn around and, like everybody else, rethink how I do things.”

This year, he is running a pilot project where about 130 students enrolled in Introduction to the Philosophy of Mind, a second-year course, will research and write essays in an on-campus computer lab under the watchful eye of a teaching assistant.

Students will bring their own laptops. The supervisors, using QR codes on their phones, will sign the students in to external servers for MATCHA , a software program that Prof. Bourget designed as a walled garden in which users can access word processors and online research materials but not AI tools.

The program, which stands for Modern Authoring Tool for Certified Human Authorship, has other features that record the work that goes into producing an essay, including research notes, early drafts and edits. Prof. Bourget co-founded a company to license the program.

The supervised nature of the lab keeps students from using AI on a secondary device, such as a phone, and typing the results into MATCHA.

As a bonus, the lab will bring students and their teaching assistants together for what would otherwise be a virtual course. Prof. Bourget will be delivering his lectures online.

“My goal,” he said, “is to make cheating hard again.”

Selma Purac, the undergraduate program chair at Western’s Faculty of Information and Media Studies, realized the traditional essay was in peril in the fall of 2023, less than a year after the launch of ChatGPT.

She was marking a batch of 40 papers for a mass communication class she had taught for years. Thirty of the essays were remarkably similar. They read nothing like the student writing she was used to grading. Twenty-eight employed a word that Prof. Purac had never seen in a student essay, one she now recognizes as a favourite of ChatGPT’s. (She declined to reveal the word, saying she’d rather not give away the AI tell.)

Prof. Purac didn’t want to abandon essays. Writing them taught her students to read critically, develop strong arguments and find their voices. “But those skills were being degraded by the way in which my students were using LLMs,” she said.

Instead, Prof. Purac decided to reimagine the essay. Two years ago, she started breaking down her assignments into worksheets. She gave her students time outside of class to conduct research and outline their arguments, including pulling direct quotes from source material. Then, she had them write their essays in class with pen, paper, their worksheets and supervision.

For example, in her third-year course, Children, Advertising and Consumer Culture, she had for years assigned a close reading of an advertisement.

Before LLMs, students selected ads and composed their assignments at home. Now, Prof. Purac distributes a three-and-a-half page worksheet, which must be completed in point form, at least three weeks in advance of a two-hour, in-class writing period.

“I really like the way it demystifies the traditional essay,” she said.

Students studying at Western’s Ivey School of Business know they’ll be expected to use AI in the workplace. So Guneet Kaur Nagpal, who teaches marketing management and digital marketing analytics to undergraduates, had to find a way to teach students to master AI without losing the ability to think critically.

Prof. Kaur Nagpal developed a marketing strategy simulation tool called plAIbook that allowed her students to use generative AI as an assistant in solving business case studies. The program caps the number of prompts students can give AI and sets strict time limits.

The tool garnered positive feedback from faculty and students after it was piloted in 10 sections of a marketing class last spring. Prof. Kaur Nagpal built it as one of Western’s Generative AI teaching fellows. She and two other professors have been seconded to the university’s Centre for Teaching and Learning for two years to develop and assess new ways of teaching with AI.

On top of developing plAIbook, Prof. Kaur Nagpal and her colleagues overhauled some classic assignments. In the pre-ChatGPT era, she gave groups of students 48 hours to compare two legacy brands and develop a marketing plan for the weaker of the two. Now she asks groups to develop marketing plans in 24 hours, using AI, for newly minted brands from sources such as the crowdfunding platform Kickstarter or the start-up incubator Y Combinator.

She also traded a week-long take-home exam for a four-hour, in-class exam with the help of AI. Unfortunately, when she quizzed students orally on the material, she discovered that some who scored well on the written final with AI couldn’t even define simple terms.

“It’s telling and it’s troubling,” she said.

Prof. Kaur Nagpal plans to increase the weight of oral tests this fall.

Western history professor William Turkel was on sabbatical in the 2024-2025 academic year when he realized that generative artificial intelligence was improving at a clip that would force him and his colleagues to teach differently.

He changed the name of his third-year Digital Research Methods class to Digital Research Methods with Artificial Intelligence. He told his students to use AI as much as they liked, including as a virtual teammate for group projects.

But he warned that the standard fare spit out by an LLM would net only an average grade.

If students wanted higher marks, they would have to do something more ambitious. One example: Dispatch an LLM or multiple LLMs to comb through thousands of digitized texts at U.S. presidential libraries, and compare what American leaders said in real time about the Vietnam War to facts that emerged later in the Pentagon papers.

Prof. Turkel is also one of Western’s generative AI teaching fellows. He thinks students are better off embracing the inescapable new technology.

“How many undergrad students become professional historians? One in 100? One in 200?” he said. “The rest of them are going to workplaces where they can’t pretend AI doesn’t exist.”

Instead, Prof. Purac decided to reimagine the essay. Two years ago, she started breaking down her assignments into worksheets. She gave her students time outside of class to conduct research and outline their arguments, including pulling direct quotes from source material. Then, she had them write their essays in class with pen, paper, their worksheets and supervision.
For example, in her third-year course, Children, Advertising and Consumer Culture, she had for years assigned a close reading of an advertisement.

Before LLMs, students selected ads and composed their assignments at home. Now, Prof. Purac distributes a three-and-a-half page worksheet, which must be completed in point form, at least three weeks in advance of a two-hour, in-class writing period.
“I really like the way it demystifies the traditional essay,” she said.

Students studying at Western’s Ivey School of Business know they’ll be expected to use AI in the workplace. So Guneet Kaur Nagpal, who teaches marketing management and digital marketing analytics to undergraduates, had to find a way to teach students to master AI without losing the ability to think critically.

Prof. Kaur Nagpal developed a marketing strategy simulation tool called plAIbook that allowed her students to use generative AI as an assistant in solving business case studies. The program caps the number of prompts students can give AI and sets strict time limits.

The tool garnered positive feedback from faculty and students after it was piloted in 10 sections of a marketing class last spring. Prof. Kaur Nagpal built it as one of Western’s Generative AI teaching fellows. She and two other professors have been seconded to the university’s Centre for Teaching and Learning for two years to develop and assess new ways of teaching with AI.

On top of developing plAIbook, Prof. Kaur Nagpal and her colleagues overhauled some classic assignments. In the pre-ChatGPT era, she gave groups of students 48 hours to compare two legacy brands and develop a marketing plan for the weaker of the two. Now she asks groups to develop marketing plans in 24 hours, using AI, for newly minted brands from sources such as the crowdfunding platform Kickstarter or the start-up incubator Y Combinator.

She also traded a week-long take-home exam for a four-hour, in-class exam with the help of AI. Unfortunately, when she quizzed students orally on the material, she discovered that some who scored well on the written final with AI couldn’t even define simple terms.
“It’s telling and it’s troubling,” she said.
Prof. Kaur Nagpal plans to increase the weight of oral tests this fall.

Western history professor William Turkel was on sabbatical in the 2024-2025 academic year when he realized that generative artificial intelligence was improving at a clip that would force him and his colleagues to teach differently.

He changed the name of his third-year Digital Research Methods class to Digital Research Methods with Artificial Intelligence. He told his students to use AI as much as they liked, including as a virtual teammate for group projects.
But he warned that the standard fare spit out by an LLM would net only an average grade.

If students wanted higher marks, they would have to do something more ambitious. One example: Dispatch an LLM or multiple LLMs to comb through thousands of digitized texts at U.S. presidential libraries, and compare what American leaders said in real time about the Vietnam War to facts that emerged later in the Pentagon papers.
Prof. Turkel is also one of Western’s generative AI teaching fellows. He thinks students are better off embracing the inescapable new technology.
“How many undergrad students become professional historians? One in 100? One in 200?” he said. “The rest of them are going to workplaces where they can’t pretend AI doesn’t exist.”

stories.title: How Tiff helped Deepa Mehta find her place in Canada
stories.summary: Over the years, Mehta has kept up her association with Tiff as a filmmaker and industry leader
stories.author: Aparita Bhandari
stories.content:
As the 51st Toronto International Film Festival takes over the city Sept. 10-20, this series of articles examines some of the Canadian directors whose lives and careers have been impacted by TIFF.

As an emerging filmmaker living in Toronto in the late ’80s, Deepa Mehta didn’t feel very Canadian.

It was a time in her life when she was deeply unhappy. Her marriage had unravelled, and walking down the city streets, she sometimes heard racist abuse hurled in her direction. In fact, she missed India, the country of her birth, so much that at one point she rang up the Indian consulate wondering if she could get a job as a receptionist if she worked for free.

So when Piers Handling, former CEO of the Toronto International Film Festival, invited her to bring her debut feature film, Sam & Me to TIFF, Mehta says she felt Canadian for the first time.

“It was a very small film, but it was important to me,” she says. “For me, Canada was defined by TIFF… It meant the world to me for my first feature to be invited.”

Mehta had met Handling at the 1991 Cannes Film Festival, where Sam & Me screened and won an honourable mention for the Caméra d’Or prize. The film is about a young Indian immigrant Nikhil (Indian actor Ranjit Chowdhry, also the screenwriter of Sam & Me ), who becomes a caregiver to Sam (Peter Boretski), an eccentric, elderly Jewish man.

The warmth she received at TIFF was wonderful, says Mehta.

“I remember it was Cameron who introduced the film,” says Mehta, referencing TIFF’s current CEO Cameron Bailey, who was a programmer at the time. “And I got to meet so many wonderful filmmakers. I got to see an aspect of Canada and its growth. Especially [seeing] what’s happening now with South Asian cinema, I feel so happy.”

Born in Amritsar, Punjab, in 1950, Mehta was pursuing a master’s degree at Delhi University when she got involved in documentary filmmaking and met Canadian filmmaker Paul Saltzman, who she later married. She came to Canada in 1973 and started making TV series and short documentaries, moving to feature films with Sam & Me .

TIFF has championed Mehta’s work throughout her career. In 1996, former TIFF programmer David McIntosh invited her to bring Fire, the first in her elemental trilogy of films (along with Earth and Water ), to the festival. By then, Mehta had established other collaborators, including her current partner and film producer David Hamilton, with whom she founded Hamilton-Mehta Productions, as well as Hussain Amarshi, founder of Canada’s leading independent film distribution company Mongrel Media.

Starring celebrated Indian actresses Shabana Azmi and Nandita Das (who would go on to become a director and bring films such as Manto and Zwigato to TIFF), Fire sparked controversy for its depiction of same-sex desire.

For Anita Lee, TIFF’s chief programming officer, watching Fire at TIFF was a revelation.

“I remember at the time, even just the fact that it was a film that took place entirely in India, it was debated – is this a Canadian film? The fact that it was a romantic relationship between two women, within that Indian context, and the taboo of that subject matter; I recall the significant international discussion that happened around that film,” says Lee, who later went on to become a producer for Mehta’s film Heaven on Earth . “It was so groundbreaking for Canada.”

Over the years, Mehta has kept up her association with TIFF as a filmmaker and industry leader. She’s been an ambassador for its Share Her Journey initiative, set up in 2017 to champion women creators. She co-directed documentary I Am Sirat , about the life of a transgender woman in New Delhi, which screened at TIFF in 2023. This year, she’s acting as a jurist for the festival’s Canadian programming, which has been a source of delight, says Mehta.

“I want to see what’s happening in Canada today, with the young filmmakers. They have added something to Canada that was never there before. And they aren’t apologetic for who they are,” she says.

“It’s just so lovely. And I think TIFF has a lot to do with it.”

TIFF’s invitation to screen Sam & Me validated its place in the Canadian canon, says Malini Guha, associate professor of film studies at Carleton University. Mehta is one of the most prolific filmmakers to be working out of Canada, despite the significant challenges she faced as a racialized woman, she adds.

“A number of her films deal with the question of migration, the struggles of migration, particularly as they pertain to labour,” says Guha. She notes that films about migration usually deal with family conflicts or romantic relationships, but Sam & Me is unusual because of its focus on South Asian men living together in a Toronto rooming house, trying to make a go of it as immigrants.

In one scene, during a birthday party, a character named Xavier dresses up in a sari and dances to a popular Hindi movie song, says Guha.

“Nikhil brings Sam into this space, and he’s watching along with the nephew of the boarding house owner Keith, who is the most explicitly queer character in the film. They have a friend, Takahito, who is Japanese. And they’re all sitting there, watching this performance,” she says.

“It’s brilliant. It’s so joyful. And there are some non-normative gender and sexual ideas. It feels remarkable for a film of its time period.”

stories.title: Ground breaks on South Britannia in B.C., home to Canada's first surf park
stories.summary: Popular tourism corridor expands with new mixed-use development
stories.author: Howard Chai
stories.content:
Over a decade after the land was sold, shovels are now in the ground at South Britannia, a new mixed-use resort-like development along the Sea-to-Sky Highway just south of the Britannia Beach community in British Columbia, about a 45-minute drive north from Vancouver.

The project is being undertaken by Tiger Bay Development, formerly known as Taicheng Development, a company owned by Chinese real estate developer Peter Cheng and his son Long Cheng – just one example of the wave of Chinese developers that entered B.C. around the aughts and 2010s. The Chengs have been involved in numerous projects in China, but South Britannia is Tiger Bay’s one and only project.

Tiger Bay acquired the land, a large gravel pit and surrounding land that total to approximately 490 acres, in the early 2010s for $30.5 million after the previous owner became insolvent and the property went through a court-ordered sales process.

Originally envisioned for the site was a resort community with more than 4,000 homes, but the project was pared down after concerns from locals and the Squamish-Lillooet Regional District about the scale. The project was refined before a rezoning application was submitted in 2019 and then approved in 2025, with the revisions having won over some opponents. The project is an instance of a sprawling resort community sprouting from the ground up – and one that’s now being constructed.

The South Britannia development will now include 900 homes, 100 market rental units, 50 below-market rental units, retail space, tourist accommodations, outdoor sports amenities, 320 acres of green space and the crown jewel: A six-acre man-made surf park, the first of its kind in Canada.

“The resistance from the Regional District was regarding job opportunities,” said Tony Petricevic, Tiger Bay’s head of development. “They didn’t want it to be another commuting community. When I came along [around 2018], there was an opportunity to build more commercial [and places to work] to not only make the project more feasible, but also just capitalizing on the location.”

From there, Tiger Bay started exploring possibilities in addition to just residential, with an eye on sports tourism opportunities, as Mr. Petricevic notes that the Sea-to-Sky corridor is one that leans heavily into an outdoorsy lifestyle and culture – winter sports on Whistler Mountain, mountain-biking around Squamish, kitesurfing on Howe Sound.

They eventually settled on a surf park, a pool-like facility with artificially generated waves. And perhaps signalling how persuasive it has been to the community, the outdoor surf park will be delivered as part of Phase One of South Britannia, with the residential, retail and amenities coming in later phases.

The overall master plan for the project was designed by Whistler-based Ecosign Mountain Resort Planners and Vancouver-based Placemark Design .

Mr. Petricevic says the concept of a sports facility being integrated within a residential community was one that was fairly new at the time, so Tiger Bay’s focus was to get the integration aspect right while ensuring the project remained viable.

They ultimately concluded that not only was the surf park financially feasible, it made the overall project more feasible as well because it made way for other commercial components to be included to support the surf park and community.

The heart-shaped surf park will span six acres – around the middle of the overall South Britannia site – and include a beach house that’s home to a restaurant, bar, cafe, retail space, meeting space, wellness facilities, surf cabins and surf academy.

Mr. Petricevic says they wanted to respect the existing surf community, so they worked with groups such as Surf Canada and the Olympic training team to make sure they were on board. The hope is that the facility will also help grow the sport, with lessons provided on site and the controlled environment to make it easier for beginners to learn.

The surf park and beach house were designed by Vancouver’s Michael Green Architecture alongside engineering firm Stantec , with Spain’s Wavegarden as the artificial wave-generation systems provider.

The development permit for the surf park was submitted earlier this year, site work began in late August and the surf park is expected to open in 2029. The timing of the remaining phases will be in part determined by market conditions but are not expected to be advanced until after the surf park is complete.

“Rather than just peel the curtain and be like ‘Boom, here’s the surf park,’ we’re actually creating a series of steps people will have to take [within the development], through the design, to…discover the experience, instead of being bluntly shown it,” said Michael Green.

Mr. Green’s colleague, Chris Knight, added that other surf parks that have been built around the world were not integrated into the landscape, so that became something they strived for.

Mr. Knight added that the form of the beach house buildings were inspired by the look of pebbles on a beach.

Knowing the surf park would be the heart of South Britannia, not to mention the first phase, Green said it was important that they kick off the project on a high note and that “having ambition around it is really important.

“To take the unbelievable landscape of B.C., this unbelievable site, put it together with this [surf] culture and the Sea-to-Sky Highway, which is one of the single-most-visited tourism corridors in Canada, and you get the perfect story of how a project can go from being good to really great.”
