stories.title: American diplomat recalls Canadian solidarity in the days after 9/11 attacks
stories.summary: The legacy of Sept. 11 is seen in the depth of the relationships between Canadians and Americans, the diplomat says
stories.author: Dylan Robertson
stories.content:
American diplomat Baxter Hunt recalls showing up to work at the U.S. Embassy in Ottawa the morning after the 9/11 terrorist attacks and finding “a mountain of flowers” outside the building.

“It was just a day that none of us will ever forget,” said Hunt, now the U.S. consul general in Toronto. “What also stuck with me was the outpouring of support that we got from Canadians.”

This Friday marks 25 years since nearly 3,000 people in the U.S. were killed when al-Qaeda hijackers slammed planes into the World Trade Center in New York and crashed into the Pentagon and a Pennsylvania field.

In the days that followed, Hunt witnessed many more displays of Canadian compassion and support for a grieving nation.

Three days after the attack, 80,000 people crowded Parliament Hill for a national day of mourning, according to an RCMP estimate reported by The Canadian Press that week.

‘’By their outpouring of concern, sympathy and help, the feelings and actions of Canadians have been clear,” then-prime minister Jean Chrétien told the crowd.

‘’And even as we grieve our own losses, the message they send to the American people is equally clear. Do not despair. You are not alone. We are with you. The whole world is with you.’’

Similar moments of silence took place at provincial legislatures and even in the heart of Canada’s financial sector on Bay Street. It was Canada’s first official day of mourning in three decades.

On the day of the attacks, the Newfoundland community of Gander famously took in 38 passenger planes carrying more than 6,500 travellers after officials closed U.S. airspace.

“Just an incredible showing of compassion by those people for complete strangers, who needed them at that time,” Hunt said. “There were also many, many stranded passengers who went to other locations around Canada, about 33,000, I understand.”

Hunt was quick to mention the 24 Canadians who were killed in the attacks alongside other non-Americans.

He was 38 and working as the embassy’s political-military officer on Sept. 11, 2001. American diplomats “naturally came together” with Canadian law enforcement and military officials to identify threats, he said.

“No one knew initially exactly what else might happen. And we wanted to make sure we weren’t vulnerable to other attacks,” Hunt said. “The response of Canadians at a time when we most needed it was incredible.”

Both countries standardized airport security. Allies took up air patrols around the U.S. The Nato military alliance invoked its collective security clause for the first time, sending Canadians and allied troops to fight the Taliban in Afghanistan. That war lasted for more than a dozen years and 165 Canadians – 158 soldiers and seven civilians – died in the conflict.

“It was an event that was a shift in how we perceived threats around the world, and something that happened in the homeland, which we really hadn’t seen before,” Hunt said.

“It was something that just reinforced the need for us to work together.”

Hunt spoke to The Canadian Press shortly before trade talks in Washington collapsed. Prime Minister Mark Carney accused the U.S. of launching an economic “war” on its erstwhile ally and U.S. President Donald Trump moved to rename Lake Ontario as “Lake America.”

Hunt said the legacy of 9/11 is seen in the depth of the relationships between Canadians and Americans throughout the ups and downs in the bilateral relationship.

“That is something that we saw big time after the 9/11 attacks. People just feeling like these are our friends and neighbours, and it is like an extended North American family. And that really came through. And that’s something that I believe is still very strong today,” he said.

“It’s great to remember that as we approach the 25th anniversary, and be grateful that we have that close, close relationship.”

The Toronto consulate is holding events this month to commemorate the anniversary.

They include an ongoing exhibition at a Toronto arts centre of pen and ink drawings by Toronto-based artist John Coburn, who was in New York after the attacks. Hunt said the exhibit includes interactive events with local college students, many of whom were born after the attacks.

On the Friday anniversary, the consulate will hold an event at the same art centre bringing together first responders and government officials to honour the victims. That event will feature Maureen Basnicki, whose husband Ken was killed at the World Trade Center.

Hunt will open the Toronto Stock Exchange that day to commemorate the city’s connections with New York. He’ll also visit a memorial walkway in St. Catharines, Ont. on Thursday.

stories.title: Nova Scotia state of emergency remains in effect after widespread flooding, rain forecast continues
stories.summary: Cape Breton Island and parts of the northern mainland have been battered by rainfall for several days due to a slow-moving weather system
stories.content:
Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston says the province is mourning a Cape Breton Island woman who died during widespread flooding across the region.

RCMP say the body of a 46-year-old woman from Cleveland, N.S., was recovered Saturday afternoon after she was reported missing earlier that day.

The Mounties say their Richmond County office received a report the woman was missing after her vehicle was found parked near her residence on the far side of a flooded bridge.

Police, volunteers and local fire services started searching for the woman, and her body was later recovered in the area at about 2:30 p.m. on Saturday, according to a news release.

RCMP said Sunday the death is not believed to be suspicious. A spokesperson for Nova Scotia RCMP added they would not provide any more information.

Cape Breton Island and parts of the northeast mainland have been battered by rainfall for several days due to a slow-moving weather system.

Nova Scotia’s Department of Emergency Management said Sunday morning that roads across the region continued to be affected by flooding. The province’s road conditions service still reported several closures Sunday afternoon.

A local state of emergency also remained in place Sunday afternoon for Inverness, Richmond and Victoria counties due to severe flooding and widespread damage.

Meanwhile, Environment and Climate Change Canada lifted its weather alerts for Nova Scotia. It issued a special weather statement for parts of northern Newfoundland, warning of heavy rain.

Houston on Sunday repeated a request by officials that people in the affected areas avoid unnecessary travel.

“Stay off the roads while the weather is bad. Your safety is our priority,” he said in a statement.

Federal Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre called on the federal government on Sunday to assist Nova Scotia and its municipalities “with any resources they need to protect people and communities.”

A spokesperson for Emergency Management Minister Eleanor Olszewski did not immediately respond to a request for comment Sunday afternoon.

Prime Minister Mark Carney said in a social media post on Saturday night that his thoughts were with everyone in eastern Nova Scotia and Cape Breton Island affected by the rain and flooding.

“Thank you to the first responders who are working around the clock to keep people safe,” Carney said.

“Our government is in close communication with the provincial government and remains ready to provide any support needed.”

stories.title: London health-tech firm lands Nato approval, first U.S. military sale
stories.summary: Deep Breathe’s AI-guided ultrasound software is aimed at helping military medics assess chest and abdominal injuries in the field.
stories.author: Norman De Bono
stories.content:
A London business has cleared a major hurdle in supplying life-saving software to NATO armed forces, the company’s founder and chief executive says.

Deep Breathe recently made the list of businesses approved to sell its technology to alliance nations and scored its first sale. It is also in talks with three European countries as well as the militaries in Canada and the U.S., said Rob Arntfield.

“We are on the world stage for military adoption,” Arntfield said.

Its first sale was to U.S. Air Force pararescue specialists, elite military first responders who rescue and treat wounded personnel, often in hostile environments.

“They’re like the James Bond of paramedics,” Arntfield said.

Deep Breathe has made a list of 15 businesses approved for NATO’s DIANA Mission Track program, for technologies that meet military needs.

“This opens the door” to sell its technology to NATO’s 32 members, he added.

“This is a list of elite companies that show the most promise. More than 3,000 companies applied and it was reduced to 150 and we are in the top 15. It highlights NATO’s intent to support commercialization and integration.”

Deep Breathe uses artificial intelligence and ultrasound to detect lung and torso issues. Its software, called ATLAS , or the AI Tactical Assessment System, uses AI-guided handheld ultrasound to assess chest and abdominal injuries. That means injuries and wounds can be diagnosed immediately in the field.

It made the list after six months of military exercises in Canada, Estonia, Spain, the United Kingdom and the United States, Arntfield said.

“What this really means is we are helping to solve meaningful problems.”

London tech firm eyes overseas growth, takes part in NATO exercises

It’s not the first time Deep Breathe has received attention from the military. In September 2024, it beat 150 other technology businesses in a U.S. Army-sponsored competition, placing first in the 2024 xTech International competition.

Although Arntfield has spent time with U.S. military officials demonstrating the technology, he said he has seen no indication of tensions between the two countries amid the current trade and tariff dispute between Canada and the U.S.

“It is not about politics. The military is all about the mission. It is refreshing,” Arntfield said.

Deep Breathe software can be used on different hardware. The company charges users a $1,000 monthly subscription fee.

Arntfield is also an intensive care physician and medical director at the critical-care trauma centre at London Health Sciences Centre.

Deep Breathe was founded in 2021.

stories.title: Missing London man found dead
stories.summary: A missing London man has been found dead.
stories.author: Kate Otterbein
stories.content:
A missing London man has been found dead.

Cole Rioux was reported missing by his family after he didn’t arrive at work on Aug. 28.

Rioux’s mother, Marla Rioux, posted to social media on Sunday that the 19-year-old was found dead.

“The family and I are sincerely thankful to all of you for your efforts in searching for Cole and spreading awareness,” she wrote.

She added a celebration of life will be held at a later date for those that knew him.

stories.title: Police recover body of kayaker, 37, missing on Lake Huron near Grand Bend
stories.summary: The Ontario Provincial Police said on Sunday that they had discovered a body off the shore of Lake Huron and confirmed it to be a kayaker who went missing one day prior near Grand Bend.
stories.author: Ryan Goodison
stories.content:
The Ontario Provincial Police said on Sunday that they had discovered a body off the shore of Lake Huron and confirmed it to be a kayaker who went missing one day prior near Grand Bend.

On Saturday at 3:40 p.m., the OPP responded to a report of a missing 37-year-old man from Kitchener who had been kayaking on Lake Huron and had not returned after several hours. Police say the man had launched his kayak from Bluewater, 10 kilometers north of Grand Bend.

The OPP notified residents in the beach community to expect a “heavy police presence” amid the search.

Shortly after 7:30 p.m., police issued new information, saying they were searching Lake Huron for a man who was last seen in a “solid blue” kayak and who was wearing a yellow life jacket.

On Sunday morning, the body of the missing kayaker was located and recovered from Lake Huron, police said in a news release. Police did publicly identify the deceased.

Police say the investigation is ongoing, and anyone with information is asked to contact OPP at 1-888-310-1122.

A driver has died following a single-vehicle collision in Southwold Township, southwest of St. Thomas, police say.

Elgin County Ontario Provincial Police and emergency crews responded to a single-vehicle collision at 7:25 p.m. Friday on John Wise Line, where police say the driver of the vehicle was pronounced dead at the scene.

John Wise Line was closed between Begg and Middle River roads for several hours to conduct the investigation and was later reopened at 3:40 a.m., the OPP said in a post to social media early Saturday.

Anyone with information is asked to contact OPP at 1-888-310-1122 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-TIPS (8477).

Windsor police say they’ve seized more than $7,000 in illegal drugs and a loaded gun after a recent arrest.

Following an investigation by the drugs and guns enforcement unit into an individual suspected of trafficking drugs, police say officers raided a home in the 100-block of Montrose Street, and searched a a vehicle, on Sept 2.

Police said they found 45.1 grams of cocaine, 45.7 grams of fentanyl, a loaded A-75 .45-calibre handgun, a .45-calibre magazine and ammunition, $164 in Canadian cash, $25 in U.S. cash, two cellphones and three digital scales.

Police estimate the total street value of the drugs seized at $7,252.

A 23-year-old man is charged with two counts of possession of a controlled substance for the purpose of trafficking and single counts of possession of a loaded prohibited or restricted firearm, possession of a prohibited firearm without a licence, contravention of section 117(H) of the Firearms Act and failure to comply with a release order.

In addition, he faces 12 counts of possession of a firearm while prohibited and four counts of failure to comply with a probation order.

An arrest warrant has been issued for a second person – a 21-year-old woman who is wanted on drug and firearm possession charges, as well as failure to comply with a release order.

–With files from The Windsor Star

stories.title: A tale of two U.S. ambassadors: Hoekstra and Heyman see Canada very differently
stories.summary: A former U.S. ambassador has shown his support for Canada with a series of social media posts, as the trade war continues to escalate.
stories.author: Ellie Hutchings
stories.content:
A former U.S. ambassador to Canada is taking a strikingly different approach to cross-border relations than the current diplomat in office, as the trade war between the two countries continues to escalate.

Bruce Heyman, who served as ambassador to Canada under U.S. president Barack Obama between 2014 and 2017, has been increasingly vocal in his support for Canada. In contrast, current U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra has offended some Canadians to the point that a parliamentary petition calling for his removal has gathered more than 260,000 signatures.

Both Midwesterners, Heyman grew up in Ohio and served as a managing director of private wealth management at Goldman Sachs before Obama appointed him as U.S. ambassador to Canada. Hoekstra spent most of his childhood in Michigan and is a long-serving Republican, first as a member of Congress representing Michigan’s 2nd District from 1993 to 2011.

Ohio and Michigan are among the states most affected by the Canada-U.S. trade war. Last year, 38 per cent of all exports from Michigan and 32 per cent from Ohio went to Canada , according to data from the U.S. Department of Commerce’s International Trade Administration (ITA), with motor vehicles and parts both states’ top northbound exports.

In a series of recent posts on X, Heyman has been emphatic in his support for Canada, writing “never underestimate a Canadian,” “this American is proudly pro-Canadian,” and “love you, Canada.”

Hoekstra's comments on Gordie Howe bridge 'a punch in the face', says ex-Harper communications chief

As the petition grows, here's what would happen if Carney actually booted the U.S. ambassador

He also shared a photo of himself wearing a hat with “Lake Ontario” stitched on the front, after U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order to rename the body of water “Lake America,” and on Wednesday claimed that he’d previously been told by senior U.S. military officers that “if they were ever stuck in a foxhole under fire and they couldn’t have an American at their side they would undoubtedly want a Canadian.”

Since leaving the role of U.S. ambassador to Canada in 2017, Heyman co-founded the company Uncharted with his wife, Vicki Heyman, which connects Canadians and Americans to create a positive impact across the Canada-U.S. relationship, political engagement and philanthropy.

Heyman’s vocal support for Canada is likely good for his business. But regardless of the motivation, his public posture stands in stark contrast to that of Hoekstra, who took on the role of U.S. ambassador to Canada in April 2025.

Among the objectionable comments Hoekstra has made about Canada are his bafflement at why Canadians are angry about “51st state” comments , suggesting Canada’s response to Trump’s actions has been “nasty and mean,” and reportedly aiming an expletive-laden rant at Ontario’s trade representative .

He also reiterated Trump’s claim that the U.S. “does not need Canada” during a radio interview in Montreal, and suggested that the U.S. president’s “51st state” comments could be taken as a “term of endearment.”

More recently, Hoekstra claimed that Canada paying to construct the Gordie Howe International Bridge was a “big myth,” a comment that former prime minister Stephen Harper’s director of communications, Andrew MacDougall, branded a “punch in the face.”

The petition calling for his removal accuses the ambassador of undermining Canada-U.S. diplomatic relations and normalizing “51st state” language, and is sponsored by Green Party MP Elizabeth May.

That said, the stark difference between the two ambassadors isn’t explained by personal politics alone.

Heyman, whose current business relies on maintaining a positive relationship with Canada, served under Obama, whose administration committed to forming stronger trade ties with Canada through instructing aides to make it easier for goods and people to move between the two nations, and looking to solve a dispute over exports of Canadian softwood lumber.

Hoekstra, meanwhile, represents Trump during a dramatically different period in the bilateral relationship, characterized by tariffs and the trade war. The fallout has caused Canadians’ views of America to become increasingly negative, with a recent Angus Reid poll finding that 45 per cent of Canadians say their views on Americans are unfavourable or very unfavourable .

And it’s not just Canada that Hoekstra has had a fractured relationship with. During his time as ambassador to the Netherlands during Trump’s first term, he was forced to apologize after making false claims that the “Islamic movement” in Europe was creating “no-go zones” and burning politicians.

Meanwhile, it would be wrong to suggest that Heyman didn’t have to navigate policy differences between Canada and the U.S. during his time as ambassador. Most notable was the Keystone XL pipeline, for which Obama denied the cross-border permit in 2015, stating the project did not serve U.S. national interests .

Heyman later wrote in a book he co-authored with his wife, Vicki, that disagreements between former prime minister Stephen Harper’s government and the Obama administration over the pipeline briefly led to an “ice age in relations.”

And yet, Heyman’s pro-Canada stance has extended beyond his time in office. After Trump first imposed tariffs in March 2025, he said in an interview on Cntv that Canada had “been there for (the U.S.) in thick and thin” and that the tariffs “shouldn’t happen.”

“I just think Donald Trump must have some other issue here, and those issues are either personal with Canada, or … personally think he’s short cash,” Heyman added.

He also called the tariffs “deeply offensive to the Canadians,” and said: “I would just say to the Canadian public, there are millions of Americans that value this relationship.”

stories.title: This beloved CNE ride has drawn crowds for decades. It takes another crowd to keep it swinging
stories.summary: From Calgary to Zimbabwe, Wave Swinger staff come together to build the attraction and get riders gracefully aloft.
stories.author: Sophie Bouquillon
stories.content:
Every year, seemingly overnight, the 192-acre Exhibition Grounds transform into the spectacular Canadian National Exhibition for 18 days. The event always reintroduces locals to some old friends — few more popular than the Wave Swinger. But few riders reflect on the attraction’s travelling entourage.

Alexander Hawkins, 20, supervises the ride, Tuesday, September 1, 2026.

Among the 61 rides, the Wave Swinger is one of the oldest, and still one of the most in-demand. Manufactured in 1979 in Germany, the hand-painted 48-seater (currently 47) has become a staple of the midway, loved and revered by riders of all ages.

In an oscillating wave-like motion, riders are flung clockwise into the cool breeze at 10.5 revolutions per minute for about two minutes, depending on the length of the line.

Rider Alicia Ferreira, 39, describes it as “not too scary” and enjoys the feeling of weightlessness, and the bird’s-eye perspective.

Behind the magic are the travelling crew members for North American Midway Entertainment who trek through 15 cities between March and November and toil for as many days as baseball players do in a regular season — 162.

stories.title: Don't want to slip and fall off the mountain? There's an app for that.
stories.summary: Calgary - When clinging to the side of a rock wall hundreds of metres in the sky, avoiding a single misstep can save your life.
stories.author: Bill Graveland The Canadian Press
stories.content:
CALGARY - When clinging to the side of a rock wall hundreds of metres in the sky, avoiding a single misstep can save your life.

Turns out there’s an app to help with that.

Ben Pearman, a rock climber since age 18, said the idea of the app came to him while his group was trying to determine the best way to climb the south face of Mount Yamnuska in southern Alberta’s Bow Valley.

“You get up there and the whole thing looks sort of like a planar surface from far away, like one big sheer cliff,” Pearman said in an interview.

When clinging to the side of a rock wall hundreds of metres in the sky, avoiding a single misstep can save your life. The ThreeTopo app can help you with that. (Sept. 6, 2026)

“The scale just swallows you. And you’re like, ‘Oh man, it’s really easy to get lost here.’”

The sheer limestone wall of this climbing route is known as Red Shirt, and Pearman said it’s the “crown jewel” of climbing in the Rocky Mountains.

The 29-year-old is a master’s student in the University of Calgary’s Department of Computer Science. He decided to turn a climbing map into a project, creating the ThreeTopo app for climbers.

He used a drone to shoot detailed photos of the 240-metre-tall climb and created a three-dimensional digital copy of that section of the rock face.

The app examines the potential for new navigation and conveys the information to climbers. Pearman said it was also important to make it so climbers could use it one-handed when they consult it at safe points during the climb.

As an example, a climber could ask the app for information on the best way forward while at one particular spot in the climb.

The app could reply: “You’ll want to start traversing left from the anchor. Once you hit the corner, start heading upwards until you reach a bolt. As soon as you get to that bolt, you need to traverse hard left, passing a pin to reach an anchor on the face.”

In the past, said Pearman, that kind of practical information came only in the form of cryptic, decades-old typewritten notes from other climbers.

Miles Abesdris, who was in a group of experienced climbers asked to test the app, said it can take some of the scary unknowns out of trad climbing.

Trad — or traditional climbing — involves the lead climber placing temporary, removable gear into the rock. They then clip in a rope to catch a fall. The second climber comes up behind and removes the devices, leaving nothing behind.

“The first little while, (trad climbing) is somewhat horrifying, but you kind of become very comfortable there after a while,” said Abesdris, 38.

“Your hands and feet are great, but you’ve got to know where to go, right?

“There’s weaknesses in the rock. And you kind of follow the weaknesses and you kind of get a Spidey sense of where to go over the years — but sometimes you can be wrong.”

Pearman intends to make his app publicly available. He hopes other climbers will follow suit by detailing data on other popular North American routes from B.C. to Nevada, making the sport safer.

“I know a bunch of people who have had to be rescued by helicopter,” he said.

“Everyone I know has gotten off route at some time.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 6, 2026.
paragraphs: CALGARY - When clinging to the side of a rock wall hundreds of metres in the sky, avoiding a single misstep can save your life.
Turns out there’s an app to help with that.

Ben Pearman, a rock climber since age 18, said the idea of the app came to him while his group was trying to determine the best way to climb the south face of Mount Yamnuska in southern Alberta’s Bow Valley.
“You get up there and the whole thing looks sort of like a planar surface from far away, like one big sheer cliff,” Pearman said in an interview.
When clinging to the side of a rock wall hundreds of metres in the sky, avoiding a single misstep can save your life. The ThreeTopo app can help you with that. (Sept. 6, 2026)
“The scale just swallows you. And you’re like, ‘Oh man, it’s really easy to get lost here.’”
The sheer limestone wall of this climbing route is known as Red Shirt, and Pearman said it’s the “crown jewel” of climbing in the Rocky Mountains.
The 29-year-old is a master’s student in the University of Calgary’s Department of Computer Science. He decided to turn a climbing map into a project, creating the ThreeTopo app for climbers.
He used a drone to shoot detailed photos of the 240-metre-tall climb and created a three-dimensional digital copy of that section of the rock face.

The app examines the potential for new navigation and conveys the information to climbers. Pearman said it was also important to make it so climbers could use it one-handed when they consult it at safe points during the climb.
As an example, a climber could ask the app for information on the best way forward while at one particular spot in the climb.

The app could reply: “You’ll want to start traversing left from the anchor. Once you hit the corner, start heading upwards until you reach a bolt. As soon as you get to that bolt, you need to traverse hard left, passing a pin to reach an anchor on the face.”
In the past, said Pearman, that kind of practical information came only in the form of cryptic, decades-old typewritten notes from other climbers.
Miles Abesdris, who was in a group of experienced climbers asked to test the app, said it can take some of the scary unknowns out of trad climbing.

Trad — or traditional climbing — involves the lead climber placing temporary, removable gear into the rock. They then clip in a rope to catch a fall. The second climber comes up behind and removes the devices, leaving nothing behind.
“The first little while, (trad climbing) is somewhat horrifying, but you kind of become very comfortable there after a while,” said Abesdris, 38.
“Your hands and feet are great, but you’ve got to know where to go, right?
“There’s weaknesses in the rock. And you kind of follow the weaknesses and you kind of get a Spidey sense of where to go over the years — but sometimes you can be wrong.”
Pearman intends to make his app publicly available. He hopes other climbers will follow suit by detailing data on other popular North American routes from B.C. to Nevada, making the sport safer.
“I know a bunch of people who have had to be rescued by helicopter,” he said.
“Everyone I know has gotten off route at some time.”
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 6, 2026.

stories.title: American diplomat recounts Canadian solidarity with U.S. after Sept. 11 attacks
stories.summary: Ottawa - American diplomat Baxter Hunt recalls showing up to work at the U.S. Embassy in Ottawa the morning after the 9/11 terrorist attacks and finding "a mountain of flowers" outside the building.
stories.author: Dylan Robertson The Canadian Press
stories.content:
OTTAWA - American diplomat Baxter Hunt recalls showing up to work at the U.S. Embassy in Ottawa the morning after the 9/11 terrorist attacks and finding “a mountain of flowers” outside the building.

“It was just a day that none of us will ever forget,” said Hunt, now the U.S. consul general in Toronto. “What also stuck with me was the outpouring of support that we got from Canadians.”

This Friday marks 25 years since nearly 3,000 people in the U.S. were killed when al-Qaeda hijackers slammed planes into the World Trade Center in New York and crashed into the Pentagon and a Pennsylvania field.

Baxter Hunt, the U.S. consul general in Toronto, was working at the American Embassy in Ottawa when the Sept. 11, 2001 attacks occurred. He recalls an outpouring of support from Canadians in the weeks that followed. (Sept. 6, 2026)

In the days that followed, Hunt witnessed many more displays of Canadian compassion and support for a grieving nation.

Three days after the attack, 80,000 people crowded Parliament Hill for a national day of mourning, according to an RCMP estimate reported by The Canadian Press that week.

’‘By their outpouring of concern, sympathy and help, the feelings and actions of Canadians have been clear,” then-prime minister Jean Chrétien told the crowd.

’‘And even as we grieve our own losses, the message they send to the American people is equally clear. Do not despair. You are not alone. We are with you. The whole world is with you.’’

Similar moments of silence took place at provincial legislatures and even in the heart of Canada’s financial sector on Bay Street. It was Canada’s first official day of mourning in three decades.

On the day of the attacks, the Newfoundland community of Gander famously took in 38 passenger planes carrying more than 6,500 travellers after officials closed U.S. airspace.

“Just an incredible showing of compassion by those people for complete strangers, who needed them at that time,” Hunt said. “There were also many, many stranded passengers who went to other locations around Canada, about 33,000, I understand.”

Hunt was quick to mention the 24 Canadians who were killed in the attacks alongside other non-Americans.

People bow their heads for three minutes of silence at a memorial ceremony in Ottawa Friday Sept 14, 2001, for the victims of Tuesday’s terrorist attacks on the United States.

He was 38 and working as the embassy’s political-military officer on Sept. 11, 2001. American diplomats “naturally came together” with Canadian law enforcement and military officials to identify threats, he said.

“No one knew initially exactly what else might happen. And we wanted to make sure we weren’t vulnerable to other attacks,” Hunt said. “The response of Canadians at a time when we most needed it was incredible.”

Both countries standardized airport security. Allies took up air patrols around the U.S. The NATO military alliance invoked its collective security clause for the first time, sending Canadians and allied troops to fight the Taliban in Afghanistan. That war lasted for more than a dozen years and 165 Canadians — 158 soldiers and 7 civilians — died in the conflict.

“It was an event that was a shift in how we perceived threats around the world, and something that happened in the homeland, which we really hadn’t seen before,” Hunt said.

“It was something that just reinforced the need for us to work together.”

Hunt spoke to The Canadian Press shortly before trade talks in Washington collapsed. Prime Minister Mark Carney accused the U.S. of launching an economic “war” on its erstwhile ally and U.S. President Donald Trump moved to rename Lake Ontario as “Lake America.”

It’s getting harder to believe that the president is a symptom rather than the cause of what’s gone off the rails in the U.S., Susan Delacourt writes.

Hunt said the legacy of 9/11 is seen in the depth of the relationships between Canadians and Americans throughout the ups and downs in the bilateral relationship.

“That is something that we saw big time after the 9/11 attacks. People just feeling like these are our friends and neighbours, and it is like an extended North American family. And that really came through. And that’s something that I believe is still very strong today,” he said.

“It’s great to remember that as we approach the 25th anniversary, and be grateful that we have that close, close relationship.”

The Toronto consulate is holding events this month to commemorate the anniversary.

They include an ongoing exhibition at a Toronto arts centre of pen and ink drawings by Toronto-based artist John Coburn, who was in New York after the attacks. Hunt said the exhibit includes interactive events with local college students, many of whom were born after the attacks.

On the Friday anniversary, the consulate will hold an event at the same art centre bringing together first responders and government officials to honour the victims. That event will feature Maureen Basnicki, whose husband Ken was killed at the World Trade Center.

Hunt will open the Toronto Stock Exchange that day to commemorate the city’s connections with New York. He’ll also visit a memorial walkway in St. Catharines, Ont. on Thursday.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 6, 2026.

stories.title: 'It's childish': Americans in Canada react to Trump's renaming of Lake Ontario
stories.summary: If you’re angered by U.S. President Donald Trump's renaming of Lake Ontario to “Lake America,” chances are that an American living in your neighbourhood might be just as outraged — if not more.
stories.author: Sharif Hassan The Canadian Press
stories.content:
If you’re angered by U.S. President Donald Trump’s renaming of Lake Ontario to “Lake America,” chances are that an American living in your neighbourhood might be just as outraged — if not more.

Many Americans who’ve made Canada their home are calling it an embarrassing, even “childish,” stunt.

Ben Davis, a retired law professor, said Trump’s executive order to change the lake’s name is “so beneath the office of the United States president.”

Ben Davis is shown in this undated photo.

“And obviously it’s another one of his distractions of the day, but it’s just pitiful,” Davis said.

He is a permanent Canadian resident who moved from Virginia in February 2025 and has since been living in Quebec, where his wife is from.

Davis noted that Lake Ontario was mentioned by that name in the 1794 Canandaigua Treaty, signed by the first U.S. president George Washington and the Six Nations after the American Revolution. Renaming it more than 230 years later is nothing short of “nonsense,” he said.

“The name was good enough for George Washington and I don’t see why it’s not good enough for Donald Trump.”

More than a million Americans, including visitors on long-term visas and dual citizens, live in Canada, according to 2023 estimates from the Association of Americans Resident Overseas.

Dawna E. Wade, who lives with her wife in Annapolis Royal, N.S., is among those who see Trump going after Lake Ontario’s name as plainly ridiculous.

“It’s not his to rename,” she said. “And even if it were in the purview of the United States, he doesn’t get to do it unilaterally.”

Trump signed the order to change the name as tensions between the United States and Canada escalated following a breakdown in trade talks, and after the president and Ontario Premier Doug Ford traded insults over tariffs. The executive order only holds water in the United States, and has been widely dismissed in Canada.

Ford and Prime Minister Mark Carney have said the large body of water shared between the two countries will always be known as Lake Ontario, regardless of what Trump calls it.

A recent Ipsos/Reuters poll suggested the lake renaming was not popular within the United States either, with only 14 per cent of roughly 1,000 Americans surveyed countrywide saying they supported the move.

For Wade, distancing herself from America is about much more than geographical names.

She said she and her wife moved to Canada from North Carolina in May because they didn’t feel safe in the United States anymore due to their sexual orientation, their Jewish faith and left-leaning politics.

Wade, who is a Canadian citizen by descent, was born in Los Angeles and spent most of her life in the United States. She said she had visited Canada only a few times before making the final move. Her wife, however, had never been in Canada.

The transition has been smooth, she said.

“We have been not only welcomed, but truly embraced. People are not only kind, but they are helpful,” she said. “I don’t know that I had any expectations before we moved, but our experience has far surpassed anything that I could have imagined.”

Chris Palermo, an American who lives in Hamilton with his Canadian wife, called the Lake Ontario name change a “useless” knee-jerk reaction by Trump after he failed to get what he wanted at the negotiating table.

The U.S. president Donald Trump’s executive order to change the name of Lake Ontario to ‘Lake America’ has sparked widespread outrage among dual citizens and Americans who live in Canada. They call the renaming of the lake U.S. and Canada a childish, ridiculous and useless move. (Sept. 6, 2026)

He said he is more disappointed in Google and Apple for changing the lake’s name on their maps for U.S. users.

Palermo, who moved from Long Island, N.Y, three years ago, said he has noticed that support for Trump’s “outrageous, outlandish actions” is diminishing rapidly even among his hard-core supporters amid a high cost of living made worse by trade disputes and the United States’ war with Iran.

Palermo said moves such as renaming Gulf of Mexico and Lake Ontario could also be part of a strategy to divert attention from the Trump administration’s domestic failures.

“Every time there is a groundswell of opposition to the Epstein files, the war in Iran, affordability, et cetera, something outrageous has to happen to take that approach away,” he said.

In addition to waging a trade war, Trump has also repeatedly threatened Canada’s sovereignty and mused about the country becoming the “51st state.”

London, Ont., resident Chris Kubinski said he was so outraged by those threats of annexation that he decided to renounce his U.S. citizenship and “divorce” Trump’s America.

Chris Kubinski is shown in this undated photo.

“Literally when he started talking about the 51st state, ‘Canada’s not a country,’ all that negative rhetoric, I just kind of went, ‘That’s it, I’m done,’” he said.

Kubinski moved to Canada with his family in the 1970s when he was a child, and later married a Canadian woman with whom he raised a family. He became a Canadian citizen two years ago.

As for Trump’s Lake Ontario renaming order, Kubinski said “it’s childish. It’s bizarre.”

“I’m actually surprised he didn’t try and name it ‘Lake Trump,’ because he likes to put his name on absolutely everything,” he said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 6, 2026.

stories.title: Here's what's open and closed in London this Labour Day
stories.summary: Many city services will be closed Monday, but some outdoor pools, recreation programs and attractions will be open for Labour Day.
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: Many city services will be closed Monday, but some outdoor pools, recreation programs and attractions will be open for Labour Day.
· Posted: Sep 06, 2026 5:00 AM EDT | Last Updated: September 6
Here is a list of what's open and closed in London this holiday.(CBC)
Labour Day is Monday, and for many Londoners, it’s the last chance to squeeze a little more summer out of the long weekend.
Here’s what you need to know about what’s open and closed around the city.

The City of London is offering a range of free recreation activities on Monday, including swimming, arts and crafts, science workshops and basketball. Some activities require registration, while others are drop-in.
And unlike some years, Londoners still have several chances to get in an outdoor swim.
Byron, Southcrest and Silverwoods pools are open Monday, although they’re closing for the season that day. Gibbons and Stronach pools will remain open beyond the holiday.
Several wading pools will also have their final day on Labour Day, including Meredith, Silverwoods and Springbank parks.
The city’s spray pads are also open, generally from 9 a.m. to 9 p.m., although the Ivey Park spray pad remains closed for the rest of the year.
If you’re looking for something beyond the pool, Storybook Gardens will be open from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. Monday. Admission is $10.70, with children under two admitted free.
Other attractions, including the London Children’s Museum at Kellogg Lane, East Park and Boler Mountain, are also open for the long weekend.
London Public Library branches will be closed Monday for Labour Day, although its digital library remains available.
If you’re planning to shop, check before you head out.
White Oaks Mall and CF Masonville Place will be closed Monday for Labour Day.
Individual stores, restaurants and grocery stores can set their own holiday hours, so it’s a good idea to check before making a trip.
Liquor and beer retailers May also have holiday closures or reduced hours.
London Transit will run on a holiday schedule Monday.
There are also several route and schedule changes taking effect Sunday, Sept. 6, so regular riders should check their route before heading out.
Banks will be closed Monday.
There will also be no regular Canada Post collection or delivery on Labour Day.
And if Monday is your usual garbage day, your collection will be pushed back one day to Tuesday, Sept. 8.
So if you're heading out Monday, check the hours first. The forecast for Monday from Environment Canada is calling for cloudy skies with a high of 23 C.

stories.title: How to help your child navigate back-to-school anxiety
stories.summary: Psychotherapist Lori Griffith shares tips on how families can manage nerves ahead of the first day of school
stories.author: Travis Dolynny
paragraphs: Psychotherapist Lori Griffith shares tips on how families can manage nerves ahead of the first day of school
The countdown to the new school year can trigger a mix of excitement and stress.

Psychotherapist Lori Griffith, a director at the Canadian Mental Health Association (Cmha) Thames Valley, offers insight into why students and parents experience back-to-school nerves, how to validate those feelings, and when it might be time to seek professional support.
Griffith spoke with London Morning host Matt Allen.
The following has been edited for length and clarity.
Matt Allen: What are some of the emotions kids might be feeling as summer winds down?

Lori Griffith: It's completely normal for students of all ages to feel some level of anxiety about going back to school. A new teacher, new routine, social pressures, academic expectations, and uncertainty can all create stress.

The goal isn't to eliminate the anxiety. Anxiety is a normal human emotion. The goal is helping students to learn that they can cope with it. What we might see before going back to school is some butterflies before the first day, worrying if friends will be in their class, feeling nervous about a new school or teacher.
LISTEN | How to help your child:
Media Audio | London Morning :
MA: Is it just the kids who are nervous right now, or parents too?

LG: I think it's everybody. Every time you're starting a new challenge or an event, it's normal to feel a little bit anxious. The normal thing is to feel uncomfortable, but try to manage through it. As long as something's not interfering significantly with daily life, we do normally see routines and the anxiety will improve once they settle into their routine.
MA: Why do kids get so nervous heading into a new grade?

LG: I think it's the fear of the unknown. I mean, I think that's common with all of us. Also, we get this idea of this anticipatory anxiety. Often kids aren't struggling with the event itself, they're struggling with imagining the event. Maybe they're worrying all weekend about Monday, or worrying all summer about school, and thinking about every possible thing that could potentially go wrong.
MA: What are some tips for parents who are trying to psych their kids up to enter a new environment?

LG: I think it's really important to acknowledge the feeling. We're not looking to avoid or remove the feeling. We're wanting to acknowledge and then express confidence in the children and encourage gradual exposure.

As an example, if a child misses school because they're nervous, they May feel better that day, but then their brains will learn, "I survived it because I avoided it." The next time, the anxiety May come back a little bit stronger.
Instead of saying, "Don't worry, there's nothing to be nervous about," we want to say things like, "I can see you're nervous. New things can feel scary, but I know you can handle this."
MA: How can parents support their children if they don't have all the answers?

LG: One of the nice things is when we're kind of exposing ourselves to a new routine is to keep routines predictable. Children feel safer when expectations are clear. Consistent sleep schedules (sleep is one of the most important things that we can do in terms of relieving some of that worry), regular meals, and then preparing. Whether that looks like preparing on the weekend for the upcoming week, or preparing that night for the school the next day.

Focus on coping, not certainty. Parents often try to reassure away anxiety. Instead of saying that "Nothing bad will happen," try saying something to your youth or your child that says, "Whatever happens, we'll figure it out." This will teach the resilience rather than dependence on certainty.
MA: How do parents know if anxiety is normal or if professional help is necessary?

LG: Anxiety, it May be there for a couple weeks as they're adjusting to that schedule. When we want to look for more support is if it's persisting for more weeks, it's getting worse rather than better, it's causing significant distress, or if it's interfering with their school attendance, their sleep patterns, their friendships, family life, or other activities.
One kind of way of thinking about it is when anxiety starts running a child's life instead of simply visiting it from time to time, that's when we become more concerned.

What we might see before going back to school is some butterflies before the first day, worrying if friends will be in their class, feeling nervous about a new school or teacher.

LISTEN | How to help your child:

Media Audio | London Morning :

MA: Is it just the kids who are nervous right now, or parents too?

LG: I think it's everybody. Every time you're starting a new challenge or an event, it's normal to feel a little bit anxious. The normal thing is to feel uncomfortable, but try to manage through it. stories.title: How Howard Lutnick became Donald Trump’s ‘ultimate disrupter’ in Canada’s trade war
stories.summary: Sometimes the U.S. commerce secretary has been described as charming and pleasant to deal with. Other times, his bare-knuckled bargaining style has been called "bananas." Everyone agrees that he's a
stories.author: Alex Ballingall
stories.content:
OTTAWA — The Americans weren’t happy. But Howard Lutnick seemed furious.

It was early March 2025, the final days of Justin Trudeau’s prime ministership, and the trade war with U.S. President Donald Trump had only just begun. Ottawa had struck back with retaliatory tariffs against the first volley of U.S. import duties. Two days later, Trudeau and his advisers gathered in his office for a phone call with the American president, according to two Canadian officials with knowledge of what happened, who agreed to speak about sensitive discussions on the condition they weren’t identified.

During the conversation, which both officials described as heated, Trump brought in Vice President JD Vance and Lutnick, the New York billionaire who serves as commerce secretary. The Americans spoke of how they would now exempt goods from tariffs if they complied with the North American trade deal that Trump had signed during his first term.

Shouldn’t the Canadians be grateful?

As it turned out, Ottawa still saw the remaining tariffs as an unjustified violation of the trade deal, and would therefore still retaliate. This, according to both officials, is what offended the Americans — and nobody more so than Lutnick.

One of the officials said Lutnick sounded shocked and angry, expressing fury that Canada had the gall to strike back when the U.S. was softening its position. The second official described Lutnick as “losing his s — t,” and said his tone became “bananas” over the course of the call.

“He’s a guy whose basic instinct is to revert to anger,” they said. “He’s been an ultimate disrupter.”

That perception of Lutnick has hardened since Prime Minister Mark Carney suspended trade talks with the Trump administration in August, declaring the U.S. had “attacked” Canada with last-minute demands that would have eroded the country’s independence.

Sources have told the Star and other media that Lutnick was a factor in the collapse of negotiations , particularly over the exclusion of trucks made in Oshawa and Oakville from American tariff relief that was on the table, while the commerce secretary and other American officials blamed the Canadian side for unreasonably pushing too hard and walking away from the best deal in Trump’s new world of tariffs and trade transactions.

The latest U.S. tariffs on more than 700 Canadian products took effect last month.

Regardless of what happened, observers — including some with direct knowledge of Lutnick as an American interlocutor — see in the commerce secretary the embodiment of the Trump administration’s transactional negotiating approach. Brash, slick-haired, cocksure, the erstwhile Manhattan financier was a key player in jockeying over the Gordie Howe International Bridge, which saw the U.S. extract further concessions from Canada allowing the opening of the $6.4-billion structure, which was financed entirely by Ottawa. Last year, behind closed doors at a conference in Toronto, Lutnick declared Canada should find something else to build in Ontario’s car-making heartland, since the U.S. planned to dominate the auto sector and “there is nothing Canada can do about it.”

Portraying Lutnick as the villain in the relationship would be simplistic, however. He can be charming and pleasant to deal with, said one Canadian official, adding that Lutnick’s bluster can also be read as a performance, and a tactic to accomplish his goals. But the official said it’s also true that Lutnick can turn on a dime, and show the edge and intensity of a ruthless New York dealmaker.

“He’ll stab you in the stomach while smiling in your face,” the official said.

Lutnick’s office did not respond to requests for comment from the Star.

It’s getting harder to believe that the president is a symptom rather than the cause of what’s gone off the rails in the U.S., Susan Delacourt writes.

Lutnick, 65, came to politics after a long career in the New York financial world. He helped raise money for Trump’s 2024 presidential run, and co-chaired his transition back to the White House as Trump met with petitioners at his Mar-a-Lago resort in Florida. A profile in The New Yorker described him as “the most Trumpian member of Trump’s cabinet,” and Lutnick has seemed to embrace the president’s style and mercantilist world view. On a podcast in 2025, he echoed Trump’s notion of a halcyon era of high tariffs in the U.S., when taxes on imports filled government coffers in the absence of personal income tax.

Accounts of Lutnick’s past describe his ascent in the 1980s and 1990s at the New York investment firm Cantor Fitzgerald. By his mid-thirties he had control of the firm following a bitter succession battle with the widow of the company’s founder, in which Lutnick was accused in the New York Times of staging a “palace coup.”

One Canadian official said that Carney’s lead cabinet minister on U.S. trade, Dominic LeBlanc, established a solid relationship with Lutnick in early 2025. The pair texted often and got along well, the official said, even as the trade war heated up.

But Canadians have observed Lutnick’s forcefulness in trade talks. He has been seen as trying to assert dominance through his oversight of sectoral tariffs on Canadian steel, aluminum and autos — import duties the Trump administration justifies on “national security” grounds.

“He’s outrageous. He is mercurial. He yells. The way he talks in public is like he talks in private. He can be extremely aggressive, unlike Trump, who in private is never really aggressive,” one former official said.

“I think he is driven by the desire to be the top dog, be admired by the president, to always come out on top.”

Lutnick’s life has been marked by death and tragedy. His mother, an art teacher, died of cancer when he was 16 in 1978, and his father died the following year after he was given the wrong dose at his first chemotherapy treatment for lung cancer, Lutnick told a U.S. Senate committee after he was nominated to Trump’s cabinet.

Cantor Fitzgerald’s Manhattan offices took up the top five floors of the north tower of the World Trade Center. When hijacked planes struck the twin towers on Sept. 11, 2001, 658 Cantor Fitzgerald employees were killed, including Lutnick’s younger brother Gary, who had lived with him in his college dorm room after their parents died. Lutnick told the Senate hearing that the only reason he wasn’t also killed is that he was taking his son to his first day of kindergarten when the attacks occurred.

Kevin O’Leary, the Canadian TV personality and investor, said Lutnick’s response to the disaster and efforts to support victims’ families and rebuild the company are “legendary” in the business community.

“He’s actually a nice guy. You know, he’s an entertaining guy with a lot of energy,” O’Leary said, describing how he last ran into Lutnick in a hotel lobby in Washington, D.C.

“You may or may not like his negotiating style,” O’Leary added. “Everybody’s got their own thing.”

And that rubs some people the wrong way. Last winter, when Lutnick gave the final speech at a dinner during the World Economic Forum in Davos, European Central Bank president Christine Lagarde walked out.

Lutnick “just bashed Europe, right, left and centre,” she told the Wall Street Journal . “That was just too much and just unnecessarily offensive.”

The commerce secretary has also faced pressure and scrutiny from fellow Americans. Steve Bannon, the right-wing commentator and former Trump adviser, panned Lutnick’s defence of Trump’s “Liberation Day” tariffs last year as an “unmitigated disaster.”

WASHINGTON (AP) — Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, in an interview with House lawmakers, backed away from a previous claim that convicted se…

Last May, after Lutnick admitted he and his family visited the Caribbean island of the disgraced late financier Jeffrey Epstein in 2012, members of the U.S. Congress accused him of lying about his interactions with Epstein — who had been Lutnick’s neighbour in New York City — and called on him to resign immediately.

One Canadian official said a big challenge in dealing with the Trump administration is reading who has more influence at any given time in what they described as a “chaotic” and at times “unclear” dynamic inside the White House.

Flavio Volpe, president of the Automotive Parts Manufacturers’ Association and member of Carney’s advisory council on economic relations with the U.S., said that U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer took the leading role in recent talks that almost landed with a deal in late August. But in the final days before talks fell apart, Lutnick got more involved, and it soon became clear to the Canadians that the U.S. would not include medium and heavy duty trucks in any tariff relief, Volpe said — something that could doom factories in Ontario.

“I know for sure that wasn’t the case going into Wednesday night,” Volpe said, citing the evening two days before the negotiations collapsed.

“We were in contact, semi-regular contact, with the negotiating team … The clarity that medium and heavy trucks were excluded came in after Canada repeatedly sought clarity on Friday,” he added. “Whether it came directly from Lutnick or not, it came after Lutnick became directly involved.”

Given Lutnick’s comments last year that Canada must surrender auto manufacturing to the U.S., Volpe said he believes the commerce secretary was responsible for this aspect of the disagreement.

“I don’t believe in coincidences,” he said.

Lutnick, meanwhile, has blamed Canada for adding last minute changes to the deal, and the U.S. maintains that medium and heavy trucks were never part of the deal. On Wednesday, a smiling Lutnick told the U.S. broadcaster CNBC that the Carney government “blew it up for political reasons only” ahead of separatist concerns in the Quebec election and Alberta referendum in October.

“We were treated disrespectfully,” Lutnick insisted.

“It’s just sad the way Canada has treated us.”

With files from Tonda MacCharles

Kevin O’Leary, the Canadian TV personality and investor, said Lutnick’s response to the disaster and efforts to support victims’ families and rebuild the company are “legendary” in the business community.
“He’s actually a nice guy. You know, he’s an entertaining guy with a lot of energy,” O’Leary said, describing how he last ran into Lutnick in a hotel lobby in Washington, D.C.
“You may or may not like his negotiating style,” O’Leary added. “Everybody’s got their own thing.”

And that rubs some people the wrong way. Last winter, when Lutnick gave the final speech at a dinner during the World Economic Forum in Davos, European Central Bank president Christine Lagarde walked out.
Lutnick “just bashed Europe, right, left and centre,” she told the Wall Street Journal . “That was just too much and just unnecessarily offensive.”

The commerce secretary has also faced pressure and scrutiny from fellow Americans. Steve Bannon, the right-wing commentator and former Trump adviser, panned Lutnick’s defence of Trump’s “Liberation Day” tariffs last year as an “unmitigated disaster.”
WASHINGTON (AP) — Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, in an interview with House lawmakers, backed away from a previous claim that convicted se…

Last May, after Lutnick admitted he and his family visited the Caribbean island of the disgraced late financier Jeffrey Epstein in 2012, members of the U.S. Congress accused him of lying about his interactions with Epstein — who had been Lutnick’s neighbour in New York City — and called on him to resign immediately.

One Canadian official said a big challenge in dealing with the Trump administration is reading who has more influence at any given time in what they described as a “chaotic” and at times “unclear” dynamic inside the White House.

Flavio Volpe, president of the Automotive Parts Manufacturers’ Association and member of Carney’s advisory council on economic relations with the U.S., said that U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer took the leading role in recent talks that almost landed with a deal in late August. But in the final days before talks fell apart, Lutnick got more involved, and it soon became clear to the Canadians that the U.S. would not include medium and heavy duty trucks in any tariff relief, Volpe said — something that could doom factories in Ontario.
“I know for sure that wasn’t the case going into Wednesday night,” Volpe said, citing the evening two days before the negotiations collapsed.

“We were in contact, semi-regular contact, with the negotiating team … The clarity that medium and heavy trucks were excluded came in after Canada repeatedly sought clarity on Friday,” he added. “Whether it came directly from Lutnick or not, it came after Lutnick became directly involved.”
Given Lutnick’s comments last year that Canada must surrender auto manufacturing to the U.S., Volpe said he believes the commerce secretary was responsible for this aspect of the disagreement.
“I don’t believe in coincidences,” he said.

Lutnick, meanwhile, has blamed Canada for adding last minute changes to the deal, and the U.S. maintains that medium and heavy trucks were never part of the deal. On Wednesday, a smiling Lutnick told the U.S. broadcaster CNBC that the Carney government “blew it up for political reasons only” ahead of separatist concerns in the Quebec election and Alberta referendum in October.
“We were treated disrespectfully,” Lutnick insisted.
“It’s just sad the way Canada has treated us.”

stories.title: How Canada’s border offices are facing a major security gap
stories.summary: The audit examined the security controls at border agencies including airports, land border crossings, mail processing centres, warehouses, telephone reporting sites and office buildings.
stories.author: Nicholas Keung
stories.content:
Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) is woefully behind when it comes to protecting its only facilities at airports, ports of entry and offices from security threat and risk, an audit found.

A recent effort to catch up on that work has exposed major shortcomings: Unauthorized people walked into secure areas through “piggybacking.” Surveillance cameras were missing or too blurry to be useful to guard the facilities. And official stamps used to process travellers and goods at ports of entry couldn’t be accounted for.

The report examined the security controls at premises of the border agency, which operates in more than 1,000 facilities across the country, including airports, land border crossings, mail processing centres, warehouses, telephone reporting sites and office buildings.

Of the 410 sites classified as “critical facilities,” 312 or 75 per cent had no records of threat and risk assessments or had one that was more than five years old — and only 69 or 40 per cent of 162 “medium and high-risk” premises had a valid evaluation, the internal audit found.

“This indicates that the agency does not have a comprehensive or up to date baseline understanding of the risks and vulnerabilities present in most of its facilities,” said the report, released on Monday.

Advocates say they are alarmed by the pushback of immigration authorities against migrants trying to exercise their right to protest.

Security and intelligence expert Wesley Wark said it’s incumbent on every federal department and agency, especially those with a role in national security, to protect their data and infrastructure.

“That level of seriousness in terms of responding to a potential threat is not there for CBSA and improvements have to be made,” said Wark, a senior fellow at the Centre for International Governance Innovation. “This is an important responsibility that needs to be done in a better, more rigorous way.”

The CBSA audit, covering the period between April 2022 and September 2025, focused on its physical security rules and oversight, internal controls and processes such as risk management, as well as monitoring and reporting of physical security activities.

Auditors reviewed more than 300 documents, interviewed over 75 people involved and affected by these measures and visited 18 sites with walk-throughs in facilities in Ontario, the Pacific and Quebec regions.

They pored over 180 physical security recommendations issued during the audit period but found only 25 per cent had been implemented, while the rest were either not carried out or could not be confirmed, indicating the identified vulnerabilities may have persisted, the report warned.

The border agency’s management attributed the lacking valid threat and risk assessments to other priorities and limited human and financial resources. Reasons for lagging implementations included insufficient funding, infeasibility and no clear order of priority.

In an email, CBSA said it’s on track to complete all ongoing threat and risk assessments by March 2027, at which time it will establish annual compliance monitoring of threat risk assessment recommendations.

“We treat this matter seriously and take immediate action whenever gaps in physical security are identified,” said the agency, which has conducted an internal analysis to ensure its physical security data is accurate and up to date.

“The CBSA has worked to address these issues over recent years by investing in physical security elements such as alarm systems, distress alarms, lighting, fences, barriers, signage, doors and windows.”

During a number of walk-throughs in various locations, audit team members were able to access all secure and non-secure floors unannounced, at various times of day, without access cards or visible CBSA identification. They were let in by occupants of the floors or entered through “piggybacking” — following an authorized person. They were only questioned on one of the six secure floors and two of the nine non-secure floors.

On two occasions, employees were found to be away from their workstations, with computer screens unlocked and unattended. Sensitive documents were left at printers, including financial documents and documentation containing personal traveller data such as names, passage dates, passport numbers and dates of birth.

“In some instances, the audit team was also able to consult paper documents with Protected B and C information, in cabinets that were left open, without being questioned,” said the report, referring to classified information pertaining to private personal data and business records.

Although all 18 inspected sites had some form of electronic surveillance or CCTV infrastructure, problems were identified at half of them, including no coverage in key operational areas and low-quality resolution:

There was no CCTV installed at one primary inspection lane that processes millions of crossing vehicles yearly;

Three other locations had no CCTV coverage in areas such as the bond rooms, where seized goods are held;

The remaining five locations had CCTV cameras with such poor resolution that in some cases images were not visible.

“The most significant deficiencies were noted in one facility that had no electronic access management system; the entire Port of Entry (POE) leveraged locks with a pin code and/or keys with the same code for the entire facility,” the audit noted.

“This facility had no intrusion alarm, although the audit notes that it is manned 24/7 with officers. Another three POE had access management systems which were deemed to be at a very high risk of failure.”

The team also audited the management of port stamps that are used to identify the date, location, purpose and duration of a traveller’s authorized stay, or the personal and commercial goods entering and exiting Canada. They authenticate documents and identify the issuing officers with their unique numbers.

They found that the government’s database was consistently out of date and didn’t match the actual stamps on hand at border crossings, while others in the system were missing, damaged, moved, reassigned or unaccounted for. There were also stamps in storage that were not in the inventory data.

“Compromise, such as a lost or stolen stamps, can directly impact the integrity of Canada’s border,” the report cautioned.

Throughout his nine years in Canada, the Egyptian man has gone through — and passed — three extensive security checks by multiple federal agencies.

Security expert Wark believes the gaps identified in the audit have more to do with what he calls the “security culture” at CBSA, rather than lacking resources because infrastructure such as access controls and CCTV cameras are not “a big money pit.”

He said a lot of people don’t understand the threat and risk until they are convinced to take it seriously, but more often than not major changes only happen after there’s a security crisis.

“The security culture at CBSA is a little more lax than they should be comfortable with,” said Wark. “It’s an important reminder that physical security matters and that there are practices and policies in place that need to be followed as rigorously as possible.”

The border agency said many historical CCTV issues have been rectified and it’s working to address known deficiencies as quickly as possible.

Following the audit, it said it conducted further review of its port stamps inventory and located some missing stamps at a different port of entry, and the records have since been updated to reflect the stamps’ actual location.

The agency said a new step-by-step guide will be ready by the end of September for how to do a yearly check across the country to make sure all security-sensitive items are accounted for, and a five-year program of work will replace access control systems at a number of sites every year.

“The CBSA maintains a safe and secure operational environment where its personnel, facilities, information and assets are guarded from security threats and vulnerabilities,” it said.

The Customs and Immigration Union, which represents more than 9,000 CBSA employees, said it’s still reviewing the audit and declined to comment.
paragraphs: Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) is woefully behind when it comes to protecting its only facilities at airports, ports of entry and offices from security threat and risk, an audit found.

A recent effort to catch up on that work has exposed major shortcomings: Unauthorized people walked into secure areas through “piggybacking.” Surveillance cameras were missing or too blurry to be useful to guard the facilities. And official stamps used to process travellers and goods at ports of entry couldn’t be accounted for.

The report examined the security controls at premises of the border agency, which operates in more than 1,000 facilities across the country, including airports, land border crossings, mail processing centres, warehouses, telephone reporting sites and office buildings.

Of the 410 sites classified as “critical facilities,” 312 or 75 per cent had no records of threat and risk assessments or had one that was more than five years old — and only 69 or 40 per cent of 162 “medium and high-risk” premises had a valid evaluation, the internal audit found.

“This indicates that the agency does not have a comprehensive or up to date baseline understanding of the risks and vulnerabilities present in most of its facilities,” said the report, released on Monday.
Advocates say they are alarmed by the pushback of immigration authorities against migrants trying to exercise their right to protest.
Security and intelligence expert Wesley Wark said it’s incumbent on every federal department and agency, especially those with a role in national security, to protect their data and infrastructure.

“That level of seriousness in terms of responding to a potential threat is not there for CBSA and improvements have to be made,” said Wark, a senior fellow at the Centre for International Governance Innovation. “This is an important responsibility that needs to be done in a better, more rigorous way.”

The CBSA audit, covering the period between April 2022 and September 2025, focused on its physical security rules and oversight, internal controls and processes such as risk management, as well as monitoring and reporting of physical security activities.

Auditors reviewed more than 300 documents, interviewed over 75 people involved and affected by these measures and visited 18 sites with walk-throughs in facilities in Ontario, the Pacific and Quebec regions.

They pored over 180 physical security recommendations issued during the audit period but found only 25 per cent had been implemented, while the rest were either not carried out or could not be confirmed, indicating the identified vulnerabilities may have persisted, the report warned.

The border agency’s management attributed the lacking valid threat and risk assessments to other priorities and limited human and financial resources. Reasons for lagging implementations included insufficient funding, infeasibility and no clear order of priority.

In an email, CBSA said it’s on track to complete all ongoing threat and risk assessments by March 2027, at which time it will establish annual compliance monitoring of threat risk assessment recommendations.

“We treat this matter seriously and take immediate action whenever gaps in physical security are identified,” said the agency, which has conducted an internal analysis to ensure its physical security data is accurate and up to date.

“The CBSA has worked to address these issues over recent years by investing in physical security elements such as alarm systems, distress alarms, lighting, fences, barriers, signage, doors and windows.”

During a number of walk-throughs in various locations, audit team members were able to access all secure and non-secure floors unannounced, at various times of day, without access cards or visible CBSA identification. They were let in by occupants of the floors or entered through “piggybacking” — following an authorized person. They were only questioned on one of the six secure floors and two of the nine non-secure floors.

On two occasions, employees were found to be away from their workstations, with computer screens unlocked and unattended. Sensitive documents were left at printers, including financial documents and documentation containing personal traveller data such as names, passage dates, passport numbers and dates of birth.

“In some instances, the audit team was also able to consult paper documents with Protected B and C information, in cabinets that were left open, without being questioned,” said the report, referring to classified information pertaining to private personal data and business records.

Although all 18 inspected sites had some form of electronic surveillance or CCTV infrastructure, problems were identified at half of them, including no coverage in key operational areas and low-quality resolution:
There was no CCTV installed at one primary inspection lane that processes millions of crossing vehicles yearly;
Three other locations had no CCTV coverage in areas such as the bond rooms, where seized goods are held;
The remaining five locations had CCTV cameras with such poor resolution that in some cases images were not visible.

“The most significant deficiencies were noted in one facility that had no electronic access management system; the entire Port of Entry (POE) leveraged locks with a pin code and/or keys with the same code for the entire facility,” the audit noted.

“This facility had no intrusion alarm, although the audit notes that it is manned 24/7 with officers. Another three POE had access management systems which were deemed to be at a very high risk of failure.”

The team also audited the management of port stamps that are used to identify the date, location, purpose and duration of a traveller’s authorized stay, or the personal and commercial goods entering and exiting Canada. They authenticate documents and identify the issuing officers with their unique numbers.

They found that the government’s database was consistently out of date and didn’t match the actual stamps on hand at border crossings, while others in the system were missing, damaged, moved, reassigned or unaccounted for. There were also stamps in storage that were not in the inventory data.
“Compromise, such as a lost or stolen stamps, can directly impact the integrity of Canada’s border,” the report cautioned.
Throughout his nine years in Canada, the Egyptian man has gone through — and passed — three extensive security checks by multiple federal agencies.

Security expert Wark believes the gaps identified in the audit have more to do with what he calls the “security culture” at CBSA, rather than lacking resources because infrastructure such as access controls and CCTV cameras are not “a big money pit.”
He said a lot of people don’t understand the threat and risk until they are convinced to take it seriously, but more often than not major changes only happen after there’s a security crisis.

“The security culture at CBSA is a little more lax than they should be comfortable with,” said Wark. “It’s an important reminder that physical security matters and that there are practices and policies in place that need to be followed as rigorously as possible.”
The border agency said many historical CCTV issues have been rectified and it’s working to address known deficiencies as quickly as possible.

Following the audit, it said it conducted further review of its port stamps inventory and located some missing stamps at a different port of entry, and the records have since been updated to reflect the stamps’ actual location.

The agency said a new step-by-step guide will be ready by the end of September for how to do a yearly check across the country to make sure all security-sensitive items are accounted for, and a five-year program of work will replace access control systems at a number of sites every year.
“The CBSA maintains a safe and secure operational environment where its personnel, facilities, information and assets are guarded from security threats and vulnerabilities,” it said.
The Customs and Immigration Union, which represents more than 9,000 CBSA employees, said it’s still reviewing the audit and declined to comment.

stories.summary: The Snowbirds’ aging fleet of CT-114 Tutor jets is being retired after this year, grounding the team until the 2030s. See what fans are saying.
stories.author: Karon Liu
stories.content:
For many spectators at Sunday’s Canadian International Air Show, the roar of the Snowbirds over Lake Ontario was more than the traditional finale to the Labour Day weekend.

Former Star photographer Dick Loek photographed this image of the Snowbirds flying past the Rogers Centre and CN Tower during a photo flight with former Snowbird member Kevin Kokotailo in 1989.

It was a farewell — at least for now.
