stories.title: Canadian journalists reflect on the triumphs, regrets and lessons learned covering 9/11
stories.summary: Twenty-five years after the attacks, journalists look back at how newsroom decisions shaped Canadians’ understanding of the events that changed global security and international politics
stories.author: Elissa Mendes
stories.content:
Like every other journalist working in a Canadian newsroom on Sept. 11, 2001, Michelle Shephard recalls the moment she learned a plane had struck the World Trade Center in New York City.

Then a crime reporter at the Toronto Star, she barely stopped to grab her passport and a notebook before rushing to the airport, which had already grounded flights and switched off television screens.

Shephard quickly switched gears and jumped into a car headed for New York with other Star reporters, joining scores of other journalists and volunteers hustling toward Ground Zero as thousands were trying to escape it.

Reporting on the 9/11 attacks required an extraordinary collective effort at a time when verifiable facts and explanations were scarce and the world was gripped with fear. The attacks also pushed journalists to their physical and emotional limits, exposing the risks of reporting on traumatic events.

Twenty-five years later, prominent journalists reflected on their triumphs and regrets in covering 9/11, and how newsroom decisions shaped Canadians’ understanding of the events that changed global security and international politics.

During their “crazy fast” drive to New York, Shephard and her colleagues got lucky.

She said her laminated Toronto Star press pass “looked like it was made in someone’s basement,” but it was enough for one official to let them into a lane marked for emergency responders.

They arrived in the eerily quiet city that night and the sight of a firefighter slumped over on the ground, weary after digging for bodies in the rubble, stopped Shephard in her tracks.

Other details from the scene are still seared in her mind a quarter-century later. The mountain of papers that fell in a blizzard from the collapsed office towers, which Shephard initially mistook for a snowbank. Thousands of eyes staring out from posters of missing people plastered across Manhattan. The repulsive, metallic smell hanging in the air.

“It was an entire city that was traumatized,” Shephard said in a recent interview.

Every other aspect of her life quickly fell by the wayside.

Shephard’s husband, fellow Star reporter Jim Rankin, had rushed off to Boston, where the flights that crashed into the towers originated. The pair realized within a few hours that in the chaos, neither had made plans for someone to look after their new kitten.

For three days, Shephard wore the same shirt and pants she had arrived in, washing off thick dust in the sink each night and blasting the clothes dry with a hotel hair dryer in the morning.

Shephard, who subsequently authored the book Decade of Fear about national security since 9/11, said she is proud of her coverage but might make some small changes if she could go back.

She recalled there being pressure in the newsroom to get emotionally charged photos, such as of a grieving wife crying. The journalism industry has since become more mindful of retraumatizing sources, she added.

Shephard believes that meeting people who became victims of post-9/11 policies early in her national security reporting career strengthened her journalism. She said many of her early stories about Islamophobia were relegated to the back of the paper, but eventually “the pendulum swung the other way.”

Despite covering funeral after funeral in the days after 9/11, Shephard said she found solace knowing her reporting was a public service.

She believes some journalists who weren’t reporting from New York may have been even more traumatized, including editors who had to watch footage of people jumping from the towers over and over.

She recalled breaking down at the end of an interview with a Red Cross official, who asked Shephard who was looking after the reporters.

“I remember that when I would put my head down, I would be teary about all that I had seen,” she said.

CBC News anchor Peter Mansbridge was at his doctor’s office when he got a call about the 9/11 attacks.

As the veteran journalist drove toward CBC headquarters in Toronto, not yet knowing that day would be the biggest of his 50-year career, he turned the fundamentals of reporting over and over in his mind: “You’re going to hear all kinds of things. There are going to be all kinds of rumours. You have to deal with fact.”

Forty-four hours of wall-to-wall coverage from the public broadcaster would follow.

Mansbridge said he was running on adrenalin and he got his first “real break” around 4 a.m. on Sept. 12, when he ducked into his private dressing room to change and take a shower.

A short voice mail from his daughter, then a university student in Winnipeg, was waiting for him.

“I just want you to know that I’m watching you,” she told her father. “And I love you.”

Hearing her voice, Mansbridge felt the emotional weight of the attacks for the first time since he sat down behind the anchor desk the day before.

“Sometimes, when you sit in the studio, it’s almost like watching a movie,” he said. “You’re watching a monitor, and sometimes as real as you know it is, it doesn’t feel real.”

The voice mail “was one of the things I used that night to remind me how big the impact of this thing was for families literally around the world – wanting to reach out and connect with each other.”

Mansbridge said the CBC’s 44 hours of intensive coverage weren’t perfect, but overall he is proud of what the broadcaster achieved.

He said the network was careful not to hazard guesses about the death toll and was judicious about replaying footage of the plane crashes.

Mansbridge said the CBC relied on experts to “keep feeding the beast” and find new ways to convey information to audiences as interns sprinted back and forth through the newsroom, hands full of marked-up scripts.

One especially helpful person was introduced as a retired pilot, and he gave detailed explanations of cockpit operations to fill airtime, inferring the planes had been hijacked.

Mansbridge said he found out weeks later that the man’s background in aviation was fabricated. Perhaps just as strangely, he recalled, “everything he said was right.”

The CBC apologized to viewers, and Mansbridge said the incident was another reminder of the importance of verification in a chaotic situation.

Mansbridge said he barely left the newsroom for a week after the attacks.

“The world would never be the same after that,” he said.

Few journalists, including those at the CBC, adequately covered the rampant Islamophobia following the attacks, Mansbridge said.

“I’m not sure that enough of us in western journalism understood what was happening (with Islamophobia),” he said. “Some did, but they were kind of lonely voices in the midst of all this.”

The bustling Canadian Press newsroom in downtown Toronto fell completely silent as journalists watched on live television another plane crash into the second tower, sending ash and debris onto the streets below.

“It was a ’holy s---’ moment,” recalled Scott White, then the news agency’s editor-in-chief. “You’re seeing it happen, right in front of you, and it just changed everything.”

Reporters mobilized as quickly as they could, hurtling south by car in fear that the border would close. The Canadian Press even paid for a traffic ticket that one reporter incurred as he sped through Pennsylvania, White said.

In New York City, Canadian Press journalists arrived at a hellscape where the iconic World Trade towers were now a tangle of steel, and watched as workers shovelled mountains of sludge and knee-deep ash.

“We saw the bodies come out and we cheered because we thought they were alive,” one worker told The Canadian Press at the time.

“But then they brought in the chaplain to read his last rites.”

In one frightening moment, a panicked Canadian Press reporter phoned a colleague to say she had heard a rumour that another plane attack was imminent. It was quickly confirmed to be a hoax, but she ran for her life for several minutes, White said.

“She was terrified, and rightly so,” he said. “That was the first time I remember worrying that something was going to happen to one of our reporters.”

As the dust at Ground Zero settled, one of the iconic post-9/11 images came from Canadian Press photojournalist Andrew Vaughan.

The photo shows Rachel Uchitel pleading for information about her fiancé, who was working on the 104th floor of the second tower when it was obliterated. Her face contorted with grief, Uchitel is almost unrecognizable from the beaming picture of her pressed against James Andrew O’Grady on his missing person poster.

Twenty-five years later, White no longer works in journalism but he’s still haunted by a correction the wire had to issue on the day of the attacks. The Canadian Press reported that borders were closing based on a tip from an official that turned out to be inaccurate.

White said it was a reminder that being right is always more important than being first.

“It still, to this day, bothers me that we misreported that element,” White said. “I don’t think we were the only ones who did it, but that’s still no excuse.”

White, who led the wire’s transition to multimedia journalism, added there were many 9/11 storylines and not enough reporters and resources to cover them all.

White said he was in constant discussions with various bureau chiefs at CP to ensure the wire avoided speculation or fear-mongering at a time when even military and government officials were flailing in the same information vacuum.

“These are high-stress times, the terrible things and emotions – seeing people fall out of the World Trade Center,” White said.

“But you have to press on. You have a job to do.”

stories.title: Regina Early Learning Centre’s preschool program at risk
stories.summary: More than 70 concerned parents are petitioning for the replacement of all board members at the Regina Early Learning Centre following months of a lack of communication.
stories.author: Hannah Sangster
stories.content:
More than 70 concerned parents are petitioning for the replacement of all board members at the Regina Early Learning Centre.

The petition is calling for the preschool program that helps low-income families, to be reinstated after it was cancelled due to financial restraints.

The centre has sat in the city’s Cathedral area since its opening in 1977 and remains a pillar to many in the community.

“You build this relationship with the support staff where they become like family,” says Courtney Kydd, whose five children all attended the program.

“It’s a beautiful thing and I’ve seen families come from hard circumstances, become the best parents they can be and then turn around and work for this organization to help.”

It all began with the late Anne Luke, a person who saw a need in the community: that low income and Indigenous families were not getting the same care and attention when it came to education. Luke made the decision to quit her steady teaching job to invest her life’s work into Regina’s less privileged families, and founded the organization.

In an interview before her passing in 2022, she said, “It bothered me a lot that there was such a gap. If you were wealthy, you could afford to send your child to a Montessori program or preschool program. If you were working, you could access daycare services. But for moms that were caught between the cracks of those situations, there was nothing … nothing for the children.

“So the reason was to fill a gap, but not just to fill a gap with the same-old-same-old, but to do it differently and bring a new vision to what early childhood education could look like.”

The preschool lies at the heart of the organization and works in conjunction with support programs for parents, focusing on the children as a family unit. This is a method called the Reggio Emilia approach , which has earned the school both provincial and national recognition. The approach is a type of early intervention education that empowers people to become their best version, in order to support their children’s education in the most holistic way.

Kydd says the program was cut without any communication to parents or teachers, adding that the food program and transportation to the school were cut this year in the same way, which the majority of its parents relied on.

The program used to cost parents only $40 a year. The switch to $ 10-a-day daycare making it no longer affordable for the majority of the parents.

Kydd says, “They completely cut parents out … but it’s our children, this is the community it serves, you should listen. I’m not asking for you to let us run everything, but you’re not even listening to us, you’re not even communicating with us at all.”

There’s still hope for some parents as advocates fight back.

Former employee, long-time volunteer and advocate for the centre, Gary Robins, says the preschool has been a stable resource in his neighbourhood for almost 50 years now, and he won’t see it go without a fight.

“It’s not that there isn’t a great need for daycare centres and daycare spaces in the city or around the province, but to close down a preschool like this and to replace it with a daycare is such a profound step backwards. And eliminates some important opportunities for most of those families in need.”

According to the regulations of the Non-Profit Corporations Act, an organization can call a special general meeting to discuss concerns if 10 per cent of the membership signs a petition. More than 90 per cent of the membership signed that petition.

“It’s led to a situation whereby there is a huge group of parents involved with the Early Learning Centre that have signed a petition wanting to remove the entire board,” Robins said. “They’ve lost confidence in the board and they’ve called for a special general meeting to remove the board and elect a new board.”

Global News reached out multiple times to the learning centre for an interview and so far has only been directed to a press release issued in June stating the change was made to address a $300,000 deficit and loss of a donor.

Hannah Sangster has more in the video above.

stories.title: Majority of Canadians now see U.S. as an enemy, and Trump is the reason: poll
stories.summary: Canadians' views of the U.S. are shifting amid Trump's trade war, with a new poll finding 41 per cent now see the country as an enemy.
stories.author: Kenn Oliver
stories.content:
For as long as anyone can remember, Canada and the U.S. have arguably been the world’s closest of allies and friends. The sibling settler-colonial nations sharing the world’s longest undefended border are deeply linked, culturally and economically, with any differences historically resolved respectfully.

But as the trade war initiated by U.S. President Donald Trump drags on, getting uglier every day, a growing number of Canadians have a very different view of America: our “enemy.”

“Donald Trump, man, he can move public opinion like nobody’s business,” Leger vice-president Andrew Enns told National Post in an interview.

More than half (51 per cent) of those 55 or older perceived the U.S. as an enemy, only 13 per cent of whom see it as neutral. Meanwhile, Quebecers were the Canadians most likely (49 per cent) see the U.S. in that light and the least likely to consider it an ally (17 per cent) or neutral (20 per cent), one of several times an “exclamation point” appeared on some Quebec results.

Enns said they related to the province’s election this fall, which the Trump factor has unavoidably entered into.

“It’s helping, I would suggest, some of those federalist parties,” he said. “It’s probably creating some grief for the PQ, the front-runner in that election, as they’re trying to sort of navigate this.”

Even with the recent sharp movement in how Canadians characterize the U.S, Leger’s results indicate most still distinguish between America the country and the Trump administration ruling it. When asked if his leaving office would change their impression, 64 per cent said yes, 21 per cent said it wouldn’t and 14 per cent were unsure.

Results indicate Quebecers and women would be most open to a change of heart, with 72 and 71 per cent saying Trump’s departure would alter their impression of the U.S. and only 16 per cent, respectively, saying it wouldn’t change a thing. British Columbians (30 per cent) and men (27 per cent) were the least amenable to a new way of thinking.

Canadians are happier than they've been in years, poll finds

Republicans split on Canada as Trump’s trade war escalates: polls

Brian Rathbun, a professor of international relations and political science at the University of Toronto’s Munk School of Global Affairs and Public Policy, said that while Canadians May recognize that most Americans don’t support the way Canada’s being treated, it’s important to remember that Americans, simply as a function of their larger economy and population, are somewhat indifferent to Canadians.

“But at some point, I think Canadians will start to get frustrated if this persists, even if it’s not what the American public wants,” Rathbun told National Post in an interview.

“They can say, ‘Why is it that no one’s standing up to this particular bully?’ Then I think that you could get into something like a deeper problem that couldn’t be fixed by kicking this guy out.”

Rathbun, himself an American who moved to Canada in April 2024 from southern California, said Canadians May be starting to realize that a change in leadership — “even with a Democratic president” — won’t fix the “basket case” the U.S. has become.

“It’s become something of an ungovernable country,” he said.

Leger landed on enemy as a “black and white” catch-all against ally or neutral for people who felt negatively towards the U.S., Enns explained, acknowledging it could mean something different to some, including those who legitimately fear the U.S. will try to invade Canada.

It’s not the first time they’ve felt this way.

Last March, after months of enduring Trump’s jabs at Canada and two weeks into Prime Minister Mark Carney’s “Elbows Up” bid to see the Liberals retain government, 43 per cent saw the U.S. as an enemy. But that number dropped precipitously to 27 per cent in a poll last June after it seemed as though cooler heads might prevail.

Fast forward to this summer, noted Enns, and Trump’s “really, really deliberate comments around Canada” have permeated into “a pretty broad sentiment across the country.”

Rathbun isn’t surprised by the 41 per cent who see the U.S. as an enemy, and reasoned that, unlike Russia, for example, many “Canadians feel like American policy is more malicious vis-à-vis Canada” because it’s more direct.

Both he and Enns agree the freshly stoked rhetoric from Trump and his administration — some of it entirely separate from the trade discussion — is only making things worse. This week alone, aside from Trump blasting Canada on Truth Social, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent took a shot at the Canadian Navy’s aging submarine fleet and Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth was accused of body-shaming Canadian cadets.

Enns said the proportion seeing the U.S. as an enemy could climb if Trump and his ilk continue to “double down” on disparaging Canada.

Rathbun highlighted the Lake Ontario-Lake America discussion as a “classic example.”

“It’s entirely unimportant what the Americans call Lake Ontario, and yet, at the same time, it probably galls us more than softwood lumber tariffs, unless we’re in the softwood lumber industry,” he said. “Why? Because it’s indicative of a lack of respect, and respect is so basic to our self-understanding of ourselves as people.”

Leger also sought to gauge Canadians’ feelings on tariffs — both those initiated by Trump and those Canada has launched or promised to in retaliation.

A large majority (87 per cent) of Canadians expect Trump’s tariffs will have some level of impact on their personal financial situation, whether small (24 per cent), moderate (40 per cent) or major (24 per cent), and 38 per cent are somewhat (22 per cent) or very (16 per cent) concerned about losing their job in the next 12 months — especially in Ontario (49 per cent) and among 18-34-year-olds (46 per cent).

As for Canada’s latest economic riposte, Ottawa announced “new countermeasures on $27.6 billion in products imported from the U.S.” effective Sept. 8. The 15 to 50 per cent levies will apply to U.S. steel, aluminum, dishwashers, refrigerators, video game consoles, cheese, beauty products, plywood, paper products and clothing, among others.

Almost three-quarters of Canadians (74 per cent) agree with the counterattack, with only 13 per cent dissenting and the remaining 13 per cent unsure or preferring not to answer.

Solidarity with Canada’s reprisal peaked among the 55-plus crowd (83 per cent) and in B.C. (80 per cent), but wasn’t far off in Quebec (78 per cent). Respondents in Manitoba and Saskatchewan were most likely to disagree (22 per cent).

Canadians by and large (78 per cent) expect Ottawa’s retaliation will result in higher prices paid by Canadian consumers, but 66 per cent agree with Canada’s clapback, with the strongest support from those 55-plus (76 per cent), men (71 per cent), and people in B.C. (72 per cent). Just over a fifth of respondents (21 per cent) are against the retaliation.

Enns said the results tell him there “are some conflicting opinions within the Canadian public and at some point, the ‘Ra-Ra, Canada-proud, sticking to the American with some tariffs,’ could start to soften if it becomes really painful for households’ pocketbook.

“If this thing just sort of settles and all of a sudden we’re into the fall going into the winter, we’re not talking necessarily about Donald Trump and maybe his insults aren’t making the front pages,” he said. “But what might be making the front pages is suddenly the impact on food prices.”

That’s a topic already on respondents’ minds, evidenced by the 35 per cent who cited inflation and rising cost of items as the top issue facing Canadians. Trump, his tariffs and U.S. aggression were the second biggest (24 per cent), followed by health care (10 per cent) in a distant third.

Enns and Rathbun warned the conflict of tariffs and the cost of living could put some heat on Carney and the Liberals.

“The big question is, and the big challenge for a leader, is how long you can persist in that course and basically how much resolve ordinary Canadians will have? We don’t know,” said Rathbun. “Because it’s easy to say this now because we haven’t really paid the price yet.”

Still, he said the “childish” and “bullying” behaviour from the U.S. side is only emboldening Canadians and likely helping Carney’s cause.

Canadians May be willing to endure blows in the trade war because national pride has surged since it began, according to polling data.

A plurality of Canadians (83 per cent) say they are proud to be Canadians, but the proportion who feel very proud (56 per cent) increased by 11 points since polling last June, and up from 40 per cent in 2024. Only 13 per cent said they weren’t very proud (eight per cent) or not proud at all (five per cent).

“The overall pridefulness of Canadians hasn’t wavered much since we started asking that question around when all this sort of stuff started happening in 2025, but the intensity really, really jumped up,” Enns said.

Since the trade war hit a fever pitch this summer, 41 per cent told Leger they feel more proud, including 45 per cent of Ontarians and men. Only 15 per cent are less proud and 44 per cent said their level of pride hasn’t changed.

Overall net pride was highest in Ontario and B.C. (85 per cent, respectively), among women (86 per cent) and 55-plus Canadians (88 per cent). And while Quebecers were the most likely to say they are not proud to be a Canadian (17 per cent), 79 per cent of them still expressed pride.

Rathbun said that sense of nationalism is understandable and offered a different perspective.

“It’s also understandable that Canadians feel more pride, even though nothing about Canada has changed — it’s the Americans that are essentially reducing American pride,” he said, “So that pride is really just a reaction to something that they don’t like somewhere else.”

Canadians also remain steadfast against becoming the 51st state (85 per cent opposed), again with Quebecers (89 per cent) and the 55-plus group (93 per cent) opposed. British Columbians (13 per cent) and the 18-34 crowd (14 per cent) showed the most support.

The survey of 1,552 respondents in Canada was conducted by Leger between Aug. 28-31. For comparison purposes, a probability sample of 1,552 respondents would have a margin of error no greater than plus or minus 2.48 per cent, 19 times out of 20.

This week alone, aside from Trump blasting Canada on Truth Social, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent took a shot at the Canadian Navy’s aging submarine fleet and Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth was accused of body-shaming Canadian cadets.
Enns said the proportion seeing the U.S. as an enemy could climb if Trump and his ilk continue to “double down” on disparaging Canada.
Rathbun highlighted the Lake Ontario-Lake America discussion as a “classic example.”

“It’s entirely unimportant what the Americans call Lake Ontario, and yet, at the same time, it probably galls us more than softwood lumber tariffs, unless we’re in the softwood lumber industry,” he said. “Why? Because it’s indicative of a lack of respect, and respect is so basic to our self-understanding of ourselves as people.”
Leger also sought to gauge Canadians’ feelings on tariffs — both those initiated by Trump and those Canada has launched or promised to in retaliation.

A large majority (87 per cent) of Canadians expect Trump’s tariffs will have some level of impact on their personal financial situation, whether small (24 per cent), moderate (40 per cent) or major (24 per cent), and 38 per cent are somewhat (22 per cent) or very (16 per cent) concerned about losing their job in the next 12 months — especially in Ontario (49 per cent) and among 18-34-year-olds (46 per cent).

As for Canada’s latest economic riposte, Ottawa announced “new countermeasures on $27.6 billion in products imported from the U.S.” effective Sept. 8. The 15 to 50 per cent levies will apply to U.S. steel, aluminum, dishwashers, refrigerators, video game consoles, cheese, beauty products, plywood, paper products and clothing, among others.
Almost three-quarters of Canadians (74 per cent) agree with the counterattack, with only 13 per cent dissenting and the remaining 13 per cent unsure or preferring not to answer.

Solidarity with Canada’s reprisal peaked among the 55-plus crowd (83 per cent) and in B.C. (80 per cent), but wasn’t far off in Quebec (78 per cent). Respondents in Manitoba and Saskatchewan were most likely to disagree (22 per cent).

Canadians by and large (78 per cent) expect Ottawa’s retaliation will result in higher prices paid by Canadian consumers, but 66 per cent agree with Canada’s clapback, with the strongest support from those 55-plus (76 per cent), men (71 per cent), and people in B.C. (72 per cent). Just over a fifth of respondents (21 per cent) are against the retaliation.

Enns said the results tell him there “are some conflicting opinions within the Canadian public and at some point, the ‘Ra-Ra, Canada-proud, sticking to the American with some tariffs,’ could start to soften if it becomes really painful for households’ pocketbook.

“If this thing just sort of settles and all of a sudden we’re into the fall going into the winter, we’re not talking necessarily about Donald Trump and maybe his insults aren’t making the front pages,” he said. “But what might be making the front pages is suddenly the impact on food prices.”

That’s a topic already on respondents’ minds, evidenced by the 35 per cent who cited inflation and rising cost of items as the top issue facing Canadians. Trump, his tariffs and U.S. aggression were the second biggest (24 per cent), followed by health care (10 per cent) in a distant third.
Enns and Rathbun warned the conflict of tariffs and the cost of living could put some heat on Carney and the Liberals.

“The big question is, and the big challenge for a leader, is how long you can persist in that course and basically how much resolve ordinary Canadians will have? We don’t know,” said Rathbun. “Because it’s easy to say this now because we haven’t really paid the price yet.”
Still, he said the “childish” and “bullying” behaviour from the U.S. side is only emboldening Canadians and likely helping Carney’s cause.
Canadians May be willing to endure blows in the trade war because national pride has surged since it began, according to polling data.

A plurality of Canadians (83 per cent) say they are proud to be Canadians, but the proportion who feel very proud (56 per cent) increased by 11 points since polling last June, and up from 40 per cent in 2024. Only 13 per cent said they weren’t very proud (eight per cent) or not proud at all (five per cent).

“The overall pridefulness of Canadians hasn’t wavered much since we started asking that question around when all this sort of stuff started happening in 2025, but the intensity really, really jumped up,” Enns said.

Since the trade war hit a fever pitch this summer, 41 per cent told Leger they feel more proud, including 45 per cent of Ontarians and men. Only 15 per cent are less proud and 44 per cent said their level of pride hasn’t changed.

Overall net pride was highest in Ontario and B.C. (85 per cent, respectively), among women (86 per cent) and 55-plus Canadians (88 per cent). And while Quebecers were the most likely to say they are not proud to be a Canadian (17 per cent), 79 per cent of them still expressed pride.
Rathbun said that sense of nationalism is understandable and offered a different perspective.

“It’s also understandable that Canadians feel more pride, even though nothing about Canada has changed — it’s the Americans that are essentially reducing American pride,” he said, “So that pride is really just a reaction to something that they don’t like somewhere else.”

Canadians also remain steadfast against becoming the 51st state (85 per cent opposed), again with Quebecers (89 per cent) and the 55-plus group (93 per cent) opposed. British Columbians (13 per cent) and the 18-34 crowd (14 per cent) showed the most support.

The survey of 1,552 respondents in Canada was conducted by Leger between Aug. 28-31. For comparison purposes, a probability sample of 1,552 respondents would have a margin of error no greater than plus or minus 2.48 per cent, 19 times out of 20.

stories.title: A new Niagara-on-the-Lake pinot noir makes a grand entrance
stories.summary: On Seven winery owner Vittorio De Stefano waited 17 years to release the first pinot noir from the farm that he and his wife bought in 2009
stories.author: Christopher Waters
stories.content:
Vittorio De Stefano, owner of On Seven winery, has waited 17 years to release the first pinot noir from the Niagara-on-the-Lake farm that he and his wife Sula bought in 2009. Working with winemaking consultant Peter Gamble, the couple studied the seven-acre property’s soil structure to determine which specific clone and rootstock combinations of chardonnay and pinot noir from Burgundy would produce the best possible wine .

The search for the ideal vines from respected nurseries in France took longer than expected. “The thinking was, let’s do this once, let’s do this properly,” De Stefano said.

The existing grapevines were removed to allow On Seven, which takes its name from the size of the estate, to build from the ground up. The five-acre vineyard is certified organic, and an adjacent eight-acre property has been purchased for future grape cultivation.

Clone 76 chardonnay vines were planted 2014, with clone 95 plants added in 2015 and clone 96 in 2018. Those early plantings meant On Seven was able to produce its first commercial release of chardonnay in 2017.

The first pinot noir vines (clone 115) went into the ground in 2017, with an additional planting of two additional clones (777 and 828) in 2019.

Each clonal variation was intentionally selected, De Stefano explained. One of the first official French pinot noir clones available from nurseries, 115 is noted for pinot noirs with balance and elegant character, he said, while 777 yields riper wines with more tannic structure. Clone 828, which is the most recently certified, in 1985, results in more aromatic red wines with fine tannins.

“We had a vision of what type of wine we would get as a result of the characteristics of the clonal and rootstock selection we ordered,” he said.

That vision becomes a reality with the Sept. 13 online launch of On Seven’s first commercial release of pinot noir from 2023. (A pinot noir rosé was produced in 2021. The 2022 crop was lost to winter frost.)

The wet growing season in 2023 meant that On Seven had to reduce the crop to allow the remaining grape clusters to ripen and stay free from mildew and other fungal diseases that would have reduced the quality of the fruit. The total production for the vintage was 71 cases of pinot noir and 86 cases of chardonnay. Pinot noirs and chardonnay made by On Seven 2024 and 2025 are aging in barrel, awaiting bottling for future release.

On Seven is open by appointment and sells its wine online, at onsevenwinery.ca . Its two 2023 releases are reviewed here along with a rare pinot blanc from another family-owned Niagara-on-the-Lake boutique winery that operates without a tasting room.

Scott and Maria Kirby operate a boutique winery from an 11-acre property on the lakeshore of Niagara-on-the-Lake. The site is home to five different grape varieties, including gamay noir, merlot and chardonnay. The concentrated and satisfying white wine made with grapes from 27-year-old pinot blanc vines is a great introduction to the Kirby’s operation, which is supported by winemaker Matt Smith and consultants Adam Lowy and Peter Gamble. The barrel-fermented character suggests a mix of citrus, peach and pear with toast and spice notes. It’s a style that’s best enjoyed over the coming few years. This has 13-per-cent ABV. Drink now to 2028. Available at the above price direct, kirbyestate.com

This alluring single vineyard chardonnay from Niagara-on-the-Lake has a rich, concentrated character that carries through to a fresh, savoury finish. paragraphs: Vittorio De Stefano, owner of On Seven winery, has waited 17 years to release the first pinot noir from the Niagara-on-the-Lake farm that he and his wife Sula bought in 2009. Working with winemaking consultant Peter Gamble, the couple studied the seven-acre property’s soil structure to determine which specific clone and rootstock combinations of chardonnay and pinot noir from Burgundy would produce the best possible wine .
The search for the ideal vines from respected nurseries in France took longer than expected. “The thinking was, let’s do this once, let’s do this properly,” De Stefano said.

The existing grapevines were removed to allow On Seven, which takes its name from the size of the estate, to build from the ground up. The five-acre vineyard is certified organic, and an adjacent eight-acre property has been purchased for future grape cultivation.

Clone 76 chardonnay vines were planted 2014, with clone 95 plants added in 2015 and clone 96 in 2018. Those early plantings meant On Seven was able to produce its first commercial release of chardonnay in 2017.
The first pinot noir vines (clone 115) went into the ground in 2017, with an additional planting of two additional clones (777 and 828) in 2019.

Each clonal variation was intentionally selected, De Stefano explained. One of the first official French pinot noir clones available from nurseries, 115 is noted for pinot noirs with balance and elegant character, he said, while 777 yields riper wines with more tannic structure. Clone 828, which is the most recently certified, in 1985, results in more aromatic red wines with fine tannins.
“We had a vision of what type of wine we would get as a result of the characteristics of the clonal and rootstock selection we ordered,” he said.

That vision becomes a reality with the Sept. 13 online launch of On Seven’s first commercial release of pinot noir from 2023. (A pinot noir rosé was produced in 2021. The 2022 crop was lost to winter frost.)

The wet growing season in 2023 meant that On Seven had to reduce the crop to allow the remaining grape clusters to ripen and stay free from mildew and other fungal diseases that would have reduced the quality of the fruit. The total production for the vintage was 71 cases of pinot noir and 86 cases of chardonnay. Pinot noirs and chardonnay made by On Seven 2024 and 2025 are aging in barrel, awaiting bottling for future release.

On Seven is open by appointment and sells its wine online, at onsevenwinery.ca . Its two 2023 releases are reviewed here along with a rare pinot blanc from another family-owned Niagara-on-the-Lake boutique winery that operates without a tasting room.

Scott and Maria Kirby operate a boutique winery from an 11-acre property on the lakeshore of Niagara-on-the-Lake. The site is home to five different grape varieties, including gamay noir, merlot and chardonnay. The concentrated and satisfying white wine made with grapes from 27-year-old pinot blanc vines is a great introduction to the Kirby’s operation, which is supported by winemaker Matt Smith and consultants Adam Lowy and Peter Gamble. The barrel-fermented character suggests a mix of citrus, peach and pear with toast and spice notes. It’s a style that’s best enjoyed over the coming few years. This has 13-per-cent ABV. stories.summary: Provincial police say a person is dead after a single-vehicle collision in the township of Southwold, Ont.
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: Provincial police say a person is dead after a single-vehicle collision in the township of Southwold, Ont.
· Posted: Sep 05, 2026 8:30 AM EDT | Last Updated: 33 minutes ago
The driver of the vehicle was pronounced dead at the scene, according to police.(CBC)
Provincial police say a person is dead after a single-vehicle collision in the township of Southwold, Ont., south of London on Friday night.
In a news release, Ontario Provincial Police said officers were called to John Wise Line shortly before 7:30 p.m.
The driver of the vehicle was pronounced dead at the scene, according to police.
John Wise Line was closed between Begg Road and Middle River Road for the investigation but has since reopened, the OPP said in a post to X Saturday overnight.
Anyone with information is asked to contact police.

stories.title: The Mississaudyssey: One hero’s epic journey into the suburbs in pursuit of a movie – and more
stories.summary: Ian Brown made the arduous trek to an Imax 70mm screening of Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey, and learned something about the value of seeking and spectacle
stories.author: Ian Brown
stories.content:
Ian Brown is a feature writer with The Globe and Mail. His latest book is Seventy: A Diary of My Seventy-First Year.

With apologies to Emily Wilson’s translation of The Odyssey, to which Christopher Nolan’s record-setting film has been compared and linked.

Tell me about a complicated trip. Muse, tell me how our man Idiotius sweated to score an IMAX 70mm ticket to Chris Nolan’s Odyssey , when every seat was snagged for weeks ahead; when IMAX 70mm theatres in the province were in number only two, and far away across the suburban steppe, in tracted Vaughan, Kingdom of Developers, or beyond the barrens brave men know and fear as sprawling Mississauga, the traditional territory of the Mississaugas of the Credit, Haudenosaunee, Huron-Wendat, and Wyandot. Tell me of the ways the demi-gods of Reddit revealed how Idiotius might snag a ticket for a seat; and how he raced through sclerotic traffic; and tell me his opinion of the blockbusting film (US$1.55-billion and counting), did he think it stinking bad or bloody brilliant, despite dire warnings of its cheesy shallows by carping critics and turgid translators who tried to founder the adventure before it even started. Then say how long It took to drive home again, in rush hour. Find that story.

Dawn’s fingers had just spread roses across the sky when Idiotius first tried to book an IMAX seat in landlocked Vaughan or burby Mississauga, he cared not which. The trickster mini-gods on Reddit implored him to call midweek, ideally Tuesday or Thursday, but after 4 p.m. the day before he hoped, with Zeus’s grace, to see Nolan’s slambam epic. Reddit’s brainy wizards claimed seats that were going to free up would do so within 12 hours before showtime. Whose commands Idiotius obeyed, only to discover his Scene card was pooched, insufficiently registered. Eons of his life swept by as he waited on the dreadful phone, ear-poisoned by canned music, while one after another of Cineplex’s customer service Spirit Dudes greeted him warmly, claimed to fix the problem, then bade him “Mmmbye!” before hanging up – the problem never truly solved. But that, as the gods have often proclaimed, is the way of the goddamned Cineplex app.

Eventually our traveller, obstinate fool that he was, found a 70mm IMAX theatre seat, at 11 a.m. on a Wednesday morning, a single reclining chair in full-frontal row E at the Mississauga Square One venue. Our stubborn hero gave no thought to his stenotic neck and the wreckage three hours of gazing way, way up would wreak upon his one and only spine. Here was a seat! He grabbed it. For glory knows no shame.

No sooner had he won it when doubts pressed in. Mississauga! Unknown kingdom of enormous malls and endless construction, the storied arrival city where the goddess McCallion once ruled since time itself began (or so it seemed). Who knew what beasts and dragons lurked within its parkades and parkways and prim cul-de-sacs, seven miles – or was it seven thousand? – to the west of downtown T.O. the Good, by car, along death-defying expressways and potholed highways in the fabled Land of Fours – the 401, 410, 403, 407, 404 and beyond. Who knew which was which?

Next day’s dawn had barely shown her bright-haired hue as Idiotius headed for the big-screen IMAX at Square One. He placed his hands at 10-and-two upon the steering wheel of his trusted silver hybrid and gently eased the faithful barque into the hooting sirened downtown Toronto traffic. The quicksilver demons of that perilous world, heedless e-bike delivery boys from distant lands, nattered back and forth across his lane, into and out of Spadina’s Laestrygonian potholes all the way to the Gardiner Expressway.

From there the nightmare worsened. Waze, his trusted helmsman, instead of leading west toward eternal sunsets and Mississauga Road, had a nervous breakdown: now Waze lured him west through canyons of high-rises – holding what lives? What agonies and exultations in their stacked and boxy towers? – and then, surprise, north to the Trans-Canada, then west again, and abruptly south to the 403 and Hurontario, once Mississauga’s main artery. All the godlike Waze cared about was saving seconds on the fastest route. Though this speedy route meant choosing between the Charybdis of the 403 and the Scylla of crossing six lanes of racing cars to make the cutoff to Hurontario. Crazy jackass drivers cut in from left and right, unseen and unheralded. A movie at 11 a.m. on a workday was thrilling. But was it worth one’s life? He wondered. And then, too soon, the gleaming spires of the great mall itself, Square One, loomed: his IMAX seat lay within.

He was an hour early; the parking lot was empty. For an hour he texted, until straggling patrons began to approach the rounded IMAX temple, arriving hypnotized from all directions, as if called by Zeus himself: in shorts and shifts and golf shirts and shower slides and unmatched socks, cellphones never far from hand. Men and women of all nations and ages, drawn to the onscreen tale of the great Odysseus, eager to see the spectacle of the day before the theatre’s doors were even opened.

Idiotius stepped forth and spoke to one pilgrim, a giant who had travelled far from storied Ajax (extensive suburb east of Pickering, not the warlord who, with Odysseus, saved the broken body of Achilles from the Trojans) in blood-red Galaxy Quest tee and cargo shorts, accompanied by a woman who wanted to be nameless. These were not bearded ancient Greek sailors, spearing meat on spits and roasting it beachside: they sat in their Honda, sipping Starbucks and texting. “Yeah,” Carl said, admitting he booked tickets a month ahead, “IMAX has been really slammed.”

The doors finally opened. Here was Andrew Fabcic, a youth of 20 who had taken a week’s vacation to make sure he could see the movie: He was two-thirds of his way through Emily Wilson’s crisp translation of The Iliad . “Right now it’s good,” he said, warily. “I got to the point where Hector gets knocked unconscious by a stone for the second time.” Here too was Daniel Willoughby, 18, tall, skinny as an exclamation point, second-year at Waterloo for mechanical engineering, also reading The Iliad . Cody and Jenny, office workers in their thirties, were playing hooky from that same office: “We’re kind of Christopher Nolan fans,” Cody said. “We’ve seen all his movies.” They were only “vaguely familiar with the details of the Odyssey.” But it didn’t seem to matter.

The theatre was open. Idiotius’s seat awaited. But before he could arrive to that safe shore, he heard the fattened sirens of the candy counter. “Make Your Movies Sweeter,” the signage sirens sang, boasting Jolly Ranchers and ropey Twizzlers. Even Oh Henry!, that chewy relic, called out to him. So did hot dogs and poutines and Squishmallow dolls. He longed for a $22.98 large popcorn, drink and candy special, but the supertall $59.99 plastic popcorn bucket in the shape of the Trojan horse was sold out. (It’s reselling for 90 bucks these days on eBay.) Idiotius finally made it to his seat, E8. He reclined. The angle wasn’t bad. A woman stepped upon his toe as she waddled to her seat. The strange, fixating voyage had begun.

And yet there lurked in him, this midday shirker, doubts about the movie version of the classic – doubts sown by Emily Wilson herself, gifted translator of Norton’s 2018 Odyssey , which some thought most brilliant and best yet, a version even Christopher Nolan quoted. Translations of The Odyssey (more than 30 in English) ooze and retract, in and out of fashion, over time: Chapman’s famous 1616 rhyming iambs yielded to Alexander Pope’s heroic couplets in 1725, then to Robert Fitzgerald’s flashy poesy in 1961, against which Richmond Lattimore’s unadorned six-beats-per-line (from 1965) reacted and corrected. Only to yield again to Robert Fagles’s (how many translations of The Odyssey have been penned by men named Robert!) zesty operatic script in 1996. Wilson’s more political (and female) translation is in the plain, strong, active, iambic, idiomatic, more readable open-verse style.

But feeble Idiotius need not have worried. For what a voyage the movie was! More engaging in IMAX 70mm – see it if you can – than in every other format, and way more vivid than page after page of the original text, with its endless cast of gods and Greeks and superfluous details, even in Wilson’s transmutation. The film’s ambition was as astonishing as its score was deafening, the theatre’s air conditioning as chilling as Odysseus’s visit to Hades and the land of the dead, the zombie graveyard of his regrets. (Nolan’s Odyssey was all about remorse, And how impossible it is to stay free of.) The special effects were especially special: Circe’s real-time massage of Odysseus’s men into living pigs was super-creepy. So was Polyphemus, “the reckless Cyclops, lacking in customs” (as Homer has it), whose lawless ways and awkward pulpy body brought to mind – of all people – Donald Trump (surely Idiotius was not alone in this?). The frightening gullibility of the mob, so easily led, the claustrophobia of drowning, the shameful thrill – but what a rush! – of Odysseus’s murderous revenge on Penelope’s entitled suitors: all of it came alive. Yes, some of the writing was pretentiously empty (“the power of the sacrifice is the cost to the person making it”), but the non-stop suspense, so skillfully built as the Ithacans unlocked the gates of Troy, made up for it: a beta blocker would have been in order. True, the dialogue was sometimes indecipherable, as it often is in a Nolan flick: everybody says this. And yes, it’s true, Troy is only a memory in the ancient poem, not a central plot point, as was the case in Nolan’s movie. But the tragic consequences of the sack of Troy are the same: Homer gave us these stories, and Homer’s dilemmas, Homer’s agonies, are on the screen, however re-ordered.

Nolan’s movie pulled modern truth from ancient matter: the challenge of love, despite our longing for impossible faithfulness; the pain of facing who we once were, and how abominably we behaved; the unintended consequences of our every decision. Because try as we might we cannot control our fates, much less the fate of the world. Modesty would so become us. The Trojans and the Ithacans and then Odysseus and his men in turn offended Zeus’s Law, a.k.a xenia – that dictum that hosts must treat strangers as they expect to be treated themselves, generously and kindly. Which became the Judeo-Christian Golden Rule: Do unto others as you would have them do unto you. It is still the unreachable longing of our godless modern world – one torn by hatred and mistrust, floods and heat waves, warmongers and billionaires, smart machines and fearsome apps. We need each other more than ever, but can never admit it. Was that Homer’s point? Maybe not. Would he – or she, or they, there’s some debate – mind if a moviegoer, watching a smackdown adaptation of the poems composed 3,000 years ago, came to that conclusion? I seriously doubt it. As Odysseus says in the movie: “The clearest vision of a man is from below,” from the depths of the failed self. It’s the most recognizable place we humans know.

It was only afterwards, as his brain raced and his ears rang and his eyes adjusted to the light, as Idiotius made his way from the IMAX palace to his parked Prius, that he spied Daniel again. The youthful engineer-in-training was bus-bound to bucolic Burlington. He was abuzz, and thrilled. The Odyssey had in a moment replaced Dune as his favourite flick of all time. Why, Idiotius asked, still shaking. “Without the story,” Daniel replied, “it still would have been a cool experience. But the story makes it a spiritual experience.” And what is it about the story that does that? Idiotius asked. “I think,” the youth declared, “I think it’s about the fact that human experience has so many levels we can’t describe. The Odyssey’s a myth. And a myth is something we hand down to make sense of human experience. Because we have so little information about who we are.” The myth, the work, lives in service to the humans who read it, not the other way around (dear Emily). The lad paused and shook his head in wonder at the spectacle he had seen. “Our minds are so much bigger than our experience. And we are so much bigger than our experience, too.” With that Idiotius bade Daniel farewell and took his leave, and searched for his car for 20 minutes in the colossus of the Square One parking lot. paragraphs: Ian Brown is a feature writer with The Globe and Mail. His latest book is Seventy: A Diary of My Seventy-First Year.
With apologies to Emily Wilson’s translation of The Odyssey, to which Christopher Nolan’s record-setting film has been compared and linked.

Tell me about a complicated trip. Muse, tell me how our man Idiotius sweated to score an IMAX 70mm ticket to Chris Nolan’s Odyssey , when every seat was snagged for weeks ahead; when IMAX 70mm theatres in the province were in number only two, and far away across the suburban steppe, in tracted Vaughan, Kingdom of Developers, or beyond the barrens brave men know and fear as sprawling Mississauga, the traditional territory of the Mississaugas of the Credit, Haudenosaunee, Huron-Wendat, and Wyandot. Tell me of the ways the demi-gods of Reddit revealed how Idiotius might snag a ticket for a seat; and how he raced through sclerotic traffic; and tell me his opinion of the blockbusting film (US$1.55-billion and counting), did he think it stinking bad or bloody brilliant, despite dire warnings of its cheesy shallows by carping critics and turgid translators who tried to founder the adventure before it even started. Then say how long It took to drive home again, in rush hour. Find that story.

Dawn’s fingers had just spread roses across the sky when Idiotius first tried to book an IMAX seat in landlocked Vaughan or burby Mississauga, he cared not which. The trickster mini-gods on Reddit implored him to call midweek, ideally Tuesday or Thursday, but after 4 p.m. the day before he hoped, with Zeus’s grace, to see Nolan’s slambam epic. Reddit’s brainy wizards claimed seats that were going to free up would do so within 12 hours before showtime. Whose commands Idiotius obeyed, only to discover his Scene card was pooched, insufficiently registered. Eons of his life swept by as he waited on the dreadful phone, ear-poisoned by canned music, while one after another of Cineplex’s customer service Spirit Dudes greeted him warmly, claimed to fix the problem, then bade him “Mmmbye!” before hanging up – the problem never truly solved. But that, as the gods have often proclaimed, is the way of the goddamned Cineplex app.

Eventually our traveller, obstinate fool that he was, found a 70mm IMAX theatre seat, at 11 a.m. on a Wednesday morning, a single reclining chair in full-frontal row E at the Mississauga Square One venue. Our stubborn hero gave no thought to his stenotic neck and the wreckage three hours of gazing way, way up would wreak upon his one and only spine. Here was a seat! He grabbed it. For glory knows no shame.

No sooner had he won it when doubts pressed in. Mississauga! Unknown kingdom of enormous malls and endless construction, the storied arrival city where the goddess McCallion once ruled since time itself began (or so it seemed). Who knew what beasts and dragons lurked within its parkades and parkways and prim cul-de-sacs, seven miles – or was it seven thousand? – to the west of downtown T.O. the Good, by car, along death-defying expressways and potholed highways in the fabled Land of Fours – the 401, 410, 403, 407, 404 and beyond. Who knew which was which?

Next day’s dawn had barely shown her bright-haired hue as Idiotius headed for the big-screen IMAX at Square One. He placed his hands at 10-and-two upon the steering wheel of his trusted silver hybrid and gently eased the faithful barque into the hooting sirened downtown Toronto traffic. The quicksilver demons of that perilous world, heedless e-bike delivery boys from distant lands, nattered back and forth across his lane, into and out of Spadina’s Laestrygonian potholes all the way to the Gardiner Expressway.

From there the nightmare worsened. Waze, his trusted helmsman, instead of leading west toward eternal sunsets and Mississauga Road, had a nervous breakdown: now Waze lured him west through canyons of high-rises – holding what lives? What agonies and exultations in their stacked and boxy towers? – and then, surprise, north to the Trans-Canada, then west again, and abruptly south to the 403 and Hurontario, once Mississauga’s main artery. All the godlike Waze cared about was saving seconds on the fastest route. Though this speedy route meant choosing between the Charybdis of the 403 and the Scylla of crossing six lanes of racing cars to make the cutoff to Hurontario. Crazy jackass drivers cut in from left and right, unseen and unheralded. A movie at 11 a.m. on a workday was thrilling. But was it worth one’s life? He wondered. And then, too soon, the gleaming spires of the great mall itself, Square One, loomed: his IMAX seat lay within.

He was an hour early; the parking lot was empty. For an hour he texted, until straggling patrons began to approach the rounded IMAX temple, arriving hypnotized from all directions, as if called by Zeus himself: in shorts and shifts and golf shirts and shower slides and unmatched socks, cellphones never far from hand. Men and women of all nations and ages, drawn to the onscreen tale of the great Odysseus, eager to see the spectacle of the day before the theatre’s doors were even opened.

Idiotius stepped forth and spoke to one pilgrim, a giant who had travelled far from storied Ajax (extensive suburb east of Pickering, not the warlord who, with Odysseus, saved the broken body of Achilles from the Trojans) in blood-red Galaxy Quest tee and cargo shorts, accompanied by a woman who wanted to be nameless. These were not bearded ancient Greek sailors, spearing meat on spits and roasting it beachside: they sat in their Honda, sipping Starbucks and texting. “Yeah,” Carl said, admitting he booked tickets a month ahead, “IMAX has been really slammed.”

The doors finally opened. Here was Andrew Fabcic, a youth of 20 who had taken a week’s vacation to make sure he could see the movie: He was two-thirds of his way through Emily Wilson’s crisp translation of The Iliad . “Right now it’s good,” he said, warily. “I got to the point where Hector gets knocked unconscious by a stone for the second time.” Here too was Daniel Willoughby, 18, tall, skinny as an exclamation point, second-year at Waterloo for mechanical engineering, also reading The Iliad . Cody and Jenny, office workers in their thirties, were playing hooky from that same office: “We’re kind of Christopher Nolan fans,” Cody said. “We’ve seen all his movies.” They were only “vaguely familiar with the details of the Odyssey.” But it didn’t seem to matter.

The theatre was open. Idiotius’s seat awaited. But before he could arrive to that safe shore, he heard the fattened sirens of the candy counter. “Make Your Movies Sweeter,” the signage sirens sang, boasting Jolly Ranchers and ropey Twizzlers. Even Oh Henry!, that chewy relic, called out to him. So did hot dogs and poutines and Squishmallow dolls. He longed for a $22.98 large popcorn, drink and candy special, but the supertall $59.99 plastic popcorn bucket in the shape of the Trojan horse was sold out. (It’s reselling for 90 bucks these days on eBay.) Idiotius finally made it to his seat, E8. He reclined. The angle wasn’t bad. A woman stepped upon his toe as she waddled to her seat. The strange, fixating voyage had begun.

And yet there lurked in him, this midday shirker, doubts about the movie version of the classic – doubts sown by Emily Wilson herself, gifted translator of Norton’s 2018 Odyssey , which some thought most brilliant and best yet, a version even Christopher Nolan quoted. Translations of The Odyssey (more than 30 in English) ooze and retract, in and out of fashion, over time: Chapman’s famous 1616 rhyming iambs yielded to Alexander Pope’s heroic couplets in 1725, then to Robert Fitzgerald’s flashy poesy in 1961, against which Richmond Lattimore’s unadorned six-beats-per-line (from 1965) reacted and corrected. Only to yield again to Robert Fagles’s (how many translations of The Odyssey have been penned by men named Robert!) zesty operatic script in 1996. Wilson’s more political (and female) translation is in the plain, strong, active, iambic, idiomatic, more readable open-verse style.

But feeble Idiotius need not have worried. For what a voyage the movie was! More engaging in IMAX 70mm – see it if you can – than in every other format, and way more vivid than page after page of the original text, with its endless cast of gods and Greeks and superfluous details, even in Wilson’s transmutation. The film’s ambition was as astonishing as its score was deafening, the theatre’s air conditioning as chilling as Odysseus’s visit to Hades and the land of the dead, the zombie graveyard of his regrets. (Nolan’s Odyssey was all about remorse, And how impossible it is to stay free of.) The special effects were especially special: Circe’s real-time massage of Odysseus’s men into living pigs was super-creepy. So was Polyphemus, “the reckless Cyclops, lacking in customs” (as Homer has it), whose lawless ways and awkward pulpy body brought to mind – of all people – Donald Trump (surely Idiotius was not alone in this?). The frightening gullibility of the mob, so easily led, the claustrophobia of drowning, the shameful thrill – but what a rush! – of Odysseus’s murderous revenge on Penelope’s entitled suitors: all of it came alive. Yes, some of the writing was pretentiously empty (“the power of the sacrifice is the cost to the person making it”), but the non-stop suspense, so skillfully built as the Ithacans unlocked the gates of Troy, made up for it: a beta blocker would have been in order. True, the dialogue was sometimes indecipherable, as it often is in a Nolan flick: everybody says this. And yes, it’s true, Troy is only a memory in the ancient poem, not a central plot point, as was the case in Nolan’s movie. But the tragic consequences of the sack of Troy are the same: Homer gave us these stories, and Homer’s dilemmas, Homer’s agonies, are on the screen, however re-ordered.

Nolan’s movie pulled modern truth from ancient matter: the challenge of love, despite our longing for impossible faithfulness; the pain of facing who we once were, and how abominably we behaved; the unintended consequences of our every decision. Because try as we might we cannot control our fates, much less the fate of the world. Modesty would so become us. The Trojans and the Ithacans and then Odysseus and his men in turn offended Zeus’s Law, a.k.a xenia – that dictum that hosts must treat strangers as they expect to be treated themselves, generously and kindly. Which became the Judeo-Christian Golden Rule: Do unto others as you would have them do unto you. It is still the unreachable longing of our godless modern world – one torn by hatred and mistrust, floods and heat waves, warmongers and billionaires, smart machines and fearsome apps. We need each other more than ever, but can never admit it. Was that Homer’s point? Maybe not. Would he – or she, or they, there’s some debate – mind if a moviegoer, watching a smackdown adaptation of the poems composed 3,000 years ago, came to that conclusion? I seriously doubt it. As Odysseus says in the movie: “The clearest vision of a man is from below,” from the depths of the failed self. It’s the most recognizable place we humans know.

It was only afterwards, as his brain raced and his ears rang and his eyes adjusted to the light, as Idiotius made his way from the IMAX palace to his parked Prius, that he spied Daniel again. The youthful engineer-in-training was bus-bound to bucolic Burlington. He was abuzz, and thrilled. The Odyssey had in a moment replaced Dune as his favourite flick of all time. Why, Idiotius asked, still shaking. “Without the story,” Daniel replied, “it still would have been a cool experience. But the story makes it a spiritual experience.” And what is it about the story that does that? Idiotius asked. “I think,” the youth declared, “I think it’s about the fact that human experience has so many levels we can’t describe. The Odyssey’s a myth. And a myth is something we hand down to make sense of human experience. Because we have so little information about who we are.” The myth, the work, lives in service to the humans who read it, not the other way around (dear Emily). The lad paused and shook his head in wonder at the spectacle he had seen. “Our minds are so much bigger than our experience. And we are so much bigger than our experience, too.” With that Idiotius bade Daniel farewell and took his leave, and searched for his car for 20 minutes in the colossus of the Square One parking lot. Torrential rain was falling from the sky like heavy curtains of reproach. He climbed aboard, and pressed the starter button, And began his long, watery trek home, to his waiting wife. He was eager to return, for it was his night to cook the dinner.

The special effects were especially special: Circe’s real-time massage of Odysseus’s men into living pigs was super-creepy. True, the dialogue was sometimes indecipherable, as it often is in a Nolan flick: everybody says this. And yes, it’s true, Troy is only a memory in the ancient poem, not a central plot point, as was the case in Nolan’s movie. content_blocks.text: Nolan’s movie pulled modern truth from ancient matter: the challenge of love, despite our longing for impossible faithfulness; the pain of facing who we once were, and how abominably we behaved; the unintended consequences of our every decision. Because try as we might we cannot control our fates, much less the fate of the world. Modesty would so become us. The Trojans and the Ithacans and then Odysseus and his men in turn offended Zeus’s Law, a.k.a xenia – that dictum that hosts must treat strangers as they expect to be treated themselves, generously and kindly. Which became the Judeo-Christian Golden Rule: Do unto others as you would have them do unto you. Would he – or she, or they, there’s some debate – mind if a moviegoer, watching a smackdown adaptation of the poems composed 3,000 years ago, came to that conclusion? I seriously doubt it. As Odysseus says in the movie: “The clearest vision of a man is from below,” from the depths of the failed self. It’s the most recognizable place we humans know.

content_blocks.text: It was only afterwards, as his brain raced and his ears rang and his eyes adjusted to the light, as Idiotius made his way from the IMAX palace to his parked Prius, that he spied Daniel again. The youthful engineer-in-training was bus-bound to bucolic Burlington. He was abuzz, and thrilled. The Odyssey had in a moment replaced Dune as his favourite flick of all time. Why, Idiotius asked, still shaking. “Without the story,” Daniel replied, “it still would have been a cool experience. But the story makes it a spiritual experience.” And what is it about the story that does that? Idiotius asked. “I think,” the youth declared, “I think it’s about the fact that human experience has so many levels we can’t describe. The Odyssey’s a myth. And a myth is something we hand down to make sense of human experience. Because we have so little information about who we are.” The myth, the work, lives in service to the humans who read it, not the other way around (dear Emily). The lad paused and shook his head in wonder at the spectacle he had seen. “Our minds are so much bigger than our experience. And we are so much bigger than our experience, too.” With that Idiotius bade Daniel farewell and took his leave, and searched for his car for 20 minutes in the colossus of the Square One parking lot. Torrential rain was falling from the sky like heavy curtains of reproach. He climbed aboard, and pressed the starter button, And began his long, watery trek home, to his waiting wife. He was eager to return, for it was his night to cook the dinner.

stories.title: CBL Playoffs: London Majors beat Welland Jackfish 6-5 to take Game 1
stories.summary: The best-of-seven Canadian Baseball League playoff series opened on Friday night at Labatt Park.
stories.author: Geoff Robins
stories.content:
London Majors player Jarrett Burney scores during the third inning of the first game of their Canadian Baseball League playoff series against the Welland Jackfish at Labatt Park in London on Friday, Sept. 4, 2026. (Geoff Robins/The London Free Press)

It took 11 innings but the London Majors beat the Welland Jackfish 6-5 on Friday night at Labatt Park, winning the opening game of their best-of-seven series in the first round of the Canadian Baseball League playoffs. The teams had identical records (31-17) in the regular season. Game 2 is set for Saturday night in Welland. Photos by Lfp’s Geoff Robins.

Welland Jackfish second baseman Jonah Weisner misses the tag on London’s Jarrett Burney during the third inning of the first game of their Canadian Baseball League playoff series at Labatt Park in London on Friday, Sept. 4, 2026. (Geoff Robins/The London Free Press)

London Majors starting pitcher Victor Payano throws a pitch during the fourth inning of the first game of their Canadian Baseball League playoffs series against the Welland Jackfish at Labatt Park in London on Friday, Sept. 4, 2026. (Geoff Robins/The London Free Press)

London Majors first baseman Trent Lenihan tags out Welland’s Carson Johnson during the fourth inning of the first game of their Canadian Baseball League playoff series at Labatt Park in London on Friday, Sept. 4, 2026. (Geoff Robins/The London Free Press)

London’s Maikol Escotto tags out Welland’s Justin Gideon during the second inning of the first game of their Canadian Baseball League playoff series at Labatt Park in London on Friday, Sept. 4, 2026. (Geoff Robins/The London Free Press) grobins@postmedia.com

stories.title: Where is the ‘common sense’ here?
stories.summary: Ripping out Toronto bike lanes is more than just a waste of money
stories.author: Marcus Gee
stories.content:
With nearly half a trillion dollars in debt and vast spending commitments for transit, highways, health and other urgent needs, the government of Ontario cannot afford to waste any money. So why on earth would we want to spend tens of millions to rip out a bunch of bicycle lanes in Toronto?

Under the past few mayors, the city has built a substantial network of lanes so that cyclists can navigate the city in relative safety. It lagged behind other cities in this effort – Montreal took the lead years ago – but it has been catching up. A cyclist can now get around most of the central city in marked and protected lanes, a huge improvement on the days of jockeying shoulder to shoulder with speeding cars.

Cities around the world have been building out their biking networks. London’s has grown fivefold since 2016, reaching 450 kilometres – more than the whole Tube system. An ambitious cycling plan introduced under former mayor Anne Hidalgo has transformed Paris into a pedalling paradise, with a vast bike-share fleet and tens of thousands of bike-rack spaces. New York, Vancouver, San Francisco, Shanghai, Amsterdam – all now have extensive cycling networks.

The result is not just safer and smoother cycling but calmer, healthier and more livable cities. Paris has a whole new feel, with streams of bikes replacing the throngs of belching cars that used to choke the streets. Those streams are as much the symbol of progressive 21st-century cities as hosts of gleaming automobiles were of 20th-century ones.

All of this seems to have sailed right over the head of Ontario’s Progressive Conservative premier, Doug Ford. Since the days he and his brother Rob ruled the roost at Toronto City Hall, he has been fixated on ending the so-called “war on the car.” Putting bike lanes on big Toronto streets such as Bloor, Yonge and University was, to him, part of that grand conspiracy against the long-suffering motorist.

He vowed that they must go, even though it cost the city $27-million to put them in and, according to a city report, would cost nearly double that to pull them out. He went as far as to bring in a law requiring cities to get a green light from Queen’s Park before building a bike lane that takes away a lane of traffic. The province also gave itself the power to rip out the offending lanes on Bloor, Yonge and University. That thwarted the clearly expressed will of Toronto’s city council, which had studied, debated and approved the lanes and was elected to make precisely this sort of local decision.

After an appeal-court ruling on Aug. 14 that said the government was within its rights to remove the lanes, Mr. Ford started revving up the bulldozers. In a social media video released this week, he told viewers that officials were already starting to hire contractors for the removal work. “We’re not wasting any time,” he said. “We’re moving fast.”

His government, he said, “was elected with a clear mandate from the people of Ontario to fight gridlock and get drivers moving again, including by taking bike lanes off our busiest streets and putting them on secondary roads.”

That sounds sensible enough: cars on big roads, bikes on smaller ones. But in fact, no efficient bike system works this way. Most big-city networks put major bike routes on bigger roads to connect to transit hubs and business or entertainment districts. Lanes on smaller streets complete the grid, linking up to major corridors and routing cyclists through quieter neighbourhoods when possible.

Paris has installed lanes on both small streets and major ones. It even put a big cycling corridor on the famous Rue de Rivoli, which runs past the Louvre and once had seven lanes for parking and traffic. New York has good, recently improved bike lanes on Sixth and Seventh Avenues in the heart of Manhattan. One of Vancouver’s busiest goes over the heavily trafficked Burrard Bridge. With good design and engineering, cars and bikes can co-exist on even the biggest roads.

Mr. Ford’s campaign against the bike lanes seems based more on animus against bike-riding pinkos – as Don Cherry described them at the inauguration of Rob Ford as Toronto’s mayor in 2010 – than any foundation of fact. Documents filed in court during the legal battle revealed that his government was shown research that removing the lanes could make collisions more likely and might not even reduce traffic congestion in the end.

But there was the premier this week, standing next to a bike lane and pledging more “common sense infrastructure decisions that will keep people moving.” If spending nearly $50-million to destroy something that already exists is his idea of common sense, we had all better hold onto our wallets.

Lanes on smaller streets complete the grid, linking up to major corridors and routing cyclists through quieter neighbourhoods when possible.

content_blocks.text: Paris has installed lanes on both small streets and major ones. It even put a big cycling corridor on the famous Rue de Rivoli, which runs past the Louvre and once had seven lanes for parking and traffic. New York has good, recently improved bike lanes on Sixth and Seventh Avenues in the heart of Manhattan. One of Vancouver’s busiest goes over the heavily trafficked Burrard Bridge. With good design and engineering, cars and bikes can co-exist on even the biggest roads.
