stories.title: Rock the Runway and Bckyrd Fest moving to Harris Park
stories.summary: have been moved to Harris Park.
stories.author: Kate Otterbein
stories.content:
have been moved to Harris Park.

The Jones Entertainment Group (JEG) said after months and multiple meetings, this decision was made to allow the event to move forward without traffic issues that were experienced at the 2025 event.

“Given the traffic challenges experienced last year, it was especially important to us that we had a plan in place that would provide a smooth, safe, and positive experience for everyone attending the festival, as well as the surrounding community,” said the group.

They said moving to Harris Park gives them the confidence needed.

“From day one, our goal has always been to create an incredible festival experience while ensuring the safety of our patrons and the surrounding community,” they added.

“When it became clear that we could not achieve the traffic plan we felt was necessary, we made the decision to move the event. Harris Park gives us the opportunity to deliver the same experience in a location that is accessible, right in the heart of the city and proven with the last 22 years with Rock the Park.”

JEG said that this location move does not change its relationship with London International Airport.

“They have been outstanding partners throughout this process, and we look forward to continuing that relationship.”

Nothing changes for ticketholders; other than the location you must go to for the event. No exchanges, updates, or further action is required.

Previously bought parking passes will be automatically refunded.

The events take place Sept. 17 and 18 at Harris Park.

stories.title: What to know as London’s first centre-running BRT lanes are set to open
stories.summary: Route 90 will begin using the new centre lanes Sunday, giving riders and drivers their first look at how the system will work.
stories.author: Jack Moulton
stories.content:
London drivers on Wellington may not agree given the current traffic headaches, but construction of the southern bus rapid transit link has reached a milestone – with buses beginning to run in some completed centre lanes. LFP’s Jack Moulton reports.

Beginning Sunday, London Transit’s Express Route 90, which runs from Masonville Place to White Oaks mall, will begin using a roughly one-kilometre stretch of completed centre-running bus rapid transit lanes on Wellington between Simcoe Street, just south of Horton Street, and Grand Avenue, where it will merge back into mixed traffic.

The idea is to get Londoners used to what will be the city’s first use of centre-running bus lanes, said London’s director of construction Jennie Dann. The lanes will make up much of the Wellington Gateway and part of the East Link BRT routes.

Dann said centre-running lanes are a preferred BRT design around the world because they reduce interactions with other vehicles, including parked ones.

“It’s a small piece in our larger rapid transit program, but it’s an important step because it gives us a chance to see how the new road design is going to work with buses, drivers, pedestrians, cyclists, all using the corridor,” she said.

“Just as importantly, it gives Londoners a chance to get used to it . . . let’s start using it and see how people respond, and if we need to make any adjustments.”

The city has already begun trialling its BRT “contraflow lane” on King Street by similarly redirecting one bus route. While it left some drivers confused and concerned , Dann said it hasn’t caused major issues.

The biggest change for drivers brought about by the new centre lanes and medians will be restrictions on left turns to and from some driveways and smaller streets, Dann said.

Drivers intending to turn left from Wellington onto a side street, or left onto Wellington from one, will instead have to proceed to the nearest signalized intersection that allows U-turns and wait for an advanced left-turn signal to complete the turn.

City hall responds as merchants group sounds alarm over Wellington BRT work

London traffic congestion ranking improves – what’s behind the shift?

“Which is actually a good thing on a busy arterial like Wellington Road – instead of people making unprotected turning movements mid-block, we’re sending them up to the next signalized intersection,” she said. “It’s actually, in a lot of ways, safer.”

The express bus, which makes only a handful of stops, will stop at the Wellington and South Street station instead of its usual Grand Avenue stop.

Riders will board and disembark from protected platforms in the middle of the road and will have to wait for the normal walk signal at the intersection to cross.

All other Route 90 stops will remain at their normal curbside locations. Routes 1 and 13, which also travel on Wellington, will continue using existing curbside stops.

“We’re going to start practising using that transition, and then allow the buses to stop at the South Street stop, get some transit users used to using that median shelter, and then they’ll continue over the (Clark’s) bridge and then at Grand Avenue they’ll merge back into mixed traffic,” Dann said.

“As we do complete more sections of centre-running that are ready to go, we’re going to start to expand using existing express routes.”

Dann said work on widening Clark’s bridge over the Thames is complete.

The third phase of the Wellington Gateway between Wilkins Street and Harlech Gate has only landscaping work left, while the section from Harlech Gate to Exeter Road still needs shelter work and landscaping.

Traffic headaches at Wellington and Commissioners Road will continue into next year, however, Dann said, adding she hopes major work on Wellington between Commissioners and Wilkins will wrap up this year.

At the same time, work is beginning on Wellington from Watson Street to Whetter Avenue, including straightening the S-curve through that stretch and installing a new sewer trunk.

Dann said the expanded sewer is large enough for her to walk through and will be buried three storeys deep.

“That’s going to take us probably through to mid-2027. At that point, we should be pretty much out of the Commissioners intersection, and then we’re going to start with . . . moving south towards Base Line,” she said.

“The main goal of that is to keep access to the hospital as open as we can throughout the construction of both these contracts.”

The Wellington Gateway is expected to begin operations in 2029.

On the East Link BRT, Dann said sections of both Highbury Avenue north of the rail overpass and Oxford Street East are nearly complete and awaiting a top coat of asphalt this fall.

The on-campus station at Fanshawe College is finished and ready for the school year.

Work on widening Highbury’s rail overpass has shifted to the east side and will likely be completed next fall, she said.

Crews hope to finish the stretch of Dundas Street west of Highbury by early next year after the road was completely closed for deep sewer upgrades.

Construction at the Dundas and Highbury intersection will begin once Dundas reopens and is also expected to last until next fall, around the time full service on the East Link is expected to begin.

The third phase of the Wellington Gateway between Wilkins Street and Harlech Gate has only landscaping work left, while the section from Harlech Gate to Exeter Road still needs shelter work and landscaping.

Traffic headaches at Wellington and Commissioners Road will continue into next year, however, Dann said, adding she hopes major work on Wellington between Commissioners and Wilkins will wrap up this year.
At the same time, work is beginning on Wellington from Watson Street to Whetter Avenue, including straightening the S-curve through that stretch and installing a new sewer trunk.
Dann said the expanded sewer is large enough for her to walk through and will be buried three storeys deep.

“That’s going to take us probably through to mid-2027. At that point, we should be pretty much out of the Commissioners intersection, and then we’re going to start with . . . moving south towards Base Line,” she said.
“The main goal of that is to keep access to the hospital as open as we can throughout the construction of both these contracts.”
The Wellington Gateway is expected to begin operations in 2029.
HOW IS THE EAST LINK PROGRESSING?
On the East Link BRT, Dann said sections of both Highbury Avenue north of the rail overpass and Oxford Street East are nearly complete and awaiting a top coat of asphalt this fall.
The on-campus station at Fanshawe College is finished and ready for the school year.
Work on widening Highbury’s rail overpass has shifted to the east side and will likely be completed next fall, she said.
Crews hope to finish the stretch of Dundas Street west of Highbury by early next year after the road was completely closed for deep sewer upgrades.
Construction at the Dundas and Highbury intersection will begin once Dundas reopens and is also expected to last until next fall, around the time full service on the East Link is expected to begin.

stories.title: N.B. regulator to review complaints about noise and odours near potato chips factory
stories.summary: The 17 residents say the Covered Bridge Potato Chips Ltd. plant brings overwhelming smells, constant noise and more traffic to their once-quiet neighbourhood.
stories.author: Eli Ridder
stories.content:
A group of residents who live near a potato chip factory in a New Brunswick town are moving forward with their case against the company.

The 17 residents say the Covered Bridge Potato Chips Ltd. plant brings overwhelming smells, constant noise and more traffic to their once-quiet neighbourhood.

Each resident filed a claim with provincial farming regulator alleging the plant was causing significant and ongoing disruption to their lives.

The company’s lawyer, Sheila Mecking, has asked the province’s Farm Practices Review Board to settle the case, arguing that the company is an agricultural operator under provincial legislation.

The New Brunswick Farm Practices Review Board says it will consider whether it has jurisdiction to settle the complaints against the popular chip-making company.

The residents’ lawyer Basile Chiasson wants to pursue the case in court and argues the board doesn’t have jurisdiction.

The regulator’s chair Maurice Maillet said on Friday that the board, made up of five people who work in agriculture, will consider the arguments and come to a decision in the near future.

Chiasson said he expects the board to pave the way for the residents to take legal action at the Court of King’s Bench.

Last year, Covered Bridge converted its storage warehouse in Woodstock into a chip-processing factory, after its previous facility in another town burned down.

Some residents have said they hope Covered Bridge, which sells its chips across North America, leaves Woodstock entirely.

stories.title: Survey on perceived safety in cities puts Quebec City on top, Winnipeg at the bottom
stories.summary: Along with Winnipeg, Edmonton, Vancouver and Toronto were all perceived as much less safe than they were a decade ago.
stories.author: Chris Knight
stories.content:
A new survey on public safety perception in Canada’s urban centres finds that Quebec City has the strongest net perceived safety score in the country, while Winnipeg has the weakest.

But the survey, updating a previous version of the study conducted almost a decade ago, also recorded a big change in several large municipalities. Edmonton, Vancouver and Toronto were all perceived as much less safe than they were in 2017. Those cities are clustered at the bottom of the list, along with last-place Winnipeg.

The survey, conducted by Liaison Strategies , asked respondents whether they consider each city very safe, somewhat safe, somewhat unsafe, very unsafe, or whether they did not know enough to say. They were also asked what most shapes their impression of city safety, including news coverage, personal experience, stories from friends or family, social media, crime statistics or a city’s general reputation.

“Net safety” is the percentage who say a city is very or somewhat safe minus those who say it is somewhat or very unsafe. By that measurement, Quebec City leads the 15 cities tested with a score of 57, followed by Ottawa at 56 and Charlottetown at 51.

Five of the cities ended up with a negative score. Saskatoon had a net safety rating of -5 followed by Edmonton and Vancouver, both at -8, then Toronto at -18 and finally Winnipeg at -28.

The firm found that Quebec City has changed the most since it did a similar study in 2017, rising from 7 to 57. Edmonton and Vancouver, meanwhile have moved sharply in the other direction, each falling from positive net scores in 2017 to -8 today.

Toronto and Winnipeg were the bottom of the list in both surveys, but their numbers also fell. Toronto had a score of -12 in the first survey and -18 in this one, while Winnipeg dropped from -18 to its current score of -28.

“We brought this study back because city safety has a long memory” David Valentin, Principal at Liaison Strategies, said in releasing the data. “Quebec City now leads on net safety, Ottawa remains very strong, and Winnipeg and Toronto remain at the bottom.”

“Winnipeg is the clearest safety concern,” Valentin added. “It ranks last on perceived safety, with only 31 per cent saying it is safe and 59 per cent saying it is unsafe. It also has the highest official Crime Severity Index among the cities tested, so in Winnipeg the perception problem and the official data are pointing in the same direction.”

The Crime Severity Index , developed by Statistics Canada in 2009, is a summary measure of the volume and severity of police-reported crime in a given area.

“Toronto is different,” said Valentin. “Toronto is perceived as almost as unsafe as Winnipeg, but the official crime-severity data does not put Toronto in the same category. That is why Toronto stands out as the clearest reputational penalty in the report.”

He added: “Only 12 per cent say crime statistics are the main thing shaping their impression of city safety. That matters. If people are mostly relying on news coverage, personal experience, and word of mouth, then city safety is not just a policing issue. It is also a reputation issue. That reputation can take years to build, and years to repair.”

The survey also noted a clear gender gap, with women seeing a sharper safety problem in several major cities, including Winnipeg, Vancouver, Edmonton and Toronto.

“A city can have one national number, but the lived meaning of safety is not the same for every audience,” said Valentin.

The survey contacted 1,500 Canadian adults between August 30 and 31, 2026. The margin of error is plus or minus 2.53 percentage points, 19 times out of 20.

stories.title: B.C. school districts crack down on e-scooters, e-bikes as emergency room visits grow
stories.summary: Highest proportion of emergency room visits for e-scooter crashes were for children aged 13 and 15, despite 16 being minimum legal age to ride
stories.author: Marissa Birnie
stories.content:
More British Columbia school districts are banning electric bikes and scooters from their properties ahead of the new school year, citing a spike in injuries among underage riders.

The Langley School District says in a letter to parents this week that e-scooters and e-dirt bikes are now banned at all of its schools, and the Nanaimo-Ladysmith school district says elementary school students cannot arrive to school on an e-bike or scooter.

“If an e-bike or scooter does come to school we will call parents to come and pick up the e-bike or e-scooter,” the Nanaimo-Ladysmith school district’s communications director Gillian Robinson said.

Both school districts say an increase in injuries among children and youth riders influenced their decision to implement bans on school property.

Dr. Genevieve Ernst, trauma medical director at BC Children’s Hospital, said the hospital has seen a steep rise in both emergency room visits and devastating brain injuries for child patients as the result of e-scooter crashes.

By law, light e-bike riders must be at least 14-years-old and e-bike or scooter riders must be 16.

But data from the Canadian Hospital Injury Reporting and Prevention Surveillance Program shows the highest proportion of emergency room visits for e-scooter crashes were for children aged 13 and 15.

There were 81 visits to BC Children’s emergency department between April 2025 and 2026 related to e-scooter use, more than double those of the previous year. Most were a result of falling off the scooter.

Ernst said e-scooters are the culprit in the most severe injuries among patients involved in e-bike or scooter crashes at BC Children’s hospital.

She said common injuries include fractures, road rash, abrasions and head injuries. More than half of those seriously injured were not wearing helmets.

“So what you can see is long-term stays at the hospital, need for critical-care surgery, and then more long-term issues with development and learning.”

Resha Sabti, a parent from Langley, said her 12-year-old twins asked for e-scooters for their birthday last year, and it was upon researching the vehicles that she learned riders must be at least 16.

She’s since had a close call with scooters, almost hitting two young girls as they rode downhill in the rain while wearing dark clothing. The girls were not wearing helmets, she added.

The Langley school district serves students in both the Township of Langley, where e-scooters are permitted as part of a provincial pilot project, and Langley City, where they are not.

Sabti, who is running for a council seat with the Township of Langley, said she’s brought her concerns about e-bikes to the township and school district because people are confused about where the rules apply.

Though she sympathizes with the need for the vehicles among youth who May lack accessible transportation in their communities, she said she also understands the need for a school ban.

“I don’t think we should wait until a child’s death,” she said.

stories.title: Five former B.C. Conservative MLAs form new provincial party
stories.summary: are forming a new provincial party they say will offer voters an alternative to both the governing NDP and the Conservatives.
stories.author: Prisha Dev
stories.content:
Five B.C. legislators who recently left the provincial Conservatives are joining forces to form a new political party, with plans to have it up and running when the legislature returns next month.

Rosalyn Bird, Bruce Banman and Áʼa꞉líya Warbus announced Friday they are joining Peter Milobar and Ian Paton in the yet-to-be-named party.

The five are among nine MLAs who have left the B.C. Conservative caucus in recent weeks under Leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay.

Milobar, who is serving as interim leader, told Global News that the group wants to create an option for voters who are dissatisfied with the governing NDP but don’t see themselves supporting the B.C. Conservatives.

“We need to form a serious, credible option for voters that are fed up with the NDP and can’t see themselves voting for the Conservative Party of B.C. moving forward,” he said Friday.

The party has not yet announced a name, but Milobar said the group is working through the process with Elections BC and hopes to have key details in place before the legislature returns Oct. 5.

“We are not doing this on a whim. We are doing this methodically and properly,” he said.

The party also plans to hold an internal leadership vote before the legislature resumes and sit with official third-party status. Milobar said he would consider seeking the permanent leadership, but said his current priority is building the party.

“I will give it some consideration, but that is not my main focus right now,” he added.

The group said in a release that its priorities will include affordability, the economy, health care, taxation, resource development and land and property rights.

Milobar said he believes there is an appetite among British Columbians for another political option, pointing to the response he and other former Conservative MLAs have received since leaving the caucus.

“My inbox has been overflowing,” he said. “All nine have said that it’s been an extremely positive response and experience in their communities for them taking that step to leave.”

Milobar said the group will continue speaking with other MLAs, but would not say whether more members are expected to join in the coming days.

Findlay narrowly won the B.C. Conservative leadership in May.

Scott McInnis and Donegal Wilson became the latest MLAs to leave the caucus on Wednesday.

– With files from The Canadian Press

stories.title: B.C. school districts crack down on e-scooters, e-bikes as emergency room visits rise
stories.summary: More British Columbia school districts are banning electric bikes and scooters from their properties ahead of the new school year, citing a spike in injuries among underage riders.
stories.author: Marissa Birnie The Canadian Press
stories.content:
More British Columbia school districts are banning electric bikes and scooters from their properties ahead of the new school year, citing a spike in injuries among underage riders.

The Langley School District said in a letter to parents this week that e-scooters and e-dirt bikes are now banned at all of its schools, while the Nanaimo-Ladysmith district said elementary students cannot arrive to school on an e-bike or scooter.

“If an e-bike or scooter does come to school we will call parents to come and pick up the e-bike or e-scooter,” said Gillian Robinson, communications director with the Nanaimo-Ladysmith district.

Both school districts said an increase in injuries among children and youth riders influenced their decision to implement bans on school property.

Dr. Genevieve Ernst, trauma medical director at BC Children’s Hospital, said the hospital has seen a steep rise in both emergency room visits and devastating brain injuries for child patients as the result of e-scooter crashes.

By law, light e-bike riders must be at least 14-years-old and e-bike or scooter riders must be 16.

But figures from the Canadian Hospital Injury Reporting and Prevention Surveillance Program show 13-year-old children made up the highest proportion of emergency room visits for e-scooter crashes at 22 per cent.

There were 81 visits to the BC Children Hospital emergency department between April 2025 and 2026 related to e-scooter use, more than double those of the previous year. Most were a result of falling off the scooter.

Ernst said e-scooters are the culprit in the most severe injuries among the hospital’s patients involved in e-bike or scooter crashes.

She said common injuries include fractures, road rash, scrapes and head injuries. More than half of those seriously injured were not wearing helmets.

“So what you can see is long-term stays at the hospital, need for critical-care surgery, and then more long-term issues with development and learning.”

Resha Sabti, a parent from Langley, B.C., said her 12-year-old twins asked for e-scooters for their birthday last year, and it was upon researching the devices that she learned riders must be at least 16.

Sabti said she has since had a close call with scooters, almost hitting two young girls as they rode downhill in the rain while wearing dark clothing. The girls were not wearing helmets, she added.

The Langley School District serves students in both the Township of Langley, where e-scooters are permitted as part of a provincial pilot project, and Langley City, where they are not.

Eleven communities in B.C.‘s Metro Vancouver and Fraser Valley regions allow e-scooters as part of the four-year pilot.

Riders can’t ride on crosswalks, double up on the scooters or ride without a helmet — rules that Sabti said she’s seen broken frequently.

The fine for breaking e-scooter rules is $109, while the fine for riding without a helmet is $29.

Other cities, such as Surrey, have banned e-scooters from public property, a prohibition that extends to school properties.

Sabti, who is running for a seat on the Township of Langley council, said she’s brought her concerns about the devices to local officials and the school district because people are confused about where the rules apply.

Though she said she sympathizes with the need for options among youth who May lack accessible transportation, she also understood the need for a school ban.

“I don’t think we should wait until a child’s death,” she said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 4, 2026.

Note to readers:This is a corrected story. A previous version said the Nanaimo-Ladysmith school district would send children home if they arrive to school on an e-scooter or e-bike. In fact, the district says it will ask that the e-scooter or bike be picked up.

stories.title: PQ leader says his immigration comments were 'distorted' by opponents in campaign
stories.summary: Montreal - Parti Québécois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon said comments he has made about immigration have been "distorted" by his opponents as Quebec's political parties wrapped up the second week of the provincial election campaign on Friday.
stories.author: Erika Morris The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal - Parti Québécois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon said comments he has made about immigration have been “distorted” by his opponents as Quebec’s political parties wrapped up the second week of the provincial election campaign on Friday.

Immigration and anglophone rights took centre stage over the week as leaders continued to campaign ahead of the Oct. 5 provincial election.

The Parti Québécois, which has maintained its lead in the polls despite growing support for the governing Coalition Avenir Québec, is facing criticism after St-Pierre Plamondon stirred up controversy with comments about immigrants in schools.

In recent days, the PQ leader has linked immigration to overcrowded schools and the decline of the French language. On Saturday, he held a press conference outside a Quebec City high school where modular classrooms are being used to accommodate students.

He said schools were “overflowing everywhere in Quebec,” and cited data about the increase that he attributed to immigrants. But the statistics he shared were actually adding up a combination of immigrants and Quebec-born children of immigrants.

Québec solidaire co-spokesperson Ruba Ghazal accused him of scapegoating immigrant children, while suggesting that the real problem was due to previous governments failing to adequately fund the education system.

“Who does the PQ consider a Quebecer? Isn’t being born here enough?,” said Ghazal on Wednesday. “My nieces and nephews were born here. They’ve never known anything but Quebec. How can we blame them for overcrowded schools? It’s hurtful.”

St-Pierre Plamondon addressed the backlash again on Friday, saying that his opponents were distorting his actual views. He said his party is “not targeting Quebecers of immigrant background.”

“To us, all Quebecers are 100 per cent Quebecers, but we just have a bad public policy that needs to be fixed,” he said. “The flip side of this issue is that many people hesitate to bring it up for fear of being accused of racism or intolerance.”

Frantz André, head of a Montreal-based migrant advocacy group, says the PQ is parroting electoral talking points from former Coalition Avenir Québec leader François Legault.

In both 2018 and 2022 — when Legault’s party formed successive majority governments — the Coalition Avenir Québec made immigration and religious minorities the focus of its campaigns. Legault had vowed to slash temporary immigration and permanent residency, and to accept fewer asylum seekers.

On the campaign trail, St-Pierre Plamondon has claimed that Legault’s government — in which current Coalition Avenir Québec leader Christine Fréchette was once immigration minister — “lost control” over its immigration system despite promises.

“The reality is we need immigrants,” said André. “Immigration is challenging, but it’s also a solution to our population decline and labour shortage.”

St-Pierre Plamondon said a PQ government would reduce the number of temporary immigrants in Quebec per year from more than 500,000 to between 200,000 and 250,000, arguing current levels have exceeded the province’s capacity to provide housing and public services. He also promised to reduce permanent immigration to 35,000 people a year, down from the government’s current target of 45,000.

But André says that number is “totally arbitrary” and does not take into consideration Quebec’s needs.

He agrees with Ghazal’s claims that the PQ is scapegoating immigrants, saying it can often be a winning strategy as seen by Legault and politicians south of the border.

Listening to St-Pierre Plamondon’s press conferences, André hears electioneering. He believes the PQ is trying to court voters who were favourable to Legault’s positions.

Philippe Fournier, who created poll aggregator 338Canada, says he has noticed a shift in the Coalition Avenir Québec’s priorities under Fréchette, who is focusing her campaign on the economy and businesses.

According to the pollster, targeting immigration is a “slippery slope” based on “risk and reward.”

“In 2022, when the CAQ focused heavily on identity and immigration, it didn’t go well,” said Fournier. “They didn’t pay the price at the polls, but Mr. Legault got bogged down a few times on the issue of immigration, and it wasn’t a winning issue for them.”

According to Fournier, the party fared best when talking about stability and good governance.

Meanwhile, Fréchette’s party was under fire after Élections Québec said language laws were forcing it to provide printed voter guides in French only.

Lobby groups representing anglophones accused the government of voter suppression after the provincial election authority said its request to be exempt from legislation forcing government entities to communicate in French only was denied. A group of lawyers also threatened to take legal action.

Liberal Party Leader Charles Milliard published an open letter addressed to Fréchette on Thursday evening expressing his disapproval.

“This decision … constitutes an unjustifiable attack on the electoral rights of English-speaking Quebecers,” he wrote.

Fournier expects the campaign to ramp up next week, after Labour Day, as party leaders prepare for upcoming debates.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 4, 2026.
paragraphs: Montreal - Parti Québécois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon said comments he has made about immigration have been “distorted” by his opponents as Quebec’s political parties wrapped up the second week of the provincial election campaign on Friday.
Immigration and anglophone rights took centre stage over the week as leaders continued to campaign ahead of the Oct. 5 provincial election.

The Parti Québécois, which has maintained its lead in the polls despite growing support for the governing Coalition Avenir Québec, is facing criticism after St-Pierre Plamondon stirred up controversy with comments about immigrants in schools.

In recent days, the PQ leader has linked immigration to overcrowded schools and the decline of the French language. On Saturday, he held a press conference outside a Quebec City high school where modular classrooms are being used to accommodate students.

He said schools were “overflowing everywhere in Quebec,” and cited data about the increase that he attributed to immigrants. But the statistics he shared were actually adding up a combination of immigrants and Quebec-born children of immigrants.

Québec solidaire co-spokesperson Ruba Ghazal accused him of scapegoating immigrant children, while suggesting that the real problem was due to previous governments failing to adequately fund the education system.

“Who does the PQ consider a Quebecer? Isn’t being born here enough?,” said Ghazal on Wednesday. “My nieces and nephews were born here. They’ve never known anything but Quebec. How can we blame them for overcrowded schools? It’s hurtful.”
St-Pierre Plamondon addressed the backlash again on Friday, saying that his opponents were distorting his actual views. He said his party is “not targeting Quebecers of immigrant background.”

“To us, all Quebecers are 100 per cent Quebecers, but we just have a bad public policy that needs to be fixed,” he said. “The flip side of this issue is that many people hesitate to bring it up for fear of being accused of racism or intolerance.”
Frantz André, head of a Montreal-based migrant advocacy group, says the PQ is parroting electoral talking points from former Coalition Avenir Québec leader François Legault.

In both 2018 and 2022 — when Legault’s party formed successive majority governments — the Coalition Avenir Québec made immigration and religious minorities the focus of its campaigns. Legault had vowed to slash temporary immigration and permanent residency, and to accept fewer asylum seekers.

On the campaign trail, St-Pierre Plamondon has claimed that Legault’s government — in which current Coalition Avenir Québec leader Christine Fréchette was once immigration minister — “lost control” over its immigration system despite promises.
“The reality is we need immigrants,” said André. “Immigration is challenging, but it’s also a solution to our population decline and labour shortage.”

St-Pierre Plamondon said a PQ government would reduce the number of temporary immigrants in Quebec per year from more than 500,000 to between 200,000 and 250,000, arguing current levels have exceeded the province’s capacity to provide housing and public services. He also promised to reduce permanent immigration to 35,000 people a year, down from the government’s current target of 45,000.
But André says that number is “totally arbitrary” and does not take into consideration Quebec’s needs.
He agrees with Ghazal’s claims that the PQ is scapegoating immigrants, saying it can often be a winning strategy as seen by Legault and politicians south of the border.
Listening to St-Pierre Plamondon’s press conferences, André hears electioneering. He believes the PQ is trying to court voters who were favourable to Legault’s positions.

Philippe Fournier, who created poll aggregator 338Canada, says he has noticed a shift in the Coalition Avenir Québec’s priorities under Fréchette, who is focusing her campaign on the economy and businesses.
According to the pollster, targeting immigration is a “slippery slope” based on “risk and reward.”

“In 2022, when the CAQ focused heavily on identity and immigration, it didn’t go well,” said Fournier. “They didn’t pay the price at the polls, but Mr. Legault got bogged down a few times on the issue of immigration, and it wasn’t a winning issue for them.”
According to Fournier, the party fared best when talking about stability and good governance.
Meanwhile, Fréchette’s party was under fire after Élections Québec said language laws were forcing it to provide printed voter guides in French only.

Lobby groups representing anglophones accused the government of voter suppression after the provincial election authority said its request to be exempt from legislation forcing government entities to communicate in French only was denied. A group of lawyers also threatened to take legal action.
Liberal Party Leader Charles Milliard published an open letter addressed to Fréchette on Thursday evening expressing his disapproval.
“This decision … constitutes an unjustifiable attack on the electoral rights of English-speaking Quebecers,” he wrote.
Fournier expects the campaign to ramp up next week, after Labour Day, as party leaders prepare for upcoming debates.
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 4, 2026.

stories.title: Vancouver police officer and youth charity founder charged over theft of more than $3M
stories.summary: Chief Const. Steve Rai says Kalwinder Dosanjh was arrested on Thursday after a covert investigation that lasted more than two years
stories.content:
A 26-year veteran of the Vancouver Police Department is facing charges of theft, fraud and breach of trust involving millions of dollars in a case the force’s chief is calling “deeply distressing.”

Kalwinder Dosanjh, who is well known for his charitable work involving a foundation called Kids Play, was arrested on Thursday in a controlled traffic stop in Surrey, B.C., after a covert investigation that lasted more than two years.

The charges relate to housing developments, with 19 alleged victims reporting losses of more that $3 million.

Chief Const. Steve Rai and other high-ranking officers spoke about the case on Friday at Vancouver police headquarters.

“These allegations are deeply troubling, not only because of their seriousness, but because they have the potential to undermine the trust that our members work very hard, very hard to build and maintain with the public,” Rai said.

“It is deeply distressing when the actions of one individual, one individual cast a shadow over the tremendous work of so many dedicated professionals who serve our city with honour every day.”

Provincial Crown prosecutors approved four counts of fraud over $5,000, four counts of theft over $5,000 and one count of breach of trust. Online court records show charges were sworn against Dosanjh along with his co-accused, Sarabjit Gill.

Police say the alleged criminal conduct happened between 2017 and 2025.

Few other details have been released by police, citing privacy and the matter being before the courts.

Dosanjh’s lawyers did not immediately provide a response to the allegations.

Dosanjh is the founder of Surrey-base Kids Play, whose website said he had served in various roles including as an undercover officer and in the department’s financial crime and drug units.

Supt. Mike Ritchie said police searched the premises of Kids Play on Thursday.

Dosanjh’s wife, Sandy, had been a council candidate for the Conservative Party of Surrey in the city’s upcoming municipal election but the party said Friday she had dropped out.

“As Sandy is no longer a candidate for public office, we ask that her privacy be respected so that she is able to focus on her family,” the party said.

Ritchie said there May be more victims in the case, and investigators have set up a dedicated phone line for anyone who May have been affected to come forward.

Ritchie said more charges were possible.

“We anticipate a number of other victims, so there is a possibility,” he said. “It is an active, ongoing investigation. The current charges are before the courts, but we do anticipate further victims coming forward.”

Police say the investigation into Dosanjh began in December 2023, when several victims reported the allegations of “criminal activity.”

It led to the establishment of a dedicated investigative team that undertook a covert investigation of more than two years.

Rai said Vancouver Police consulted the RCMP on which jurisdiction should carry out the investigation before forming the team to investigate its own officer.

“It was a two-plus-year investigation,” he said. “That takes a lot of resources and a lot of expertise and in B.C., let’s be frank, only a large department can lead that kind of investigation in this province – that’s the RCMP or ourselves.

“And we had discussions with the RCMP, and with what’s going on in the region with transition, bodies, resources, it was determined with collective judgment that we would maintain the file for the expertise required and the resources.”

Dosanjh has been suspended, removing his powers as a police officer, and his service weapon had been seized, Ritchie told the news conference.

Rai recommended to the Vancouver Police Board that Dosanjh’s suspension be without pay for the duration of any proceedings.

“If the Police Board adopts my recommendation, this suspension will remain in place while the criminal proceedings move through the courts and until any disciplinary proceedings under the Police Act are concluded,” he said.

stories.title: Special city council meeting called over leak of confidential Calgary budget docs
stories.summary: Preliminary budget documents obtained by Global News show a large property tax increase would be required to pay for the funding requests in front of Calgary city council.
stories.author: Adam MacVicar
stories.content:
Calgary city council will take part in a special meeting behind closed doors to seek legal advice, after a trove of confidential and preliminary budget documents were obtained by Global News.

As first reported by Global News on Wednesday, the confidential documents showed a significant property tax increase would be required to cover all the spending requests in front of city council in the upcoming four-year budget.

The preliminary documents were presented to city council during a closed-door meeting July 28, in which city council directed administration to whittle down the requests and present an updated budget scenario later this month with a 15 per cent property tax increase in 2027.

Calgary mayor Jeromy Farkas said the figures are simply a “wishlist” and no decisions have been made regarding a property tax increase.

The release of the documents resulted a clash on Thursday between Farkas and Ward 14 Coun. Landon Johnston , after Johnston took to social media and claimed he leaked the information.

The situation has prompted Farkas to call a special meeting of council.

It will take place after the long weekend on Tuesday morning, following the start of a busy Executive Committee meeting in which city councillors will need to endorse an option for the downtown leg of the Green Line LRT project.

A notice sent to city councillors said the meeting to is to receive “legal advice regarding unauthorized disclosure of 2027-2030 budget cycle information.”

Farkas’ office declined an interview with Global News on Friday morning.

Ward 3 Coun. Andrew Yule told reporters Wednesday he was disappointed the information was released, but isn’t confident there will be any repercussions, as the council code of conduct was eliminated by the provincial government last year and replaced with a provincewide one .

Calgary city council will deliberate the next four-year budget on Nov. 23 after the proposed spending plan is released publicly in early November.

More to come…

stories.title: Denying EI to women laid off after maternity leave is unconstitutional: appeal court
stories.summary: MONTRÉAL - The Federal Court of Appeal has ruled that it's unconstitutional to deny employment insurance job loss benefits to women who recently received maternity and parental benefits.
stories.author: Lia Lévesque The Canadian Press
stories.content:
MONTRÉAL - The Federal Court of Appeal has ruled that it’s unconstitutional to deny employment insurance job loss benefits to women who recently received maternity and parental benefits.

The three-judge panel ruled in favour of a group of Quebec women who were denied EI after being laid off shortly before, during, or just after their maternity leaves.

The court sided with a lower tribunal, which had found that some provisions of the Employment Insurance Act violate the section of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms that guarantees equal rights for men and women.

Initially, the workers had won their case before the Social Security Tribunal’s general division, but the decision was overturned on appeal.

A summary of the decision says the existing rules create a sex-based distinction that disproportionately affects women because they are the ones who give birth and take the majority of parental leave.

The court has declared the contested provisions of the Employment Insurance Act invalid, but suspended its decision for one year to give the federal government time to adjust the program.

The six female workers mounted a legal case after being told they had not accumulated enough insurable hours to receive EI benefits due to having taken maternity or parental leave close to the time they were laid off.

A summary of the decision says the impact of the EI rules, as written, were discriminatory to women even though they apply to both sexes. That’s because “only women can become pregnant and give birth,” and most people who receive parental benefits are women, it noted.

“The court also found that denying EI job loss benefits to women who have recently received maternity and parental benefits perpetuates the long-standing economic disadvantage associated with pregnancy and motherhood by diminishing unemployment protection available to women precisely because they bear children and assume childcare responsibilities after giving birth,” the decision summary read.

“Under the EI Act, the price for receiving maternity and parental benefits is the loss of job loss benefits for those in the applicants’ situation, and this price is disproportionately paid by women.”

The women had all testified in court that their job loss and EI denial created financial problems that forced them to use savings, rely on their partners, or borrow from loved ones. They also testified on how they felt the provisions of the EI law discriminate against women who have children.

The Mouvement Action-Chômage de Montréal, an advocacy organization that led the challenge on behalf of the plaintiffs, welcomed the decision but noted the federal government has 60 days to indicate whether it will try to bring the case to the Supreme Court of Canada.

“At MAC, we believe it would be shameful for the Carney government to appeal this ruling, as its predecessor did. It would be a slap in the face to the six women we have supported for the past seven years, but also to the hundreds, if not thousands, of others across Canada who are currently awaiting this decision because they find themselves in the same situation,” said Fanny Labelle, a mobilization and community engagement coordinator, in a social media post.

A spokesperson for Employment and Social Development Canada said the federal government would carefully review the decision before deciding on its next steps.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 4, 2026.

stories.title: Vancouver police officer Kalwinder Dosanjh charged over theft of more than $3M
stories.summary: Vancouver - A 26-year veteran of the Vancouver Police Department is facing charges of theft, fraud and breach of trust involving millions of dollars in a case the force's chief is calling "deeply distressing."
stories.author: Chuck Chiang The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Vancouver - A 26-year veteran of the Vancouver Police Department is facing charges of theft, fraud and breach of trust involving millions of dollars in a case the force’s chief is calling “deeply distressing.”

Kalwinder Dosanjh, who is well known for his charitable work involving a foundation called Kids Play, was arrested on Thursday in a controlled traffic stop in Surrey, B.C., after a covert investigation that lasted more than two years.

The charges relate to housing developments, with 19 alleged victims reporting losses of more that $3 million.

Chief Const. Steve Rai and other high-ranking officers spoke about the case on Friday at Vancouver police headquarters.

“These allegations are deeply troubling, not only because of their seriousness, but because they have the potential to undermine the trust that our members work very hard, very hard to build and maintain with the public,” Rai said.

“It is deeply distressing when the actions of one individual, one individual cast a shadow over the tremendous work of so many dedicated professionals who serve our city with honour every day.”

Provincial Crown prosecutors approved four counts of fraud over $5,000, four counts of theft over $5,000 and one count of breach of trust. Online court records show charges were sworn against Dosanjh along with his co-accused, Sarabjit Gill.

Police say the alleged criminal conduct happened between 2017 and 2025.

Few other details have been released by police, citing privacy and the matter being before the courts.

Dosanjh’s lawyers did not immediately provide a response to the allegations.

Dosanjh is the founder of Surrey-base Kids Play, whose website said he had served in various roles including as an undercover officer and in the department’s financial crime and drug units.

Supt. Mike Ritchie said police searched the premises of Kids Play on Thursday.

Dosanjh’s wife, Sandy, had been a council candidate for the Conservative Party of Surrey in the city’s upcoming municipal election but the party said Friday she had dropped out.

“As Sandy is no longer a candidate for public office, we ask that her privacy be respected so that she is able to focus on her family,” the party said.

Ritchie said there May be more victims in the case, and investigators have set up a dedicated phone line for anyone who May have been affected to come forward.

Ritchie said more charges were possible.

“We anticipate a number of other victims, so there is a possibility,” he said. “It is an active, ongoing investigation. The current charges are before the courts, but we do anticipate further victims coming forward.”

Police say the investigation into Dosanjh began in December 2023, when several victims reported the allegations of “criminal activity.”

It led to the establishment of a dedicated investigative team that undertook a covert investigation of more than two years.

Rai said Vancouver Police consulted the RCMP on which jurisdiction should carry out the investigation before forming the team to investigate its own officer.

“It was a two-plus-year investigation,” he said. “That takes a lot of resources and a lot of expertise and in B.C., let’s be frank, only a large department can lead that kind of investigation in this province — that’s the RCMP or ourselves.

“And we had discussions with the RCMP, and with what’s going on in the region with transition, bodies, resources, it was determined with collective judgment that we would maintain the file for the expertise required and the resources.”

Dosanjh has been suspended, removing his powers as a police officer, and his service weapon had been seized, Ritchie told the news conference.

Rai recommended to the Vancouver Police Board that Dosanjh’s suspension be without pay for the duration of any proceedings.

“If the Police Board adopts my recommendation, this suspension will remain in place while the criminal proceedings move through the courts and until any disciplinary proceedings under the Police Act are concluded,” he said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 4, 2026.

stories.title: Alberta thinks it has a health care fix. Ottawa, as always, is skeptical
stories.summary: The question is not just whether it works. It's whether Ottawa and Alberta can drop the usual script — Western grievance vs federal lecture.
stories.author: Donna Kennedy-Glans
stories.content:
Can Ottawa and Alberta actually work together?

Adriana LaGrange is not waiting for permission. Alberta’s minister of hospital and surgical health services is rolling out a dual-practice model that lets some surgeons work in both the public system and a private-pay lane at the same time — something no other province allows. The question hanging over it is not just whether the model works. It is whether Ottawa and Edmonton can drop the familiar script — Western grievance versus federal lecture — and treat a provincial experiment as a chance to fix something both sides say is broken.

When I catch up with LaGrange in late August, she is not in campaign mode. She is in implementation mode. Legislation passed last December created a new category of “flexibly participating” physicians, mainly surgeons. Starting this fall they can do publicly funded work and, ON a case-by-case basis, privately paid elective procedures: hip and knee replacements, cataracts, hernia repair, selected ENT, gynecology, dermatology and plastic surgery. Emergency care, cancer treatment and family practice stay fully public.

Right now, she says, Alberta has two camps: physicians who are “fully opted out” or “fully opted in.” She puts the opted-out group at about 15 — doctors who do only private work. Everyone else stays inside the public system. Dual practice is the attempt to stop the binary. Doctors keep a public contract, meet a minimum number of public hours with Alberta Health Services or Covenant Health, then add private volume in approved facilities. At first, those will be accredited non-hospital surgical facilities.

The Alberta Medical Association neither endorses nor opposes the plan. It has spent months pressing for guardrails so the private lane does not lengthen public waits, poach staff, or slide into queue-jumping by ability to pay. LaGrange says that is her test too. “What we want to do, pre-emptively, is make sure we have those strong guardrails in place so we are protecting our public system first and foremost.” Dual-practice doctors, she says, “would have to put the minimum public surgery hours in before they could actually do private surgeries.”

Her pitch: Albertans already leave the province — and the country — for these surgeries. “Alberta doctors are flying out, Alberta patients are flying out, and we have other provinces, their patients and their doctors flying here to do those surgeries here. It just doesn’t make sense.” Keep the work here, she argues, and you add capacity, keep complications inside a system that will treat them anyway, and give patients a local choice for elective care.

She keeps drawing the line. “I emphasize elective, not medically needed at this moment, because of course if it was an emergency or if it was cancer, that would be done here, no cost, no impediment to that whatsoever.”

Federal Health Minister Marjorie Michel is not convinced the model fits the Canada Health Act. In mid-August she told the Toronto Star she was “very concerned” and did not see how dual practice could operate within the Act. Her office confirmed a July 24 letter asking Alberta to protect the public system. Reporting around that interview floated discretionary penalties — an unusual step beyond the deductions Ottawa already takes from health transfers when provinces allow patient charges.

That is where the relationship gets tested. LaGrange says Alberta had already sent Ottawa the draft regulations “and some of our thoughts around the safeguards that we’re putting in place to protect the public system.” The letter back, she explains, was that Ottawa would “monitor,” had “some concerns that it May not adhere to the spirit of the Canada Health Act,” and that the two departments should keep talking. Then came the Star piece. “That’s why I was quite surprised by the tone and somewhat implied threat of discretionary penalties.”

She is still waiting for a straight answer. “From their perspective, they would say it’s not in keeping with the spirit of the Canada Health Act, and I keep asking for clarity on that. So that’s where I would say we differ, because I do believe it does keep with the spirit of the Canada Health Act.”

The federal statute dates to 1984 and has never been rewritten. Long waits, workforce shortages and private delivery already exist across the country under different provincial rules. Alberta’s claim is that simultaneous public-and-private practice for the same elective procedures is compatible with the Act.

She still describes the working relationship as good. “I do believe Minister Michel wants to improve the overall health-care system in Canada. She also knows the challenges of the funding for health care that all the provinces are experiencing.” The disagreement is definitional. Ottawa hears “ability to pay.” Alberta hears “choice for elective surgery, with public hours locked in first.”

LaGrange wants time to prove the model increases surgical volume without starving the public list. Michel wants proof it will not create two queues for the same medically necessary procedure. The money argument sits underneath everything.

“When health care was first envisioned in Canada, it was a 50/50 split with the federal government. Right now, we receive about 21 per cent,” says LaGrange. Premiers have spent years asking Ottawa to lift that to 35 per cent; some now talk about a 50/50 split again. The Canada Health Transfer rises 5 per cent to $57.4 billion in 2026-27. Alberta’s portion is about $7 billion, against a $34.4-billion provincial health budget.

What galls LaGrange is the mix of a shrinking cash share and a growing list of conditions. “The fact that the number continues to decline … and yet they would like to have more and more strings attached to it and more and more say on what happens in what is a provincial jurisdiction, I think is problematic.”

LaGrange is not only defending dual practice. On Oct. 19, Albertans will vote in a referendum on a constitutional question: should Alberta work with other provinces to let a province opt out of federal programs in health, education and social services — and keep the cash? She says she will vote yes, that the ballot language is aimed at programs such as pharmacare and the federal dental plan.

Her line is that individual provinces should run health care because individual provinces’ needs are not the same. That is a legitimate constitutional argument. It is also why a letter about the “spirit” of the Canada Health Act lands like a warning. Alberta is asking Ottawa to trust a new surgical model in the same season it is asking voters to weaken Ottawa’s leverage.

Alberta’s surgery experiment is an opportunity for clarity: If dual practice shortens public waits and keeps surgeons in Alberta, the collaboration argument gets easier. If it does not, Ottawa will have its evidence and Alberta will have a political problem it created.

stories.title: Four sentenced in connection with killing of 19-year-old Burnaby man
stories.summary: Four people have been sentenced to prison after pleading guilty to manslaughter in connection with the 2023 killing of 19-year-old Ryan Nagy in Burnaby.
stories.author: Prisha Dev
stories.content:
Four people have now been sentenced in connection with the 2023 killing of a 19-year-old man in Burnaby, B.C.

In its latest update Friday, the Integrated Homicide Investigation Team ( Ihit ) said all four have since pleaded guilty to manslaughter and have been sentenced with prison terms ranging from six to 10.5 years.

On June 29, 2023, Burnaby RCMP were called to a home following a home invasion in the 7600-block of 17 Avenue shortly after 7 a.m.

Officers found Ryan Nagy suffering from life-threatening injuries. Despite efforts by first responders, he died at the scene.

A woman was also found with non-life-threatening injuries and taken to hospital.

Ihit took over the investigation, working alongside Burnaby RCMP, forensic investigators and the BC Coroners Service.

In September 2024, the BC Prosecution Service approved manslaughter and forcible confinement charges against Ali Shamkhi, Rais Usman, Ousmane Keita and Rhoda Diabikulu, investigators said in the release.

Shamkhi was sentenced in March to a global sentence, meaning a single overall sentence a court imposes for multiple offences, rather than giving a separate sentence for each charge.

Shamkhi will serve 10.5 years for manslaughter and unrelated firearms offences after pleading guilty in October 2025.

Usman was sentenced in April to six years for manslaughter after pleading guilty in October 2025 as well.

Keita received a six-year sentence in June after pleading guilty in March.

Most recently, Diabikulu was sentenced Sept. 1 to seven years in prison after pleading guilty to manslaughter in March.

All four received credit for time already spent in custody. The court also imposed lifetime firearms prohibitions and DNA orders, according to the release.

“Thanks to the quick response from the Burnaby RCMP and the subsequent teamwork with Ihit investigators, all four individuals responsible for Ryan’s death have been held accountable,” Ihit Sgt. Freda Fong said.

“Our thoughts are with Ryan’s loved ones and the surviving victim as they continue their healing journey from this traumatic event.”

stories.title: Marcus Nordmark gives London Knights major firepower up front
stories.summary: The Anaheim Ducks first-rounder joins a loaded import group that already includes Maksim Sokolovskii and Luca Santala.
stories.author: Ryan Pyette
stories.content:
The London Knights have assembled one of the best import classes in junior hockey.

The Ontario Hockey League club signed Anaheim Ducks first-rounder Marcus Nordmark Thursday after trading defenceman Linus Funck to the Oshawa Generals for a second- and third-round draft pick.

The 18-year-old Swedish forward will join Russian defenceman Maksim Sokolovskii, a Philadelphia Flyers first-rounder, and Finnish forward Luca Santala, who is expected to be a high pick in the 2027 NHL draft, at Canada Life Place this season.

Nordmark is a prime candidate to play for Tre Kronor at the world junior tournament in Edmonton and Red Deer this year. He helped Sweden win world under-18 gold this past season and led the recent Hlinka Gretzky Cup in scoring with seven goals and 12 points en route to a silver medal.

The six-foot-two, 190-pound Stockholm native’s 12 points ranked sixth all-time in tournament history. He also led the 2024 World Under-17 Hockey Challenge in points per game, averaging 2.00 with eight points in four games.

“We are very excited to add a player of Marcus’ calibre to our hockey club,” London GM Mark Hunter said. “He is a gifted offensive player that has size and plays the game the right way. Any time you are adding an NHL first-round pick to your team, it’s exciting for the players and our fans.”

Nordmark, Sokolovskii and Jaxon Cover (Senators) give the Knights three of the 32 picks from the first round of the NHL draft at Buffalo in June.

Last year, Nordmark was one of three 17-year-olds to record a point in the Swedish Hockey League, the country’s top circuit. He spent most of the season with Djurgarden’s top junior squad and posted 14 goals and 38 points in 25 games.

He has the bloodlines, too. His father, Robert, played 236 NHL games with St. Louis and Vancouver, while his brothers Eric and Steven currently skate in the pro ranks at home.

The Knights took a flyer on Marcus in the third round, 180th overall, of the 2025 Canadian Hockey League draft. But it was a calculated risk because Robert Nordmark has long-standing ties to Mark Hunter.

The former defenceman was a teammate of Hunter on the Blues in 1987-88 and was hired as a scout by the Toronto Maple Leafs in 2015 while the current London GM was still working for the team.

The 18-year-old Nordmark has spent the past few weeks working out with Sweden’s men’s national hockey team. There is no timetable for his arrival in London, with Ducks rookie camp set to begin next week.

The Knights are spending this weekend in British Columbia for a pair of exhibition games against the Western Hockey League’s Victoria Royals.

stories.title: Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe heading to U.K. for nuclear symposium
stories.summary: Regina - Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe is heading to the United Kingdom next week for the World Nuclear Symposium.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The province says Moe will be leading a trade and investment mission to reinforce Saskatchewan’s position as the jurisdiction of choice in nuclear co-operation.

The World Nuclear Symposium in London is set to start Tuesday.

Moe is also to participate in a panel event profiling Saskatchewan’s nuclear industry.

Article continues below

Toronto Island waitlist life: why one man will never give up his dream of living lakeside

The government says that over the past five years, Saskatchewan exports to the U.K. increased almost 178 per cent.

It says the growth has been driven by the province’s uranium, which in 2025 accounted for about 57 per cent of its total U.K. exports.

“Our province has what it takes to be a world leader in nuclear energy development with our extensive uranium resources, nuclear research infrastructure and supply chain capabilities, and Saskatchewan-based businesses and research organizations are at the forefront of the global nuclear renaissance,” Moe said in a news release Friday.

“The U.K. has been a vital gateway to growing Saskatchewan’s nuclear sector and I look forward to building on our relationships.”

Jeremy Harrison, minister of Crown Investments Corporation, is to join the symposium after representing Saskatchewan at the International Defence Industry Exhibition in Poland alongside federal and provincial counterparts.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 4, 2026.

stories.author: Devin Stevens The Canadian Press
stories.content:

By Devin Stevens The Canadian Press

Education Minister Brendan Maguire said Thursday that his department will spend $500,000 to buy bus passes from the city for students that need them.

He said the Department of Opportunities and Social Development will spend another $600,000 to provide passes to youth in families on income assistance, for a total funding of $1.1 million.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Toronto Island waitlist life: why one man will never give up his dream of living lakeside

The government previously announced it would be reducing the program’s funding in its March budget, but said it planned to maintain support for families on income assistance.

Maguire says the provincial funding will cover about 1,700 students for students in Grade 7 to Grade 12.

The city says it will fund passes for all other students, including those attending private school.

stories.title: 4 tornadoes landed in the Prairies during Sunday’s storm, researchers confirm
stories.summary: The Northern Tornadoes Project has confirmed two additional tornadoes landed in Manitoba during Sunday's storm, bringing the regional total to four.
stories.author: Tavi Dhillon
stories.content:
Two additional tornadoes hit Manitoba during Sunday’s storm, the Northern Tornadoes Project (NTP) has confirmed.

These new verifications bring the total number of twisters from last weekend to four in the Prairies. Three were said to have hit Manitoba, in addition to the previously confirmed EF-1 storm in Maryfield, Sask., approximately 35 kilometres from the Manitoba-Saskatchewan border.

The now-confirmed tornado in the community of Kola, Man., caused damage to a barn on a property north of it, according to the project. It said the maximum wind speeds from the weather event hit 140 km/h after it landed around 5:30 p.m., causing damage to trees and crops.

NTP also said two tornadoes occurred around Elkhorn, Man. Its initial report from Monday could only confirm one, noting that others were being investigated.

The earlier, and more intense, of the two hit around 6:35 p.m. and was described as a “rain-wrapped tornado,” with wind gusts at 155 km/h.

“Damage to several structures, including barns, farm outbuildings, grain bins and homes, along with tree and crop damage was reported,” according to the project, who said it was an EF-1 tornado.

Then, the second, weaker EF-0 twister in the Elkhorn area landed around 6:50 p.m., damaging bins and several farm outbuildings, it continued.

No injuries were reported in any of whirlwinds, NTP said.

stories.title: No time to waste for Milobar as ex-B. C. Conservatives join new party of five MLAs
stories.summary: It's been a busy three weeks for Peter Milobar.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
It’s been a busy three weeks for Peter Milobar.

Since announcing he was leaving the British Columbia Conservative caucus on Aug. 14, setting off an exodus from the party, Milobar has gathered with fellow defectors into what is being billed as the “stable, serious” alternative to the NDP.

On Friday, three fellow ex-Conservatives said they would join Milobar and Ian Paton in that as-yet-unnamed new party announced 10 days ago, after weeks of chaos in the official Opposition under leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay.

The recruits are among nine legislature members who have recently quit the Opposition during a time that has seen Findlay’s chief of staff resign and the RCMP looking into allegations that MLAs were offered jobs if they resigned.

“We simply don’t have the time and the luxury to just sit back and quietly work in a backroom for four or five months,” Milobar said Friday in an interview.

“We need to try to be gathered and cohesive going into a legislative session, and that gets very, very hard if you’re trying to be a group of, you know, X number of independents operating all independently yet together.”

Rosalyn Bird, Bruce Banman and A’a:liya Warbus said in a joint statement Friday that they’re joining the new party, with Milobar as interim leader until a vote can be held.

Milobar said those involved in forming the party have been “incredibly open and transparent” as they try to pull together what’s required at lightning speed, in time for the fall legislative session that is scheduled to begin on Oct. 5.

“This is admittedly a little bit bumpy, but it’s also necessary. It’s what we need to do to be able to fight a general election with some eventual stability into this process and moving forward,” Milobar said.

Those who have quit the Conservative caucus have been unhappy with Findlay’s leadership and those in her orbit, with Banman this week calling out what he called a “purity test” of whether MLAs are “hard right enough.”

The Conservatives came out of the 2024 election with 44 seats in the legislature. But a series of defections, first under former leader John Rustad and now under Findlay, have seen their ranks shrink to 28.

Milobar said that since he and Paton announced plans to start a new party, “there’s been a huge groundswell of people wanting to know what’s going on” as they continue to work through the required paperwork to get official status with Elections BC.

“Frankly we also don’t and can’t afford to have multiple groups putting in months and months and months of parallel work, knowing that only one group can move forward if we’re going to have any chance of success,” he said.

“And that group needs to have MLAs attached to it, or you know, it’s just not going to be a viable option for the electorate in their minds.”

The legislators’ statement said the new party is to hold a leadership vote before the legislature resumes, when it hopes the party will sit with official third-party status.

Milobar said it’s too soon to have a full platform and policy points to release but that the five members have had a chance to meet to discuss the future of the party.

“This is about creating (a) serious and stable political party that is focused on the economy and focused on natural resource development, focused on health care, focused on protecting private property rights, in a way that the public sees themselves in and trusts, and that’s ultimately what we’re creating,” he said.

“(Voters are) fed up with the NDP. They cannot see themselves voting for the BC Conservatives, and they’re asking for something like this that is not so hardcore ideologically driven, but better reflects how people live their daily lives and their daily thought process.”

The B.C. Conservatives referred a request for comment to Findlay’s byelection campaign in the Abbotsford-Mission riding, which did not immediately respond.

Warbus said people who oppose the governing New Democrats must focus on defeating Premier David Eby’s government in the next election.

“We have, at most, two years to be election-ready to defeat the NDP, and joining Peter and Ian is a commitment to making sure voters have a strong alternative when that election comes,” she said in Friday’s joint statement.

“There’s no time to waste — Peter and Ian have been moving forward at full-steam ahead and I’m ready to get to work alongside them.”

Banman, meanwhile, said he hopes the new party will provide right-of-centre voters with a choice other than the B.C. Conservatives.

“British Columbians want options, and we intend to give them a strong one,” he said.

Emily Lowan, the leader of the B.C. Green Party, which is currently the third party in the legislature with two seats, shrugged off the new party in a statement Friday.

“I’m less concerned about the drama the Conservatives and their offshoots are creating and more concerned that they’re a distraction from the urgent needs British Columbians are facing from an out-of-control affordability and climate crisis,” she said.

Meanwhile, the NDP caucus took its first swing at the new party in a statement Friday, saying both conservative parties would make life harder for British Columbians.

“B.C.’s newest party is a conservative spinoff that would make cuts and continues to welcome MLAs who push far-right conspiracy theories,” the statement said.

Gaining official party status would mean a budget from the legislature.

A statement from the clerk’s office said for each member, a caucus receives a budget of $121,240 annually, pro-rated from the date of its formation.

The statement said the leader of an opposition caucus other than the official Opposition receives an additional budget of $455,587, also pro-rated.

The clerk’s office said it doesn’t have information yet on how office space or time during question period would be divided.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 4, 2026.

— With files by Chuck Chiang

Ashley Joannou, The Canadian Press

Since announcing he was leaving the British Columbia Conservative caucus on Aug. 14, setting off an exodus from the party, Milobar has gathered with fellow defectors into what is being billed as the “stable, serious” alternative to the NDP.

On Friday, three fellow ex-Conservatives said they would join Milobar and Ian Paton in that as-yet-unnamed new party announced 10 days ago, after weeks of chaos in the official Opposition under leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay.

The recruits are among nine legislature members who have recently quit the Opposition during a time that has seen Findlay’s chief of staff resign and the RCMP looking into allegations that MLAs were offered jobs if they resigned.
“We simply don’t have the time and the luxury to just sit back and quietly work in a backroom for four or five months,” Milobar said Friday in an interview.

“We need to try to be gathered and cohesive going into a legislative session, and that gets very, very hard if you’re trying to be a group of, you know, X number of independents operating all independently yet together.”
Rosalyn Bird, Bruce Banman and A’a:liya Warbus said in a joint statement Friday that they’re joining the new party, with Milobar as interim leader until a vote can be held.

Milobar said those involved in forming the party have been “incredibly open and transparent” as they try to pull together what’s required at lightning speed, in time for the fall legislative session that is scheduled to begin on Oct. 5.

“This is admittedly a little bit bumpy, but it’s also necessary. It’s what we need to do to be able to fight a general election with some eventual stability into this process and moving forward,” Milobar said.

Those who have quit the Conservative caucus have been unhappy with Findlay’s leadership and those in her orbit, with Banman this week calling out what he called a “purity test” of whether MLAs are “hard right enough.”

The Conservatives came out of the 2024 election with 44 seats in the legislature. But a series of defections, first under former leader John Rustad and now under Findlay, have seen their ranks shrink to 28.

Milobar said that since he and Paton announced plans to start a new party, “there’s been a huge groundswell of people wanting to know what’s going on” as they continue to work through the required paperwork to get official status with Elections BC.

“Frankly we also don’t and can’t afford to have multiple groups putting in months and months and months of parallel work, knowing that only one group can move forward if we’re going to have any chance of success,” he said.
“And that group needs to have MLAs attached to it, or you know, it’s just not going to be a viable option for the electorate in their minds.”
The legislators’ statement said the new party is to hold a leadership vote before the legislature resumes, when it hopes the party will sit with official third-party status.
Milobar said it’s too soon to have a full platform and policy points to release but that the five members have had a chance to meet to discuss the future of the party.

“This is about creating (a) serious and stable political party that is focused on the economy and focused on natural resource development, focused on health care, focused on protecting private property rights, in a way that the public sees themselves in and trusts, and that’s ultimately what we’re creating,” he said.

“(Voters are) fed up with the NDP. They cannot see themselves voting for the BC Conservatives, and they’re asking for something like this that is not so hardcore ideologically driven, but better reflects how people live their daily lives and their daily thought process.”
The B.C. Conservatives referred a request for comment to Findlay’s byelection campaign in the Abbotsford-Mission riding, which did not immediately respond.
Warbus said people who oppose the governing New Democrats must focus on defeating Premier David Eby’s government in the next election.

“We have, at most, two years to be election-ready to defeat the NDP, and joining Peter and Ian is a commitment to making sure voters have a strong alternative when that election comes,” she said in Friday’s joint statement.
“There’s no time to waste — Peter and Ian have been moving forward at full-steam ahead and I’m ready to get to work alongside them.”
Banman, meanwhile, said he hopes the new party will provide right-of-centre voters with a choice other than the B.C. Conservatives.
“British Columbians want options, and we intend to give them a strong one,” he said.
Emily Lowan, the leader of the B.C. Green Party, which is currently the third party in the legislature with two seats, shrugged off the new party in a statement Friday.

“I’m less concerned about the drama the Conservatives and their offshoots are creating and more concerned that they’re a distraction from the urgent needs British Columbians are facing from an out-of-control affordability and climate crisis,” she said.
Meanwhile, the NDP caucus took its first swing at the new party in a statement Friday, saying both conservative parties would make life harder for British Columbians.
“B.C.’s newest party is a conservative spinoff that would make cuts and continues to welcome MLAs who push far-right conspiracy theories,” the statement said.
Gaining official party status would mean a budget from the legislature.
A statement from the clerk’s office said for each member, a caucus receives a budget of $121,240 annually, pro-rated from the date of its formation.
The statement said the leader of an opposition caucus other than the official Opposition receives an additional budget of $455,587, also pro-rated.
The clerk’s office said it doesn’t have information yet on how office space or time during question period would be divided.
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 4, 2026.
— With files by Chuck Chiang
Ashley Joannou, The Canadian Press
